12302021.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12302021.value: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) characterized by a progressive neuronal loss and cognitive decline is the most prevalent form of neurodegenerative dementia. Currently, there is still no single confirmative clinically approved test to diagnose AD yet although one of the neuropathological hallmarks of AD, cerebral senile plaques can be visualized by positron emission tomography (PET). The plaques are mainly composed of amyloid-β (Aβ) peptides. It is known that deposition of Aβ appears a decade or more prior to the onset of any clinical symptoms of the disease. To achieve early detection and diagnostics of high-risk and pre-symptomatic subjects for AD, development of reliable diagnostic AD biomarkers and their detection tools/techniques are urgently needed for early intervention and treatment of the disease. The oxidative stress, overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS), is one of the prominent causes of neurotoxicity induced by Aβ, which is shown to eventually lead to neuronal cell death and then dementia. ROS is also shown to be an important therapeutic target in AD. Therefore, it is of great interest to develop a smart tool and/ technique that can directly detect and monitor the presence and the amount of Aβ-induced ROS in the high-risk and diseased brains as an alternative and reliable AD biomarker for disease diagnosis and evaluation of drug treatment efficacy. Toward this end, we propose herein the design and development of novel ratiometric two-photon fluorescent probes for sensing and monitoring of endogenous ROS in cell models of AD, living AD brain tissue and an AD mouse model in vivo. With such versatile probes, an investigation of the pathological effect of ROS, an evaluation of the disease progression for early diagnosis of AD and an assessment of drug treatment efficacy would then be achievable. 阿爾茨海默病 (AD) 以神經元逐漸丟失和認知能力下降為特徵，是神經退行性癡呆最普遍的類型。目前，儘管 AD 的神經病理學標誌之一，腦老年斑可以通過正電子發射斷層掃描 (PET) 進行可視化，但仍然沒有單一的經臨床批准的用作診斷確診 AD 的測試。斑塊主要由澱粉樣蛋白-β (Aβ) 肽組成。眾所周知，Aβ 的沉積在該疾病的任何臨床症狀出現之前十年或更長時間出現。為了實現對 AD 高危和出現症狀前群组的早期檢測和診斷，有迫切需要開發可靠的 AD 診斷生物標誌物及其檢測工具/技術，以便對該疾病進行早期干預和治療。氧化應激，由於過度產生活性氧 (ROS) 是 Aβ 誘導所引起的神經毒性的主要原因之一，最終導致神經元細胞死亡，然後導致癡呆。 ROS 也被證明是 AD 的重要治療靶點。因此，開發一種智能工具和/技術可以直接檢測和監測高風險和患病大腦中 Aβ 誘導的 ROS 的存在和數量，作為用於診斷另一可靠的 AD 生物標誌物和藥物治療效果的評價具有重要意義。為此，我們在此提議設計和開發新型比率雙光子熒光探針，用於感測和監測 AD 細胞模型、活體 AD 腦組織和 AD 小鼠體內模型中的內源性 ROS。有了這種多功能探針，就可以對 ROS 的病理作用進行研究，對 AD 早期診斷的疾病進展進行評估，並評估藥物治療效果。

12302021.label: Realisation of objectives
12302021.value: (1) We have reported the first Aβ-targeted ratiometric H2O2-responsive fluorescent probe for realtime detection and monitoring of the Aβ-induced H2O2 level in cell and AD mouse models. The H2O2-responsive probe is constructed based on a methylamino-substituted quinolinium-based cyanine as the fluorescence moiety and a phenylboronate ester as the sensing reaction site. This sensing probe exhibits a large emission wavelength shift of ∼87 nm upon reacting with H2O2, a high binding selectivity for Aβ, and a faster response toward H2O2 in the presence of Aβ, concomitant with an enhanced fluorescence intensity, hence greatly boosting the sensitivity of in-situ H2O2 detection. This biocompatible and nontoxic probe is capable of ratiometrically detecting and imaging endogenous H2O2 induced by Aβ in a neuronal cell model. Remarkably, this Aβ-targeted H2O2-responsive probe is also able to detect, monitor, and differentiate different Aβ-induced H2O2 levels in real time in different age groups of transgenic AD mice in which the cerebral H2O2 level increases age dependently concomitant with the plaque contents. Therefore, this smart probe can act as a powerful tool to diagnose high-risk subjects and diseased brains of AD and to further study the role of ROS in AD pathology. (2) We have developed a simple, stable, highly sensitive and specific H2O2-responsive theranostic probes with Aβ targeting capability for imaging and monitoring of endogenous H2O2 ratiometrically in AD mouse model as well as serving as a pro-drug to treat AD. One of the probes synthesized in this study namely, HY3 was shown to possess superior multifunctional properties including low cytotoxicity and good biocompatibility, strong binding with Aβ and large Aβ binding-induced fluorescence enhancement, excellent H2O2 specificity, superior stability, and of particular importance, rapid response, and high sensitivity toward H2O2 in the presence of Aβ for selective imaging and monitoring of endogenous H2O2 in real time in AD mouse model. Molecular docking revealed the difference in the binding motif and interactions of the probe HY3 and its H2O2-oxidized product, HY2 with Aβ fibrils giving rise to the difference of Aβ binding-induced fluorescence enhancement between them. Impressively, with the promotion of Aβ, HY3 was able to detect the endogenous H2O2 level ratiometrically in AD cell model and differentiate the difference between the normal and AD cells. More importantly, the excellent BBB permeable and biocompatible HY3 probe enabled it to target the senile plaques and serve as an effective and highly sensitive ratiometric fluorescent probe to image and monitor endogenous H2O2 level in vivo in different age groups of AD mice. Furthermore, the inhibitory function against Aβ aggregation of HY2 offers an additional benefit for the therapeutic use of this versatile probe. Our results suggested that H2O2 could be a useful and reliable biomarker for AD and HY3 is a highly promising and effective tool in the detection of Aβ-induced H2O2 level in vivo for more precise diagnosis of AD as well as can serve as a potential pro-drug to treat AD. (3) In addition to H2O2-responsive probes, we have developed an Aβ and ONOO– synergistically activated NIR fluorescent probe for highly selective imaging of Aβ-induced ONOO– level in vivo. Importantly, this responsive probe exhibits not only synergistically strong enhancement of fluorescence at 655 nm upon reacting with ONOO– in the presence of Aβ but also high sensitivity down to 13 nM with minimal interference. The strong Aβ binding and low cytotoxicity enable the probe to successfully apply for detecting and visualizing endogenous ONOO– level induced by Aβ in AD cell model. Remarkably, this ONOO–-responsive probe can be applied effectively to detect, monitor, and distinguish varying ONOO– levels induced by Aβ in different age groups of AD mice, in which cerebral ONOO– level rises with increasing age of AD mice along with Aβ plaque accumulation. Furthermore, the potent neuroprotection against Aβ-induced toxicity and anti-Aβ aggregation effect of the ONOO–-reaction product of the probe offer an extra therapeutic advantage of this ONOO– -responsive probe. In essence, this multifunctional theranostic probe can serve as a highly sensitive and specific imaging tool for visualizing and monitoring of ONOO– level in the presence of Aβ in vivo, thereby facilitating more accurate early diagnosis and therapy of AD. (4) The formation of neurotoxic amyloid-β (Aβ) oligomers begins much earlier than the deposit of plaques in AD, which still poses a great challenge to detect and monitor for early diagnosis and intervention of the disease. The rational design and development of a series of novel multifunctional heteroaromatic-derived and ethylene π-bridge free near-infrared (NIR) cyanine probes with high Aβ42 oligomers selectivity and sensitivity for real-time imaging of Aβ aggregates was reported. Intriguingly, these heteroaromatic-derived fluorophores showed selectively large fluorescence turn-on up to a 53-fold increase and strong binding affinity with dissociation constant (Kd) of 198–525 nM upon interacting with Aβ42 oligomers. Molecular docking analyses revealed that the strong binding selectivity and interactions were synergistically driven by the hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces between those probes particularly with acetamido-substituent and Aβ42 tetramer model. Because of excellent Aβ oligomers selectivity, biocompatibility, and blood-brain barrier penetrability, the application of the probe, SLTAD for real-time detection and visualization of Aβ aggregates in different age groups of AD mice was demonstrated. Additionally, SLTAD was found to inhibit Aβ42 aggregates/fibrils formation (IC50 = 312 nM) and attenuate neuronal toxicity induced by Aβ, underscoring its uniqueness as a theranostic Aβ oligomers probe for AD.

12302021.label: Major findings and research outcome
12302021.value: Two novel Aβ-targeted ratiometric hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-responsive fluorescent probes and an Aβ and peroxynitrile (ONOO)-dual-activated NIR fluorescent probe have been designed and developed to detect and monitor oxidative stress in Alzheimer’s Disease. These biocompatible, bio-safe and BBB permeable ROS-responsive probes were capable of selective detecting and imaging endogenous H2O2 and ONOO–-induced by Aβ in a neuronal cell model. Importantly, these Aβ-targeted NIR H2O2-selective and ONOO–-selective responsive probes were also capable of selectively detecting, monitoring, and differentiating different Aβ-induced H2O2 and ONOO– level in real time in different age groups of transgenic AD mice in which the cerebral H2O2 and ONOO– level increased age dependently concomitant with the plaque contents. Therefore, these ROS-responsive probes are a powerful tool to diagnose high-risk subjects and diseased brains of AD and to further study the role of ROS in AD pathology. In addition, a heteroaromatic-derived cyanine skeleton that shows high Aβ42 oligomers selectivity and sensitivity for real-time imaging of Aβ aggregates was developed, which is highly useful and viable for the development of Aβ oligomer-targeted ROS-responsive fluorescent probe(s) upon incorporating with a specific ROS sensing moiety.

12302021.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12302021.value: Multimodal imaging probes can provide multiple imaging capabilities from a single administration with the same pharmacokinetics and colocalization of the signal for each modality. They are emerging as a more powerful and holistic tool in which different imaging modalities can provide complementary and expanded information on the region of interest. Multimodal probes with imaging capabilities of Aβ-targeted NIR imaging, responsive sensing of Aβ-induced ROS, and magnetic resonance (MR) imaging of Aβ aggregates in a single entity would be highly valuable and indispensable for etiological studies, precise disease diagnosis, and the investigation of the treatment efficacy and the mode of action of new therapeutic agents. As a result, the ROS responsive molecular probes developed in this project will be used to explore for the fabrication and development of such multifunctional multimodal nanoprobes.

12302021.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12302021.value: Amyloid-β (Aβ), the pathological hallmarks of Alzheimer disease (AD), is known to induce oxidative stress due to the overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and peroxynitrite (ONOO–) leading to neurotoxicity and ultimately, neuronal death. Therefore, the level of Aβ-induced ROS is an important marker to be detected and monitored for precise diagnosis of AD. However, tools that can directly detect and monitor the presence and amount of Aβ-induced ROS are rarely known due to the blood-brain barrier impermeability and lack of Aβ-targetability of the existing ROS-responsive probes. In this project, several novel ROS responsive molecular probes that can selective and specific detect and monitor Aβ-induced H2O2 or ONOO– in real-time in AD cell and mouse models have been successfully developed for more precise diagnosis of AD. Besides, some of these probes showing potent neuroprotection against Aβ-induced toxicity and anti-Aβ aggregation effect of the ROS-reaction product of the probe offer an extra therapeutic advantage of these ROS-responsive probes. Thus, these developed multifunctional theranostic probes can act as a powerful tool to diagnose high-risk subjects and diseased brains of AD.

12302421.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12302421.value: Cell motility plays a crucial role in diverse physiological and pathological processes. Most biophysical and statistical studies of cell motility examine the migration of bacteria and epithelial cells, and we know much less about the quantitative principles underlying immune cell motion. In this proposed project, we aim to elucidate the dynamic control over the chemotactic motion of an important immune cell type, Natural Killer (NK) cells. NK cells are cytotoxic lymphocytes that detect and eliminate virus-infected cells and cancer cells. The strong cytotoxicity of NK cells against cancer targets render NK cells promising therapeutic candidate for cancer treatment. However, despite data showing directed NK cell migration towards the cancer targets is the rate-limiting step of NK-tumor cell interaction in vivo, our quantitative and mechanistic understanding of this critical motility process is very limited. We have previously developed single-cell microscopy assays to measure the real-time dynamics of NK-cancer cell interactions, and employed machine learning-assisted single cell tracking to quantify the target-directed NK cell motion. We found NK cell polarization played an important role in regulating its migration and such polarization-modulated motility varied significantly in response to different target cell types, likely due to variable target secretion of chemotactic cytokines/chemokines. Building on these novel observations, in this project we will expand the measurements to obtain large NK cell motility datasets under a variety of NK-target cell interaction conditions, and then construct a mathematical model for NK cell chemotaxis based on the in-house experimental data. Computational analysis will be performed to explore the model behaviors, in particular the NK cell response to environmental cues in relation to their nonrandom motility. The key and previously unresolved questions that our study will address include: (1) how the polarization-modulated NK cell chemotactic motion quantitatively depends on the target cells, particularly via the differential cytokine/chemokine microenvironment; (2) how chemotaxis depends on NK cell population density (i.e., collective group behavior); and (3) what quantitative features of the chemotactic signaling can be inferred from the differential NK cell migration dynamics. Overall, the wealth of data generated through targeted experiments in this project will enable us to propose and quantitatively evaluate the critical search strategies employed by NK cells to detect and migrate towards abnormal cell targets. The integrated approach that we adopt is highly novel and will also serve as a protocol for elucidating the chemotactic dynamics of other important immune cell types, e.g., T cells. 細胞運動在不同的生理和病理過程中都起著至關重要的作用。細胞運動的生物物理學和統計學研究主要集中於細菌和上皮細胞的運動規律，而我們對免疫細胞運動的定量原理知之甚少。因此，本研究項目旨在闡明人體免疫系統中一重要免疫細胞類型，即自然殺傷 (NK) 細胞，的趨向運動動態特徵和調控機制。 NK 細胞是毒性淋巴細胞，具有發現並消除病毒感染的細胞和腫瘤細胞的功能。 NK細胞對腫瘤細胞的強細胞毒性使 NK 細胞成為癌症細胞療法的重要研發方向。然而，儘管數據顯示NK 細胞向腫瘤細胞的定向遷移是體內 NK 細胞與腫瘤細胞相互作用的限速步驟，但我們對這一關鍵過程的定量機制的認知與理解仍非常有限。 我們的前期工作已成功研發了單細胞顯微成像實驗手段，可對NK 細胞與腫瘤細胞相互作用進行實時動態測量，並採用以機器學習輔助的單細胞追踪來量化NK 細胞的定向運動特徵及參數。我們發現 NK 細胞極化對調節其定向運動起著重要作用，並且這種極化調節的運動會因應不同的腫瘤細胞類型而有顯著變化，其原因可能是不同腫瘤細胞分泌了調控NK細胞運動的不同細胞因子和趨化因子。基於這些新的觀測結果，本研究項目將擴展實驗測量與分析，獲取在不同 NK 細胞與腫瘤細胞相互作用條件下的NK 細胞運動特徵綜合數據集，然後基於實驗數據構建 NK 細胞定向運動的數學模型，並對模型進行計算分析以探索模型行為，特別是 NK 細胞的非隨機運動如何受到環境因子的調控。我們的研究擬解決的關鍵問題包括：（1）極化調節的 NK 細胞運動如何受腫瘤細胞類型的影響，特別是微環境中腫瘤細胞分泌的不同細胞因子和趨化因子； (2) NK 細胞運動如何取決於 NK 細胞密度（即集體行為）； (3) 從不同的 NK 細胞定向運動特徵推斷出趨化信號的定量特徵。 總體而言，本研究項目通過單細胞成像實驗獲取的大量動力學數據將使我們能夠提出並定量評估 NK 細胞發現和遷移到異常細胞目標的關鍵搜索策略。我們採用的單細胞實驗與理論模型分析相結合的綜合方法非常新穎，將可應用於研究其他重要免疫細胞類型的動力學行為，例如 T 細胞。

12302421.label: Realisation of objectives
12302421.value: Objective 1: Measure the migration dynamics of NK cells in the presence of normal versus different cancer cell targets by single cell imaging; Quantify the experimental data using machine learning-assisted single cell tracking; This objective has been fully accomplished. Specifically, we have developed a 3D image analysis pipeline that incorporates multiple Machine Learning strategies for automatic single-cell image segmentation, single-cell phenotype classification and tracking to extract NK cell dynamic data from the live-cell imaging movies of NK cells in coculture with 3D tumor organoids. Using this 3D image analysis pipeline (SiQ-3D, Single-cell image Quantifier for 3D), we acquired extensive datasets of NK cell motility in response to gastric tumors of two distinctive molecular subtypes, i.e., GX048-TO (MSI) and GX068-TO (Intestinal), as well as their paired normal. In the presence of normal cells, NK cells mostly exhibited random Brownian motion, as expected. In contrast, in the presence of the NK cell-sensitive tumor organoid, GX048-TO, we observed directed NK cell migration towards the tumor target (measured by Mean Squared Displacement (MSD), Migration angle and NK cell density distribution), within a region of 50-80 microns from the tumor surface. Intriguingly, NK cells exhibited unexpected chemorepulsive motion (i.e., actively moving away from the tumor target) near the tumor surface of GX068-TO. This novel result indicates that GX068-TO can evade NK cell surveillance by secreting chemorepellent that induces NK cell reverse chemotaxis (i.e., moving down-gradient away from the tumor target). Objective 2: Measure the effect of NK cell population density on differential NK cell motility; This objective has been fully accomplished. Given that the NK cells exhibited two distinctive migration modes depending on the tumor target subtype, we analyzed the NK cell population effect on these two migration modes, respectively. Upon interaction with GX048-TO, NK cells exhibited directed motion towards the tumor target (i.e., chemoattraction) about 4-5 hours after the NK-tumor cell coculture started. As the density of NK cells increased, we observed NK cell chemoattractive motion faster (about 2-3 hours after the coculture started), and the near tumor region where directed NK cell migration towards the tumor target was observed also expanded to about 80-100 microns. Further mechanistic and quantitative analysis revealed that this NK cell population effect on accelerating the onset of NK cell chemoattractive motion and expanding the chemoattractive field is due to increased NK-tumor cell contacts at higher NK cell density. Specifically, we found that the secretion of key NK cell chemoattractants by GX048-TO, such as CXCL9, CXCL10 and CXCL11, was upregulated by NK-tumor cell contact. Therefore, increased NK-tumor cell contacts at high NK cell density resulted in GX048-TO generating a larger chemoattractive field faster to direct NK cell motion. In contrast, higher NK cell density did not alter the characteristics of NK cell chemorepulsive motion upon interaction with the tumor organoid, GX068-TO. This result makes intuitive sense. Due to chemorepulsive motion, NK cells made few contacts with GX068-TO, even at high NK cell density. Therefore, chemokine secretion by GX068-TO largely depends on the tumor alone and is not impacted by the NK-tumor cell contact frequency or NK cell density. Objective 3: Measure the effect of key cytokines and chemokines on modulating NK cell motility; This objective has been fully accomplished. NK cell activation and migration most critically depend on cytokines, IL-2/IL-15, and chemokines, CXCL10/CXCL11. We therefore investigated their respective effects on modulating the NK cell migration dynamics that we observed in the presence of distinctive tumor organoids. We found IL-15 is a stronger activator of NK cell chemoattractive migration than IL-2. NK cells showed more persistent directed motion towards GX048-TO under IL-15 treatment, and the chemoattractive field, where non-random, directed NK cell motion was observed, was significantly larger under IL-15 than IL-2. Moreover, IL-15 substantially attenuated the chemorepulsive motion of NK cells in the presence of GX068-TO. Further flow cytometry analysis of the expression of NK cell chemotactic receptors revealed that the IL-15 treatment, and to a lesser extent the IL-2 treatment, significantly upregulated the expression of chemoattractant receptors in NK cells, such as CXCR3, which promoted NK cell chemoattractive migration while dampening chemorepulsion. As for the effect of chemokines, CXCL10/CXCL11, secretome profiling showed NK-tumor cell contacts, in particular in the presence of GX048-TO, upregulated these two chemokines. The upregulation of CXCL10/CXCL11 synergized with the IL-2/IL-15 effect on increasing CXCR3, the cognate receptor of CXCL10/CXCL11 expressed on NK cells, thus strongly promoting chemoattractive over chemorepulsive migration of NK cells towards the tumor targets. Overall, these results illustrated how key cytokines/chemokines modulate NK cell motility, in particular how they promote chemoattractive over chemorepulsive motion towards the tumor targets. Objective 4: Based on the dynamics data, develop mathematical model for NK cell chemotaxis; conduct computational analysis of the model to identify key dynamic parameters and the statistical mechanical mechanism underlying NK cell chemotaxis. This objective has been fully accomplished. Based on the detailed NK cell motility data obtained in Objectives #1, #2 and #3, we established the mathematical formulation of NK cell motility using the Langevin equation, in which the migration velocity of individual NK cells is governed by a frictional force, a fluctuating force, and an external chemotactic force that depends on the tumor subtype and cytokine/chemokine. We first simulated the Langevin equation in the absence of an external chemotactic force, which corresponds to the scenario of no tumor target or normal target being present. And we obtained NK cell trajectories that were of random nature. By comparing the simulated results with experimental data, we were able to parameterize the Langevin equations, including the NK cell mass, the frictional force and the fluctuating force. Next we simulated the NK cell motility under an external chemotactic force field, which corresponds to the scenario of tumor targets being present. We assumed the chemotactic force is driven by chemokines secreted by the tumor organoid and subsequently diffusing into the 3D microenvironment. Based on the Keller-Segel model for chemotaxis, this chemotactic force depends on the concentration gradient of the chemokines. Given that we found NK-tumor cell contacts upregulated chemoattractant secretion (results acquired under Objectives #2 and #3), for the chemoattractive field generated by GX048-TO, we further defined the chemokine concentration to be dependent on the number of NK-tumor cell contacts. Simulation of the Langevin equation with the above chemotactic field not only produced NK cell motility trajectories that agreed with the experimental data but also identified the chemotactic sensitivity for both the chemoattractive and chemorepulsive migration of NK cells induced by distinctive tumor targets. Results acquired for Objective #1 has been published in Cancer Research (Liu et al, 2024). The detailed methods and protocol are reported in another manuscript currently under peer review (Zhu et al, Three-dimensional Single-cell Imaging Analysis of Tumor-Natural Killer Cell Interaction Dynamics in Multi-cell type Tumor Organoid Models). Results acquired for the Objectives #2, #3 and #4 have been presented and discussed in the PhD thesis of Bodong LIU. A manuscript based on the PhD thesis is under final preparation, and will be submitted for peer review and publication shortly.

12302421.label: Major findings and research outcome
12302421.value: (1) We developed a Machine learning-powered 3D image analysis pipeline that can automatically extract multi-dimensional kinetic data from complex 3D live-cell imaging movies comprising multiple interacting cell types. The pipeline, named SiQ-3D (Single-cell image Quantifier for 3D) outperformed other existing open-source and commercial image analysis software packages in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. We have deposited the Python-based software codes in Github and Code Ocean for all interested users to access and use for free. (2) Using novel 3D single-cell imaging assay of NK cell-tumor organoid coculture and the SiQ-3D image analysis pipeline, we quantified in details NK cell migration dynamics in the presence of distinctive tumor targets. We uncovered a novel chemorepulsive mode of NK cell motion, in which NK cells actively move away (i.e., reverse chemotaxis) from the tumor target, revealing a previously unknown mechanism for “immunologically cold” tumor to evade NK cell surveillance. (3) We found higher NK cell density promotes chemoattractive migration of NK cells by increasing NK-tumor cell contacts and subsequently upregulating secretion of chemoattractant by the tumor targets. (4) We also elucidated that cytokines, IL-2 and IL-15, as well as chemokines, CXCL10/CXCL11, promote chemoattractive over chemorepulsive migration of NK cells by upregulating expression of chemoattractant receptor on NK cell surface and increasing chemoattractant secretion by the tumor targets. (5) Based on the extensive experimental data on NK cell motility, we established a mathematical model using the Langevin equation and the Keller-Segel framework for chemotaxis. By simulating single NK cell migration trajectories as a function of tumor subtypes and cytokines and comparing the simulated results with the experimental data, we were able to parameterize the mathematical model and determine the chemotactic sensitivity underlying the chemoattractive and chemorepulsive migration of NK cells, respectively. Our findings have resulted in three manuscripts, one published in 2024 (Liu et al, Cancer Research, 2024), one currently under peer review, and one under final preparation (please refer to Part C for details). The project findings also constitute the PhD thesis of Bodong LIU, who was supported by this grant and awarded the PhD degree in 2025.

12302421.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12302421.value: Our results revealed a novel chemorepulsive migration mode of NK cells, which was not reported or studied before. Such chemorepulsive motion, in which NK cells actively move away from the tumor targets (i.e., reverse chemotaxis), is potentially a new mechanism for “immunologically cold” tumor to evade NK cell surveillance, and likely of great interest from the clinical perspective. We are following up on this novel NK cell migration mode by performing secretome profiling to identify the chemorepellent involved. We are also doing pulldown by immunoprecipitation to identify the chemorepellent receptor expressed on NK cells. Once the chemorepellent and its cognate receptor on NK cells are identified, we will investigate how their interactions modulate the actin-integrin signaling cascade to direct NK cell motility down-gradient of the tumor-secreted chemorepellent. Moreover, we are further developing a user-friendly interface for SiQ-3D so that users without any programming knowledge can easily customize and use it for different image analysis tasks. We are also exploring different machine learning strategies to extract dynamic characteristics from the large number of single NK cell trajectories that we experimentally acquired, and aim to develop methods that can more robustly detect kinetic features that define unique NK cell motility.

12302421.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12302421.value: Natural Killer (NK) cells are cytotoxic lymphocytes that detect and eliminate abnormal cancer cells. The strong cytotoxicity of NK cells against cancer targets renders NK cells promising therapeutic candidate for cancer treatment, especially for removing residual cancer cells after conventional therapy. In this project, we performed quantitative single cell imaging and machine learning-powered 3D image analysis to measure the real-time interaction dynamics of NK cells and tumor targets of distinctive molecular subtypes. Together with computational modeling, we not only identify the quantitative mechanism by which NK cells detect and migrate towards abnormal cancer targets but also uncover a novel NK cell migration mode, i.e., chemorepulsive motion away from tumor targets, which enables “immunologically cold” tumor to evade NK cell surveillance. Insights from our study, which identify functional heterogeneity and rate-limiting control in NK cell dynamic response to different tumor subtypes that are missed by traditional bulk assays, could be of great importance in the clinical context and will help guide future developments of NK cell-based cancer therapy. The imaging assays and analysis tools that we develop may also be directly useful for measuring the activity of NK cell batches prior to adoptive cell transfer in individual cancer patients.

12302621.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12302621.value: Many time series in real life exhibit a periodic component as well as a trend. Sometimes, the period of a time series may be unknown and an accurate estimate is necessary for further estimation, prediction and inference. In addition, the period or amplitude of the periodic component may change along time which makes it harder to study. Moreover, there may be some covariate effects which are important in their own rights and may have an influence on the estimation and inference for the periodic and trend terms. Motivated by examples concerning global warming, monthly total import and export by China and hospital admissions of respiratory and cardiovascular disease patients in Hong Kong, we study time series that contain a periodic component with an unknown period and an unknown changing amplitude, a trending behavior and other complex covariate effects. Specifically, our model allows the amplitude function to change at some unknown change-points, and we add to the classical time series decomposition model some covariate effect functions. The covariates may have different effect mechanisms and their effects may vary with time. Also, there may be functional covariates as functional data are increasingly common in various subject areas. We suggest a three-stage estimation procedure to estimate more accurately the period, change-points, periodic sequence, trend and covariate effects. First, we estimate the period with the trend and covariate effects being approximated by B-splines rather than being ignored. Since there are change-points along the periodic sequence, here we apply a segmented penalized least square method. Then, we suggest a new method inspired by binary segmentation to estimate the change-points. Finally, we estimate the entire periodic sequence, trend and covariate effects with the latter two approximated by B-splines. Asymptotic results will be derived and simulation studies will be conducted to examine asymptotic properties and finite sample performance of the proposed method. We will apply the proposed methods to analyze the above-mentioned motivating datasets to demonstrate its utility. Next, since functional data are increasingly common, we will extend our method to deal with functional time series with a similar dynamical periodicity, trend and covariate effects. While this emerges as an important topic, the relevant literature is limited. Also, such an extension and the theoretical study are nontrivial. We will conduct a simulation study and apply the proposed method to analyze a functional time series concerning climate change. 在實際應用中許多時間序列顯示含有週期性結構和趨勢結構。有時候，其中的週期性結構的週期是未知的，因而有必要準確的估計它，而且週期和震幅函數還可能隨時間變化，這使得問題更加困難。另外，有些時間序列還受解釋變數影響，這些影響本身有其重要性，同時可能對週期性結構和趨勢結構的估計和推論造成衝擊。我們在全球氣候、中國進出口、香港呼吸道和心血管疾病研究的實際時間序列數據中，觀察到這些現象，因此，我們研究俱動態週期性結構、趨勢結構及複雜解釋變數影響的非穩定時間序列的統計分析，特別是我們的統計模型容許週期震幅函數有多個未知變點，而且解釋變數影響隨時間變化。我們提出一個三階段估計程序：首先我們估計週期，當中使用樣條函數逼近趨勢結構和解釋變數影響，然後我們創造一個新方法用來決定變點個數和估計它們的位置，最後我們估計整個動態的週期性結構、趨勢函數和解釋變數影響。我們將推導這三個估計步驟的大樣本理論性質、使用模擬實驗探討它們的有限樣本表現、並且應用前面提到的實際數據分析以得到對全球氣候、中國進出口、香港呼吸道和心血管疾病數據準確的了解。此外，我們預計將我們的統計模型、方法和理論推廣到函數時間序列。近二十多年來由於資料收集和儲存技術進步函數資料常見於各種領域包含化學氣象生物醫學財務等，但是關於函數時間序列的文獻仍然稀少，我們在這方向的方法和理論工作將是創新而重要的。我們將進行模擬實驗用以檢驗有限樣本下表現，也將應用在一組氣候資料的分析。

12302821.label: Realisation of objectives
12302821.value: The stated project objectives have been fully and satisfactorily achieved. [Objective #1] The formation mechanism of 2-butene-1,4-dial (BDA) and its substituted analogues (BDAs) during chlorination was investigated using bisphenol S (BPS) as a model phenolic compound. A UHPLC-QTOF-MS analytical method was first developed to detect and identify BDAs as N-α-acetyl-lysine (NAL) adducts in chlorinated BPS samples. Subsequently, the effects of initial NaOCl dosage, pH, halides, dissolved organic matter (DOM), and ammonia on the formation of BDA and chlorinated BDA (Cl-BDA) were systematically examined: • Chlorine Concentration: BDA production increased with higher chlorine levels. Cl-BDA was only detected when the NaOCl dose was ten times the BPS concentration. • pH Influence: Acidic (pH 5–6) and neutral (pH 7) conditions favored the formation of both BDA and Cl-BDA, with peak yields observed at pH 7. Alkaline conditions (pH 8) resulted in lower formation rates. • Halide Effects: Bromide ions (Br⁻) inhibited BDA formation in a concentration-dependent manner, while iodide ions (I⁻) showed no significant impact on BDA or Cl-BDA yields. • Dissolved Organic Matter: Humic acid (HA) did not suppress BDA formation, suggesting its negligible role in BDA generation during BPS chlorination. • Ammonia Addition: The presence of ammonia significantly reduced BDA and Cl-BDA formation, especially when the Cl₂/N ratio was below 1. Increasing ammonia concentrations led to up to 6-fold and 2-fold reductions in BDA and Cl-BDA formation, respectively, compared to chlorination alone. Preformed chloramine further suppressed BDA formation relative to direct chlorination. Finally, the impact of multi-step chlorination was evaluated. When the total NaOCl dose was divided into 1 to 8 fractions and administered over 120 minutes, the yields of both BDA and Cl-BDA decreased with increasing number of steps. Notably, the peak area from 8 split injections was less than half that of a single injection. [Objective #2] To identify BDAs formed during chlorination, chlorinated BPS samples were analyzed using UHPLC-QTOF-MS. In addition to the previously known BDA and Cl-BDA, a novel sulfonated analogue, SO₃-BDA, was discovered. Moreover, in the presence of bromide ions (Br⁻), a brominated derivative, Br-BDA, was also detected. The identified BDAs—detected as N-α-acetyl-lysine (NAL) adducts—and the transformation products (TPs) of BPS generated during chlorination are summarized. Time-course profiling of BPS TPs and BDAs revealed four TPs with significant temporal decline, suggesting their involvement in BDA formation. Specifically: • Electrophilic Substitution (ES) Pathway: TP-283 and TP-351 • Electron Transfer (ET) Pathway: TP-127 and TP-207 These TPs showed strong correlation with BDA formation. Based on these insights, a novel transformation pathway for BPS chlorination is proposed. This pathway branches from the ET mechanism and involves the formation of a BPS phenoxy radical. This radical undergoes cleavage to yield phenoxy and sulfonyl phenoxy radicals, which then proceed through ring-opening and chlorine substitution reactions, ultimately leading to the formation of various BDAs. [Objective #3] To expand understanding of BDA formation from other phenolic micropollutants, three additional bisphenols—bisphenol F (BPF), 4,4'-dihydroxybenzophenone (4,4'-DHB), and 4,4'-dihydroxydiphenyl ether (DDE)—were subjected to aqueous chlorination. The BDA yield followed the descending order: BPS > 4,4'-DHB > BPF > DDE, which correlates with the electron-withdrawing strength of their bridging groups: –SO₂– > –CO– > –CH₂– > –O– Comparable Cl-BDA yields for 4,4'-DHB and BPF are attributed to the oxidative conversion of BPF into 4,4'-DHB, which then undergoes chlorination to form Cl-BDA. This trend suggests that stronger electron-withdrawing bridging groups promote greater BDA formation. Mechanistically, this is explained by the enhanced stability of radical intermediates at the para-position—particularly for –SO₂– and –CO– groups—which facilitates preferential cleavage from the substituent. In contrast, bisphenols with less electron-withdrawing bridging groups (e.g., BPF) exhibit reduced radical cleavage propensity, resulting in lower BDA yields. These findings underscore the pivotal role of bridging group electronics in governing radical-mediated ring cleavage and subsequent BDA formation. This systematic analysis provides a foundation for developing mitigation strategies based on precursor structural characteristics.

12302821.label: Major findings and research outcome
12302821.value: In this study, the formation of butenedial derivatives (BDAs) resulting from the chlorination of bisphenol S (BPS) was systematically investigated. Key parameters including NaOCl dosage, pH, and water matrix components were found to significantly influence the yields of BDA and its chlorinated analogue, Cl-BDA. BDA production increased with higher chlorine concentrations, whereas Cl-BDA was only detected when the NaOCl dose was tenfold greater than the BPS concentration. Multi-step chlorination markedly reduced the yields of both BDA and Cl-BDA, with eight split injections producing less than half the peak area observed from a single injection. This suggests that multi-step chlorination may effectively mitigate exposure to BDAs in treated drinking water. The highest BDA formation occurred under neutral conditions (pH 7), surpassing yields observed under alkaline conditions. Bromide ions (Br⁻) inhibited the formation of both BDA and Cl-BDA, while iodide ions (I⁻) and humic acid (HA) exhibited negligible effects. Ammonia strongly suppressed BDA formation, with increasing concentrations leading to a progressive decrease in both BDA and Cl-BDA yields. Four BDAs were identified and characterized: three previously known compounds (BDA, Cl-BDA, and Br-BDA) and one newly discovered sulfonated derivative (SO₃-BDA). The mechanism of BDA formation during BPS chlorination was elucidated through the identification and structural characterization of BPS transformation products (TPs). Time-course monitoring revealed that TP-283 and TP-351 (from the electrophilic substitution pathway) and TP-127 and TP-207 (from the electron transfer pathway) served as key intermediates in BDA generation. A revised transformation pathway was proposed, involving the formation of phenoxy radicals via the electron transfer route, followed by radical cleavage and ring opening. Comparative analysis of bisphenol analogues revealed a descending order of BDA yields: BPS > 4,4′-DHB > BPF > DDE. This trend correlates with the electron-withdrawing strength of their bridging groups (–SO₂– > –CO– > –CH₂– > –O–). Stabilization of the radical intermediate at the para-position by electron-withdrawing groups (e.g., –SO₂– and –CO–) facilitates preferential cleavage and subsequent BDA formation via ring opening. In contrast, analogues with less electron-withdrawing bridging groups exhibited reduced cleavage tendencies and lower BDA yields. These findings demonstrate that chlorination of phenolic micropollutants produces not only conventional disinfection byproducts (DBPs) and chlorinated transformation products, but also ring-cleavage DBPs such as BDAs. The insights gained from this systematic investigation provide a foundation for developing mitigation strategies based on precursor structural characteristics. A journal article summarising all the research outcomes has been published in the Journal of Hazardous Materials, 2023, Volume 459, Article 132128.

12302821.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12302821.value: The present study provided fundamental insights into the formation of butenedial derivatives (BDAs) during the chlorination of bisphenol S (BPS) and elucidated the transformation pathways and formation mechanisms of BDAs from various bisphenol analogues. Building on these findings, the proposed transformation pathways offer a valuable framework for further investigations into BDA formation from other phenolic micropollutants during chlorination. Given the widespread presence of natural phenolic compounds in environmental waters, further evaluation of BDA occurrence in aquatic environments, particularly in drinking water sources, is warranted. In addition, a systematic toxicological assessment of the newly identified BDAs and associated transformation products (TPs) is essential to determine their potential risks to both environmental and human health. While chloramination presents a clear advantage over chlorination in reducing BDA formation, it is also known to produce toxic and unregulated nitrogenous disinfection byproducts (N-DBPs). Future research should therefore focus on evaluating the overall trade-off between the reduced formation of BDAs and the potential increase in N-DBPs. This line of inquiry holds significant public health relevance, as N-DBPs are generally more toxic than many conventional carbonaceous DBPs. Ultimately, the overarching goal of these studies is to establish a scientific foundation for the development of advanced treatment technologies aimed at mitigating the formation of BDAs and other harmful DBPs, thereby safeguarding the quality and safety of our water resources.

12302821.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12302821.value: 2-butene-1,4-dial (BDA), a toxic metabolite known for its genotoxic and carcinogenic properties, was recently identified as a disinfection byproduct (DBP) formed during chlorination. Our research revealed that the formation of BDA and its analogues (BDAs) is significantly influenced by disinfection parameters. By monitoring the time profiles of transformation products (TPs) of bisphenol and its analogues (BPs analogues) alongside BDA formation, we elucidated the underlying formation mechanisms of BDAs from these compounds. The findings indicate that chlorination of phenolic micropollutants produces not only the well-known DBPs and chlorinated TPs, but also ring-cleavage DBPs such as BDAs. This comprehensive study, encompassing the effects of disinfection parameters, transformation chemistry, and mechanistic pathways, provides critical insights for future research on BDAs, which have long been overlooked due to analytical challenges despite their toxicological significance. Moreover, these findings lay the groundwork for the development and refinement of water disinfection strategies aimed at minimizing the formation of toxic DBPs, thereby contributing to the protection of both water quality and public health.

12302921.label: Project Objectives
12302921.value: Study the formation and characterization of T7-conjugated, red blood cell membrane coated, doxorubicin loaded persistent luminescence nanoparticles (TRPD). (i) Bioconjugation of T7 and red blood cell membrane (RCM) to form T7-RCM. T7, a peptide with both BBB penetration and glioma targeting properties, will be selected. Streptavidin-PEG3400-DSPE and biotin-PEG3500-T7 will be synthesized and conjugated with RCM to form T7-RCM. (ii) Drug loading to form persistent luminescence nanoparticles with doxorubicin (PD). Coating of T7-RCM and RCM, respectively, on PD to produce T7-RCM-PD (TRPD) and RCM-PD (RPD). (iii) The yield of the synthesis of each step will be measured using 1H-NMR and FTIR. Structure characterizations of TRPD will be conducted using SEM and TEM. The size and zeta-potential of the TRPD will be investigated by DLS. The encapsulation efficiency and drug loading of DOX, respectively, will be measured using UV-visible spectrometer. The renewable persistent luminescence of TRPD will also be studied. Study the in vitro stability and controlled release of TRPD. The in vitro stability of TRPD, RPD, and PD, respectively, will be studied on the release of DOX in PBS with serum and simulated cerebrospinal fluid, respectively. The released DOX will be measured using UV-visible spectrometer. The structure and size changes of the nanoparticles (NP) will be observed using SEM and TEM. The release profiles will be built. Study the in vitro cytotoxicity, the mechanisms of cell apoptosis and necrosis and cellular uptake of TRPD using the glioma cell model. (i) The in vitro cytotoxicity of TRPD, RPD, PD, and DOX, respectively, will be studied using U87 MG glioma cells. (ii) The cytotoxicity effects after the treatments of TRPD, RPD, PD, and DOX, respectively, will be interpreted on the apoptosis and necrosis conditions of the cells, which will be visualized using a fluorescent microscope with the help of fluorescent stains, including propidium iodide (PI) and Hoechst 33258. (iii) The cellular uptake of TRPD, RPD, PD, and DOX, respectively, will be studied using fluorescent microscope, live cell imaging, and confocal laser scanning microscope. In vivo study of the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, diagnostic imaging, and anti-glioma efficacy of TRPD using the orthotopic glioma mice model. (i) Normal nude mice and U87 MG-Red-Fluc cell-derived orthotopic glioma mice will be used for the in vivo studies. (ii) Pharmacokinetics: TRPD, RPD, PD, and DOX, respectively, will be administered to nude mice model via tail vein injection. At selected time points, blood samples will be collected and the DOX contents will be measured. (iii) Biodistribution and diagnostic imaging: TRPD, RPD, PD, and DOX, respectively, after the initial excitations by UV light will be administered to the orthotopic glioma mice model. At selected time points, the persistent luminescence will be renewed using LED and the in vivo autofluorescence-free images will be obtained and analyzed. The effects of BBB penetration and glioma targeting will be evaluated. At predefined time points, the mice will be sacrificed and the drug concentrations in the blood and organ samples will be measured. Major organs will also be sampled for ex vivo fluorescence imaging. (iv) The anti-glioma efficacy: TRPD, RPD, PD, and DOX, respectively, will be administered to the orthotopic glioma mice model. Tumor volume and body weight will be recorded daily. The evaluations of the therapeutic effects, including tumor weight index, tumor volume, and histological observation of the major organs, will be conducted. Study the in vivo toxicity, biocompatibility, and immunogenicity of TRPD. Healthy normal mice will be administered with various concentrations of TRPD, RPD, PD, and DOX, respectively. The survival and body weight of the mice will be monitored and recorded. The histological analyses, hematology, hemolysis test, and blood biochemistry will also be conducted.

12302921.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12302921.value: 腦腫瘤，尤其是神經膠質瘤，是兒童和成人最常見的實體瘤之一。某些類型的膠質瘤，如膠質母細胞瘤（GBM），呈浸潤性且具有侵蝕性，難以通過手術治療。並且由於大多數藥物無法穿過血腦屏障，以及藥物在殺滅腫瘤細胞的同時不可避免會導致正常組織損傷，因此即使採用手術切除和常規治療相結合的方式，GBM患者的平均生存期僅有5-12個月。 臨床上，磁共振成像 (MRI) 是膠質瘤診斷和治療評估的主要成像方式，在造影劑（CA）的幫助下，可以確定腫瘤邊緣。但是CA無法通過完整的血腦屏障增強診斷時的 MRI 信號。此外，CA 的體內迴圈時間短，且不具有靶向性，阻礙了它們的應用。因此，具有血腦屏障通透性、長體內迴圈時間和高靶向性的造影劑/探針是研究的重點。 本項目將能夠持續標記神經膠質瘤並實現無自發螢光的腫瘤成像功能的近紅外長餘輝納米顆粒，以及具有血腦屏障和神經膠質瘤雙重靶向功能的 T7 肽相結合，製造了 TRPD，即紅細胞膜 (RCM) 修飾的 T7 偶聯的多柔比星 (DOX) 負載的發光納米顆粒，用於膠質瘤的成像和協同治療。TRPD 具有五個關鍵特徵，包括：(i) 可用於診斷和協同治療； (ii) 可通過血腦屏障； (iii) 無背景干擾，可持續成像； (iv) 腫瘤靶向性； (v) 延長了納米顆粒的體內迴圈時間和負載藥物的釋放時間。本項目已獲得前期結果的支持，包括（i）成功製備TRPD； (ii) 體外細胞毒性證實了 TRPD 對神經膠質瘤細胞具有殺傷作用； (iii) 通過皮下神經膠質瘤動物模型證實了TRPD可實現體內可持續和無自發螢光成像； (iv) 延長了納米顆粒的體內迴圈時間和負載藥物的釋放時間。對於TRPD的生物安全性，已有研究使用類似的合成方法對不同的配體和細胞膜進行偶聯。據報導，所涉及的材料和合成的納米顆粒均沒有免疫原性問題。 本項目將對TRPD的理化特性進行表徵，使用原位膠質瘤小鼠模型對 TRPD 的性質、功效和安全性進行體外和體內評估。本項目將成為膠質瘤診斷成像和協同治療的開創性工作，該結果將促進腦部相關疾病的靶向治療的發展，並為非侵入性腦成像帶來新的可通過血腦屏障的CA。

12302921.label: Realisation of objectives
12302921.value: 1. Study the formation and characterization of T7-conjugated, red blood cell membrane coated, doxorubicin loaded persistent luminescence nanoparticles (TRZD). All objectives have been completed, and the results were discussed in the previous report. 2. Study the in vitro stability and controlled release of TRZD. All objectives have been completed and the results were discussed in the previous report. 3. Study the in vitro cytotoxicity (including cell apoptosis and necrosis), the cellular uptake, the biosafety, and the permeability through BBB of TRZD. All objectives have been completed and the results were discussed in the previous report. 4. In vivo study of the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, diagnostic imaging, and anti-glioma efficacy of TRZD using the orthotopic glioma mice model. All objectives have been completed. The results of pharmacokinetics were discussed in the previous report. a. Biodistribution and diagnostic imaging. Ex vivo NIR luminescence imaging was used to investigate the biodistribution and diagnostic imaging of CUDZ in the orthotopic tumor mice model. 24 h after the intravenous injection of ZM, DZ, UDZ, and CUDZ, respectively, the major organs of the mice were obtained, and the luminescence intensities were measured. Results: The maximal luminescence intensity was detected in the tumor of the CUDZ group, which verified the highest accumulation of CUDZ at the tumor site. The reason was that CUDZ had an enhanced targeting ability to GBM by CLTX, a GBM-homing effect and a highly reduced RES uptake due to the GCM coating, which made CUDZ a nanoprobe with high potential for imaging and targeted therapy of GBM. Ex vivo NIR luminescence imaging was used to investigate the biodistribution of CUDZ in the orthotopic tumor mice model. The highest luminescence intensity in the tumors was observed in the CUDZ group. The luminescence intensity, which was corresponding to the amount of the NPs in the tissue, was measured. The results revealed that the accumulation of UDZ and CUDZ in the brain was higher than that of ZM and DZ. Compared with UDZ, CUDZ not only showed higher luminescence intensity but also accumulated in the right hemisphere, where the GBM tumor was inoculated . It verified that CUDZ exhibited an improved targeting to GBM by CLTX and a combination of GBM-homing effect and highly reduced RES uptake due to the GCM coating. b. Anti-glioma efficacy. To study the anti-GBM activity, PBS, DOX, ZD, RZD, and TRZD, respectively, with the DOX equivalent concentration of 10 mg/kg was administered every four days to the six groups (n = 10) of randomly divided mice. The size of the tumors and the body weight of the mice were monitored and recorded. The tumor volumes were estimated based on the tumor diameters measured using a vernier caliper. Results: A subcutaneous GBM mice model was applied to study anti-GBM activity of CUDZG. The tumor size of mice treated by CUDZG was the minimum at 17 d after the first injection compared with the other groups. And the size of the tumor in CUDZG group almost showed no change in the 17 days, indicating a good suppression of the tumor growth by CUDZG. CD31 and TUNEL staining of the slices of the tumor tissues were further applied to study the anti-GBM effect of CUDZG. The CUDZG treatment exhibited the highest degree of apoptosis and lowest degree of angiogenesis, which suggested that CUDZG presented the optimal performance in the inhibition of GBM cell growth. The histopathological analysis was also conducted on the tissues of the major organs of the subcutaneous GBM mice model. There was no obvious damage to the major organs of all the treatment groups. The results proved that, as a brain targeting nanoprobe for imaging and therapy, CUDZG exhibited no side effects on the major organs. 5. Study the in vivo toxicity, biocompatibility, and immunogenicity of TRZD. All objectives have been completed. a. In vivo toxicity and biocompatibility. The cytotoxicity of CUDGZ on the U87-MG cells was studied using CCK-8. The hemolytic assay of the NPs was performed to verify the biosafety of the NPs. Gboxin, ZG, DZG, UDZG, and CUDZG was cultivated with the mouse blood for 2 h at 37 ℃. PBS and DI water were set as negative and positive controls. Results: Gboxin exhibited a dose-dependent cytotoxicity after incubated with the cells for 48 h. The IC50 of Gboxin was 22.14±1.98 μM. While ZM exhibited insignificant cytotoxicity to U87-MG cells at the Gboxin equivalent concentrations of 0.5, 1, 5, and 10 μg/mL, demonstrating good biocompatibility of ZM. CUDZG showed stronger cytotoxicity than UDZG at the same Gboxin equivalent concentration, which demonstrated that CLTX on the surface of CUDZG improved both the targeting and cellular uptake of NPs to U87-MG cells, and the cytotoxicity to the cells was thus increased compared to that of UDZG. The group of DI water generated hemolysis, while no noticeable hemolysis was recognized in the groups of PBS, Gboxin, ZG, DZG, UDZG, and CUDZG. Moreover, no noticeable hemolysis was recognized with the increased concentration of CUDZG as high as 1000 μg/mL, showing the excellent biocompatibility of CUDZG. b. In vivo immunogenicity of NPs To study the anti-GBM activity, 200 μL of PBS, Gboxin, ZG, DZG, UDZG, and CUDZG, respectively, with the Gboxin equivalent concentration of 10 mg/kg were intravenously injected to the six groups (n = 6) of randomly divided mice with orthotropic GBM every three days from Day 1. The size of the tumors and the body weight of the mice were monitored and recorded. Results: The representative images of the subcutaneous GBM mice models and the representative ex vivo images of the tumors of various groups were obtained. The tumor size of mice treated by CUDZG was the minimum 17 d after the first injection compared with the other groups. And the size of the tumor in CUDZG group almost showed no change in the 17 days, indicating a good suppression of the tumor growth by CUDZG . The average body weight of mice of each treatment group showed no obvious change through the duration of the study. CD31 and TUNEL staining of the slices of the tumor tissues were further applied to study the anti-GBM effect of CUDZG. The CUDZG treatment exhibited the highest degree of apoptosis and lowest degree of angiogenesis, which suggested that CUDZG presented the optimal performance in the inhibition of GBM cell growth compared with other groups. Further, after finishing all the objectives of the GRF, we continue the work of the design, formation, and in vitro and in vivo evaluation of brain-targeting nanoparticles for the therapy of glioma. We designed a new brain tumor-targeting drug delivery system self-assembled from zein to explore the drug Dactolisib (Dac) for GBM therapy while avoiding its toxicity. We finished the following objectives, and the work was published on Materials Today Nano. 1. Formation of the nanoencapsulation of Dac and conjugation of RVG29 and zein-Dac_NPs. 2. Characterization, including DLS, FTIR, NMR, and in vitro drug release, of various NPs. 3. In vitro cytotoxicity of zein-RVG-Dac_NPs, zein-RVG_NPs, and Dac was measured using an MTS assay. 4. Evaluation of anti-GBM activity of NPs using the in vivo fluorescence imaging system. The immunofluorescence histochemistry and immunohistochemistry analysis were also conducted. 5. Biosafety assessments, including H&E staining, of the NPs.

12302921.value: Major findings: For the diagnosis and treatment of GBM, CUDZG, a NIR PLNP capable of BBB penetration was formed. 12302921.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12302921.value: This research offer hope for creating NIR PL nanoprobes capable of penetrating the BBB for accurate diagnosis and treatment of GBM and other CNS diseases. The suggested approach includes thorough preclinical safety and toxicology assessments to determine a suitable therapeutic window, followed by efficacy testing in advanced animal models that closely mimic human GBM. To improve clinical relevance, the rechargeability mechanism should be refined for better tissue penetration, possibly by investigating alternative light sources for in vivo reactivation. Additionally, the capabilities of this BBB-penetrating nanocarrier should be examined by incorporating other powerful, previously hard-to-deliver neurotherapeutics, thus broadening its potential use beyond Gboxin to address various central nervous system diseases, including other aggressive brain cancers and neurological disorders.

12302921.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12302921.value: This research project tackles the challenging diagnosis and treatment of glioblastoma (GBM), a very aggressive brain cancer. A dual-functional novel NIR-PLNP for imaging and therapy of GBM was formed. it can be seen glowing through pinpoint the tumor's location, and it carries a powerful anti-cancer drug directly to the cancer cells. Its major significance is its ability to cross the protective blood-brain barrier, a huge obstacle for most drugs. It achieves this using a combination of a special targeting peptide and a coating made from cancer cell membranes, which acts as a disguise. The particle is also designed to release its drug only when it detects the unique environment of the tumor, minimizing harm to healthy cells. The value of this work is a new, highly precise method that could lead to earlier diagnosis, more effective treatment with fewer side effects, and ultimately longer survival for patients with this devastating disease.

12303321.label: Project Objectives
12303321.value: To characterize and compare microplastics in outdoor air from Guangzhou and Taiyuan, China. Previously, we have established platforms for the collection of outdoor atmospheric fallouts in the northern and southern cities of China. In this study, we aim to collect and characterize airborne microplastics from Taiyuan and Guangzhou. The latter city, located about 300 kilometers from Hong Kong SAR, is one of the densely plastic contaminated areas in China. Comparison will be made regarding the physicochemical properties of airborne microplastics, such as types, shapes, sizes and adhered toxicants in are from the two cities. To conduct in vivo and in vitro experiments for the investigation of lung toxicity induced by airborne microplastics exposures. Because lung is one of the primary organs withstanding the toxicity induced by atmospheric fallouts. This objective aims to establish in vitro cell and in vivo rat models and evaluate the toxicity induced by airborne microplastics exposures. Human lung cell lines, including the lung epithelial cells, lung fibroblast cells and lung adenocarcinoma cells will be used for the investigation of acute biological responses, such as oxidative stress and inflammation drive by airborne microplastics exposure. A real-ambient exposure system allows whole-body inhalation exposure of airborne microplastics in rats. The obtained results will be validated by laboratory animal experiments with collected airborne microplastics and commercial fluorescent microplastics. To analyze microplastics in biological fluids and lung tissues of experimental animals. The appearance and location of microplastics in biological fluids and lung tissue samples will be investigated. The results of this study are expected to clarify whether the airborne microplastics with different size distributions can enter the lung and circulatory fluids of experimental animals via inhalation. To investigate the differential metabolites and perturbed metabolic pathways by mass spectrometry-based metabolomics and to verify the identified biomarkers and relevant metabolic pathways at enzymatic level. This objective aims to identify biomarkers and perturbed metabolic pathways induced by airborne exposure. Non-targeted metabolomics will be used to measure the metabolic profiles of lung cell lines, rat plasma and tissues. Interested metabolites will be accurately determined by using targeted metabolomics analysis. In addition, biological verification of the metabolite biomarkers at the enzymatic level will be carried out in the study. The results will be collectively taken into consideration for the interpretation of toxicological mechanisms of airborne microplastics.

12303321.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12303321.value: 微塑料（小于 5 毫米）已经被报道普遍存在于水、空气和食物等各类环境介质中，成全球性环境污染物，其摄食和吸入被认为是人类接触微塑料的主要途径。据报道，每年有近74000至121000 个微塑料颗粒会进入人体，其中吸入约占每年接触量的二分之一。有证据表明，生物反应如炎症、基因毒性和细胞凋亡与摄入微塑料有关。然而，很少有人注意到吸入微塑料的毒性。在本研究中，我们将从分子水平研究空气中微塑料的肺毒性过程和机制。首先，室外空气样本将在太原和广州这两个华北和华南的经济和产业结构明显不同的特大城市中采集，后者是中国塑料污染最密集的地区之一。我们将通过表征手段比较两个地区的空气中微塑料的类型、形状、大小和粘附的毒物种类。其次，将建立体内细胞和体外大鼠模型，以研究空气中微塑料暴露引起的肺毒性。除了实验室暴露外，真实环境暴露系统也将应用于评估微塑料在污染大气环境中的暴露。第三，将对照组和暴露大鼠的血浆和肺组织等生物样本中的微塑料进行相关性研究，这可以为空气中的微塑料是否可能进入暴露动物的肺和循环系统提供直接证据。最后，我们也将应用基于质谱的代谢组学手段去研究暴露在空气中的微塑料对代谢物和代谢途径所产生的扰动。我们希望本项目的结果能为解释空气中微塑料引起的生物效应和毒理学机制以及评估通过吸入空气中微塑料的潜在监管阈值提供有价值的信息。

12303321.label: Major findings and research outcome
12303321.value: To establish a comprehensive framework for microplastic (MP) toxicity, we first reviewed the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) of MPs in humans, highlighting inhalation as a critical exposure pathway (Wu et al., 2022). Building on this foundation, environmental correlates of MP pollution were disentangled in the coastal waters of Southern China (Wu et al., 2025), establishing a regional pollution baseline. Specifically addressing outdoor air (Objective 1), a fragmentation pattern-based mass spectrometry strategy was developed, successfully identifying multiple emerging tire-wear contaminants (e.g., 6PPD-quinone and novel analogues) in air particulates from Taiyuan (Wang et al., 2024). Regarding toxicity mechanisms and metabolic profiling (Objectives 2 & 4), in vitro experiments demonstrated that polystyrene nanoplastics (80 nm) internalized into human lung epithelial cells (BEAS-2B), causing mitochondrial damage and ROS overproduction. High-resolution metabolomics revealed significant perturbations in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and glutathione metabolism (Lin et al., 2022). We further corroborated these findings using quantitative proteomics in the model organism C. elegans, which showed that nanoplastics disrupt proteome homeostasis and upregulate energy metabolism-related proteins (Huang et al., 2023). This cross-model validation confirms that metabolic reprogramming and mitochondrial dysfunction are conserved mechanisms of MP toxicity. For contaminant analysis in lung tissues (Objective 3), in vivo toxicokinetic studies utilizing stable isotope tracing revealed that microplastic-derived contaminants were rapidly absorbed into the bloodstream and distributed to lung tissue, exhibiting a half-life of ~20.7 hours. This confirms the potential for bioaccumulation of airborne plastic-associated chemicals within the respiratory system (Zhang et al., 2024, Sci. Total Environ.). Validating these findings, we also successfully detected the contaminants in human biofluids using novel UPLC-HRMS methods (Zhang et al., 2024, J. Inst. Anal.).

12303321.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12303321.value: The current research established a critical link between inhaled microplastics, their chemical additives, and mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming. This offers significant potential to further elucidate the vector mechanism, wherein microplastics act as carriers facilitating the respiratory uptake of toxic organic pollutants. To advance this understanding towards realistic human health risk assessment, the proposed course of action focuses on three directions of further development. First, future studies may be conducted on transition from 2D cell cultures to 3D lung organoid models to better recapitulate the physiological complexity of the alveolar barrier under long-term, low-dose exposure scenarios. Second, the existing research outcomes may be expanded to evaluate the combined toxicity of weathered, environmentally sampled microplastics and their leached chemical cocktails, moving beyond pristine polymer standards to reflect actual atmospheric conditions. Finally, we propose to validate the identified metabolic biomarkers—specifically perturbations in the TCA cycle and glutathione pathways—in human clinical samples, such as bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. This translational approach aims to develop non-invasive diagnostic indicators for monitoring early-stage respiratory injury induced by airborne plastic pollution.

12303321.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12303321.value: Microplastics are ubiquitous pollutants found not only in food but also in the air we breathe. While the risks of ingestion are recognized, the health impacts of inhaling these particles remain poorly understood. This project investigated the lung toxicity of airborne microplastics, particularly those originating from tire wear. By analyzing urban air samples, we detected toxic chemical additives adhering to these particles. Using advanced laboratory techniques, we demonstrated that these tiny particles can penetrate human lung cells and impair their mitochondria (the cell’s energy generators), forcing the cells to disrupt their normal metabolism to survive. Furthermore, our animal studies confirmed that these associated chemicals are absorbed into the bloodstream and accumulate specifically in lung tissue. This research is significant as it demonstrates that airborne microplastics function as carriers for hazardous substances, effectively delivering toxic chemicals deep into the respiratory system. These findings provide critical scientific evidence to help policymakers establish air quality standards and safety thresholds to protect public health from this emerging airborne threat.

12303421.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12303421.value: Meta-analysis is a statistical technique to synthesize the research findings from multiple studies for decision making. It has been increasingly popular in recent years, mainly due to its wide application in evidence-based practice. Also in the past several years, the PI and collaborators have made some significant progress in advancing statistical methods for meta-analysis, in particular for the newly developed methods for data transformation that are capable to serve as “rules of thumb” in meta-analysis and evidence-based practice. The main purpose of this proposal is to further advance the literature by developing new models and methods for meta-analysis. Specifically, there are three major projects in the proposal. The first project is to develop a unified framework for simultaneous synthesis of the odds ratio (OR) and the risk ratio (RR) in meta-analysis with binary outcomes. The second project is to propose an Intrinsic measure for Quantifying the heterogeneity in meta-analysis, referred to as the IQ statistic, to overcome the limitations in the I^2 statistic. The third project is to develop new estimation and model selection methods for the fixed-effects model (FEM) with application to meta-analysis with few studies. We plan to accomplish, but not limited to, the proposed three projects in a three-year research plan. All three projects are of particular importance, and upon a successful completion, we expect that the new models and methods from our proposed studies will have potential to be widely applied in meta-analysis and evidence-based practice. 薈萃分析是一種綜合多項研究之研究結果的統計方法。近年來，它在決策研究中越來越受歡迎，特別是在循證實踐中的廣泛應用。在過去的幾年裡，項目負責人和合作者在推進薈萃分析的統計方法學方面已取得了一些重大的進展，特別是他們最近提出的數據轉換的新方法，已經成為薈萃分析中的經驗法則並已被廣泛用於循證實踐。在本項目中，我們將進一步開發新的薈萃分析模型和方法，從而讓薈萃分析達到一個新的高度。具體而言，本項目將包括三個主要研究課題。第一個課題是開發一個能同時綜合優勢比 (OR) 和風險比 (RR)的統一模型；第二個課題是提出一種新的用於量化薈萃分析中異質性的內在度量，稱為 IQ 統計量，以克服現有的 I^2 統計量的局限性；第三個課題是在稀疏情況下，基於固定效應模型 (FEM) 開發新的模型估計和選擇的方法。這三個課題都具有特別重要的現實意義，一旦成功完成，我們預計所提出的新模型和新方法將有可能被廣泛應用於薈萃分析和循證實踐。

12303421.label: Realisation of objectives
12303421.value: To realize the first objective, we developed and validated a unified framework for synthesizing odds ratios (ORs) and risk ratios (RRs) in meta-analyses of binary outcomes, addressing a longstanding challenge in evidence synthesis. Traditional approaches typically rely on approximations or indirect transformations, which can introduce bias when studies report different effect measures or designs. We overcame these limitations by introducing a bivariate random-effects model that jointly synthesizes ORs and RRs from both cohort and case-control studies, making optimal use of within-study covariance. This flexible framework can incorporate studies reporting only OR, only RR, or both, and removes constraints inherent in previous single-effect and transformation approaches. Our model and practical recommendations are detailed in a published paper in Statistical Methods in Medical Research (2023) and a second manuscript currently under review. Extensive simulations and applications to real-world data demonstrate that our approach provides unbiased estimates, valid confidence intervals, and improved robustness over existing methods. To support broad adoption and maximize the practical impact of these advances, we have developed accessible online calculators and R package modules for binary outcome meta-analysis, extending previous tools designed for continuous outcomes. We have also tackled practical issues such as incomplete reporting and missing baseline risk, refining imputation strategies and offering clear, actionable guidance for practitioners. Dissemination through presentations, workshops, and comprehensive documentation ensures that these methodological improvements are accessible to both researchers and clinicians. Collectively, these achievements represent a significant step forward, equipping the medical and public health communities with more reliable tools for evidence synthesis and clinical decision-making. To achieve the second objective, we addressed the well-known limitations of the I^2 statistic in quantifying heterogeneity. Although I^2 is widely reported, its dependence on study sample size can distort the interpretation of heterogeneity, sometimes leading to inappropriate analytical choices. Our recent publication in Statistics in Medicine (Yang et al., 2025) provided both theoretical and empirical evidence that I^2 may approach 1 with large sample sizes, even when actual differences between study populations are minimal, thus overstating heterogeneity and justifying random-effects models unnecessarily. To resolve this, we introduced the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for meta-analysis and new measures including the ANOVA and I_A^2 statistics, which are invariant to sample size and better reflect true population diversity. Simulations and real-world applications confirmed that these metrics offer more robust and interpretable assessment of heterogeneity across a range of effect types. Clear formulas, guidance, and visualizations were provided to support implementation in practice, and we recommend reporting I_A^2 alongside conventional I^2 for more informed model selection and interpretation. These advancements set a new methodological standard, empowering analysts to make more precise and clinically relevant decisions in meta-analytic evidence synthesis. For the third objective, we advanced meta-analytic methodology in two essential areas: synthesizing evidence from few studies and rigorous detection of inconsistency in network meta-analysis (NMA). Recognizing that many meta-analyses include just two or three studies, we demonstrated that the fixed-effects model is often the best choice in these cases, as both common-effect and random-effects models can be unreliable—particularly when heterogeneity or unstable variance estimates are present. We developed an optimal estimator for the unweighted average effect, offering improved accuracy and stable inference, which supports more reliable conclusions from small-scale meta-analyses. At the same time, we made important progress in the detection of inconsistency in NMA, which is critical when comparing multiple interventions using both direct and indirect evidence. Through analytic comparison and comprehensive simulations, we systematically evaluated the design-by-treatment interaction model and side-splitting approaches—the leading methods for inconsistency detection in current practice. By reframing NMA as a missing data problem, we showed that side-splitting models are specific cases of the broader design-by-treatment interaction approach. Our results demonstrated that the design-by-treatment interaction model is generally more robust and sensitive for global inconsistency detection, especially in complex or sparse networks, while side-splitting is an effective supplementary tool for identifying local inconsistency. We provided clear analytical tools and recommendations for practitioners, thereby strengthening the reliability of NMA results and contributing to more nuanced and trustworthy evidence synthesis.

12303421.label: Major findings and research outcome
12303421.value: During the reporting period, we achieved all principal objectives with significant methodological and practical advances in meta-analysis. These results address central challenges in evidence synthesis for binary outcomes, heterogeneity quantification, and small or networked meta-analyses. First, in line with Objective 1, we developed and validated a unified bivariate random-effects framework for the joint synthesis of odds ratios (ORs) and risk ratios (RRs) in meta-analyses involving binary outcomes. Traditional approaches often relied on restrictive transformations, introducing bias when studies differed in reported effect measures or design. Our novel model accommodates studies reporting only OR, only RR, or both, and incorporates within-study covariance, thus overcoming these limitations. As described in our published work (Statistical Methods in Medical Research, 2023) and a manuscript under review, this approach consistently yields unbiased estimates, valid inference, and greater methodological robustness. We also produced user-friendly online calculators and R packages to facilitate practical adoption. Second, addressing Objective 2, we tackled the well-known limitations of the I^2 statistic in measuring heterogeneity, specifically its dependence on study sample size that can lead to overestimated heterogeneity and inappropriate model selection. Our research, detailed in Statistics in Medicine (Yang et al., 2025), introduced the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for meta-analysis alongside new, sample size-invariant estimators (I_A^2 and ANOVA statistics). Simulations and applications confirmed these measures provide more accurate, interpretable heterogeneity assessments and better inform model selection. We now recommend reporting I_A^2 alongside conventional I^2 in future analyses. Third, consistent with Objective 3, we advanced methods for meta-analyses with few studies and for network meta-analysis (NMA). We showed that the fixed-effects model and our newly developed optimal estimator offer superior accuracy and reliability when only two or three studies are available, outperforming standard common-effect and random-effects models. Our comprehensive evaluation of inconsistency detection methods in NMA demonstrated that the design-by-treatment interaction model is more robust for global inconsistency detection than side-splitting models, particularly in complex networks, while side-splitting remains useful for targeted, local assessment. We disseminated practical recommendations and tools to support their use in research and practice. Collectively, these accomplishments establish a suite of reliable, broadly accessible methods and tools for meta-analysis. Through publications, community workshops, and open-source resources, our findings are already empowering researchers and clinicians in medicine and public health to make stronger, more informed decisions.

12303421.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12303421.value: There is strong potential for further development of this research by extending the new statistical methods and software tools to address increasingly complex challenges in medical data analysis. Future work could focus on adapting our techniques for use with large-scale and diverse data sources, such as electronic health records, genomics, and patient registries, which present unique hurdles beyond traditional clinical studies. Enhancing our methods to better accommodate real-world evidence, including data from observational studies and community-based research, will further broaden their utility and impact in healthcare decision-making. To advance these goals, we propose building collaborations with clinical researchers, data scientists, and healthcare providers to pilot and refine our approaches across various medical fields. We will prioritize gathering user feedback and updating the tools to ensure they remain practical, accessible, and relevant to evolving user needs. Additionally, we plan to promote adoption through workshops, training materials, and open-access resources, encouraging wider use of evidence synthesis in both research and clinical practice. By pursuing these actions, we aim to support ongoing innovation and ensure our work continues to improve patient outcomes and inform effective health policies.

12303421.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12303421.value: Medical research often combines results from several studies to determine which treatments and approaches are most effective. However, differences in study design, sample sizes, and measurement methods can make it challenging to combine this evidence accurately. Our project addressed these obstacles by developing innovative statistical techniques that allow researchers to merge findings from diverse studies with greater precision, even when data is limited or studies are not perfectly aligned. We also introduced rigorous methods to assess the reliability and consistency of the combined results, ensuring that conclusions drawn from this process are trustworthy and reproducible. To support wider adoption and practical use, we created user-friendly software tools and made them freely available to scientists and health professionals. These advances help improve the quality of evidence available for making medical decisions, ultimately strengthening patient care and informing health policies that benefit the public. By enabling more accurate and reliable synthesis of research findings, our work empowers researchers and clinicians to make better use of existing data, paving the way for improved healthcare outcomes and public well-being around the world.
