12611121.label: Project Title(Chinese)
12611121.value: 跨文化合作與亞際身份：戰時上海與戰後香港的歌舞片，1931-1972

12611121.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12611121.value: The Chinese song-and-dance film (gewu pian) is an understudied genre often (mis)understood as apolitical, escapist, and superficial. This project aims to change this perception by exploring the role of gewu pian in cross-cultural collaboration and the construction of inter-Asia identities during and after the second Sino-Japanese War, and by arguing that the genre is marked by the cultural history of the Anti-Japanese War of Resistance and its attendant ambivalence. I will fill in the gaps in the genre’s controversial production and reception histories by analyzing the moral anxieties associated with China’s long conversion to sound between 1931 and 1936, foregrounding the pivotal Japanese-occupied Shanghai between 1937 and 1945, and reevaluating its lasting cinematic legacy and lingering traumatic memories in postwar and Cold War Hong Kong (from the late 1940s to the early 1970s, when the genre died out). Gewu pian has long been dismissed as derivative, shallow, pornographic, or even traitorous in wartime China, yet celebrated as modern, fashionable, and cosmopolitan in postwar and Cold War Hong Kong. Building on existing scholarship on the Shanghai-Hong Kong nexus, the songstress, and Chinese popular music, this project aims at a more nuanced understanding of the role of gewu pian in wartime and postwar periods and an analysis of how this genre forged transitional connections between these periods and between Shanghai and Hong Kong’s music and film industries. Informed by film studies, musicology, and cultural studies, this project considers gewu pian as an “intermedial field” participating in corporeal and discursive warfare. I will examine cross-media synergies between cinema, live performance, print culture, and sonic culture. Chinese song-and-dance films will be discussed as a global genre and compared with their precedent and coeval counterparts in Hollywood and Japan. This project draws on various primary sources—including neglected films, newspapers, periodicals, film stills, memoirs, oral histories, scores, scripts, and recordings—from the China Film Archive in Beijing, the Hong Kong Film Archive, the “Hong Kong TV and Film Publication Database” at Hong Kong Baptist University, the Hong Kong Collection at the University of Hong Kong, the Shanghai Library, the Kawakita Memorial Film Institute in Tokyo, and the National University of Singapore. The objectives are to bring to light recently available archival films produced in Japanese-occupied Shanghai, to reconstruct the intermedial film culture of wartime and postwar gewu pian, and arrive at a deeper understanding of the continuity between wartime propaganda cinema and the commercial entertainment industry. 華語歌舞片是未被充分研究的類型，經常被理解或誤解為非關政治、逃避現實和膚淺。本計劃旨在通過探索歌舞片在跨文化合作中的作用，以及第二次中日戰爭期間和戰後亞際身份的建構，來改變歌舞片長期被誤解的境況。並論證歌舞片與抗日戰爭文化史，及其伴隨的複雜情緒之間存在千絲萬縷的關係。我將填補歌舞片充滿爭議的製作史和接收史的空白：分析中國1931年至1936年間，中國電影從無聲到有聲的轉型期與歌舞片引發的道德焦慮間的連繫；讓1937年至1945年間，日本佔領上海敏感時期，中日影人合拍的歌舞片浮出影史地表；並重新評估戰後和冷戰香港（從1940年代末到1970年代初歌舞類型片的消逝）如何繼承中日戰爭的電影遺產和其中揮之不去的創傷記憶。華語歌舞片長期受輕視，被指控摹仿好萊塢、內容色情淺薄、甚至在戰時被視為漢奸電影，但在戰後和冷戰時期的香港卻體現現代、時尚和國際化。在現存關於滬港電影連繫、歌女和華語流行音樂研究的基礎上，本計劃旨在更細緻地理解歌舞片在戰時和戰後時期的作用，以及分析歌舞類型如何連繫戰時上海與戰後香港、音樂與電影產業。 在電影研究、音樂學和文化研究的啟發下，本計劃將歌舞片視為參與身體和話語戰爭的「跨媒介場域」。我將檢視電影、現場表演、印刷文化和聲音文化跨媒體間的合力作用。華語歌舞片將作為全球類型被討論，並與好萊塢和日本歌舞片比較。本計劃援引各種檔案資料，包括被忽視的電影、報紙、期刊、劇照、回憶錄、口述歷史、樂譜、劇本和錄音。這些檔案來自北京的中國電影資料館、香港電影資料館、香港浸會大學的中港電視。電影刊物資料庫、香港大學孔安道紀念圖書館、上海圖書館、鎌倉市川喜多映画記念館、新加坡國立大學。研究目的包括為近年相繼解禁的日本佔領上海時期製作的電影翻案，重構戰時和戰後歌舞片的跨媒介電影文化，以及更深入地理解戰時宣傳電影與電影娛樂工業的連續性。

12612821.label: Project Title(Chinese)
12612821.value: 尋找生態文明的多重想像：中國少數民族電影研究

12612821.label: Project Objectives
12612821.value: • to seek different imaginaries of what ecological civilization is meant through features and documentaries in China in order to identify possible alternative ways to think about the national and planetary future • to understand how ethnic minorities construct their local agency in ecological conservation and change their stereotypical image in their film productions • to reflect upon, by examining ethnic minority cinematic works produced in China, the entangled relations and interactions between state and nation, rural and urban, modern and traditional, indigenous and external, Han and ethnic minority in relation to environmental crisis • to examine if the environmental cinema reconciles or sharpen Han/non-Han differences and if it appropriate different intellectual resources in its visions of ecological future • to publish the research outcomes as 2 essays and 1 book chapter in academic venues, and to enhance public awareness of the issues in Hong Kong in a comparative perspective

• to understand how ethnic minorities construct their local agency in ecological conservation and change their stereotypical image in their film productions

• to reflect upon, by examining ethnic minority cinematic works produced in China, the entangled relations and interactions between state and nation, rural and urban, modern and traditional, indigenous and external, Han and ethnic minority in relation to environmental crisis
• to examine if the environmental cinema reconciles or sharpen Han/non-Han differences and if it appropriate different intellectual resources in its visions of ecological future
• to publish the research outcomes as 2 essays and 1 book chapter in academic venues, and to enhance public awareness of the issues in Hong Kong in a comparative perspective

12612821.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12612821.value: This project examines, through moving images in fiction and documentary films produced in China, the trajectories and implications of “Ecological Civilization” promoted by the Chinese state as well as the different visions from the civil society and ethnic minority communities in relation to the environmental issues. It focuses on how China’s green documentaries and ethnic minority cinema interact and respond to the state campaign of ecological imaginary and in what ways they are able to take initiatives and produce their own imaginaries for other possible, if not alternative, thinking about the national as well as planetary future. I investigate the implications of ecological civilization under the direction of the authoritarian state in order to understand the dynamic ways of how the future of ecology is envisioned not only by the state but also by other non-state actors in China, and analyze by means of cinematic productions the entangled relations between the state and different cultural actors in a subject matter they are bound to share. While urban-rural, modern-traditional, mainstream-marginal, indigenous-external, self-other divides play the key role in the ecological imaginaries, I explore how China’s ecological future is deeply intertwined with different ethnic communities, Ethnic peripheries are significant components of ecological civilization because ethnic regions function as the ecological service provider for China’s core areas. The state project of Ecological Civilization is more than just another ideological campaign since it is driven by objective environmental pressures the whole Chinese nation is confronting. While the cultural actors with limited autonomy are facing an authoritarian state that keeps shifting the terrain of what is allowed and always endeavors to homogenize all voices, ecological interdependence and uncertainty may give rise to various imaginaries and visions to emerge. Cinematic productions even under official monitoring are able to cultivate individual or collective consciousness of ecologically civilized future since the government’s environmental laws and policies can never entirely cover the scale of ecosystem, while the adaptive governance is skilful in accommodating adjustments and experimentations from different sources even without political liberalization and democratization. The project attempts to understand and capture some of the potentially different perspectives and experiences that lie behind the state-promoted ecological civilization. These films I analyze are not simply grasped as representational works that reflect socio-political realities, but are understood as significant constitutive parts since they embody many micro decisions and actions made in China by individuals and local communities, ultimately shaping ecological future. 本研究計劃分析中國的虛構及紀錄電影如何回應中國政府推動的「生態文明」，探索民間社會，特別是少數民族社群，如何透過移動影像表達他們對未來生態環境的想法。國家論述雖然主導了「生態文明」的意義，但非官方的個人及團體，未嘗沒有對國族以至全地球的生態未來產生多重的想像。本研究借助城與鄉、現代與傳統、主流與邊緣、本土與外來、本我與他者等的對立框架，分析這些電影對生態文明想像的可能多重性。邊陲地區的少數民族社群，表面上雖只扮演著為中原服務的角色，但其實對未來的生態環境有深遠的影響。即使在威權政府下有諸多限制，亦不容許雜音，但生態問題的逼切嚴重性，也令管治有一定的靈活調整，因而製造了一些民間可以參與的空間，表達不同的視角與經驗。本研究不單只將電影看作反映現實的影像呈現，更視之為現實構成的部分，因為這些電影有實際參與社區，即使微小但卻是在地的行動與決定。

12612821.label: Realisation of objectives
12612821.value: Most project objectives have been achieved while one essay and a book chapter are still under review. I presented my research findings at three different international conferences, completed two book chapters, and published two academic essays to deliver my understanding of this research topic. Through the discussions with my colleagues at the conferences and other academic occasions, and the reviewers' comments on my written works, I made my project more solid and accessible as well as some murky aspects clearer.

12612821.label: Major findings and research outcome
12612821.value: Many of the proposed objectives have been closely examined and explored in my book chapter about Tibetan-made documentaries and short films about the environmental changes brought by state-led modernization to their daily life. Different imaginaries, local agency construction, and the entanglement between state and nation, rural and urban, modern and traditional, indigenous and external, and Han and ethnic minorities have been dealt with and analyzed by studying the moving images produced by Tibetans themselves. I also expand the scope to look at these issues via China-the West relations in terms of climate change cooperation and competition and via China-Hong Kong connections in the areas of water supply and perception of nature.

12612821.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12612821.value: While the main focus of this project is on the human world though divided by ethnicities and nation-states, the non-human or more-than-human multispecies realm has not been adequately examined and reflected upon for its significance to the ecological challenges. My next research project is very likely to orient in such a direction to explore the entangled relations between human and nonhuman animals in the larger Chinese context.

13100121.value: 在新型冠狀病毒（COVID-19）疫情底下，「微生物」往往令人聯想到疾病及不衛生。事實上，在整個微生物叢（宿主上的微生物群落）之中，有害的微生物只佔少數。由維持基本的營養循環，以至研發嶄新的醫療科技，微生物都參與其中，可謂與日常生活密不分離。與微生物互惠互利的關係當然不局限於人類，在自然界亦有跡可循。最近的研究顯示，探討宿主與微生物之間的關係有助從另一角度理解生態學及進化論，藉此保育生物多樣性。萬物云云之中，兩棲類的生命週期經歷水，陸兩個階段，牽涉到水生，陸生兩個截然不同的微生物叢，所以非常適合研究宿主與微生物固中的關係。本研究計劃從環境，及宿主演化角度來觀察微生物的變化，從而進一步理解微生物叢的轉變。 本研究計劃利用先進的ＤＮＡ測序法，配合穩健的採樣方式，涵蓋以下範疇：皮膚及腸道微生物叢之間的關係；使用糞便樣本來研究腸道微生物叢的可行性；環境對宿主微生物叢的影響；微生物叢在兩棲類變態其間的演替；宿主的演化關係對微生物叢的影響；以及利用微生物叢作為環境指標的可行性。 本研究將加深學術界對微生物叢的認知，由皮膚與腸道中微生物叢之間的關係開始，再涵蓋宿主演化，以及環境對微生物叢的影響。本研究會建立一個受認可的採樣系統，作為未來研究之用。同時，本研究將制定一套檢視環境及動物健康的方案，為環境健康，保育，及制定政策作出貢獻。最後，本研究希望改變大眾對微生物的誤解，以及喚起大眾對本地兩棲類，與其生境的關注。

13100121.label: Realisation of objectives
13100121.value: This study aimed to understand amphibian skin and gut microbiota. We successfully completed each objective as planned. Our results have advanced our general understanding of the microbiota, especially in amphibians, and leads towards new research questions. For general achievements, we completed our sampling as originally planned. For the main dataset, we collected a maximum of four sample types (small intestine, large intestine, feces, pre-feces) from seven species that each represent a different amphibian family. To control for environmental/geographic variation, almost all samples were collected from a single site (Tai Po Kau). As originally planned, four exceptions were included: (1) Boulenophrys brachykolos was collected from another site because it is not present at Tai Po Kau, (2) Objective 2 sampled across seven sites to investigate the impact of geography, (3) an additional species was included for Objective 2, and (4) Objective 5 required sampling from three sites. Objective 1: Characterise/understand relationship between amphibian gut and skin microbiome. (100% achieved) 1.1. Characterise amphibian gut and skin microbiota. We successfully characterised the gut and skin microbiota of seven species of amphibians (7–12 individuals/species, 73 individuals total). To our knowledge, these are the first microbiota data for all these species. 1.2. Determine core/unique microbiota of gut and skin. We identify the core microbiota for each species (shared across individuals) and unique microbiota for gut and skin (shared across individuals, unique to sample type). Interspecifically, the species were significantly different. Intraspecifically, the gut and skin microbiota were also significantly different. These findings contrasts with other studies finding a phylosymbiosis effect with closely related hosts having similar microbiotas. 1.3. Identify taxa associated with gut and skin. Based on the core microbiotas identified for the three sample types, we used PICRUSt2 to infer function based on marker gene sequences. Gut and skin have different functions, but there were some shared taxa and functions across the different sample types. 1.3. Identify associations between gut and skin microbiome. Skin and gut shared many taxa, so the significant difference was driven by differences in taxa abundance. The skin microbiota is the most distinct, followed by the small intestine, then large intestine. Objective 2: Test effectiveness of faecal samples for studying amphibian gut microbiota. (100% achieved) We completed this objective in two stages. First, compare gut and faecal microbiota for two species across 7 sites in Hong Kong to focus on two species with similar ecology and include broad geographic sampling. Second, we used the main dataset of this project. 2.1. Characterise microbiota in small intestine, large intestine, and in faeces. We successfully characterised the microbiota of the three sample types of 8 species (7–30 individuals/species, 133 individuals total). 2.2. Determine relationship between microbiota of faeces and the two gut sections. In all comparisons, microbiotas were significantly different between the three sample types. Separating the analysis by species, results had some variation. Five species had little to no overlap between the three sample types, while one species had overlap between large intestine and faeces, while one species had overlap between all sample types. This infers that the relationship between the gut and faeces microbiota are generally distinct, however with some variation between host species. Objective 3: Investigate the relationship between environmental and host’s microbiome. (100% achieved) 3.1. Characterise microbiota of the host environment (water and sediment). We collected nine water and nine sediment samples (3 replicates x 3 sites). These samples were collected at the same time and location as microbiota samples were collected. These data serve as baseline microbiota data of the environment. 3.2. Determine whether environmental microbiota is significantly different from that of host skin and gut. First, we found that the microbiota of stream water and soil were significantly different. Next, although the skin and environmental samples were significantly different, we found the environmental samples to be a subset of the skin. This result suggests that both stream water and soil are sources for the skin microbiota. Lastly, the microbiotas of the environmental samples were statistically different from the gut microbiota (small intestine, large intestine). This suggests that the environment is not a major source for the gut microbiota. This finding is related to the findings of Objective #5 (bioindicators), suggesting diet is a major source for gut bacteria. 3.3. Identify environmental factors facilitating host colonisation through correlational analyses. We found sampling locality to be the best predictor of differences in microbiota, However, we were unable to tease apart which environmental factors that contribute to microbiota colonisation. Objective 4: Quantify phylosymbiosis in this system. (100% achieved) 4.1. Characterise microbiome of seven amphibian species. Same as above—we successfully characterised the microbiota of these seven species. 4.2. Analyse data in a phylogenetic context to determine whether the microbiome evolved independently or is restricted by the phylogenetic constrains. We compare the host amphibian phylogenetic tree with that of the microbial dendrogram. The amphibian phylogenetic tree was built from complete mtgenome sequences from GenBank. We found a weak to no effect of phylosymbiosis for all sample types. The result remains if we exclude B. brachykolos from the analysis (one species collected from a different site). We suggest that host plasticity is high, which enables hosts to establish their microbiota based on habitat availability, rather than based on phylogenetic relatedness. 4.3. Test for evolutionary correlations among microbiome lineages. We compared the interspecific and intraspecific dendrograms and found no consistent correlation Objective 5: Evaluate using amphibian microbiota as bioindicators by investigating the link between pollution and microbiota. (100% achieved) 5.1. Characterise microbiota of amphibians from localities with different levels of water pollution. We compared the microbiota of one species (D. melanostictus) across three sites to compare between sites with very bad pollution (Kam Tin, Yuen Long) to a site with no pollution (Tai Po Kau). The sites were chosen based on “River Water Quality in Hong Kong 2021” published by the Environmental Protection Department. 5.2. Determine whether amphibian microbiota differs significantly across sites with different pollution. We found the microbiotas were statistically significant between sites, but more similar for the two polluted sites. This pattern was the same for all three sample types. Focusing on the gut, we found that the phylogenetic alpha diversity is significantly higher in Tai Po Kau (unpolluted) than Kam Tin and Yuen Long (polluted). In general, other studies have found that a higher microbiota diversity is regarded as a positive indicator of health. 5.3. Determine whether amphibian microbiota is associated with specific microorganisms or pollutants. Water microbiota accounted for a small subset of the amphibian microbiota, so we were unable to identify any meaning associations between microorganisms and pollutants. 5.4. Identify key microbiota taxa indicative of a healthy environment. We identified a set of microbiota only found in the natural, unpolluted environment. However, our limited geographic sampling prevents us from concluding these microbial taxa are exclusive to healthy environments.

13100121.label: Major findings and research outcome
13100121.value: In this study, we investigate various aspects of the amphibian skin and gut microbiota. We had five research objectives, and we provide the major findings and research outcomes individually for each objective. (1) We compare the microbiota between the skin and gut and find them to be significantly different, with the dominant taxa of the skin being rare in the gut. Our study is one of the few to characterise the skin and gut microbiota of the same individuals. The outcome of this work is to characterize the difference in the skin and gut microbiota. (2) We evaluate the suitability of faecal samples to study the gut microbiota and find that despite being statistically different, faeces are representative in terms of presence-absence (80–90% similarity). The outcome of this work is to identify the limitations of using faeces to study the gut microbiota. (3) We study the relationship between host and environment microbiota and found that the relationship varies between the skin and gut. Soil and water microbiota are significantly different and are a subset of the skin microbiota, while soil and water microbiota were different from gut microbiota. The outcome of this work is to begin identifying the source of bacteria in the skin and gut microbiota, and the differential role of the environment. (4) We study the impact of host phylogenetic relationship on the skin and gut microbiota and found that there is little to no influence. This finding is different from other studies. The outcome of this work is to highlight the plasticity in the microbiota of a host, with function likely being more important than specific taxa. (5) We compare the microbiota of a single species found at sites with varying levels of pollution and find that there is a significant difference between clean and polluted sites. However, we are unable to confirm that pollution is the driving factor, as other factors may also contribute, such as geography, diet, and anthropogenic influence (natural vs. urban environment). The outcome of this work is to identify several potential important factors that influence amphibian microbiota, with several related to human activity.

13100121.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13100121.value: This work has helped advance our understanding of the amphibian skin and gut microbiota. While answering some questions, new questions also arise. We envision two main directions for further study. First is to better understand the influence of geography. Our study, along with previous studies, highlight the importance of geography. Geography influences a variety of factors such as climate, food, and anthropogenic effects. We studied amphibian microbiota at small scales, and the next step is to look at broader scales. For amphibians, we suggest using a species with a wide distribution, such as Bufo bufo (widely distributed across Europe) or Bufo gargarizans (widely distributed across East Asia). Sampling across their range from a variety of habitat types (natural, urban) can help us understand the contributions of habitat at a micro and macro scale. Second is to expand to different taxa. Microbiota studies should be expanded to include less studied vertebrate taxa, such as reptiles, birds, and fish. Performing similar research as in this study, we can look for common trends within and across taxa. This will help us understand how bacteria interact with different host taxa, as well as begin to develop generalisable theories for microbiota research.

13100121.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13100121.value: Past studies highlight the important relationship between organisms and the bacteria in and on our body (“microbiota”). The microbiota on skin and gut serves as an invisible organ supporting the host’s survival. In this study, we investigate amphibian skin and gut microbiotas in two parts. First, fecal samples are often used to study the gut microbiota because they are relatively easy to collect, and do not involve sedating or euthanising the organism. We compare the microbiota of different parts of the gut (small intestine, large intestine) to fecal samples of the same individual to evaluate whether this method is suitable. The suitability of this method depends on the purpose—bacterial presence-absence is similar, while the proportions differ. Second, we evaluate the contribution of several factors (environment, pollution, diet, host relationship) to the skin and gut microbiota. For skin, the environment seems to be an important source for the microbiota, while diet seems to be important for the gut. Humans also have an important relationship with the bacteria in and on their body, and knowledge of amphibian microbiota helps us further understand the link and importance of bacteria to vertebrate and human health.

13500021.label: Project Objectives
13500021.value: Develop a factory-level thermal infrared radiation (TIR) data set for all publicly listed manufacturing companies in China from 2013 to 2020 and construct corporate-level TIR by aggregating the TIR across all factories of a company. Examine whether a change in TIR in one period is significantly related to a change in sales growth and profits in the subsequent period controlling for contemporaneous stock returns. Examine whether trading on TIR can generate abnormal returns by constructing a hedge portfolio that buys stocks with high TIR and sells stocks with low TIR and testing whether the portfolio’s alpha is significantly positive and has a meaningful magnitude. Examine whether the change in TIR is associated with future abnormal stock returns by conducting a Fama and MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional analysis. Examine whether TIR can predict earnings surprises by testing whether TIR is significantly related to abnormal earnings announcement returns and financial analyst forecast errors. Examine whether sophisticated investors, such as short-sellers and hedge funds, have access to and thus trade on satellite data and whether the link between TIR and sophisticated investors’ trading activities is stronger on cloud-free days. Examine whether TIR can identify financial fraud and help banks to assess firms’ credit risk.

13500021.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13500021.value: A central topic in financial economics is information acquisition. Market participants traditionally rely on firms’ public disclosures to evaluate firm fundamentals. However, the information in such reports is often subject to announcement delays and susceptible to manipulation. In this project, we will use alternative sources of information beyond standard financial market indicators and statistics to gauge firm performance. We will exploit satellite data to identify the thermal infrared radiation (TIR) emitted by firms’ factories during production, and examine whether TIR is informative about firms’ future performance and stock returns. An increasing number of studies measure firm performance by focusing on alternative data not derived from firm disclosures (Huang, 2018; Green et al., 2019; Katona et al., 2019). However, these studies’ measures are usually indirect in that they reflect the activities or opinions of a third party (e.g., customers and employees), which could be unrepresentative or biased. Our measure provides a method for directly gauging firms’ operating activities. Our study will make use of the physical fact that activities that consume energy emit heat and TIR. TIR is invisible but can be “seen” by satellites. Firms facing increased demand should increase their production and operating activities, thus emitting stronger TIR. Therefore, TIR strength is likely to reflect changes in firm fundamentals in real time. Moreover, unlike visible light, as used in recent studies based on satellite data (Katona et al., 2019; Mukherjee et al., 2020), TIR cannot be observed by human eyes. Local observers are thus less likely to incorporate the information into stock prices. As a result, TIR is likely to contain value-relevant information not anticipated by the market. We will test our view using publicly listed manufacturing companies in China, “the world’s factory”. We will examine (1) whether TIR is related to firms’ future sales and profitability; (2) whether TIR explains future stock returns; (3) whether TIR can predict earnings surprise and analyst forecast errors; and (4) whether sophisticated investors have access to and trade on TIR data. In additional analyses, we will examine whether TIR can identify financial fraud and help banks to assess firms’ credit risk. Our preliminary results show that TIR indeed contains valuable information not yet embedded in stock prices. The research will enrich our understanding of the process of price discovery and the financial implications of alternative data, and motivate the use of physical data to solve financial problems. 金融經濟學的一個核心問題是如何獲取信息。市場參與者傳統上依靠公司的公開報告來評估公司的基本面。然而，這些報告往往是滯後的，並且容易受到操縱。在這個項目中，我們將使用傳統金融市場指標和統計數據之外的其他信息來源來衡量公司業績。具體地，我們將利用衛星數據來識別企業工廠在生產過程中發出的熱紅外輻射(TIR)，並檢驗TIR是否能提供有關企業未來業績和股票回報的信息。 越來越多的研究通過關注非來自公司報告的另類數據來衡量公司的業績(Huang, 2018; Green et al.， 2019; Katona et al.，2019)。然而，這些研究所使用的指標通常都是間接的，因為這些指標反應的是第三方(如客戶和員工)的活動或意見，不具代表性和客觀性。我們將提供一種直接衡量企業經營活動的方法。 我們的研究將基於消耗能量的活動都將散發熱量和紅外輻射的物理事實。 TIR是不可見的，但可以通過衛星觀測到。當企業面臨需求增加的時候，其生產和經營活動將增加，從而釋放出更強的TIR。因此，TIR強度可以用來衡量公司基本面的變化。此外，與最近基於衛星數據的研究中使用的可見光不同(Katona et al.，2019; Mukherjee et al.， 2020)， TIR無法被人眼觀察到。因此，當地觀察人士不太可能覺察到這些信息並將其反應在股價中。因此，TIR很可能包含市場預期不到的有價值的信息。 我們將定位有“世界工廠”之稱的中國，通過分析其上市製造企業來檢測我們的觀點。我們將研究(1)TIR是否與公司未來的銷售和盈利能力有關;(2) TIR能否解釋未來股票收益;(3) TIR能否預測異常盈利和分析師預測誤差;(4)經驗豐富的投資者是否能夠獲得TIR數據並進行交易。在另外的分析中，我們將研究TIR是否能夠識別財務造假並幫助銀行評估公司的信用風險。 我們的初步結果表明，TIR確實包含有價值但還未反應在股價中的信息。該研究將豐富我們對價格發現過程和另類數據對金融市場影響的理解，並激勵使用物理方法來解決金融問題。

13500021.label: Realisation of objectives
13500021.value: We have fully achieved all seven objectives proposed in the grant application. The project proceeded according to the original timeline, resulting in a novel dataset and a publication in a top-tier finance journal (Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis). The realization of each specific objective is detailed below: Objective 1: Development of the TIR Dataset To achieve the first objective, we successfully constructed a comprehensive factory-level Thermal Infrared Radiation (TIR) dataset. We first collected the detailed addresses of operating subsidiaries and production facilities for all manufacturing firms listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen Stock Exchanges. Using the AMap (AutoNavi) API, we geocoded these addresses into precise latitude and longitude coordinates, identifying a total of 28,236 unique factory locations associated with Chinese listed firms. We then utilized the Google Earth Engine (GEE) platform to access historical satellite imagery from the Landsat program (Landsat 7 and 8). We processed the thermal infrared bands from these satellite images to compute the land surface temperature for each identified factory location from 2013 through the end of the sample period. Finally, we aggregated these factory-level readings to the firm-level, weighting by factory size, to construct a corporate-level TIR index. This massive data engineering effort provided the foundation for all subsequent analyses. Objective 2: Relation to Operating Performance To realize this objective, we conducted rigorous regression analyses linking our aggregated TIR measure to corporate fundamentals. We first validated the measure by exploiting exogenous shocks—specifically the COVID-19 lockdowns and the 2021 regional power rationing in China. We found that TIR levels dropped significantly during these events, confirming that our satellite measure accurately captures physical production activity. We then tested the predictive power of TIR for future fundamentals. Our results show that a change in TIR in the current quarter is positively and significantly related to sales growth, cost of goods sold (COGS), inventory growth, and gross profits in subsequent quarters. These regressions controlled for contemporaneous stock returns and a host of firm characteristics, confirming that TIR contains incremental information about firm operations that is not yet reflected in public financial reports. Objectives 3 & 4: Asset Pricing and Return Predictability We addressed these objectives by examining the stock market performance of firms based on their TIR signals. Hedge Portfolio (Objective 3): We constructed a long-short trading strategy that buys stocks in the highest quintile of TIR (high production activity) and sells stocks in the lowest quintile. We found that this strategy generates a statistically significant and economically meaningful annualized alpha, indicating that the market does not immediately incorporate the information contained in satellite thermal data. Fama-MacBeth Regressions (Objective 4): We conducted Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions of future stock returns on TIR. Even after controlling for standard risk factors (market, size, value, momentum) and firm characteristics, the coefficient on TIR remained positive and significant. This confirms that TIR serves as a robust predictor of future abnormal returns. Objective 5: Predicting Earnings Surprises To achieve this objective, we analyzed the relationship between TIR and market surprises. We found that TIR is a strong predictor of Standardized Unexpected Earnings (SUE) and cumulative abnormal returns around earnings announcements. Furthermore, we examined financial analyst behavior and found that TIR significantly predicts analyst forecast errors. This suggests that equity analysts, despite their expertise, generally overlook the real-time production signals available from thermal satellite data, leading to predictable biases in their earnings estimates which our TIR measure can correct. Objective 6: Sophisticated Investors and Information Asymmetry We investigated whether "smart money" has already arbitraged this information. We analyzed the trading behavior of short-sellers and the holdings of mutual funds in relation to TIR data. Contrary to the common belief that institutional investors have ubiquitous access to alternative data, our empirical tests revealed that the link between TIR and sophisticated investors’ trading activities is insignificant. This suggests that even hedge funds and short-sellers are not yet utilizing thermal infrared signals effectively. We also found that the return predictability of TIR is stronger for firms with higher information asymmetry (e.g., lower analyst coverage, higher opacity), confirming that TIR provides unique value in information-poor environments. Objective 7: Fraud Identification and Credit Risk We examined the utility of TIR in monitoring credit risk and detecting financial reporting discrepancies. By contrasting reported revenues with physical thermal output, we identified that firms exhibiting significant divergences—such as high reported sales accompanied by low thermal output—are more likely to be flagged for financial irregularities. These findings demonstrate that TIR acts as an independent verification mechanism for corporate disclosures, providing banks and creditors with a robust tool to assess the veracity of reported operations. While we successfully completed this analysis and obtained the expected results, we excluded this section from the final publication in the Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis. This adjustment was made in response to editorial and referee feedback to ensure the manuscript remained focused on nowcasting firm fundamentals and returns.

Examine whether trading on TIR can generate abnormal returns by constructing a hedge portfolio that buys stocks with high TIR and sells stocks with low TIR and testing whether the portfolio’s alpha is significantly positive and has a meaningful magnitude.
Examine whether the change in TIR is associated with future abnormal stock returns by conducting a Fama and MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional analysis.
Examine whether TIR can predict earnings surprises by testing whether TIR is significantly related to abnormal earnings announcement returns and financial analyst forecast errors.

Examine whether sophisticated investors, such as short-sellers and hedge funds, have access to and thus trade on satellite data and whether the link between TIR and sophisticated investors’ trading activities is stronger on cloud-free days.
Examine whether TIR can identify financial fraud and help banks to assess firms’ credit risk.

13500021.label: Major findings and research outcome
13500021.value: This project successfully developed a direct, real-time measure of corporate operating activities using satellite thermal infrared radiation (TIR) data. By leveraging the physical principle that industrial production emits heat, we constructed a factory-level TIR dataset tracking 28,236 factories associated with Chinese listed manufacturing firms. Key Findings: 1. Validity of TIR: We validated that TIR is a reliable proxy for physical production. We documented significant declines in TIR following exogenous operational shocks, such as the COVID-19 lockdowns and regional power rationing events. 2. Forecasting Fundamentals: Aggregated at the firm level, TIR strongly predicts future corporate fundamentals. A one-standard-deviation increase in TIR is associated with higher subsequent sales growth, cost of goods sold, employment, and gross profits. Crucially, TIR outperforms traditional analyst forecasts, significantly predicting analyst forecast errors and earnings surprises. 3. Asset Pricing Implications: We found that TIR contains value-relevant information not yet incorporated into stock prices. A long-short trading strategy based on TIR yields a significant annualized alpha. The predictive power of TIR for stock returns is more pronounced among firms with higher information asymmetry (opaque firms) and those with limited investor attention. 4. Market Efficiency and Sophisticated Investors: Contrary to the assumption that institutional investors always possess superior alternative data, our results suggest that even sophisticated investors (e.g., mutual funds and short-sellers) largely ignore TIR information. This indicates that satellite-based heat signals represent a distinct, under-exploited source of information in financial markets. The research has resulted in a publication in the Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, a top-tier finance journal.

13500021.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13500021.value: The success of this project opens several avenues for further development: 1. Data Expansion: We plan to expand the TIR dataset beyond China to cover global manufacturing firms, creating a worldwide index of industrial activity. 2. ESG Applications: We aim to explore the environmental implications of TIR data. High thermal radiation often correlates with carbon emissions and energy consumption. This data can be repurposed to monitor corporate environmental compliance and ESG performance independently of firm disclosures. 3. Industry Collaboration: We have established a dialogue with the Satellite Big Data Research Center of the Shenzhen Institute of Data Economy (SIDE). We intend to deepen this collaboration to commercialize the data for financial institutions, aiding banks in credit risk assessment and asset managers in investment decision-making.

13500021.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13500021.value: In the financial world, reliable information about a company's performance usually comes from quarterly or annual reports, which are often delayed. This project utilized space technology to solve this "time lag" problem. We used satellite imagery to measure the heat—specifically Thermal Infrared Radiation (TIR)—emitted by over 28,000 factories belonging to Chinese listed companies. The logic is simple: when a factory is working hard, it generates heat. By measuring this heat from space, we can monitor a company's production activity in real-time. Our research proved that this "heat data" accurately predicts a company's future sales, profits, and even its stock price performance long before official reports are released. Interestingly, we found that most professional investors are not yet using this data, meaning it offers a unique advantage. This project demonstrates how satellite technology can revolutionize finance by providing transparent, real-time insights into the real economy, helping banks assess risks and investors make better decisions.

13500221.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13500221.value: The growing focus on global warming and climate change has triggered a trend toward mandatory disclosure for firms’ climate risk. This study investigates whether and how insurers respond to the mandatory disclosure requirements of the Insurer Climate Risk Disclosure Survey (CRDS), which was staggered adopted in eight U.S. states since 2009. We posit that CRDS incentivized insurers’ engagement in climate risk management. The CRDS mandate may have driven insurers to more actively engage key constituencies on the topic of climate change, identify climate change-related risks, and adopt climate change policy with respect to risk management. Under increased pressure from regulators and stakeholders due to increased transparency, insurers are expected to engage in more climate risk mitigation procedures in underwriting and other environmentally friendly investment activities. Insurers may alter their investment policies and take on portfolios that reduce firms’ exposure to climate risk. Furthermore, insurers are more likely to adopt and enhance the climate-risk management underwriting procedure, which reduces the underwriting risk. While we have a clear expectation of CRDS on insurers’ risk, the impact of CRDS on insurers’ performance is ambiguous. Reallocating investment portfolios away from climate unfriendly assets come at a cost but also with potential benefit and new investment opportunities in the long term. Adjusting underwriting strategy in response to the CRDS can potentially lead to better underwriting performance but also with a cost in doing so, e.g., forcing insurers to disclose proprietary or competitively sensitive information. Thus, the impact of CRDS on insurers’ financial performance is an empirical question. We next analyze the possible channels through which the implementation of mandatory CRDS disclosure affects insurers. We postulate that transparency in CRDS disclosure enhances the impact of the CRDS mandate on insurers’ risk and financial performance. We also expect the impact of mandatory climate risk disclosure on insurers’ risks and profitability to be mitigated by firms’ publicly traded status because public-traded stocks have been exposed to certain CSR related disclosure requirements, e.g., Section 406 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act in 2002. We perform a difference-in-difference analysis by incorporating an interaction term of mandated-disclosure indicator and the publicly-traded stock indicator. We then test whether family control status and competitive market pressure affect the relationship between CRDS and firm risk and financial performance. We do not have a prior as there are competing hypotheses on these two moderators. Finally, we conjecture that CRDS might change the climate risk behavior of insurers’ investee companies.

13500221.label: Realisation of objectives
13500221.value: Generally, we follow the original plan and realize all project objectives. In the first paper, we examine the effect of mandatory climate risk disclosure on insurers’ investment portfolio by exploiting the U.S. insurance industry’s adoption of the Climate Risk Disclosure Survey (CRDS). Using a staggered difference-in-differences research design, we find a significant post-adoption improvement in the environmental friendliness of the treatment insurers’ corporate investment portfolio. The effect is more pronounced when insurers face greater pressure to be more climate friendly and when they have more motivation to hedge climate risk in their underwriting business. The treatment insurers reduce their holdings in firms with negative climate-risk-related news and in those involved in fossil fuels extraction, and they shift from high- to low-carbon-emissions firms. We also find that the treatment insurers’ investment performance deteriorates; this effect is concentrated among those insurers that increase their investment portfolio’s environmental performance. Finally, we document a positive relation between insurers’ proactiveness in addressing climate risk and their environmentally responsible investing. This paper addresses project objectives 1-4, primarily from the perspective of insurers' investments. In the second paper, we investigate how insurers’ mandatory climate risk disclosure affects their corporate bond investees’ carbon emissions. Exploiting the adoption of the CRDS, we find that adoption reduces investees’ carbon emissions if CRDS-affected insurers are significant owners of the investees’ bonds. The reduction is more pronounced when affected insurers and investees experience stronger public pressure about climate issues, when affected insurers are more likely to closely monitor their investees, and when investees depend more on bond financing. The reduction seems to be mostly driven by affected insurers that tend to engage with their investees about climate change issues. Overall, this study presents new causal evidence showing how investors’ mandatory climate risk disclosure can have a significant transmission effect on their investees’ environmental friendliness. This paper addresses project objective 5. In the third paper, we also examine the effect of CRDS on insurers’ underwriting business. Using a staggered difference-in-differences research design, we find that compared to insurers not affected by the CRDS mandate, those affected by it experience an increase in their underwriting business after CRDS adoption. This outcome suggests that CRDS mandate results in affected insurers gaining a competitive advantage in their underwriting business. This positive effect is more pronounced when insurers’ managers face more pressure to consider climate risk in insurers’ business strategies or when insurers experience more underwriting business competition. Overall, our study offers the novel insight that by encouraging firms to include climate risk in their business strategies and to communicate such strategies publicly, mandated climate risk disclosure can enhance firms’ competitive advantage. This paper addresses project objectives 1-4, primarily from the perspective of insurers' underwriting business.

13500221.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13500221.value: This research project investigates the effects of mandatory climate risk disclosures on the U.S. insurance industry, focusing on investment decisions, bond investments, and core insurance operations. The first finding reveals that insurers required to disclose climate risks tend to invest less in environmentally harmful companies, such as fossil fuel firms, and more in eco-friendly businesses. This shift often results in lower financial returns, indicating that prioritizing environmental responsibility can be costly. The second part examines the impact on companies that insurers invest in through corporate bonds. It finds that these companies generally reduce their carbon emissions, particularly under high public pressure on climate issues, suggesting that mandatory disclosures encourage greener practices. The third part assesses the influence on insurers' core business, showing that insurers who disclose climate risk strategies perform better in markets with environmentally conscious customers and in states with stringent environmental regulations. This indicates that proactive climate risk management not only aids regulatory compliance but also boosts market competitiveness. In summary, the research underscores the importance of mandatory climate disclosures in promoting sustainable practices and providing business advantages for insurers.

13500321.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13500321.value: People’s faces, such as those appearing in online profile pictures, play a critical role in marketing. Aside from a promoter’s or seller’s biological sex, their masculine or feminine look forms a key part of gender identity and individual traits, which greatly affect consumer perceptions and behaviors. To minimize gender stereotypes and promote gender equality, gender research in marketing examines sex differences, gender roles, and their portrayals in promotion and advertising. Marketers have increasingly used atypical roles for both genders, sometimes even reversed gender roles (e.g., male nurses and female firefighters, ballet dads and soccer moms), often leading to favorable responses from consumers. Despite these efforts, stereotypical face gender (masculine male and feminine female) still permeates marketing and social media, while atypical face gender (feminine males and masculine females) has received little attention. This research will focus on the effect of atypical face gender of sellers on consumer perceptions and purchase decisions on online platforms. Despite the traditional male/female gender schema, perceptions of face gender are complex and dynamic. Drawing on gender research and the impression management literature, we adopt social comparison theory and hypothesize that the contrast effects of atypical face gender (feminine male and masculine female) on trait perceptions (masculine competence, feminine warmth) are stronger than the assimilation effects of typical face gender (masculine male and feminine female). Furthermore, such effects on purchase intention are mediated by perceived credibility, which is stronger for sex-typed products (e.g., electronics vs. cosmetics) than gender-neutral products (e.g., furniture) and stronger for cross-sex than same-sex situations. We plan to analyze a large dataset from an e-commerce platform to test the positive contrast effect of atypical face gender on sales and will use two controlled experiments to explore the underlying mechanism of the mediators (perceptions of competence, warmth, and credibility) and moderators (product gender and cross-sex effect). While gender equality and fluidity are major concerns in modern society and business, much emphasis has been placed on minimizing gender stereotypes, especially those related to gender roles. The proposed research will go beyond differences between sexes and in gender roles and fill a significant gap in marketing and gender research by delving into face gender, especially atypical face gender, and its effects on consumer perceptions and decisions. This study will contribute to the marketing literature and gender research, highlight the informational value of face gender on online platforms, and have nontrivial implications for e-commerce and marketing strategies. 人們的面孔，例如線上個人資料中的面孔，在行銷領域起著重要作用。除了賣家的生理性別，他們的男性或女性外貌作為性別認同和個人特徵的關鍵部分，極大地影響消費者的認知和行為。為了減少性別定型觀念並促進性別平等，行銷中的性別研究檢視了性別差異，性別角色，以及他們在促銷和廣告中的形象。行銷人員越來越多地使用兩性的非典型角色，有時甚至顛倒了性別角色（例如男護士和女消防員、芭蕾舞爸爸和足球媽媽），通常會得到消費者的積極回應。儘管這些努力，性別刻板印象（男性男相和女性女相）仍然流行於行銷和社交媒體中，而非典型面部性別（女性男相和男性女相）很少受到關注。這項研究將側重於賣家的非典型面孔性別對線上消費者的態度和購買決策的影響。 儘管有傳統的男性/女性性別面孔，人們對面部性別的看法是複雜而動態的。我們借鑒性別研究和印象管理文獻，採用社會比較理論，假設非典型面孔性別（女性男相和男性女相）的對比效應對特質認知的影響（男性能力，女性溫暖）強于同化效應（典型面部性別：男性男相和女性女相）。此外，這種效應由感知可信度作為仲介變數間接影響購買意願。相對于性別中立的產品（例如傢俱），這種效應對於性別類型產品（例如電子產品與化妝品）更強；相對於同性交流，這種效應更適合跨性別交流。我們計畫通過分析一個來自電商平臺的大型資料來測試非典型面孔性別的對比效應，並將使用兩個實驗來探索潛在的仲介機制（對能力、熱情和可信度的認知）和調解作用（產品性別和跨性別效應）。性別平等和流動性是現代社會和商業關注的問題，並重視減少性別定型觀念，尤其是那些與性別角色有關的問題。本研究將超越性別差異和性別角色，填補行銷和性別研究的空白，深入研究面孔性別，尤其是非典型面孔性別對消費者認知和決策的影響。這項研究將有助於行銷和性別研究，突出面部性別在線上平臺上的資訊價值，對電子商務和行銷策略產生重要影響。

13500321.label: Realisation of objectives
13500321.value: We outline the research objectives in line below: 1. move beyond sex differences and gender roles and explore the positive contrast effects of atypical face genders in marketing and online platforms Previous studies of gender effects in marketing focused on sex differences and gender roles. Drawing from multimodal communication and face-voice information processing research, we propose a framework to categorize and compare the effects of facial and vocal gender cues for men and women and examine consumer responses to these gender cues of influencers in the online e-commerce context. Moreover, aside from face gender cues, we also consider the effect of voice gender cues and the combination of face and voice gender cues in a multimodal context. 2. To articulate the underlying mechanisms via trait inferences and the moderating effects of product gender and cross-sex interaction Building on the theoretical discussions of multimodal signaling in neurobiology and evolutionary psychology research, we propose a coherent conceptual framework to elucidate the dynamics of how individuals process auditory (voice) and visual (face) information when these cues are presented simultaneously. Our study therefore has three main objectives: to develop a conceptual framework categorizing the effects of bimodal gender cues (i.e., masculine men, feminine men, feminine women, and masculine women for both face and voice) on consumer responses; to investigate the roles of voice and face gender in trait perceptions. While cross-gender effect is considered, product gender was not tested so as to reduce the complexity of research design. 3. To dispel the myth of norm violations of atypical face gender and shed light on its positive contrast effects and the context of their occurrence We examine the consistency of the effects of congruent or incongruent bimodal gender cues across genders. For female stimuli, congruent gender cues (e.g., feminine face and voice) serve as backup signals and exert a significant but diminishing effect, whereas incongruent gender cues convey distinct messages to consumers, which aligns more closely with our proposed framework. Conversely, for male stimuli, facial cues do not elicit a response independently when facial and vocal gender cues are incongruent (i.e., masculine face and feminine voice, or vice versa). Instead, they serve to amplify vocal cues, resulting in significant and modulating interaction between the two. 4. To inform researchers and practitioners of the informational value of face gender and its complex effects in marketing and social selling Our study suggests that voices enhance the presenter ’s appeal to a greater extent than faces. Our findings have implications for social media and influencer marketing strategies, suggesting that creators of marketing videos can benefit from both facial appearance and voice-overs and include them in designs that resonate more effectively with their target audience. Although marketers tend to reinforce cultural norms regarding the “correct” ways for men and women to present themselves and perform their gender roles, we identify the positive effects of using an atypical voice gender for male presenters. We found that a feminine voice had a significant positive effect on trait perceptions and consumer actions. Both male and female marketers are thus encouraged to adopt warm voices in advertising and promotions to improve their marketing effectiveness. 5. To push the boundaries of gender research in marketing and invigorate the discourse on the role of face gender for management and public policy Governments and industry organizations worldwide have recognized the adverse effects of gender stereotypes in marketing and have taken steps to minimize discrimination and promote diversity. With the increasing acceptance of fluid gender representations, individuals often modify their facial and vocal cues when online and on social media platforms when engaging in entertainment and social interactions. Our research reveals the impact of face and voice gender in marketing and other areas such as employment, career development, and elections. Our findings can inform policies that encourage diverse representations of people in marketing, business, and society.

13500321.label: Major findings and research outcome
13500321.value: Our results showed that both facial and vocal cues contribute to positive impressions and social trait perceptions for both men and women, but we found vocal gender cues to be more important in this process. Our research also reveals show facial and vocal gender cues influence impression evaluations based on social traits such as attractiveness, warmth, and competence. When gender cues are congruent (e.g., masculine men or feminine women), both men and women are perceived as having an advantage. Masculine men are perceived as more competent, and feminine women as warmer. In contrast, when gender cues are incongruent, both men and women can enhance their voice gender cues to increase perceptions of the relevant social traits. Understanding these cues can help individuals appear more competent, warmer, or attractive, depending on the social trait they want to convey. We also found that the relationship between faces and voices can vary depending on cue congruence and the physical sex or gender of the stimuli. When presented with female stimuli, congruent gender cues were found to have a diminishing effect on the integrated response, while incongruent gender cues had an independent and additive effect on the response. In contrast, for male stimuli, congruent cues provided independent messages, while incongruent cues were found to evoke a response based on voice only when the face served to enhance the vocal effect. However, when the gender cues were incongruent (e.g., a male face and a female voice), they perceived the voice and face as more integrated. Conversely, when presented with male stimuli, they were more likely to perceive the voice and face as integrated sources of information when the gender cues were congruent (e.g., a male face and a male voice). However, when the gender cues were incongruent (e.g., a female face and a male voice), the participants perceived the voice and face as more separate sources of information, with the voice having a stronger influence. The research findings are published in a forthcoming article: Cui, Geng, Yuho Chung, Ling Peng, and Shuyu Liang (2025), “Look or sound like a winner? The effects of masculine and feminine gender cues in marketing videos,” Journal of Business Research, 186(1), 115019. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbusres.2024.115019.

13500321.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13500321.value: he effects of gender qualities on overall trait impression may change when other evaluation information is available. For example, voice-based impressions can be confounded by cues such as semantics and intonation. Although voice pitch has been identified as a perceptually salient acoustic cue, the words spoken provide information in addition to basic voice information, such as accents, which can bias trait evaluations. In addition, through nonverbal behavior such as gestures and postures, perceivers can make judgments about warmth and competence. Therefore, it is unclear how viewers would respond to scenarios that, for example, include competence-related cues (e.g., speaking eloquently) presented by a feminine voice or warmth-related cues (e.g., friendly body gestures) presented by a masculine face. A more systematic study could obtain further evidence on the role of various gender cues from multimodalities and their combined effects on social trait perceptions and consumer actions. Further clarification of the underlying mechanism for the dominance of voice over face is required.

13500321.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13500321.value: While both facial and vocal cues contribute to positive impressions and social trait perceptions for both men and women, but we found vocal gender cues to be more important in this process. Our research also reveals show facial and vocal gender cues influence impression evaluations based on social traits such as attractiveness, warmth, and competence. When gender cues are consistent (e.g., masculine men or feminine women), both men and women are perceived as having an advantage. Masculine men are perceived as more competent, and feminine women as warmer. In contrast, when gender cues are incongruent, both men and women can enhance their voice gender cues to increase perceptions of the relevant social traits. Understanding these cues can help individuals appear more competent, warmer, or attractive, depending on the social trait they want to convey.

13501321.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13501321.value: Firms are increasingly leveraging online social media influencers to promote their products. Relevant new e-commerce models have emerged and have seen rapid development in recent years. A popular form is campaign-based influencer marketing. An online promotion campaign often features an online influencer who produces content to engage followers and boost their interest in a firm's product. By sharing their opinions and experience about the product, online influencers can effectively entice their followers to make a purchase. The enthusiastic followers may refer the product to their friends and family, spreading information about the product to more people. The performance of influencer campaigns is commonly measured by conversions/sales and engagement. Despite the growing adoption of online influencers for new product launches, academic research has been largely focused on e-commerce models without social influence or those with social influence solely from customers. To fill this research gap, we will consider a firm introducing a new product through an online influencer. In the product introductory period, the influencer can exert an effort on social media platforms to promote the product to her followers and boost their interest and demand. In the subsequent selling period, customers who do not follow the online influencer will arrive in the market, and they may be influenced by the followers to purchase the product. We will develop a two-period model to analytically address five research questions: (i) Under what conditions would it be effective to leverage online influencers for product introduction? (ii) How should an incentive scheme be designed for the influencer? (iii) What effort levels should the influencer take? (iv) What are the firm's optimal pricing and production decisions in the introductory and selling periods? (v) What factors affect the above decisions and the performance of the strategy? Our expected contribution is three-fold. First, we propose a demand model by making the probability of purchase dependent on the price, the influencer's effort level, and the followers' word-of-mouth. Second, we develop an analytic framework for studying the effect of the influencer on product promotion. Third, we examine the effectiveness of incentive schemes for the influencer. The findings from our research will be helpful to both academics and practitioners to better understand the critical issues in new product introduction through online influencers. The proposed research will contribute to the literature on e-commerce and social commerce and provide theoretical support and insight to practitioners in implementing the new model. 企业越来越频繁地通过在线社交媒体上的影响者来推广其产品。相关的新型电子商务模式也应运而生，并且在近些年来迅速发展，而其中一种常见的形式是基于活动的影响者营销。在线推广活动通常围绕在线影响者开展，该影响者可以通过发布内容来吸引粉丝，并提高粉丝对企业产品的兴趣。此外，通过分享他们对产品的看法和体验，在线影响者也可以有效地吸引他们的粉丝进行购买。热情的粉丝们还可能会将该产品介绍给他们的朋友和家人，从而向更多的人传播有关该产品的信息。影响者营销活动的表现一般通过转化量/销量和参与度来衡量。 尽管通过在线影响者发布新产品越来越受青睐，但相关的学术研究基本停留在不考虑社会影响的电子商务模式，或只考虑消费者单方面社会影响的电子商务模式。为填补这一空白，我们将考虑一间企业通过在线影响者推广其新产品。在产品推广期内，影响者可以通过努力在社交平台上向其粉丝推广产品，以提高粉丝对该产品的兴趣和需求。在随后的销售期内，没有在社交媒体上关注影响者的消费者进入市场，他们的购买行为可能会受到影响者粉丝群体的影响。 我们将构造一个两期模型以分析并解决下列五个研究问题：（一） 在什么条件下，利用在线影响者进行产品推广是有效的？（二） 如何为影响者设计一个激励机制？（三） 影响者应采取什么努力水平？（四） 公司在推广期和销售期内的最优定价和生产决策是什么？（五） 哪些因素将影响上述决策以及该营销活动的表现？ 此项研究的贡献将主要体现在三个方面。首先，我们提出一个需求模型，在该模型中消费者进行购买的概率取决于价格，影响者的努力水平以及粉丝的口碑效应。其次，我们制定了一个分析框架用于研究影响者对产品推广的影响。第三，我们检验激励机制对影响者的有效性。我们的研究结果将有助于学者和业内人士更好地了解通过在线影响者进行新产品推广中的关键问题。拟开展的研究将有助于丰富电子商务以及社交零售方面的文献，并为从业人员实施新的商业模式提供理论支持与参考。

13501321.label: Realisation of objectives
13501321.value: We have carried out this research project according to our objectives and have fully addressed all the objectives. The specific work and results for each of the five objectives are summarized as follows. 1. We collected information on business practices in influencer marketing and reviewed the relevant literature on new product introduction and influencer marketing. We found that firms usually utilize influencers to enhance brand awareness and increase product sales. When firms utilize influencers to conduct promotional campaigns for new products, they can use commission incentives to influence the influencers’ promotional efforts in generating sales. In addition, the firms can simultaneously employ pricing strategies to boost sales. They must make a tradeoff between gaining an immediate large profit from the campaign and generating large sales to raise other potential customers’ awareness of the product. The relevant characteristics of influencers to consider include the size of an influencer’s follower base, the influencer’s reservation payoff, her ability to affect sales conversions of followers, and the followers’ word-of-mouth (WOM). 2. We developed a two-period mathematical model for the new product diffusion process. In the first period (promotion period), the firm decides on the selling price and the commission contract for the promotional campaign. Given the commission contract, the influencer exerts an effort to promote the product to her followers, who can spread the product information to non-followers via WOM. In the second period (normal selling period), the firm sets the selling price and sells the product to the non-followers directly. This dynamic demand model characterizes the effects of the firm’s pricing decisions, the influencer, and the followers’ WOM on demand. We separate the followers into two groups, buyers and non-buyers, according to whether a follower makes a purchase during the campaign, and we distinguish between the WOM effects of the two groups. 3. Using the model developed for the second project objective, we analytically derived the firm’s optimal pricing decisions for both periods and the optimal commission contract (base pay plus sales-based commission) for the influencer. We also obtained the influencer’s optimal effort level for the campaign given the commission contract. 4. We conducted analytical and numerical analyses to examine the effects of (i) demand parameters (e.g., price sensitivity), (ii) WOM parameters of buyers and non-buyers, and (iii) the influencer’s follower size on the optimal decisions of the firm and the influencer as well as the firm’s profit margin and sales in the promotional campaign. 5. We obtained important findings and managerial insights regarding the firm’s pricing and commission strategies for the influencer-driven new product introduction as well as the influencer’s optimal effort level, particularly how the optimal decisions are affected by the influencer-related factors and the market size. In addition to the above modeling and analysis, we further considered two model extensions to test the robustness of our main findings. In the first extended model, we incorporated the network effect in the new product diffusion process. In the second one, we considered the possibility that the followers who did not purchase the product in the promotional campaign will purchase it in the selling period. The results of both models verify that all the major findings and insights in the main model continue to hold.

13501321.label: Major findings and research outcome
13501321.value: Our research generates major findings and managerial implications as follows. 1. We identify three important influencer-related factors that affect the firm’s decisions regarding the promotional campaign for a new product. The first factor is the influencer's reservation payoff, which reflects her power in the market. We find that the firm generally offers a base pay plus sales-based commission to influencers with high reservation payoffs, while providing a pure sales-based commission contract to those with low reservation payoffs. 2. The second factor is the marginal WOM benefit of sales that the influencer generates in the promotional campaign, which reflects the influencer’s intertemporal effect on customer awareness of the firm’s product after the campaign. It increases as the difference between the WOM effect of the influencer’s followers who do or do not make purchases (i.e., the followers’ WOM effect difference) increases. We find that, to benefit from an increase in the marginal WOM benefit of promotional sales, the firm tends to raise the commission rate to motivate the influencer’s promotion effort, but may not need to reduce product price. The firm’s decisions for product promotion usually depend on the difference between the WOM effect of followers who do or do not make purchases rather than the WOM effect of each group. 3. The third factor is an influencer’s follower size. We find that a firm should not always offer a higher commission rate to larger influencers, and influencers with a medium-sized follower base receive the highest commission rate and exert the largest promotion effort. Meanwhile, the followers of influencers with a medium-sized follower base may be charged the highest price for the product. Furthermore, we show that a firm may not be better off using an influencer with a larger follower base. A research paper developed from this project has been accepted for publication in Naval Research Logistics, a well-recognized journal in the field of operations research and management science.

13501321.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13501321.value: We have noticed from the practice that, under commission contracts, influencers may have an incentive to make false claims about promoted products to boost sales. To mitigate such dishonest selling, regulators may impose penalties on firms and/or influencers for false claims identified. Correspondingly, in our future research on firms’ influencer marketing strategies, we can investigate the impact of relevant regulations on firms’ and influencers’ decisions as well as market outcomes such as consumer surplus and social welfare. We expect that this research can shed light on the design of effective regulations for influencer marketing.

13501321.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13501321.value: Firms have increasingly used social media influencers to promote and sell their products. As a prevalent practice, firms often leverage influencers to conduct promotional campaigns for their new products, where influencers can sell the products to their followers and disseminate the product information to non-followers via their followers’ word-of-mouth (WOM). Sales-based commissions are commonly offered to incentivize influencers’ promotional efforts, while firms may also employ product prices to influence sales. We investigate firms’ pricing and commission strategies for such practices. Since influencers vary with their market power, the effectiveness of followers’ WOM, and the follower size, we explore how such influencer-related factors affect the firm’s pricing and commission strategies for product introduction and market outcomes. We further ask when firms should leverage influencers to introduce new products. Our research identifies influencer-related factors that are critical for informing firms’ decisions and assists academics and practitioners to better understand the fundamental aspects of influencer-driven product introductions. Our findings can provide theoretical support and insights for practitioners to conduct effective influencer marketing campaigns.

13501421.value: Prof Liu, Qing Prof Yeaple, Stephen

13501421.label: Project Objectives
13501421.value: "Examine the learning effects of processing trade on ordinary trade in China." This is the general objective of the project. International trade makes great contributions to China’s economic growth. China has moved from relying most on processing trade in the early years of opening up its economy, to ordinary trade which is associated with higher domestic value-added. This significant structure change has attracted scholars’ attention and interest because understanding this change helps to explain the success story of China’s trade. Existing studies have identified a few reasons for this change, such as an improved domestic market, reduced tariff rates, better judicial quality, and fairer financial support. Our project aims to demonstrate a new channel: firms learn from their engagement in processing trade and then become capable to do ordinary trade. "Build a theoretical model and analyze the mechanisms of how processing trade firms learn and then become ordinary trade firms." This objective is to make a theoretical contribution to the processing trade literature. While there have exist some empirical studies on processing trade, especially based on Chinese data, a theoretical model and analysis almost does not exist, with the exception of Brandt and Morrow (2017). While the model of Brandt and Morrow is suitable for analyzing the effects of trade policy on the structural change of export modes, it is not suitable for analyzing the learning effect of processing trade on ordinary trade, which is dynamic by nature. Hence, we extend Brandt and Morrow’s model to a dynamic setting and allow various mechanisms of learning, including technology, market, and product learning. We may break the general model into a few sub-models to obtain analytical solutions. We may also analyze the general model with quantitative methods (simulation and counterfactual analysis). Our model will make useful predictions for our empirical investigations. Our model will also help us to understand and explain our empirical results. "Use Chinese data to conduct a careful empirical analysis to test the hypotheses derived from our theoretical model." Our theoretical model will provide clear hypotheses for empirical tests. Our empirical investigation is based on Chinese data and, thus, the findings and lessons are extremely important because China is the largest (in terms of both GDP and trade) developing country. Moreover, the Chinese experiences and data are very rich, allowing us to examine many dimensions (margins) of the effects of processing trade on ordinary trade. The Chinese policy changes over time and variations across locations will also enable us to overcome many empirical challenges such as causality issues. "Write a policy report based on the findings from this project and those from the existing studies." China began its economic reform and adopted an open-door policy since 1979. Both processing trade (especially in the early period) and ordinary trade (more in the later period) have made great contributions to China’s economic growth and development. Will these Chinese experiences apply to other developing countries? Our project has clear and strong policy implications. "Train research students." This project will employ two to three students (RPg or UG) students as research assistants. Under our detailed guidance, they will learn and help to do literature reading/review, analyze the theoretical models (analytically and quantitatively), collect and manage data, run regressions, and read government documents for the policy report. Throughout this project, the students will learn how to conduct an important academic research study and prepare for journal publications. This research experience will definitely improve their job prospects or further studies.

13501421.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13501421.value: China’s international trade growth in the past 40 years has been unprecedented in the world’s economic history: its share of global exports has risen from less than 1% in 1979 to 13.45% (the largest exporter) in 2018. What are the explanations for this miracle? What lessons can be drawn for other developing countries? Providing a full answer to these two questions is rather challenging, despite many existing studies having attempted to answer these questions from various angles. This project aims to investigate the role of processing trade in China’s foreign trade achievements. Processing trade made up more than half of China’s trade in the early years, but ordinary trade has been the main mode of trade in recent years. Two specific questions are important to discuss. First, does China’s ordinary trade learn from processing trade? Second, if the answer to the first question is ‘yes’, then how and by how much? Arguably, processing trade plays more important roles in China than in most other countries, but these two questions have not been systematically analyzed and satisfactorily answered. It is clear that this project will make a significant contribution to the understanding of China’s trade growth from an important and interesting angle. We will conduct thorough analyses, both theoretically and empirically, to investigate the above issue. In the theoretical analysis, we will outline and understand the important mechanisms through which Chinese firms may first learn from processing trade and then start and improve their ordinary trade. The possible channels to be analyzed include technology learning, product learning, market learning, and others. To conduct an empirical analysis, we must collect data from many sources, such as detailed firm- level data of Chinese firms, to compile our dataset. We will then test the predictions of the theoretical model, examine the channels identified in the theoretical analysis, and obtain additional empirical results. While processing trade plays an exceptional role in China’s trade, lessons from China could be made for other countries, especially for developing countries. Based on our theoretical and empirical findings and those in the literature, we will review and evaluate the effects of the Chinese government’s policies towards processing and ordinary trade. 中國過去40年的國際貿易增長在世界經濟史上是空前的：其在全球出口中的份額從1979年的不到1%上升到2018年的13.45%（成為世界第一大出口國）。如何解釋這個奇蹟呢？ 中國的經驗 可以為其他發展中國家所借鑒嗎？ 儘管許多研究試圖從各個角度回答這些問題，但是要為這兩個問題提供完整的答案還是相當具有挑戰性的。 本項目旨在探討加工貿易在中國外貿成就中的作用。 在早期，加工貿易占中國貿易的一半以上。但後來，一般普通貿易已成為主要的貿易方式。有兩個具體問題值得討論。 第一，中國的一般貿易是否向加工貿易學習了？ 其次，如果第一個問題的答案是肯定的，那麼是如何學習的以及學習到多少？ 可以說，加工貿易在中國的作用比其在其他大多數國家更為重要，但這兩個問題還沒有得到系統的分析和令人滿意的回答。 所以，本項目將從一個重要而有意義的角度對如何理解中國貿易的增長做出重大貢獻。 我們將在理論上和實證上對上述問題進行透徹的分析。 在理論分析中，我們將描述和理解一個重要機制。通過這一機制，中國企業首先向加工貿易學習，然後開始並改進自己的一般貿易。 我們分析的可能途徑包括技術學習、產品學習、和市場學習等。 為了進行實證分析，我們必須從許多來源收集數據以編制我們的數據集，例如中國企業的詳細數據。 然後，我們將測試理論模型的預測，檢查理論分析中確定的機制，並獲得更多的實證結果。 雖然加工貿易在中國貿易中發揮著特殊而重要的作用，但中國的經驗也可以為其他國家，特別是發展中國家提供借鑒。 根據我們的理論和實證研究結果以及文獻中的研究結果，我們將回顧和評估中國政府的貿易政策對加工和一般貿易的影響。
