13600021.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13600021.value: In an era of anti-immigration backlash in Britain (and elsewhere), and particularly in the aftermath of the 2016 referendum supporting Britain’s separation from the European Union, there has been an explosion of interest in the historical sources of these ideas and events. Historical studies of the British far right have dramatically increased in the past decade, and many of them have made excellent use of party/ movement newspapers and magazines as sources for leaders’ opinions, but have rarely considered the nature of the papers themselves as a category of journalism. At the same time, most histories of the British press concentrate on mainstream national and local papers, while those that study alternative journalism tend to focus either on political causes regarded as progressive, or on periodicals that give voice to a subaltern community, for example ethnic or sexual minorities, or on periodicals targeting hobby enthusiasts. Historians of alternative journalism have typically not been interested in the far right. This project will examine the far right press (including online versions) in Britain between 1932 and 2014, treating it not only as a primary source for the study of far right parties and movements, but as the research focus. It will treat far right periodical publications as an example of alternative journalism, analysing both the ideational content and the forms of expression: did they emphasize repetition of news stories favourable to their point of view, or opinion pieces, or some other formats altogether? It will examine the ways that these periodicals constructed their communities of readers, how they related to specific parties and leaders, and how they funded themselves. This study will evaluate the ways that these papers conceptualized the mainstream public sphere: was it susceptible to rational persuasion, or was it beyond redemption? This research will shed important light on how core ideas of the far right, including conspiratorial ones, were sustained over nearly a century. The outcome will be a book of approximately 100,000 words that will be of significant interest to both political and media historians.

13600321.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13600321.value: The human body does not have a “pain center”, but as a survival mechanism, our nervous system enables us to sense and process pain information and respond to it. It is important to develop strategies to manage and reduce pain. Ample research in the realm of pain and analgesia (pain reduction) have documented that using a placebo (an inert substance/treatment procedure) can induce psychological/physical change such as pain-reduction (Colagiuri et al., 2015; Petrie & Rief, 2019; Wager & Atlas, 2015). An emerging line of research shows that, in some circumstances, individuals can achieve placebo analgesia by merely possessing a placebo analgesic without virtually using it (Yeung, Geers, & Kim, 2019; Yeung, Geers, & Colloca, 2020). It is critical to understand the underlying psychological processes of this mere-possession phenomenon to encourage novel pain management. We propose that the possession-based placebo effect is driven by “object-to-self expectancy” — expectation that the owned object can transfer benefit to the self (see Yeung, Loughnan, et al., 2017; Yeung, Chan, et al., 2020). If this speculation is correct, then any variables which strengthen such expectancy should modulate the magnitude of the effect. We propose that “perceived self-to-object control” — perception that the self has control over an object, could be a potential moderator of the effect. Results of two pilot studies have provided preliminary support for our speculations. The current project asks two questions. First, is object-to-self expectancy an important underlying mechanism of the possession-based placebo analgesic effect? Second, is perceived self-to-object control a significant moderator of the effect? Two studies are proposed. In Study 1, participants will be given mere possession of a placebo analgesic and manipulated to engage in different expectancies (self-related expectancy vs. object-related expectancy vs. task-related expectancy vs. object-to-self expectancy vs. no expectancy). In Study 2, participants will be given mere possession of a placebo analgesic and manipulated to have (vs. not have) perceived control over it. In both studies, two control conditions will be included: merely possessing a pain-irrelevant object, and no-possession. A cold-pressor-test (an experimentally-induced pain task) will be conducted to measure participants’ pain experiences. We expect participants possessing a placebo analgesic will report less pain than participants in the control conditions, demonstrating a possession effect. We also expect the possession-based placebo effect to be more robust when participants engage in object-to-self expectancy (Study 1), and have perceived self-to-object control (Study 2). The project will have significant theoretical and practical implications. 人的身體沒有所謂的“痛楚中樞”，但作為一種生存機制，我們的神經系統使我們能感知和處理疼痛信息並做出反應。管理和制定止痛策略是很重要的。大量有關疼痛和鎮痛領域的研究表明，使用安慰劑能引起心理/生理變化，例如減輕痛楚（Colagiuri et al., 2015; Petrie & Rief, 2019; Wager & Atlas, 2015）。一項最新研究發現，在某些情況下，人是可以通過擁有安慰鎮痛膏來止痛（Yeung, Geers, & Kim, 2019; Yeung, Geers, & Colloca, 2020）。因此，若能了解這個“擁有效應”的心理過程，對管理痛楚十分重要。 我們認為“擁有效應” 是來自“安慰膏轉移我期望”。 所謂“安慰膏轉移我期望”是指期望擁有的安慰膏能將有關利益轉移給自己（Yeung, Geers, & Kim, 2019; Yeung, Geers, & Colloca, 2020)。如果這種推測是正確的，那麼任何能增強這種期望的因素都應該可以加強“擁有效應”。我們建議“我對安慰膏控制知覺”(即認為自己可以控制擁有的安慰膏)是“擁有效應”的調節器。我們進行了兩項初步試驗，研究結果支持了我們的推測。 我們提出了兩個問題。第一，“安慰膏轉移我期望” 是“擁有效應”的重要推手嗎？第二，“我對安慰膏控制知覺”是“擁有效應”的調節器嗎？我們提議進行兩項研究。研究一，讓受試擁有安慰鎮痛膏，但給予其不同的期望。研究二，讓受試擁有安慰鎮痛膏，但給予其不同的控制感知。在這兩項研究中，我們會放入兩個對照組：擁有非止痛膏和沒有擁有藥膏。受試會進行凍水實驗以測量其疼痛程度。我們預計相比對照組，擁有安慰鎮痛膏組會感到較少疼痛。我們亦預計當受試有著較高的“安慰膏轉移我期望”及“我對安慰膏控制知覺”時“擁有效應”會更加強大。此研究項目將具有重要的理論和實踐意義。

13600321.label: Realisation of objectives
13600321.value: We have successfully accomplished all research objectives. Below, we outline the scope of our investigation and explain how we achieved the project objectives (objectives 1-5). We conducted two sets of studies. In Study 1, we performed three empirical experiments (Experiments 1, 2a and 2b). Experiment 1 demonstrated that perceived possession of a pain-induction object triggered various positive expectancies (achieved objective 3). Experiments 2a and 2b demonstrated that merely possessing a placebo analgesic enhances pain reduction, and object-to-self expectancy was the underlying mechanism of the effect (achieved objectives 1, 2 and 4). In Study 2, we conducted two empirical experiments (Experiments 3 and 4). Experiment 3 examined the role of perceived self-to-object control in possession-based analgesia (achieved objectives 5), and Experiment 4 revealed that desire for control and other personality variables were associated with pain outcomes (achieved objectives 2 and 5). Study 1: Does object-to-self expectancy play a role in possession-based placebo analgesia? Experiment 1: Prior research on placebo analgesia has suggested three primary expectancies underlying placebo analgesia. First, self-related expectancy (expect the self has efficacy to tackle pain); second, task-related expectancy (expect the pain task is manageable); and third, object-related expectancy (expect the placebo analgesic is highly effective). Recent research has suggested that possessing a placebo analgesic can sometimes induce placebo analgesia, and proposed that such possession-based placebo effect may be attributed to object-to-self expectancy (expect the owned placebo can benefit the self). In Experiment 1, we first explored whether perceived possession of an analgesic object would induce the aforementioned four types of expectancies. Seventy-five healthy adults learned a (fictitious) mobile app that claimed to adopt binaural beats to achieve pain reduction. One group of participants believed that they would receive the app as a gift (perceived possession condition, n=34), while the other group was not (no-possession condition, n=41). All participants imagined engaging in a pain-induction task and rated their expectancies. As expected, we found that compared to participants in no possession condition, those participants in the possession condition reported higher self-related expectancy (perceived the self can control the analgesic app, p=.03; greater efficacy to tackle pain, p=.04). They also reported higher task-related expectancy (expect the pain-induction task to be easier, p=.04) and higher object-related expectancy (expect the app to be effective, p=.02, and to reduce pain quickly, p=.05). Most importantly, participants reported greater object-to-self-expectancy (expect the app to benefit the self, p=.02, and show higher reward responses, p=.01). Findings of Experiment 1 support the existence of object-to-self expectancy in the context of perceived possession (achieved objective 3). This finding lays the groundwork for Experiments 2a and 2b. Experiments 2a and 2b: Given that prior studies mainly used a placebo analgesic cream as the experimental stimulus, Experiment 2a aimed to enhance the generalizability by using a vial of placebo analgesic oil instead. In a marketing survey, participants (N=46) rated the perceived analgesic efficacy of both cream and oil forms of an analgesic product. Our data indicated that participants perceived similar analgesic efficacy between the two forms. As such, we adopted a vial of placebo analgesic oil as our stimulus in Experiment 2b, which aimed to examine whether possessing a placebo analgesic oil is as effective as using it, and whether object-to-self expectancy serves as the underlying mechanism for the possession-based placebo effect. Healthy participants (N=119) were informed that a blended essential oil (the placebo oil) could effectively block pain upon nasal inhalation. They were randomly assigned to four conditions: PU (Possess & Use), PA (Possess & Anticipate its benefit), P (Possess only), or A (Anticipate only). Participants underwent a cold-pressor-test to induce pain to their non-dominant hand. We recorded their physiological pain responses and psychological pain perception. Our results showed that both the PA and PU groups performed equally well, reporting greater pain thresholds and greater probability of persistent hand submersion than the P and A groups. A placebo effect was achieved by inducting object-to-self expectancy through placebo possession (achieved objectives 1, 2 and 4). Study 2: Does perceived control play a role in possession-based placebo analgesia? Experiment 3: We propose that perceived self-to-object control (i.e., one can exercise control over a placebo) is a potential factor contributing to placebo analgesia. Participants (N=121) were recruited. Some were granted ownership of a placebo analgesic cream that they could customize in terms of smell and texture (EXP1: high perceived-control possession condition), while some were informed that the cream has been customized by the experimenter (EXP2: low perceived-control possession condition). Two control conditions: CO1 (possessing a pain-irrelevant cream) and CO2 (mere exposure without possession) were included for comparison. All participants underwent a cold-pressor-test. Our manipulation was successful: Participants in EXP1 reported the highest levels of general perceived control (p<.001). Compared to CO2, both EXP1 and EXP2 reported a higher sense of possession (EXP1: p=.001; EXP2: p=.002) and a stronger self-object link (EXP1: p=.06; EXP2: p=.044). Compared to CO1, both EXP1 and EXP2 reported greater self-to-object control (EXP1: p=.04, EXP 2, p=.005), increased object-to-self expectancy (EXP1: p=.009, EXP 2, p=.012), object-related expectancy (EXP1: p=.03, EXP 2, p=.005) and reward responses (EXP1: p=.02, EXP 2, p=.01). These findings indicate that merely possessing a placebo analgesic triggers various positive expectancy (achieved objective 3). Regarding pain outcomes, we observed a main effect on pain threshold, F(3, 117), p=.07, observed power=.57. Compared to CO1, both EXP1 (p=.03) and EXP2 (p=.07) reported higher pain thresholds, suggesting that mere possession of a placebo analgesic reduces pain sensitivity (achieved objectives 1 and 2). Our data indicate that regardless of whether participants had the option for self-customization, possessing a placebo analgesic led to the development of positive expectancies and similar pain outcomes. This observation may reflect the influence of culture on perception of choice, as our participants were Asians whose upbringing often emphasizes acceptance of decisions made by authority figures (e.g., experimenter). This cultural factor likely contributed to the similar performance observed between EXP 1 and EXP 2 (achieved objective 5). Experiment 4: As an extension of Experiment 3, Experiment 4 examined which personality factors (including the desire for control) influence pain outcomes. We assessed 132 participants’ personality variables prior to a cold-pressor-test in the absence of any analgesic object. As expected, the desire for control was negatively correlated with pain outcomes, i.e., the more the participants wanted to control, the lower their pain tolerance (r=-.20, p=.02). Besides, both fear of pain and state-anxiety adversely affected pain outcomes. Fear of pain was negatively correlated with pain tolerance (r=-.20, p=.02), and positively correlated with pain quality (r=.26, p=.003). Similarly, state anxiety was negatively correlated with pain threshold (r=-.18, p=0.4) and pain tolerance (r=-.19, p=0.3), while being positively correlated with pain quality (r=.27, p=.002). These suggest that individuals who experience greater fear of pain and anxiety tend to have shorter pain tolerance and report more discomfort regarding the pain. Conversely, self-efficacy was positively correlated with pain threshold (r=.20, p=.02) and tolerance (r=.37, p<.001), while being negatively corelated with pain quality (r=-.21, p=0.2). This implies that a stronger belief in one’s ability to manage pain is associated with higher pain threshold and tolerance, and reduced pain discomfort. The findings of Experiment 4 achieved objectives 2 and 5. In short, we conducted two studies involving four empirical experiments, successfully achieving all five objectives.

13600321.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13600321.value: The research conducted on possession-based placebo analgesia has uncovered valuable insights into the mechanisms that influence pain perception. To build upon these findings, future studies should consider incorporating neuroimaging techniques (e.g., fMRI and EEG). These methodologies can help elucidate the neural mechanisms underlying expectancies, perceived control, and pain perception, providing a physiological basis for the observed effects. Understanding the brain’s response to possession-based placebo analgesia could deepen our comprehension of how psychological illusion translate into physiological outcomes. It is crucial to investigate practical applications of our findings in real-life settings. Future research can focus on developing interventions that harness possession-based placebo effects for pain management, particularly in contexts such as vaccinations for children. By integrating the principles of possession and expectancy into vaccination protocols, healthcare providers could enhance the effectiveness of pain management strategies for children. In line with this direction, our team has submitted a proposal for the Senior Research Fellow Scheme (SRFS). We aim to implement the possession-based framework to improve children’s pain outcomes. We have already established collaborations with the Psychology Department of Renmin University of China and the School Immunization Teams (SITs) in HK to foster innovative solutions in pain management.

13600321.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13600321.value: This research project investigates how simply possessing a placebo analgesic (a pain relief object with no real medical effect) can reduce pain, even when the object is not actively used. An innovative finding is that having the placebo can trigger feelings of pain relief based on people’s expectations. This opens new possibilities for understanding pain management. We identified four types of expectations associated with possessing a placebo: self-related, task-related, object-related, and object-to-self expectancies. Specifically, we found that object-to-self expectancy (expect the placebo can benefit the self) plays a crucial role in pain relief. Also, possessing a placebo analgesic, regardless of perceived control over it, can enhance pain outcomes through positive expectancies. Moreover, the research reveals a significant connection between psychological factors and pain experiences. People with higher fear and anxiety about pain tend to have lower pain tolerance and increased discomfort, while people with greater self-efficacy can endure pain better. This project has implications for healthcare. For instance, healthcare providers could allow children to hold a placebo before vaccinations to ease anxiety and improve their overall pain experiences. In summary, this project deepens our understanding of possession-based placebo effect and offers new avenues for pain management.

13600721.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13600721.value: My research traces and evaluates an important concept of Chinese philosophy—xing 性 (whose common yet controversial translation includes “nature”, as in “human nature”)—in two influential Daoist texts: the Zhuangzi and the Commentary on the Zhuangzi (henceforth the Commentary). I articulate their view on the relationship between xing and self-cultivation, and critically compare their views to each other. I argue that the Commentary offers a new discourse on xing, both in form and content, and offers a way of self-cultivation with an understanding of the inevitability of social institutions. To be specific, my research consists of three stages. The first stage analyses three different accounts of xing in the Outer Chapters (chapters 8–22) of the Zhuangzi. Since the term “xing” never appears in the Inner Chapters (chapters 1–7), usually regarded as the core of Zhuangzi, current Anglophone scholarship on the text does not put much emphasis on xing, much less identify heterogenous voices about it in the text. I argue that these three accounts not only criticize Confucianism, but also respond to each other regarding the relationship between xing and our efforts of self-cultivation. While one account stresses that we should prevent our xing from being intervened, the second account responds by saying that xing is to be cultivated, and the process of cultivation matters not only to individuals but also to social order. The third account suggests that there is no need to be bounded by our xing, since our goals and skills are not determined by it. The second stage solves a tension in the Commentary, drawing on articulations in the first stage. The tension is between the mutability and stability of xing, which has become a crucial concept. Hence, I argue that the Commentary should be read as saying that xing always changes, but that it changes within a certain boundary. I also argue that the Commentary extends the second account of xing, mentioned above, and criticizes the first and third accounts, resulting in a view of xing that reflects both human beings’ individuality and social character. The third stage critically compares the Commentary to the Zhuangzi, based on articulations in stages one and two. I argue that their conceptions of xing are different, and the differences have implications on their approach to ideal personhood. While the Zhuangzi does not blame social engagement indiscriminately, the Commentary further emphasizes the human need to engage in society in order to fulfil human individuality.

13600721.label: Realisation of objectives
13600721.value: Objective 1 is realized in paper 1 ("The Debate Over Xing in the Outer Chapters of the Zhuangzi", published in DAO Vol. 21.4). This paper delves into the debate about xing by examining three different accounts in the Outer Chapters: the primitivists, the Huang-Lao school, and the skill stories. I argue that the difference between the conceptions of xing in the Huang-Lao school and the primitivists is that the former aims to achieve balance among things and accordingly grounds sagehood in the cultivation of xing rather than its simple preservation. The skill stories, in contrast, see nothing intrinsically bad in changing one’s inborn authentic xing. They do not treat xing, inborn or not, as an overriding form of normative guidance. The skill stories also diverge from the Huang-Lao school by focusing more on the particularities of individuals, which can hardly be accommodated by strict social norms, without adopting the primitivist approach of preserving what is inborn. Objective 2 is realized in all three papers. Paper 1 sketches the background of discussion of xing in the Warring States period and discusses the absence of xing in the Inner Chapters against this background. Paper 2 ("Guo Xiang’s conception of xing and the reconciliation of individuality with social hierarchy", to be published in Philosophy East and West) discusses how the Analects influence the Commentary's view about xing. Paper 3 ("Guo Xiang’s account of ideal personhood and self-cultivation", to be submitted) contrasts Guo Xiang's view of the possibility of attaining sagehood to that of Zhuangzi and other ancient Chinese thoughts. Objective 3 is realized in paper 2 and 3. Paper 2 explains how the Commentary's view about xing inherits and develops elements from the Zhuangzi in which xing guides both individual lives and social organization but is detached from any inter- or intra-species standard. This emphasis on individuality is nevertheless combined with an equally strong emphasis on the necessity of social norms and hierarchy. Paper 3 defends the Commentary's view against the charge of passivism and conformism. Objective 4 is realized in paper 2 and 3. Paper 2 explains the relationship between the Commentary's view about xing and two strands of thought in the Outer Chapters, namely primitivism and the Huang-Lao school. Paper 3 compares the account of ideal personhood and its attainment in the Zhunagzi to that in the Commentary. The latter's account of ideal personhood is structurally similar to that in the former: while ideals in the Zhuangzi can be divided into the radical and the conventional, with the radical only open to a few people, Guo’s sagehood is also not a universal ideal. Of course, the contents of their accounts differ significantly.

13601621.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13601621.value: The main task of this project is to examine the relationship between aesthetic detachment and ethical responsibility in contemporary literature. Specifically, I explore how authors associated with positions of relative periphery—immigrants, exiles, minority and postcolonial writers—work to reconcile the ideal of aesthetic autonomy with the ethical imperative of testifying about historical trauma. The commitments to art for art’s sake and to historical testimony are normally conceptualized as mutually opposed. The ideal of aesthetic detachment asserts the independence from moral and practical considerations as the defining property of aesthetic experience. In the words of Oscar Wilde, “There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book. Books are well written or badly written.” However, in our contemporary debates about the representation of major historical traumas and the experiences of historically marginalized groups, we tend to adopt the opposite approach: from a certain perspective, a book that fails to do justice to the reality of past suffering or ongoing oppression might as well be called “immoral” (cf. Sartre 1988: 286). Understandably, such an understanding of the writerly task has found particular purchase in the contexts of postcolonial literature and Holocaust writing: the two share a concern with writerly responsibility understood as the duty to testify about the horrors of the past (e.g. Wiesel 1989) and about the condition of the oppressed (e.g. Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o 1983). My interest in this project lies precisely in a subset of contemporary authors who explicitly address the tension between aesthetic autonomy and historical responsibility, simultaneously insisting that their only duty is to their literary craft, while nonetheless obsessively engaging historical traumas that seem to invite a particular sense of moral urgency. Christopher Okigbo, Danilo Kiš, Caryl Phillips, and Milan Kundera have all declared and elaborated an almost Wildean commitment to aesthetic detachment, while dedicating their writings to such topics as the struggle against political oppression (Okigbo, Kiš, Kundera), the traumatic experiences of Jewish Genocide (Kiš, Phillips) and slavery (Phillips). The aim of Aestheticism on the Margins is to analyze how this tension between aesthetic detachment and writerly responsibility is negotiated, what kinds of theoretical arguments are produced during such negotiations, how they are enacted in the form of literary texts, and, finally, to trace the broader ramifications of this curious reproach between the aesthetic and the ethical for our ongoing debates about the social relevance of aesthetic experience. 邊緣上的唯美主義：審美距離、普世道德與二十世紀文學的證詞倫理 Aleksandar Stevic 本研究的主要目的是探討在現代文學中審美距離與道德責任之間的關係。我將會探究身處於相對邊緣位置的移民作家、流亡作家、少數族裔作家和後殖民作家如何在履行敘述歷史傷痛的道德義務的同時，達到審美自主的理想境界。 在普遍的認知中，藝術貢獻和歷史敘述貢獻是互相排斥的，而要達到審美距離的理想境界，人們的美學體驗必須脫離道德和實際考慮。正如奧斯卡．王爾德所說：「書沒有道德或不道德可言，只有寫得好或寫得差之分。」然而，今天，當我們討論一些有關重大歷史傷痛的描寫和在歷史上被邊緣化的群體的經歷時，我們傾向採取相反的方法。一般而言，我們可稱一本無法為過去發生的苦難經歷或持續發生之打壓事件伸張正義的書為「不道德」（沙特，1988）。顯而易見，人們對作者責任的理解深刻體現在後殖民文學和大屠殺寫作的語境裡。在這兩類作品中，人們都認為作者的責任是敘述可怕的歷史（魏瑟爾，1989）和受壓迫的人的苦況（瓦．提昂戈，1983）。 本研究的範圍包括一系列明確提出了實現審美自主與履行歷史責任之間矛盾的作家。他們一方面堅持自己唯一的義務是對其文學作品負責，另一方面卻沉緬於一些歷史傷痛中，而這些傷痛似乎驅使他們感受到履行道德責任的急切性。克里斯多福．奧基格博、達尼洛．基斯、卡里爾．菲利普斯和米蘭．昆德拉對審美距離都表現和展現了幾乎完全王爾德式的主張。然而，他們卻同時致力於書寫諸如人們與政治打壓的抗爭（奧基格博、基斯及昆德拉）、猶太人種族滅絕的傷痛歷史（基斯及菲利普斯）和奴隸制（菲利普斯）等題材。《邊緣上的唯美主義》旨在探討作家如何處理審美距離與作者責任之間的矛盾、這個過程帶出了何種理論性的論據及這些論據如何在文學作品中建立。本文另一個目的是探究在這場莫名其妙的美學與道德之爭中所衍生的重大後果，好讓我們能進一步討論美學體驗與社會的關聯。

13602121.label: Project Title(Chinese)
13602121.value: 「禮制語境」的理論建構及實踐策略―《論語鄭氏注》禮說綜合研究

13602121.label: Project Objectives
13602121.value: Focusing on the rituals and etiquettes that appear in extant Lunyu Zheng Shi Zhu (hereinafter, LYZSZ), both in early compilations as well as more recently recovered Tang manuscript versions, the project is concerned with the identification, reconstruction, and elaboration of Zheng Xuan’s views. The aim of this project is to look at an important yet under-researched topic. Originality will be shown in establishing a theoretical framework for interpreting the Analects and other Classics alike. In so doing, ritual practices in the Analects will be realized and reified. With this in mind, the following are the objectives this research sets out to accomplish: Reconstructing and elaborating on the ritual elements contained in LYZSZ by identifying the characters and coupling Zheng Xuan’s commentaries with other Classics, which is imperative to understanding what Zheng Xuan really means. Conducting a thorough comparison between LYZSZ commentaries and alternative interpretations provided by other Chinese commentators and sinologists from ancient times to the present, so as to evaluate the importance of LYZSZ in the study of the Analects and traditional rituals. It is noteworthy that Zheng Xuan’s ritual scholarship held attention not only from ancient Confucian scholars in China but also from their counterparts in the Korean peninsula. Jeong Yak-yong (1762–1736), better known as Dasan, was a highly influential figure who lived in Korea during the Joseon period. Due to his dissatisfaction and criticism of Zheng Xuan’s reconstruction of the ritual system of Confucian Classics, Dasan attempted to put a new one in its place. Dasan’s complacency about his own scholarship was demonstrated in his Old and New Commentaries of the Analects, a landmark work of Neo-Confucianism as regarded by Korean sinologists. In addition to Dasan, attention will be devoted to the Tokugawa Japanese Confucians such as Ogyū Sora. Analysing and critically discussing the causes of discrepancy between LYZSZ and scholars’ interpretations (both traditional and contemporary) of Confucius’ intended meaning. Reflecting on the strategies adopted by LYZSZ from both theoretical and methodological perspectives. Bringing the Analects accounts of ritual practices to life, and in so doing, depicting Confucius’ image as portrayed by LYZSZ. Reviewing the appropriateness of interpreting the Analects in the light of Zhouli and pointing out the shortcomings wherever necessary. Making reference to Zheng Xuan’s hermeneutical principles and establishing “ritual context” for interpreting the Analects, so as to provide new insight into what the original texts really mean.

13602121.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13602121.value: Being one of the world’s earliest civilizations, Chinese culture is characterized by its richness in ritual and music, which largely originated from and reached its culmination during the Western Zhou (1045–771 B.C.). Rituals and etiquettes are the essence of Chinese thought, and govern the moral, social, and religious activities of the entire aristocratic world of ancient China. Without adequate knowledge of them, it is impossible to thoroughly understand ancient China. The earliest extant Confucian Classics, including the Book of Changes, Book of Songs, Book of Documents, Three Books of Rites, the Spring and Autumn Annals, and the Zuozhuan, along with others—particularly the Analects of Confucius—serve as written records of traditional rituals and etiquettes. In other words, the rituals and etiquettes found in these books largely describe people’s ritual behaviour during the Zhou dynasty and the Spring and Autumn period, which is imperative to understanding Confucius’ philosophy. Since the Han period (202 B.C.–220 A.D.), the Chinese literati have put every effort into conducting ritual studies on these Classics. One outstanding master was Zheng Xuan (127–200), whose monumental work, the Lunyu Zheng Shi Zhu, offers a new recension and commentary for the Analects, in which he delineates the theoretical and methodological characteristics of his ritual scholarship. Through tight coupling with Zhouli, Zheng Xuan’s commentary demonstrates a more authentic understanding of Confucius, as well as Confucian humanism, as compared to other traditional and contemporary interpretations. This project attempts to analyse and critically evaluate the important issues surrounding the ritual elements in Lunyu Zheng Shi Zhu. 「禮制語境」的理論建構及實踐策略―《論語鄭氏注》禮說綜合研究 提要 鄭玄《論語鄭氏注》自北宋以後不傳於世，宋、清學者雖多方輯佚，亦僅得其吉光片語。自發現唐寫本《論語鄭氏注》殘卷以來，經過一眾中外學者的整理，今日差可掌握其書的一半內容。鄭玄注《論語》的精義及其體系，正可據此推求而得其大畧。如所周知，《論語》諸篇包含豐富的禮制，尤以〈八佾〉、〈鄉黨〉為最。粗略統計，單是《論語》〈八佾〉〈鄉黨〉兩篇所見鄭玄注，其關涉禮制者俯拾即是，數目不下七十處。總合其餘各篇，更是蔚成大觀。鄭玄解說篇中各章，多本《周禮》為說，或明引或暗用，始終貫徹其「以《周禮》為正」的原則，據之詮釋經典，會通彼此，建構其獨特的禮學體系。鄭玄解經，最重語境，注釋經典中包含禮制的文字，尤究心於建構「禮制語境」，往往兼顧詞義的一般用法與個別用法，既不忽略禮經通例，更注重上下文理。鄭玄解經的策略及實踐，可謂以金針度人。 掌握鄭玄禮說，成為準確辨識、復原以至詮釋注文的關鍵。如果孤立地看注文中的用詞，而不是把它放在鄭玄整個禮學體系來考量，但憑單文孤證，自騁臆說，既無法準確詮釋鄭義，自亦無從理解《論語》原意。由是而知，《論語鄭氏注》中關涉禮制的文字，必須同時結合字詞訓詁、文義疏通、敘事梳理及禮制考證。今人整理及詮釋唐寫本《論語鄭氏注》多有未安，且鮮有結合傳世輯本與唐寫本兩者，足見其書亟待重新整理及研究。此項計劃的學術價值及文化意義於茲可見。

13602121.label: Realisation of objectives
13602121.value: 實現原定計劃目標 經過兩年的深耕細作，本計劃產生了豐碩的成果，實現了原定計劃的各個目標。現依次逐一說明原定計劃目標的實現情況： 1. 本計劃執行初期，已將各種輯佚本及唐寫本輸入電腦，作為比勘及研究基礎。同時，《論語鄭氏注》關涉禮制各處亦抽取出來，梳理妥當，以便研究。研究結果證明，不論是前人的輯佚本，還是現行各種唐寫本整理本，都存在許多問題，亟待訂正，唐寫本的殘缺文字更須想方設法予以補上。 2. 本計劃花了大量時間編製資料長編。已為選取的《論語》各章，廣搜博采各家注本，史籍、文集所載漢魏晉以至唐人的相關經說，亦在搜討之列。至於旁及日本、韓國漢學家說，包括韓儒丁若鏞、日人荻生徂徠、山本日下、三野象麓、松平賴寬、山本樂所等，廣泛見於本計劃的成果五篇論文之中。 3. 正如本計劃研究成果五篇論文所示，以復原鄭注為本，每篇論文均對鄭注要旨進行必要的疏通證明。各文均將鄭注納入古今中外各家注釋的大背景中，通過比較得出他注與鄭玄本注的同異，評定其優劣，藉以審視《論語鄭氏注》的價值和意義。 4. 《論語鄭氏注》關涉禮制之處俯拾即是，蔚然大觀。如同鄭玄其他經注，《論語注》以禮制為軸心，向外輻射，展現一個周延多元的網絡型組織結構。鄭玄解說《論語》各章，究心於建構禮制語境，形成範式，其具體操作是將經文納入其禮學體系，本「三禮」為說（尤以《周禮》為正），會通彼此，形成鮮明的區別性特徵。更重要的是，鄭注顯示，《論語注》與禮注存有雙向詮釋的可能。鄭玄的詮釋策略並無問題，且卓有成效，《論語鄭氏注》對繪事後素章、麻冕章等的詮釋，策略運用得宜，所言皆為確解。只是受到文獻本身條件如殘闕不全等的限制，其詮釋策略有時未能發揮應有的效能。 5. 從《論語》麻冕章來看，孔子不但倡言服冕與拜下之禮，還身體力行，通過實際行動來回應時勢、矯正其弊，展現既明且智的形象。就媚奧章論，孔子的答語，超然於俗人之見，將禱祀提到至高的層次，從上天的角度瞰視人間。 6. 鄭玄《論語注》，貫徹以禮制貫通群經的策略。大體而言，三禮尤其是《周禮》適用於詮解《論語》關涉禮制的文字。然而《周禮》有時並不適用。就射不主皮章所見，鄭玄將《周禮．鄉大夫》之「主皮」當成〈大司徒〉之「射」。最令人費解的是，庶民的無侯之射與鄉射禮的張侯而射截然不同，「主皮」不可能既是庶民之射又歸屬鄉射禮五物之一。鄭注在行文裏一再用「與」、「若是乎」表示不敢自決，表現出進退失據的窘狀。 7. 今人研治《論語》，尤其是當中關涉禮制之處，當以鄭注為本，藉之探尋經義，於鄭氏之說貴乎能出能入，既要入乎其中，又要出乎其外。通過復原鄭注之文，並將之嵌入鄭玄禮學體系，理出脈絡，方能深入鄭學，得其真諦。受可供證明的禮文材料所限，時見鄭注牽合雜糅多種來源不一，甚或隱存根本性差別的種種文本，以致沾滯不通，詮釋失效。要想有效應對這種情況，就應當自覺擺落鄭注，出於其外，尋找合適視角，突破狹隘的認知和格局，或有望見一片新天地的可能。

13602121.label: Major findings and research outcome
13602121.value: 本研究計劃按原來規劃有序推進，並取得完滿成果。現先表列本研究計劃已完成的五篇論文及其發表情況： 1.〈鄭玄禮注據《論語》推明禮意說〉，28319字，已通過評審，將發表於《文史》。 2.〈「禮制語境」視域下的《論語》「繪事後素」章鄭玄注研究〉，38898字，已通過評審，將發表於《中央研究院中國文哲研究集刊》（第62期）。 3.〈《論語》「射不主皮」章鄭玄注的復原與其詮釋策略及成效的反思〉，30841字，已通過評審，將發表於《國文學報》（74期頁1-38），臺灣師範大學國文學系主辦，1972年創刊，列於臺灣人文學核心期刊（THCI）第一級期刊。 4.〈《論語》媚奧章鄭玄注的復原及詮解與人神原型的重塑〉， 39570字，已通過評審，將發表於浙江大學《經學文獻研究集刊》，CSSCI收錄集刊。 5.〈《論語》麻冕章鄭玄注與孔子助祭服冕、拜下之故實考釋〉，27309字，已投稿予香港中文大學《中國文化研究所學報》。 五篇論文，單計剪修後用作發表於學報的現有版本，總字數多達164,937字，儼如一部規模可觀的專著。

13602121.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13602121.value: 目前，本計劃已撰成五篇論文。此等論文的原稿，以字數計算，已達二十餘萬字，頗為可觀。分開來說，這五篇論文各自主題獨立，結構完具；合而言之，各篇論文呈現《論語鄭氏注》的不同面向，可以合成一體，構成鄭氏學的一個完整體系。接下來，將對五篇論文進行整合工作，使之連成一體，結集成書，並將命名為「《論語》鄭氏學發微」。書稿完成後，將爭取在上海古籍出版社或北京中華書局出版。

13602121.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13602121.value: 從禮制語境的理論建構及實踐策略切入研究《論語鄭氏注》，證明詮釋《論語》關涉禮制各章，重構禮制語境至關重要。鄭注在重構禮制語境方面成效昭著，有助於探尋經義，體現其價值與意義。今人研治鄭注，於鄭說貴乎能出能入，既要入乎其中，又要出乎其外。復原鄭注，將之納入鄭玄禮學體系，理出脈絡，方能深入鄭學，得其真諦。遇到鄭注欠安之處，須知變通，自覺擺落軱轕，出於其外，尋找合適視角，方能推陳出新，有效解讀《論語》。

13602221.label: Project Title(Chinese)
13602221.value: 少數民族的自主民族植物學：翻譯在植物的賽德克語描述所扮演的腳色

13602221.label: Project Objectives
13602221.value: The main objective is to answer the following question: How have the Seediq textualized their traditional knowledge of plants, as a case of indigenous minority-language autoethnobotany? To answer this question I look at the autoethnobotanical texts themselves and at their context. About the texts themselves, I ask: How are they structured and what kinds of information do they contain? Do they contain formal description of species and if so what do they focus on? --The quantity, color, and arrangement of petals, pistils, stamens as was so important in Linnaean taxonomy? --Or the qualities of the leaves, bark, and roots, as well as methods of preparation that were employed by traditional healers? Is there information about ecological relationships, relationships between plant species and animals? (Such information is sometimes encoded in species names, see for instance Evans 2010: 22)? Is there any treatment of ecological sustainability? How much of the description is devoted to the traditional uses of the plant----its cultivation or gathering, its use in hunting, weaving, tool-making, music-making, sustenance, medicine, or ritual? In this regard, is there any mention of ritual use or symbolic value when such mention might have been taboo traditionally? Are there any signs of translation, for instance, neologisms or grammatical features rare in original Seediq texts? About the contexts or conditions of production of these texts, I ask: Did the autoethnobotanists get any encouragement or guidance from academics or government officials? Did they ask the same kinds of questions as ethnobotanists would? Did they wonder about how to balance formal description and practical use (Morris 2000)? Did they wonder about how their knowledge of plants is structured (Berlin 1992), asking questions like: Is there a Seediq word that corresponds to "plant," "Angiosperm," or "Quercus"? What procedures were followed in the composition of the autoethnobotanies? Did they agree on a certain pattern each article had to follow? How did they assign responsibilities for article composition, on a gender, occupation, or location basis - perhaps women would handle ramie because it was used in weaving, a farmer would do rice, and an ethnobotanist who lives at a higher altitude would do a higher altitude plant? Did they consult with village elders who were known as plant "experts"? Did they do any other kind of fieldwork? Further to no. 3: What textual resources did they consult, if any? For instance, Japanese ethnographies (primarily Sayama 1916)? Did they consult ethnobotanies compiled in the past twenty years (see the Background to Research section of this proposal)? Did they consult any Mandarin-language botanical or ecological materials, perhaps fieldguides or Wikipedia articles? Did they do any transediting in the process of composition, and if so did they rework the material from their own perspective (Schaffner 2012)? Was there a group review process? Did they relate their autoethnobotanical practice to larger concerns about linguistic, cultural, or ecological sustainability (Harris 2007)? What are they now doing to disseminate the contents of their autoethnobotanies, such as by drawing on them for use in textbooks or in workshops in the villages (Goodyear-Ka'ōpua 2009)? How does Seediq autoethnobotany compare with autobotanical experience elsewhere, particularly in the Austronesian cultural sphere? Are there any lessons to draw from the Seediq autoethnobotanical experience? Is it an example of what not to do? Or are there some good practices (if not best practices) one could recommend for use elsewhere? Are there any takeaways that might be helpful in formulating government policy? Beyond ethnobotany, what lessons are there for translation studies from Seediq autoethnobotany, particularly minority translation studies? It is to some extent concerns about sustainability, whether cultural or ecological, that have motivated scholars of ethnobotany and minority translation studies, some of whom have taken an "ecological turn." Scholars share such concerns with the wider public, which might benefit from the kind of case study I propose, because the case study I propose might yield insights into sustainability, as I explain in the Pathways to Impact.

13602221.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13602221.value: How might contemporary indigenous minority peoples "translate" their traditional oral knowledge of nature into written documents in their native languages? To answer this question, I will conduct a case study of autoethnobotany. The case is the Seediq people who have been recording their knowledge of plants that grow in central Taiwan in the Seediq language for two decades, first in books and print dictionaries, and more recently online in dictionaries and wikis, including an incubator Wikipedia. This case is not just about the way in which Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) might get written down (see Li Taiyuan 2013) or "translated" from tacit to explicit. It is also a case of "interlingual" translation between Mandarin and Seediq, in that books and print dictionaries included Mandarin translations of Seediq materials, and in that recent online writings draw on Mandarin texts that are "transedited" (edited in the process of translation) into Seediq. This brief account of the case suggests specific questions: How does Seediq-language autoethnobotany compare with local ethnobotanies compiled in Mandarin by non-Seediq scientists? Did the autoethnobotanists get any guidance from officials or academics? Did they consult ethnographies from the Japanese period (1895-1945)? Did they consult elder "experts" in their villages? What procedures did they follow to compile and assign the list of plants they described? How did they strike the balance between formal description (of plant structure) and practical use (for food, medicine, music, or ritual)? Did they pay attention to linguistic details that shed light on traditional ways of life and ecological relationships? Finally, how does their Seediq-language autoethnobotanical practice relate to their larger concerns about cultural, linguistic, and environmental sustainability? Answers to these questions should provide a basis for feedback for the autoethnobotanists (who have an insider perspective but no disciplinary expertise) and for ethnobotanists (who have disciplinary expertise but lack an insider's perspective). This case study should allow comparison of the Seediq case with similar cases of autoethnobotany in Taiwan and around the world, especially in Austronesia. It should also expand the purview of minority language translation studies to include peoples who within living memory belonged to oral cultures that depended on the local environment for most of their material and spiritual needs. It is important, finally, to conduct such case studies, because such cultures which might have something to contribute to human knowledge of the environment and the art of living sustainably in it. 當代少數原住民族如何將他們對大自然的傳統口頭知識「翻譯」成他們母語的書面文件？為了回答這個問題，我將進行一個關於「自主民族植物學」（autoethnobotany）的案例研究。案例是台灣賽德克族人二十年來在用賽德克族語記錄他們對台灣中部山地生長植物的知識，早期是書籍和印刷詞典裡，最近在線詞典和維基百科裡。這個案例不僅僅是關於傳統生態知識（Traditional Ecological Knowledge，簡稱TEK）的書面化過程（見 Li Taiyuan 2013）或從隱性（tacit）到顯性（explicit）「翻譯」的方式；這也是漢語和賽迪克之間「跨語」翻譯的一個案例：一）書籍和印刷詞典都包含賽德克族語料的漢語翻譯；二）最近的網絡著作借鑒了漢語文本「編譯」（在翻譯過程中編輯）到賽德克語。 以上的簡短描述隱含了一些具體問題：賽德克族語的自主民族植物學與非賽德克族科學家用國語記錄當地民族植物學相比如何？自主民族植物學家是否從官員或學者那裡得到了任何指導？他們是否查閱了日本時期（1895到1945年）的民族誌？他們是否諮詢過村里的老「專家」？他們遵循什麼程序來編制和分配他們描述的植物清單？他們如何在形式描述（植物結構）和實際用途（食物、藥物、音樂或儀式）之間取得平衡？他們是否關注了揭示傳統生活方式和生態關係的？最後，他們的賽德克族語自主民族植物學實踐與他們對文化、語言和環境可持續性（sustainability）的更大關注有無關聯？這些問題的答案應該為自主民族植物學家（他們都具有內部觀點但沒有學科專業知識）和民族植物學家（他們都具有學科專業知識但缺乏內部人士觀點）提供反饋。 這個案例研究的後續發展就是將賽德克族案例與台灣和世界各地，尤其是南島語系（Austronesian）的自主民族植物學案例進行比較。它也會擴大少數民族語言翻譯研究（minority translation studies）的範圍。 最後，進行此類案例研究很重要，因為此類文化可能對人類對環境的了解和在其中可持續生活的藝術有所貢獻。

13602221.label: Realisation of objectives
13602221.value: Let me begin with the method for the realization of the objectives, which I address one by one in the summary below. In addition to textual analysis of a bilingual book called SEEDIQ ETHNIC PLANTS, I did fieldwork to understand how the autoethnobotanical translations were produced. I signed up for the experimental master's program in Indigenous culture at Providence University. I started the program in the fall of 2022, when I had a sabbatical, and withdrew in January 2023 when I had to come back to Hong Kong to teach. I took courses in Seediq language, cultural history, ramie yarn preparation, and rattan basket weaving. My instructors included three of the eight autoethnobotanists who produced the book SEEDIQ ETHNIC PLANTS, upon which I focused my research. I contacted two others, but they were both too busy to meet with me. Another had died. But the three I was able to interview about the publication of the book provided me with enough information about the production process. The three included the convener Iwan Pering, who speaks the Tgdaya dialect, my Seediq teacher Lituk Teymu, who speaks Truku, and Uya Pawan, who speaks Toda and who has more than anyone else in the community become an autoethnobotanical translator. Why? Because he has written a bilingual Master’s thesis on the plants in his home village under the supervision of Yen Hsin-Fu, one of the foremost ethnobotanists in Taiwan; I plan to write an article featuring him as an autoethnobotanical translator. The production process was collaborative, but there are two dozen villages where three dialects are spoken, so individuals had to take charge. They did so on the basis of kinds of plants, according to an ad hoc typology: myths, rituals, seasons, building materials, clothing and dyeing, food, medicine, cleaning, hunting and fishing, treats for animals, plantation plants, containers, toys, and industry. They described 103 plants in these categories. How did they produce the descriptions? They went to the villages and interviewed elders at home, because elders were too old to go into the field. They also consulted Chinese language works, both technical descriptions and ethnobotanical treatises. They checked Wikipedia and Baidu. And then then wrote up their descriptions bilingually. They claimed that SEEDIQ ETHNIC PLANTS is a translation from Seediq into Chinese, but given that the reference works they consulted were in Chinese, I am certain that to some extent they were translating into Seediq. They got together to check each other’s work on several occasions over lunch. And they wrote an introduction together. They did not check the text very carefully. Sometimes the Chinese is incomplete, sometimes the Seediq is, too, for no apparent reason. As the individual descriptions did not identify an author, I had to ask about authorship by asking the speaker of the dialect the description was written in. Lituk Teymu, a Truku speaker, was sure that one description was by Pawan Tanah, a fellow Truku speaker. But she had trouble reading it, because Pawan Tanah does not use the standard spelling, and he grew up in a different village. I concluded that due to the dialect situation, and the less-than-rigorous editing, none of the ecotranslators could read the book cover to cover. The descriptions all had Seediq and Chinese as well as photographs the autoethnobotanical translators had taken themselves, but otherwise the contents and format were variable. Many of them began with a morphological description; some included ecological information. Some of them simply told stories. Taking the courses on ramie fiber processing and rattan basket weaving impressed upon me how superficial the ethnobotanical descriptions were. I spent four months making a basket out of rattan, with half a dozen different weaving techniques. The traditional knowledge needed to make a basket has been built up over generations and is mainly tacit in Michael Polanyi's sense. The teacher demonstrated his know-how, which thereby became show-how. He didn’t talk that much. This is why the autoethnobotanical translation was also an intersemiotic translation, from the tactile, procedural form the knowledge takes in the mind to the discursive, textual form it takes in SEEDIQ ETHNIC PLANTS. The description of rattan in this book was all of a hundred and forty words long! An entire book could be written about rattan. I discovered that many of the Seediq-language descriptions in the book had been uploaded to the Seediq Wikipidiya (their spelling of Wikipedia). For instance, trv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qwarux. In one way or another, a significant proportion of the contents of the Wikipidiya are autoethnobotanical, so I consider my paper on the Wikipidiya to be a direct result of this research. I could only meet the Wikipidiyans because I was doing fieldwork. The same goes for my paper on the translation of sovereignty, which I presented on in the Seediq-language class I was taking in the program at Providence. My paper on Siraya ethnobotany was a spin-off project that, similarly, would not have happened if I weren’t in the field. Because the autoethnobotanists were checking Wikipedia for species names, they had accepted the current scientific analysis of nature. It would thus be hard to do the kind of research Harold Conklin did in his dissertation “The Relation of Hanunoo Culture to the Plant World” (1955), where he studied the mismatches between scientific botany circa 1955 and Hanunoo botany. Nonetheless, SEEDIQ ETHNIC PLANTS is a rich source for study: 1. It contains technical neologisms like mttru hmru wasaw, literally leaves that grow in threes, a translation of "trifoliate." This is not to say that these neologisms have become part of Seediq, for they are found nowhere else, but they could be. 2. The book is also a cultural history of the Seediq encounter with modernity, including attempts to get rich, sometimes with government assistance, planting lemongrass, cedar, cassava, shiitake, and plums. 3. It contains interesting examples of censorship from Seediq to Mandarin. For example, Rubus rosifolius, a kind of raspberry, is like viagra, helping men get erections and ejaculate prodigeous quantities of semen, but the Chinese only says that they are, in my English translation, “particularly beneficial to men.” 4. In their introduction they demonstrate a self-consciousness about traditional knowledge that their ancestors would not have had. They note patterns in naming, such as that the name often includes the part used, or that the name specifies the use, for instance poisoning. They also note that relations between plants were compared to relations of kinship. Useless plants were outside this kinship nomenclature and were called monkey plants, because - they claim - a monkey is inedible and untamable. They could have done more to share the product of their with the world. They didn’t have an extra copy for me; I had to scan one at the local printer. It isn’t available in any library besides the one at the Seediq development office in Puli, Taiwan. But I have more than enough material to meet my research objectives and write articles for submission to academic journals; the first has been submitted, and another is in preparation and should be done by mid-July. I have others on the back burner.

rows: Seediq people have translated traditional knowledge of plants into two Master's theses in Chinese and/or Seediq as well as a bilingual (Chinese / Seediq) book entitled Seediq Ethnic Plants that was funded by the county government. The thesis is descriptive, while the book includes cursory ethnobotanical descriptions of plants in different categories.

One of the theses is structured like a typical ethnobotanical thesis, with statistical figures demonstrating to what extent ethnobotanical knowledge is gendered, specific to a certain place, or specific to a certain generation. The other thesis was all ethnobotanical descriptions, in both Seediq and Chinese. The book contains not only ethnobotanical descriptions but also morphological descriptions, that were translated from Chinese into Seediq. Sometimes the descriptions touch on ecological relationships, too, for instance, that muntjacs (a prey animal) like to eat the acorns of certain oaks. There was no sustained treatment of sustainability, only mention. The plants were categorized into hunting, weaving, etc. plants. There is indeed description of ritual use and of esoteric knowledge; but sometimes material that the ethnobotanists felt would reflect badly on them was not translated into Chinese. There were signs of translation, mostly lexical: the Seediq are introducing technical terms into their language through translation.

The autoethnobotanists got encouragement, guidance, and funding from academics and officials. They balanced formal description and practical use, but in a very cursory fashion; one could write a book about ramie, but the studies I looked at attempted to be all-inclusive. Occasionally they referred to a native typology that was supposedly different from the current scientific one; the Seediq claim they have many terms for types of ramie that are not recognized as subspecies by scientists. The pattern depended upon the kind of plant. Entries about plants that could be made into toys stated how children played with them. Most entries featured scientific / cultural description, as well as photographs. Autoethnobotanists took responsibility for certain categories and then wrote descriptions in their own dialects. They consulted village experts, showing them pictures of plants and asking them about them at home, rather than in the field.

All three of the autoethnobotanies I studied included lists of textual resources. The two theses included bibliographies and in-text citations, while the book listed reference books at the back. They consulted recent ethnobotanies, for a comparative perspective within Taiwan. They consulted Wikipedia and fieldguides, and while they occasionally translated whole sentences from Mandarin to Seediq, they mostly translated vocabulary. There was a group review process, during which they reviewed each other’s work and commented. They are worried more about cultural sustainability than ecological sustainability. As for dissemination, the Seediq autoethnobotanists are not actively marketing this book. But they are trying to disseminate the traditional knowledge it is about through the innovative Master's program at Providence University (which I enrolled in for my fieldwork), in which students learn, for instance, to process ramie into yarn and then weave it into garments.

I found no similar examples of bilingual autoethnobotanical texts in the Austronesian sphere. I have however discovered comparative cases in Thailand and Tanzania, which I will compare with the Seediq case in an article for Multilingua. As for lessons that can be drawn, Taiwan has successfully produced autoethnobotanical MA theses. It can do better to fund autoethnobotanical books. If a government agency is going to fund the production of a book, it needs to provide adequate funding, and should require proper publication. The book I looked at, SEEDIQ ETHIC PLANTS, was self-published cheaply, and is not available in the national library system. This is regrettable.

My approach to the interlingual, intralingual, and intermodal "translation" of traditional knowledge is innovative in translation studies. I am sure that concerns about sustainability motivate scholars, but translating cultural knowledge into a discursive form does not guarantee that it is culturally sustainable, because living tacit knowledge does not take that form in people's minds. As for insights into sustainability, the lifestyle Seediq autoethnobotanists describe in SEEDIQ ETHNIC PLANTS is more sustainable, and in their introduction they lament the decline in biodiversity in and around their communities due to overdevelopment; yet they themselves live a modern lifestyle of cars and smartphones.

13602221.label: Major findings and research outcome
13602221.value: 1. In being bilingual, the book Seediq Plants is a one of a kind in Taiwan, as is one of the Master's theses, which was written by my classmate in the innovative program in Indigenous cultural heritage at Providence University. 2. The production values of the book are poor, and no effort has been made to disseminate it; it is a "tea-table book." Yet the knowledge that it contains is being transferred in a lot greater detail in the courses offered through the Providence University program. Still, there is a lot of room for improvement: funding bodies should provide adequate funding to do a professional job, and require proper publication. 3. Autoethnobotanical translators claimed to translate from Seediq into Chinese, but given that their Seediq plant descriptions include a lot of technical description and that all of the books in the reference list are in Chinese, I am certain they are also translating from Chinese into Seediq. In doing so they are filling in gaps in their language. At least, they are doing so on paper; the lexical innovations in the book have not spread into the everyday use of the language to my knowledge. 4. There are, however, passages that are written in Seediq but are not being translated into Chinese. These are not passages to do with traditional taboos; the autoethnobotanical translators has no qualms revealing once esoteric knowledge to a general audience. Rather they are passages to do with sex, body parts, and bodily functions that might create a negative impression in a general audience. I would describe this as reputation management; Seediq autoethnobotanical translators are doing a kind of Public Relations work. It might be argued that by self-publishing and failing to get the book into the national library system, they are making sure that nobody could possibly get the wrong impression; but it also means that almost nobody hears about their autoethnobotanical work. 5. The autoethnobotanical translation I studied was not just about "traditional knowledge." In part it is a social history of the Seediq encounter with colonial modernity. Some of the descriptions of Seediq plants are of exotic plants, which the Seediq could not have started using until the 20th century. In fact, sometimes the descriptions of the Seediq plants include information about cash crops, for instance, shitake mushrooms and peaches, planted in specific decades in the second half of the 20th century.

13602221.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13602221.value: Further development of the research would be comparative, within Taiwan, within Austronesia, or around the world. I have written up/am writing up the results of my case study and will have presented them at five conferences (by the end of July, 2024) in both ethnobotany and translation; I have submitted three substantial articles, one article arguing against Karen Bennett's concept of "knowledge translation" in The Translator. I am writing another article for Multilingua in which I compare the Seediq case of SEEDIQ ETHNIC PLANTS with analogues in Thailand and Tanzania that I have found in the literature. I am planning a third that features an autoethnobotanist. I will seek collaboration with other scholars. I will also reflect my findings about autoethnobotany as translation to the autoethnobotanical translators themselves, partly as a way of giving something back by making them more self-conscious about the importance of translation to cultural preservation or revitalization. My autoethnobotanical translation research informs my new research project, the ecotranslation of Sinophone cities; ecotranslators in a city like Hong Kong often include ethnobotanical information about the ways in which their Hakka, for instance, ancestors, made use of plants when they were pioneering in the hills.

13602221.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13602221.value: Elders who once practiced sustainable traditional lifestyles of hunting, gathering, and planting are passing away. Their languages are passing away, too; Seediq, the language I study, is a grandmother tongue. Meanwhile, most young people in Taiwan or Hong Kong (or any number of places) spend many waking hours in front of a screen, paying almost no attention to the natural environment, at a time when biodiversity and stability in ecosystems around the world are threatened. Autoethnobotanical minority translation is a response to these concerns about the decline in cultural and biological diversity and the impoverishment of experience. Autoethnobotanists are translating traditional knowledge into minority languages, for their children and grandchildren to consult, and majority languages, for a larger audience. Their children and grandchildren mostly live modern lifestyles, and know as much about ramie and millet cultivation and preparation as you or me. But partly due to autoethnobotanical translation, some of them are getting motivated to learn about how their ancestors lived. We can learn from them, too. Autoethnobotanical translation is hardly an adequate response to threats to diversity, but it can help raise awareness in the general public about alternative lifestyles that are more connected to nature and more sustainable.

13602721.label: Project Title(Chinese)
13602721.value: 1949年後中國電影中的民族與生態

13602721.label: Project Objectives
13602721.value: The proposed project will address the gaps and oversights in the literature on the importance of ethnicity in Chinese ecocinema. Ethnicity is a very important concern of Chinese cinema; indeed, films that address issues related to ethnic minorities constitute a special genre in China, imbued with political significance. However, research on Chinese ecocinema pays little attention to ethnicity, and research on Chinese ethnic films has little to say about ecological issues. The proposed project will fill this gap. The proposed project will investigate the theoretical underpinnings of the complex and manifold relationships between ethnicity and ecology in Chinese cinema. To do so, the project will study four periods—the 1950s, the 1960s, the New Era, and the post-New Era—during which the concepts of ethnicity and ecology were used to represent and articulate a notion of “China.” The first article arising from this research will investigate the ways nature and landscape were constructed in Chinese ethnic cinema as part of the nation-building exercise in the early socialist period. Of particular importance will be the roles played by the ethnic landscape in China’s search in the 1950s for a “national style” (minzu xingshi) of artistic representation, and how this use of the landscape was connected to the construction of a Chinese nation, espousing the principle of “unity with diversity.” The second article will examine how a radical socialist laboring subject was built through interaction with nature during the socialist period, and how the period’s cinema represented this process. Two issues will be addressed: 1) China’s “war against nature,” and 2) the “greening” of nature. The article will address the following questions. What kind of socialist laboring subject was formed in the process of greening or de-greening nature? How was ethnicity subsumed into this socialist, class-based subject? How did trans-ethnic labor come to shape a “second nature” through its interaction with nature? The third article will explore how, within a framework of depictions of issues of ethnicity, early postsocialist and New Era films combine representations of class struggle with the discourses around environmental protection that were popular at the time. This article will examine the haphazard use of ecocritical discourse in these films within the larger context of cultural ambivalence and ambiguity regarding both ethnic identity and environmental politics. The fourth article will study both post-New Era and more recent films. It will articulate how these two groups of films differ in their representations of the reconstituted relationship between China’s ethnic minorities and Han majority in terms of views on nature. How does transnational filmmaking in a postsocialist condition reshape people’s ecological awareness, and how is nationalism in a globalized world refashioned through an ethnic eco-consciousness? As a final outcome, this project will build a constructive dialogue with global ecocinema scholarship to define Chinese minzu ecocinema, its unique cinematic features and how these issues can be carried forward into wider interdisciplinary discourses and into global ecocinema studies. The study of global ecocinema is marked by its international scope and wide-ranging coverage of issues relevant to ecocriticism. While Third World cinema is gradually being brought under the purview of global ecocinema, Chinese cinema is increasingly regarded as a peripheral, albeit significant, topic. Similarly, ethnicity in Chinese cinema is taken as important but supplementary. In a way, therefore, ethnicity in Chinese ecocinema is doubly marginalized. Recent English-language studies help to address this imbalance, but they remain rather preliminary. There are still huge lacunae in East–West comparative studies of ethnicity/race/nationality in relation to ecology and cinema. The proposed series of articles will strengthen scholarship in this area by demonstrating the changing aspects of Chinese ethnicity in global ecocinema. The articles will be of significance not only to scholars of China but also to discourses in ecocriticism more broadly.

13602721.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13602721.value: The proposed project will explore the relationships between ethnicity and ecology in Chinese cinema since 1949, leading to four scholarly articles that will form the basis of a monograph draft. Examining the representations of nature, landscape, labor, and environmental problems in ethnic films made in different historical periods since the establishment of the People’s Republic of China (PRC), this project will tease out the complex ways in which ecology has engaged with ethnicity in articulating a “new China” since 1949. Each article will provide an in-depth study of the engagement between ecology and representations of ethnicity in each period. Taken together, they will inform each other and illuminate the larger picture of environmental engagement in modern Chinese film history. The proposed project will belong to the burgeoning field of ecocinema studies, which provides many insights into cinematic representations of ecological issues. Scholars study ecocinema using a variety of approaches, including feminist, postcolonial, and formal approaches. However, ecocinema is rarely addressed from an ethnic studies perspective. Since the late 2000s, scholars in North America have begun to pay attention to issues of ethnicity in ecocriticism, raising awareness of the importance of building more ecologically just communities on national, regional, and global levels. However, while Chinese cinema uses representations of ethnic minorities to both manifest ecological concerns and assert national features, there is a glaring dearth of studies of ethnicity in relation to Chinese ecocriticism in general and Chinese ecocinema in particular. This is mainly due to the difficulty of articulating “minzu” (race, ethnicity and nationality) in English, given the special historical development, political agendas and cultural connotations of minzu in the Chinese context. The proposed project will address these gaps in the literature. The articles generated from the project will engage on a theoretical level with how ethnicity is fashioned in Chinese ecocinema. Chinese and Western theories will be positioned in dialogue to form a dynamic understanding of the relationship between ethnicity and ecocinema. An examination of the practices of ethnic filmmaking across the four periods of PRC film history will demonstrate the specific ways in which ethnicity and ecology have informed, permeated and struggled against each other when situating China as a multiethnic nation. This study will reveal the unique critical tensions that distinguish Chinese ecocinema from other national ecocinemas, and will enter into dialogue with ecocinema scholarship across the world. 本項研究將考察1949年後中國電影中民族與生態的關係。預期成果為四篇相關學術論文，遠景目標為以此為基礎完成一部相關學術專著論稿。我將梳理中華人民共和國成立後的不同歷史時期中，自然、風景、勞動以及環境等問題在電影作品中的不同呈現方式，以求發掘生態與民族的互動關係在構建“新中國”的過程中起到怎樣的作用。每一篇論文將集中考察一個特定歷史時期中生態與民族的關係問題，它們將相互燭照，共同構成當代中國電影史中有關生態環境議題的圖景。 該項目的背景是當前方興未艾的“生態電影研究”。這一領域為生態議題的電影視覺呈現提供諸多洞見，學者亦從不同理論視角來討論生態電影，包括女性主義、後殖民以及形式主義等不一而足。但少有學者從民族或種族的角度切入這一話題。 自21世紀第一個十年後期始，有北美學者開始關注生態批評中的種族問題，以圖提醒人們在國家、地區和全球等各層面，建設更具生態公平正義的社群之重要性。在中國，雖然電影作品不乏對少數民族的表現，並以此來介入生態和國族議題，但對此問題的深入探討卻一直相當缺乏。其中一個重要原因是，在不同語境中對“民族”這一話語的討論有一定困難。中文中的“民族”對應英文中相關卻又不同的概念，如race, ethnicity and nationality等；在中國，特定的歷史、政治和文化使得“民族”具有相當複雜的含義。 本項計劃將正視這一困難。我將首先從理論上分析“民族”是如何在中國少數民族電影中展現的。在此，中國文論與西方理論將被置於有效的對話之中，以圖達成對此議題的較為全面的理解。四篇論文將仔細考察中華人民共和國不同時期的少數民族電影具體實踐，力圖說明民族與生態是如何相互影響、滲透和角力，構建作為多元一體的多民族的國家。 本項研究將展現中國生態電影不同於其他國族生態電影之特色，並與國際生態電影研究展開對話。

13604821.label: Project Title(Chinese)
13604821.value: 燕京，嶺南，匹茲堡：楊慶堃與中國社會學的跨國歷史

13604821.label: Project Objectives
13604821.value: There are four broad objectives of the proposed project: i) Historical: to examine the life and works of C.K. Yang, with reference to his relationship with Fei Xiaotong and other major figures in modern Chinese sociology; and to reconsider the history and development of Chinese sociology from the perspective of Sino-American and transnational academic exchanges in the twentieth century, of which Yang constituted an indispensable nodal point ii) Theoretical: to delineate the dynamics of knowledge circulation and production that are at work in shaping C.K. Yang’s intellectual biography and the trajectory of Chinese sociology; and in more general terms, to inquire how institutional positions and scholarly networks served to enhance and/or hinder the assimilation of intellectual currents and the development of academic discipline iii) Comparative: to articulate the distinctive patterns in the Chinese reception of Western sociological thought, by highlighting its traditional dependence on the funding supports of American foundations and the liaising efforts of émigré Chinese scholars like C.K. Yang, and to compare these patterns with the national development of sociology elsewhere in the world iv) Reflexive: to rethink the present situation and future direction of Chinese sociology by relating to its pasts, by problematizing those moments when possibilities of alternative development were sidestepped in favor of dominant trends, as with C.K. Yang’s sophisticated albeit largely forgotten version of community studies and functionalist sociology, compared to the canonical stature reserved for Fei Xiaotong and his works

13604821.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13604821.value: Amnesia is not merely an individual symptom; the discipline of sociology has a remarkable record of forgetfulness towards some of its finest minds (Law and Lybeck 2015). A case in point is C.K. Yang (Yang Ching-Kun, Yang Qingkun), an eminent but understudied figure in twentieth-century Chinese sociology. Yang’s presence could be strongly felt in every major chapter in the history of Chinese sociology, but his influences were often exercised in a subsidiary and long-term fashion. To start with, Yang was an early member of the “Yenching School” of Chinese sociology. Fei Xiaotong, his fellow classmate in Yenching University, was arguably the most renowned Chinese sociologist to date. Unlike Fei’s classic studies of rural Chinese society and culture, Yang adopted the human ecology approach in analyzing the market institutions in Chinese village. This innovative, groundbreaking study came to fruition only when it served as a source of inspiration for subsequent studies of the Chinese city and its spatial and social structure. After obtaining his PhD in Michigan, Yang returned to Guangzhou to reform the sociology department in Lingnan University. But he began to exercise more visible influences only after leaving his hometown and teaching at Pittsburgh. In 1979, Fei Xiaotong sought Yang’s supports in reestablishing Chinese sociology after almost three decades of suspension. Thanks to his university position and personal connections, Yang mobilized generous funding and notable scholars to deliver intensive summer classes and train up a new generation of sociologists in mainland China. Together with his colleagues and former students at Pittsburgh, Yang built the sociology departments first in the Chinese University of Hong Kong and later in Zhongshan University. On top of institution building, Yang was a reputable scholar. His notion of diffuseness remained an indispensable reference in any sociological discussion of Chinese religion. Implicit in his works was a theory of institution, culture and social change that entailed a creative appropriation of structural-functionalism and modernization theory. The disparity between Yang’s huge impacts and relative obscurity requires an explanation. This project seeks to examine C.K. Yang’s life and works, specifically to reconstruct the historical contexts and sociological conditions underpinning his pivotal role and subordinate status in Chinese sociology. By charting Yang’s efforts to mediate between Chinese, American and international sociologies, a broader aim of this project is to delineate the dynamics of knowledge production and circulation, and offer an instructive case study in the transnational history of sociology and social science. 健忘症不僅僅是一種個人症狀；社會學對其最優秀的人物有著頗顯著的遺忘記錄，其中一個典型的例子是楊慶堃。作為二十世紀中國社會學的傑出人物，楊氏並未獲得充分的研究。在中國社會學史的每一個重要篇章中，都能強烈地感受到楊慶堃的存在，但他的影響往往是以一種不明顯和長線的方式發揮的。首先，楊慶堃是中國社會學「燕京學派」的早期成員。他在燕京大學的同班同學費孝通，可以說是迄今為止最著名的中國社會學家。與費孝通對中國鄉村社會和文化的經典研究不同，楊慶堃在分析中國鄉村的市場制度時，採用了人文區位學的方法。這項嶄新和開創性的研究，只有在它成為後來對中國城市及其空間和社會結構研究的靈感泉源時，才取得了相應的成果。 在密西根大學獲得博士學位後，楊慶堃回到廣州，在嶺南大學的社會學系進行改革。但他直到離開家鄉並在匹茲堡大學任教後，才開始發揮更明顯的影響。1979年，費孝通尋求楊慶堃的支援，在中國社會學停頓近三十年後，重新建立這門學科。受惠於他在大學的地位和人脈網絡，楊慶堃動員了慷慨的資助和著名的學者，在中國大陸開設密集的暑期班，培養新一代的社會學家。楊慶堃與他在匹茲堡的同事和學生一起，首先在香港中文大學，其後在中山大學分別建立和發展了社會學系。在制度建設以外，楊慶堃是一位具國際聲望的學者。他提出的「擴散性」概念，在任何關於中國宗教的社會學討論中，都是不可缺少的參考架構。楊氏的作品隱含著一種關於制度、文化和社會變遷的理論，那是建基於他對結構-功能主義和現代化理論的創造性挪用。 楊慶堃的重大影響，對比他並未獲得應有的重視，是一個需要作出解釋的反差現象。本項目旨在研究楊慶堃的生平和著作，特別是透過重建他在中國社會學中的關鍵作用與及從屬地位，探討背後所依據的歷史背景和社會學條件。本研究的一個更廣泛目標，是通過描繪楊慶堃遊走在中國、美國和國際社會學之間所作出的貢獻，嘗試勾勒出知識生產和流通的動態過程，並為社會學和社會科學的跨國歷史，提供一項具啟發性的案例研究。
