15303521.label: Major findings and research outcome
15303521.value: To address the objectives set in the proposal, we explored the physical mechanisms of bound states in the continuum (BICs) and leveraged them to design and realize various metasurfaces for applications requiring strong field enhancement, such as harmonic generation. During this exploration, several key findings were obtained and published. Work 1 revealed that reducing the structural height of metallic nanoarrays induces a transition from localized surface plasmon resonances (LSPRs) to nonlocal surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs). This geometric dimensionality reduction dramatically decreases intrinsic metallic loss, expanding mode volume, and transforming bright radiative modes into dark trapped SPPs. As a result, the resonant quality factor increases by nearly two orders of magnitude, providing a general design principle to overcome the intrinsic Q-factor limit of plasmonic structures. Work 2 demonstrated that dielectric metasurfaces exploiting BICs can achieve ultra-high-Q resonances for nonlocal Huygens metalenses. By optimizing structural asymmetry and leveraging the generalized Kerker effect, the design reached a Q-factor of ~10^4 and transmission efficiency up to 55%, exceeding theoretical limits. The metalens exhibited robust wavelength selectivity, efficient focusing, and rotational tolerance, establishing a practical platform for narrowband imaging, nonlinear optics, quantum light sources, and advanced wavefront control applications. Work 3 focused on metallic metasurfaces combining nonlocal effects with asymmetric split-ring geometries. The interplay between local dipole and quasi-BIC modes enabled strong spatial scattering contrast and pixel-level edge emission without introducing additional defects. This work highlights the potential of nonlocal metasurfaces for flexible spatial modulation, enhanced light–matter interactions, and the design of novel optical devices relying on engineered scattering and emission properties. Work 4 presented a hybrid lithium niobate (LN) metasurface with quasi-BIC resonances for enhanced nonlinear optical conversion. By integrating subwavelength amorphous silicon nanorods on X-cut LN thin films, the structure achieved high-Q resonances with strong field confinement aligned along the LN z-axis, maximizing the nonlinear coefficient d33. Experimental SHG measurements confirmed a significant enhancement compared to unpatterned films, demonstrating the role of quasi-BICs in boosting nonlinear efficiency. This design offers a compact, efficient platform for harmonic generation and paves the way for integrated nonlinear photonic devices for quantum light generation, frequency combs, and advanced nanophotonics. Overall, these works provide fundamental insights into BIC physics, demonstrate general design strategies for high-Q and low-loss metasurfaces, and establish practical platforms for nonlinear optics, quantum photonics, and other applications relying on strong light-matter interaction.

15303521.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15303521.value: The demonstrated BIC-based metasurfaces offer broad opportunities for advancing photonics that demand strong field enhancement. Future developments include extending designs to multifunctional or reconfigurable metasurfaces, integrating emerging materials such as 2D materials or nonlinear crystals, and exploring applications in nonlinear optics, quantum light generation, and frequency conversion. Systematic optimization may further increase Q-factors, efficiency, and sensitivity for practical deployment in imaging, sensing, and integrated photonic devices. We propose to combine theoretical modeling, computational design, and precision nanofabrication to realize next-generation BIC-enhanced metasurfaces. This includes iterative simulation-experiment cycles to optimize geometry and material parameters, characterization of linear and nonlinear responses, and exploration of reconfigurable or multifunctional functionalities. The approach aims to translate fundamental BIC physics into versatile, high-performance photonic platforms suitable for both fundamental studies and technological applications.

15303521.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15303521.value: The proposed research focuses on how to confine light in ultra-thin and compact photonic devices called metasurfaces to achieve strong field enhancement. To realize this goal, the studies explore the underlying physics of bound states in the continuum (BICs) and use this mechanism to guide the design of various metasurfaces. By confining light into tiny regions and reducing losses, these devices enable extremely sharp optical resonances and enhanced light–matter interactions. This opens up applications such as ultra-precise imaging, compact devices for generating new colors of light, efficient nonlinear optical processes like frequency doubling, and potentially quantum light sources. The work provides both a fundamental understanding of light confinement and practical strategies for building high-performance, miniaturized photonic devices, offering versatile tools for future technologies in sensing, communications, displays, and advanced optical research.

15303921.label: Realisation of objectives
15303921.value: There are two objectives in this project, and both the two objectives have been 100% achieved. 1. At process scale, developing a high-accuracy computational model for the simulation and optimization of the valorization processes for waste-to-X from poultry litter. As for objective 1, this project has developed multiple processes including conventional and plasma gasification, supercritical gasification, and pyrolysis, etc. These primary biomass (poultry litter) valorization processes have been further extended to secondary and tertiary processes like anaerobic digestion+ CHP (P1), anaerobic digestion + CHP+ hydrotreating + hydrocracking (P2), gasification +CHP+SOFC (P3), gasification +FT synthesis + hydrocracking (P4), gasification + methanol synthesis (P5) and pyrolysis + hydrotreating + hydrocracking (P6) at downstream to improve the overall process sustainability. Apart from this process development, these objectives were achieved through the development and integration application of advanced AI, machine learning (ML), and hybrid modeling techniques like High dimensional model representation (HDMR) to simulate, predict, and optimize complex thermochemical conversion processes. Neural networks, ensemble regressor, and gradient boost-based AI-models have been developed to predict H2, CH4, CO2, and CO in syngas produced by gasification process. By using different dataset combinations, the study aimed to find the most reliable prediction model with higher R² and lower MSE, MAE, and MAPE. The XGB model outperformed others, achieving coefficients of determination between 0.85 and 0.95 with low error metrics. The results based on AI models reveal that hydrogen, methane, and carbon monoxide mole fractions can be increased by using biomass with higher hydrogen and oxygen content and by increasing temperature and biomass residence time in gasification. The Aspen Plus-based analysis of Gasification to SOFC and CHP demonstrates a highly efficient tri-generation system for biomass waste valorization. Process optimization identified ideal parameters at 600°C in gasification, 0.25-0.33 biomass to air ratio (BMR), and 850-950°C SOFC temperature. The XGBoost model confirmed high prediction accuracy (R² > 0.97), with BMR being the most influential input. The optimized process shows significant improvements in exergy efficiency than standard gasification and an improvement of 6% of DME production efficiency. Economically, the optimized process is also better, with a shorter payback period and higher economic feasibility even at a lower process efficiency (70%). The optimized process excels in exergy and economic performances. Furthermore, the environmental analysis confirms that producing DME from syngas (generated by PL gasification) is more favorable than that from coal. As a whole of objective 1, this project has (i) determined the training database for machine learning/deep learning, achieving data process and cleaning, and building both physical models and black box models for process simulation and optimization; (ii) developed thermodynamic equilibrium /kinetic models for modelling the upgrading processes for poultry litter valorization; (iii) developed the mechanisms-based Aspen Plus models for the simulation of the upgrading processes; and (iv) developed the process optimization model for determining the optimal operating conditions. In summary, this project has successfully developed high-accuracy computational models by creating a methodology that integrates process simulation with advanced AI/ML surrogate models (such as deep learning and gradient boosting models) for objective 1. This approach can help to achieve precise prediction of key output metrics (e.g., syngas yield and hydrogen production) and the efficient optimization of process parameters for the thermochemical valorization of poultry litter. Therefore, this project has successfully achieved objective 1. 2. At life-cycle scale, developing a multi-criteria decision-making method for prioritizing the waste-to-X routes from life cycle perspective. As for objective 2, this project has developed novel life cycle sustainability Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) frameworks that integrate life-cycle thinking, sustainability assessment, and advanced MCDM methods to evaluate and rank different waste valorization pathways. The LCA was used to evaluate those environmental factors of those processes designed in objective 1. Based on that, advanced decision-making technique of Interval Valued Fermatean Fuzzy with integrated CODAS have been developed for the optimum waste valorization process selection. This framework is specifically designed to handle the complexity and inherent uncertainty in sustainability data and expert opinion by incorporating Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) for weights calculation, Interval Valued Fermatean Fuzzy Sets (IVFFS) to effectively handle the ambiguity and imprecision in qualitative judgments, Entropy method for weights calculation in an objective way, and CODAS (Combinative Distance-based Assessment) to perform a robust ranking of different waste valorization alternatives based on the weighted criteria (AHP and entropy). A robust and novel MCDM methodology was successfully developed by addressing the major concern of expert’s biasness through fair expert selection criteria and weights calculation through entropy weighting method which does not involve the opinions of the experts. This research project has successfully established a novel and comprehensive life cycle sustainability decision-support framework, precisely designed to address the intricate and multifaceted challenges inherent in sustainable waste valorization planning, particularly under conditions of profound technological and market uncertainties. The utilization of IVFFS-CODAS with Dombi operator integration reveals gasification as the most sustainable process across economic, environmental, technological, and social-governance criteria, compared with HTG, which ranks as the least sustainable while the pyrolysis secures the 2nd rank, with anaerobic digestion following in 3rd place. The basis of this methodological advancement is a rigorous and two-tiered analytical approach that seamlessly integrates advanced process modeling with multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA). The first tier involves systematic enhancement of waste conversion technologies by initiating with thermochemical processes such as pyrolysis and thermal gasification. These primary pathways were upgraded and refined into more complex industrial systems, namely more sophisticated secondary and tertiary configurations, with each iteration being subjected to an extensive sustainability assessment. To comprehensive analysis of these processes, sustainability analysis of these processes has also been performed in terms of energy, exergy, economics, environment, and safety (4E, 1S). This assessment is grounded in a life-cycle perspective and standardized through comprehensive 4E and 1S including detailed evaluations of Energy efficiency, Exergy (or thermodynamic quality), Economic viability, Environmental impact, and critical Safety protocols to generate a robust and consistent dataset for comparison. To synthesize this complex, multi-dimensional data into actionable intelligence, the second tier of our framework introduces a sophisticated hybrid decision-making model. This model innovatively employs the Best-Worst Method (BWM) to structure the problem and weigh the relative importance of the 4E & 1S criteria, which is then integrated with other MCDA techniques to calculate a unified, dimensionless Sustainability Index score for each potential waste-to-X route. This index provides a powerful, transparent, and scientifically defensible metric, enabling the clear and objective prioritization of technologies based on a holistic understanding of their sustainability performances, thereby ensuring that selected pathways are not only technologically feasible but also economically sound, environmentally superior, and operationally safe. Therefore, objective 2 has also been successfully achieved. This project has successfully solved the problems existing in the previous work by overcoming a number of significant hurdles, including complex computational model convergence issues, dynamic simulation instabilities, and the inherent uncertainties associated with subjective or incomplete life-cycle inventory data. The outcomes including the novel integrated methodology and the significant findings derived from its application constitute a substantial contribution to sustainable poultry litter valorization. The rigor and innovation of this research have been formally recognized through the outcomes published in several high-impact and top-tier peer-reviewed scientific journals, and 23 peer reviewed papers have been presented in Part C of this report for references.

15303921.label: Major findings and research outcome
15303921.value: There are 23 peer reviewed papers published at top tier journals along with 3 conference presentations. Overall summary of this project is given below: This study conducts a comprehensive evaluation of sustainable biomass (poultry litter) waste valorization pathways using an integrated analytical framework combining Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats (SWOT) along with a comprehensive 4E+1S (environmental, economic, energy, exergy, and safety) sustainability assessment. Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) results reflect that thermal conversion technologies like gasification and pyrolysis exhibit better environmental and sustainability performance as compared to conventional land disposal and biological processes such as anaerobic digestion, especially at commercial scale. A detailed investigation of supercritical water Hydrothermal Gasification (HTG) employed artificial intelligence-driven optimization, with the Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) algorithm emerging as the most accurate predictive tool for syngas composition. Optimal operating conditions were identified at approximately 540 °C and 25 MPa, yielding maximum hydrogen and methane production alongside a process energy efficiency of 61% and production costs at least 10% lower than fossil-derived steam. LCA results show that HTG method is environmentally friendly as compared to direct land disposal, especially in terms of human health, ecosystem quality and climate change. The research further proposes and optimizes innovative tri-generation systems integrating biomass gasification with solid oxide fuel cells (SOFC) and combined heat and power (CHP) units. One advanced configuration achieved a 34.6% improvement in exergy efficiency relative to simple gasification process. The PL to DME process is economically feasible and the IRR of the optimized process varies from 26.8 to 3.3% when the process efficiency drops from 100 to 70%, whereas the base process (no AI-optimization) is not feasible when the process efficiency is <90%. Similarly, an optimized plasma-assisted gasification tri-generation process increased dimethyl ether (DME) yield by 6%, attaining a sustainability index of 2.509 and an economically attractive payback period of 7.2 years. A techno-economic, environment, energy, exergy, social, and governance multi-criteria decision-making method based on Interval Valued Fermatean Fuzzy Sets (IVFFS) has been applied reflecting gasification as the highest-ranked sustainable process, followed by pyrolysis and HTG. However, a dedicated safety evaluation identified HTG as the safest thermal option with the lowest risk profile, primarily due to its comparatively moderate operating temperatures. Finally, the primary gasification-based process is selected as the most sustainable technology for large-scale biomass waste valorization at current stage.

15303921.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15303921.value: This research provides a framework for the design of circular bio-economies. Future work will focus on scaling the optimized processes from simulation to pilot and commercial scales, validating their techno-economic feasibility in real-world settings. A key vision is the development of an integrated AI-driven digital twin platform that dynamically controls biorefineries, using real-time data to maximize product yield and minimize environmental impact. Furthermore, research will expand to include a wider variety of mixed waste feedstocks and explore the catalytic synthesis of higher-value chemicals beyond syngas and DME, such as sustainable aviation fuels. This research is a foundation for future smart, waste-to-energy networks. The immediate course of action is a three-phase plan. First, PI will seek industrial partnerships to fund and co-develop a pilot-scale gasification plant, using the validated models for its design. Second, PI will initiate a Life Cycle Costing and social acceptance study to complement the existing technical and environmental analyses, providing a truly holistic sustainability assessment for stakeholders and policymakers. Finally, the findings will be synthesized into a comprehensive policy white paper to promote for the support mechanisms identified in the research, such as subsidies and green investment, bridging the gap between scientific innovation and practical implementation.

15303921.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15303921.value: This research focuses on developing sustainable technologies for converting biomass waste, particularly poultry litter, into value-added products rather than disposing of it. By utilizing poultry litter, we can generate clean energy and high-value products. The project aims to simulate and optimize various biomass waste valorization processes using high-accuracy computational models. The life cycle multi-criteria decision-making models will then prioritize these processes. Our objective is to compare different valorization methods and identify the most sustainable options through life cycle sustainability assessments and multi-criteria decision making. The selected technologies will be optimized to enhance their economic, environmental, and social sustainability, promoting their adoption in place of landfilling and incineration. We also used computer models and advanced software to ensure these processes are safe, energy-efficient, and cost-effective. The significance lies in its practical approach to transforming waste into energy and valuable products. By providing a clear framework for companies and governments to implement biomass valorization technologies, we aim to reduce pollution, generate energy, and progress toward a more sustainable future with minimal waste. In addition, this study also has broad impacts by contributing to different SDGs such as SDG 7 (affordable and clean energy) and SDG 11 (sustainable cities and communities).

15304121.label: Project Objectives
15304121.value: To develop functionalized cyclopentadienyl ligand sets for facile reversible redox changes of the ferrocene complexes: We will prepare some defined ferrocenium complexes bearing electron-donating and -withdrawing substituents on the cyclopentadienyl ligands. Their catalytic activity toward intramolecular C-H amidation will be examined. Our goal is to establish a correlation of the catalytic C-H amidation activity with the redox potentials of the ferrocenium complexes. To determine the structure-activity relationship of some defined ferrocene complexes and the electrophilic aminating reagents: We aims to develop a mechanistic model for the nitrene transfer reaction and delineate the desirable steric and electronic properties of the ligands and the reagents for selective transformations. Stoichiometric reactions of the ferrocenium complexes and selected aminating reagent will be investigated in a hope to isolate or trap the reactive nitrene species for characterization. It is expected that good working model can be developed for later stage application. To develop enantioselective amidation reactions based on chiral ferrocene complexes as catalysts: With the working model for the catalytic nitrene transfer reactions being developed, we would pursue the more challenging enantioselective amidation reactions. Conformationally rigid chiral ansa-ferrocene complexes containing tethered bridged chiral cyclopentadienyl moieties will be chosen for this study. We plan to prepare a focus library with range of chiral cyclopentadienyl structures, the chiral landscapes presented by the ligands will be analyzed with reference to the enantioselectivity for designing more effective chiral catalysts.

15304221.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15304221.value: Nucleic acid testing (NAT) is undoubtedly one of the most powerful methods for a wide spectrum of applications such as medical diagnostics and food safety monitoring. The current NAT gold standard is real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR for deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA); reverse transcription-PCR (RT-PCR) for ribonucleic acid (RNA)), which features simultaneous amplification (thermocycling) and detection (fluorescence). Typically, an internal control (a different template than a target template/sequence) is added to the same reaction tube to rule out false negative result (caused by unexpected error(s) in sample preparation, amplification, and/or detection). A valid result must be accompanied by the successful amplification and detection of the internal control. Different fluorescently labeled oligonucleotide detection probes are used to monitor the amplification of the internal control template and target template independently, i.e., multiplex assay. Real-time PCR is mainly performed in centralized laboratories because the instrument is expensive and bulky. Decentralized NAT (e.g., testing at primary doctors' clinics, home, and poultry farms) with low-cost and small-size instrument/setup is highly desired to address the unmet needs. In this regard, colorimetric isothermal nucleic acid amplification assays are the most promising candidates. Among various isothermal amplification techniques, loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP; also RT-LAMP) has great potential to be another gold standard (similar sensitivity and specificity as PCR, yet shorter assay time). To date, several colorimetric LAMP platforms have been developed. However, all of them do not permit the inclusion of an internal control in multiplex format owing to the indirect colorimetric readout schemes (i.e., universal reporter irrespective of the amplified sequences). In this proposed project, our team aims to develop first-of-its-kind multiplex colorimetric LAMP that 2 to 3 different templates can be independently detected in a single reaction tube. A new type of colorimetric reporters is designed, i.e., colored silica nanoparticles with surface-bound polyethylene glycol (PEG)-primer conjugates, the dispersion/precipitation behavior of each colored reporter is correlated with the absence/presence of a specific sequence (complementary to the primer bound on that particular reporter). Over the past few years, our team successfully developed 2 singleplex colorimetric LAMP platforms by using gold nanoparticle-based reporters (one with carboxyl modification and another one with carboxyl and PEG co-modification). Our preliminary data herein with PEG-bound and primer-bound gold nanoparticles provide a solid basis for the rational design of the PEG-primer conjugate-coated colored silica nanoparticles. We believe this new multiplex colorimetric LAMP platform can become the next standard technique for decentralized NAT. 核酸檢測 (NAT) 無疑是醫療診斷和食品安全監測等廣泛應用中最有效的手段之一。目前NAT的金標準是即時定量聚合酶連鎖反應（PCR用於去氧核醣核酸（DNA）和反轉錄PCR（RT-PCR）用於核醣核酸（RNA）），其特點是同時的熱循環擴增和熒光檢測。通常，內源性對照模板（不同於目標模板）會被添加到同一反應管中以排除由樣品製備、擴增和/或檢測中意外錯誤引起的假陰性結果。因而一個有效的檢測結果必須伴隨著內源性對照的成功擴增和檢測。不同熒光標記的寡核苷酸檢測探針被用於獨立監測內源性對照模板和目標模板的擴增，即多重檢測。由於相應儀器昂貴且笨重，即時定量 PCR 主要在中央實驗室裡進行。因此，迫切需要具有低成本和小型儀器/設置特點的分散式 NAT（例如可在家庭醫生診所、家居和家禽場進行測試）以解決未實現的檢測需求。在這方面，比色恆溫核酸擴增檢測是最有希望的候選者。在各種恆溫擴增技術中，恆溫環形核酸增幅法（LAMP或RT-LAMP）因具有與 PCR 相似的靈敏度和特異性以及更短的檢測時間，具有成為另一個金標準的巨大潛力。迄今為止，研究者已經開發出若干比色LAMP檢測平台。然而，由於間接比色的讀出原理，現有平台均不能實現含有內源性對照的多重檢測（即採用了與擴增序列無關的通用指示物）。在本提議項目中，我們團隊旨在開發首創的可在單個反應管中獨立檢測兩到三個不同模板的多重比色 LAMP系統。我們設計了一種新型的比色指示物，即具有表面結合的聚乙二醇（PEG）-引物復合物的有色二氧化硅納米顆粒。每種有色指示物的分散/沉澱行為與特定序列（與結合在特定有色指示物上的引物序列互補）的缺失/存在相關。在過去幾年中，我們團隊通過使用基於金納米顆粒的指示物（一種為羧基修飾，另一種為羧基和PEG共修飾）成功開發了兩種單重比色 LAMP 平台。本文中涉及與引物結合以及與 PEG 結合的金納米顆粒的初步數據為合理設計 PEG-引物復合物修飾的有色二氧化硅納米顆粒提供了堅實的基礎。我們相信這種新型多重比色 LAMP 平台可以成為分散式NAT 的下一個標準技術。

15304721.label: Project Title(Chinese)
15304721.value: 用于求解大規模非凸優化問題的自適應篩法及其在模型壓縮中的應用

15304721.label: Project Objectives
15304721.value: In this project, we will focus on a class of important nonconvex optimization problems with special structures: the regularized composite multi-difference-of-convex (MDC) programming, which includes a broad class of state-of-the-art models in practice as special instances. The goal of this project is to develop efficient algorithms to solve large (huge) scale MDC problems, which can also be expected to solve the MDC programming with cardinality constraints as a natural extension. In order to design efficient and provable algorithms and to release the full power of the big data, we shall investigate and propose efficient and practical dimension reduction techniques for large scale nonconvex optimization models. Specifically, we expect to generalize the adaptive sieving technique, which has been introduced by the PI and his co-author recently for a class of convex sparse optimization problems, to the large scale MDC programming. Considering the special structure of the regularizations involved in MDC programming and other large scale optimization problems with coupled structured sparsity, we shall first investigate the adaptive sieving technique for large (huge) scale convex composite programming with coupled structured sparsity. We shall investigate and propose the adaptive sieving techniques to generate the solution paths of the MDC programming. We shall design efficient algorithms with a sharp convergence guarantee to solve the reduced MDC problems, which are generated by the adaptive sieving techniques. Finally, we expect to develop an efficient and robust software for solving a class of important instances of the MDC programming.

15304721.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15304721.value: 非凸優化模型在大數據时代扮演着非常重要的角色，已在多个應用领域中取得成功。設計具有良好理論保證的高效數值優化算法用于求解大規模（超大規模）的非凸優化模型是一個亟待解決卻又充滿挑戰的研究课题。研究者們普遍認爲求解大規模（超大規模）非凸優化問題的主要難度來自於所求解問題的高維度，在具有良好性質的駐點意義下。現有的大規模非凸優化問題求解算法，例如一階隨機優化算法，主要通過每一步對數據進行小規模隨機采樣，來迭代更新當前的解。然而，解的稀疏性是大規模優化問題的内蘊性質，值得更進一步的研究与探索。因此，爲了設計更加高效、具有收斂性保證的優化求解算法，发挥大數據的真正威力，應該探索更好的方法来直接利用解的稀疏性。在本研究項目中，我們將针对一類大規模 multi-difference-of-convex （MDC）優化問題，研发降维技术以实现高效求解。具體地，本项目计划將由该項目負責人和其合作者提出的一種用於高效求解稀疏凸優化問題的自適應篩法（Adaptive Sieving）拓展到 MDC 優化問題當中。同时，為了高效求解降維后的 MDC优化問題的子問題，本项目將研究基於非光滑稀疏牛頓算法的 Majorization-Minimization (MM) 算法。我們希望所提出的優化算法框架可以求得 MDC 問題的一个具有良好性质的驻点，特别是方向駐點解。此外，本項目所提出的技術可以进一步拓展到求解一類帶有基數約束的 MDC 問題上。本項目的研究成果将对機器學習的模型壓縮和許多具有存儲限制的移動端應用問題具有重要意义。

15304721.label: Realisation of objectives
15304721.value: All the objectives proposed for this research project have been achieved. The main challenge in solving large/huge-scale regularized composite multi-difference-of-convex (MDC) programming is twofold: (i) dimension reduction to identify and retain only the truly relevant variables/structures, and (ii) efficient and reliable solution of the reduced subproblems, supported by sharp convergence guarantees and robust implementations. Eight papers based on the research of this project have been written to address these challenges. Among them, seven papers have been published in top journals/conferences in optimization and data science. The major outcomes corresponding to each objective are summarized below. (1) Objective 1 — Efficient algorithms for large (huge) scale MDC programming. To strengthen the algorithmic foundation needed for large-scale MDC models, we developed and analyzed scalable first-order splitting and proximal-point-type frameworks that can serve as core routines for handling the structured components arising in MDC formulations and their reduced surrogates; in particular, [C8.4] establishes an acceleration mechanism for preconditioned ADMM through a degenerate proximal point mapping viewpoint and proves nonergodic O(1/k) (and even o(1/k)) guarantees for KKT residuals (and objective gaps), while [C8.7] provides ergodic convergence analysis for Peaceman–Rachford splitting with semi-proximal terms, offering a solid theoretical basis for applying PR-type schemes to large convex subproblems encountered in MDC-related procedures. Together with the dimension-reduction and solution-path machinery developed under Objectives 2–3 and the fast reduced-subproblem solvers developed under Objective 4, these results form an end-to-end algorithmic pipeline for efficiently solving large/huge-scale regularized composite MDC instances; moreover, the same pipeline naturally supports extensions with cardinality-type constraints by combining active-structure identification (sieving) with efficient reduced-problem solvers (2) Objective 2 — Dimension reduction techniques for large-scale optimization problems; generalize adaptive sieving to MDC. To address dimension reduction, we developed practical and provable mechanisms that progressively identify active structures and restrict computation to substantially smaller subproblems; specifically, [C8.3] establishes the adaptive sieving framework as a general dimension-reduction strategy for sparse optimization; [C8.2] develops a sieving-based secant/level-set approach for sparse optimization with least-squares constraints where sieving sharply reduces the subproblem size and the analysis supports rapid progress of the root-finding updates; [C8.1] studies a representative model with coupled structured sparsity (exclusive lasso), providing algorithmic insights that are directly relevant when extending sieving ideas to coupled patterns as in MDC regularizations; and [C8.5] investigates random projection for convex clustering with cluster recovery guarantees, complementing sieving by another principled dimension-reduction tool for high-dimensional structured models. (3) Objective 3 — Adaptive sieving techniques to generate solution paths of MDC programming. To enable efficient solution-path generation (e.g., across a range of regularization parameters) for MDC-type models, we developed sieve-based methodologies that reuse identified active structures and solve only a sequence of reduced problems along the path; in particular, [C8.3] provides a framework that supports path computation by stabilizing active sets and reducing dimension across parameter values, and [C8.2] complements this with a path-following/level-set + secant mechanism in which repeated solves are systematically organized, while sieving substantially lowers the per-solve cost and improves overall path efficiency. (4) Objective 4 — Fast solution of reduced subproblems with sharp guarantees; software and implementation. To ensure that the reduced problems produced by sieving can be solved efficiently in practice, we developed algorithms and implementation-oriented techniques that target computational speed, robustness, and provable performance; specifically, [C8.1] develops a dual Newton based proximal point algorithm (PPDNA) that exploits second-order structure for high efficiency on large-scale structured sparse models, making it a strong inner solver for reduced subproblems, [C8.4] provides accelerated schemes with nonergodic O(1/k) and o(1/k) rates for KKT residuals, offering sharp guarantees for key splitting components, and [C9.1] (ICLR) establishes a tight complexity analysis for an inexact stochastic proximal point algorithm, broadening the methodological toolkit toward data-driven and stochastic composite settings. Moreover, [C8.6] delivers an open-source, implementation-oriented solver for large-scale linear programming with extensive benchmarking evidence, providing a concrete software artifact and practical validation of the project’s large-scale algorithmic developments. In our implementation framework, these released solver components (together with the sieving modules and fast reduced-subproblem solvers developed in [C8.1]–[C8.4]) are used to solve representative reduced instances arising from the targeted MDC workflow, thereby providing an efficient and robust software basis for a class of important MDC instances.

15304721.label: Major findings and research outcome
15304721.value: This project developed an end-to-end methodology for large/huge-scale regularized composite multi-difference-of-convex (MDC) programming by addressing two key bottlenecks: (i) dimension reduction to identify and retain only the truly relevant variables/structures, and (ii) fast and reliable solution of the reduced subproblems, supported by sharp convergence guarantees and robust implementations. On dimension reduction, we established adaptive sieving as a practical and provable framework that progressively detects active structures and solves only a sequence of substantially reduced problems ([C8.3]). We further developed a sieving-based secant/level-set methodology for constrained sparse optimization, enabling efficient repeated reduced solves and supporting solution-path computation ([C8.2]). Complementarily, we investigated random projection for convex clustering and proved cluster recovery guarantees, providing another principled reduction mechanism in high-dimensional settings ([C8.5]). On fast reduced-subproblem solvers, we developed both second-order and first-order algorithmic engines. In particular, we developed a dual Newton-based proximal point algorithm (PPDNA) and demonstrated its effectiveness on large-scale structured sparse models (e.g., exclusive lasso), making it a powerful inner solver for reduced subproblems ([C8.1]). From a splitting perspective, by reformulating preconditioned ADMM as a (possibly degenerate) proximal point method, we derived accelerated variants with nonergodic O(1/k) (and even o(1/k)) complexity for KKT residuals (and objective gaps) ([C8.4]), and established ergodic convergence analysis for Peaceman–Rachford splitting with semi-proximal terms ([C8.7]). We also provided a tight complexity analysis for an inexact stochastic proximal point algorithm in stochastic composite optimization, extending the toolkit to data-driven settings ([C9.1]). Finally, we delivered software impact through an open-source, implementation-oriented solver for large-scale linear programming with extensive benchmarking evidence ([C8.6]), which serves as a key computational component in the project’s MDC-oriented workflow.

15304721.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15304721.value: The PI plans to leverage the techniques developed in this project to tackle more challenging problem classes related to MDC programming, such as mixed-integer optimization (MIP) formulations. In particular, we will strengthen the reduced-subproblem engine by integrating the second-order inner solvers and accelerated splitting/proximal-point schemes developed in this project, together with practical stopping and parameter-update rules, and implement these components in a GPU-accelerated manner. This will improve robustness and time-to-solution for the large reduced convex subproblems that arise after dimension reduction in MDC workflows. Since many MDC-related MIP formulations require solving a sequence of closely related reduced subproblems, accelerating and stabilizing this reduced-subproblem engine on GPUs provides a direct path to making such challenging large-scale instances computationally tractable.

15304721.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15304721.value: Many modern data-analysis tasks require solving very large optimization problems where only a small number of variables should be “active” in the final model. This project studies an important family of such problems, called regularized composite multi-difference-of-convex (MDC) programming, which covers many state-of-the-art models used in practice. The main difficulty is scale: directly solving these problems can be too slow when the data dimension is huge. Our research tackles this by (1) developing “dimension reduction” techniques that automatically identify and keep only the variables that truly matter, and (2) designing fast and reliable algorithms to solve the resulting smaller subproblems with provable performance guarantees. The project produced new theory, practical algorithms, and software components, including an open-source solver validated on large benchmark tests. These outcomes make it more feasible to solve large-scale MDC-type models accurately and efficiently, and they provide a foundation for future high-performance solvers for challenging real-world applications in machine learning, signal processing, and model compression.

15304821.value: Prof Leighton, Patrick A. Prof Liao, Jinbao

15304821.label: Project Objectives
15304821.value: Since this project develops and applies mathematical arguments to investigate biologically oriented problems, strong biological justifications are needed in the model formulation and model parameterization parts, as well as proposing the questions under investigation. An extensive review will be performed on the current studies of various physiologically structured models with seasonal effects, as well as updated biological advances on tick ecology. Formulate a physiologically structured model with seasonal effects, in particular, the seasonal diapause. The model will be reduced into a periodic delay integral form, with the aid of general inverse functions, which is suitable for describing population growth of two-stage species. The well-posedness of the model system, in terms of existence and positiveness of solutions, will be established. The basic reproduction number will be determined and the global dynamics of the model will be investigated through developing periodic dynamical system theories for the periodic delay integral equations. The model framework will be justified with field data, in particular: (i) the modeling framework will be extended to be suitable for ticks, in particular, to accommodate more growth stages; and (ii) model simulation with the annual pattern of staged-population sizes and tick distribution will be compared with data collected from field observations to validate theoretical modeling frameworks. Based on the data-validated model, it will be used to address the following ecological problems: (i) the effect of diapause on the tick seasonal patterns in a specific habitat; (ii) the contribution of diapause on the ticks' northward range expansion in eastern Canada; and (iii) possible impacts of climate change on tick seasonality and range distribution.

15304821.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15304821.value: The environment supporting the species growth, especially the climate, is expected to change acceleratingly, which poses important and interesting questions to understand not just how species distribution will adjust, but also whether their population sizes will go up or down. Various theories are based on simple population growth models where all individuals within a population are assumed to be identical. Sometimes, this assumption is oversimplified, as individuals in most populations are distinct from different aspects, such as spatial location, age, body size, sexual maturation and so on. The models, with structured individual states, allow estimating species fitness under novel conditions and predicting the response of species distribution to climate change. Ticks serve as efficient vectors of multiple diseases including Lyme disease and human babesiosis. For example, Lyme disease is regarded as the most frequently reported vector-borne disease of humans in USA and costs estimated USD 712M to 1.3B per year to the healthcare system alone. Due to the important role ticks play in the disease transmission, it is pivotal to understand the tick population dynamics, in particular, to predict the possible northward region expansion under the scenario of climate change. A range of factors regulate the tick population establishment and geographic distribution, including biotic factors and abiotic factors such as climate, in particular temperature and humidity. To fairly describe the tick population dynamics, we should integrate these factors on the tick growth, development, and survival in various stages. In tick ecology, diapause, with greatly reduced or interrupted rates of development and activity, is regarded as the most important strategy to survive through unfavorable seasons in a year. Motivated by tick population growth, the current project is going to propose a physiologically structured population growth model, in the form of a partial differential equation (PDE) with periodic parameters and seasonal diapause, through a delicate balance between biological realism and mathematical tractability. For the ease of mathematical analysis, this PDE will be reformulated into a periodic delay integral equation. Then dynamical system theories will be developed to analyze the derived model. Furthermore, the integral equation will be extended to study the tick population, in terms of tick establishment and tick seasonality. Model parameters will be fitted by realistic data, and the model will be validated to the seasonal patterns of ticks through numerical simulations. 15304821.label: Realisation of objectives
15304821.value: All the objectives outlined in the original proposal have been successfully achieved. Comprehensive literature reviews were conducted, and the latest biological findings were incorporated into model formulation and parameterization. Physiologically structured models with seasonal effects have been developed, rigorously analyzed for well-posedness and global dynamics, and sometimes reduced to a periodic delay integral form. Some models were extended and validated using field data, particularly for tick or mosquito populations, and simulations were compared with observed annual patterns. Finally, the data-validated model was applied to address key ecological questions regarding the effects of diapause, range expansion, and climate change on disease-vector populations. The results from these studies collectively demonstrate the successful fulfillment of all proposed objectives. The following topics have been investigated: (1) The manuscript "A periodic delay differential system for mosquito control with Wolbachia incompatible insect technique" was published in Nonlinear Analysis: Real World Applications 73 (2023) 103867. This study proposed a delayed periodic stage-structured model that incorporates seasonal temperature variations and larval competition. The model differs from existing models by including a density-dependent death rate due to larval competition, which introduces a density-dependent survival probability for larvae. Solution behaviors were explored through dynamical system analysis, and the impacts of seasonal factors were evaluated using numerical simulations; (2) The manuscript "A reaction-diffusion model with spatially inhomogeneous delays" was published online in March 2023 in the Journal of Dynamics and Differential Equations. This study was motivated by spatial heterogeneity in tick population growth, particularly spatially inhomogeneous development delays. It is the first comprehensive study to model and analyze systems with spatially dependent delays. The general approach developed here can be substantially extended to other population dynamic problems; (3) The manuscript "Modeling insect growth regulators for pest management" was published in the Journal of Mathematical Biology in April 2024. This study formulated a mathematical model to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of insect growth regulators (IGRs) for pest management. Key features of the model include temperature-dependent insect growth and realistic impulsive IGR release strategies. The impulsive releases are modeled by counting the number of applications during an insect's temperature-dependent development duration, which introduces a survival probability determined by a product of terms corresponding to each release; (4) The manuscript "Global dynamics of a partially degenerate nonlocal model for mosquito-borne disease transmission" was published in August 2025 in Studies in Applied Mathematics. In this work, a partially degenerate nonlocal dispersal Ross-Macdonald model was developed and analyzed to investigate how host mobility and environmental heterogeneity affect mosquito-borne disease transmission. The study identified the basic reproduction number as a key threshold for disease dynamics and addressed analytical challenges using comparison arguments in the appropriate function space. The asymptotic behavior of the basic reproduction number under varying host dispersal rates was characterized, and numerical simulations demonstrated that both host mobility and spatial heterogeneity significantly influence disease persistence and transmission risk. Notably, the results indicate that models assuming only local dispersal may underestimate transmission risks, and that epidemic size does not always increase monotonically with the basic reproduction number; (5) The manuscript "Getting jab or regular test: observations from an impulsive epidemic COVID-19 model" was published in Bulletin of Mathematical Biology (2023) 85:97. In this work, a population-based model using impulsive differential equations was developed to evaluate optimal COVID-19 testing frequencies among unvaccinated individuals, accounting for personal decision choices, vaccine efficacy, and uncertainties in epidemic transmission. The model incorporates different testing intervals and uses key epidemiological indices, including the basic reproduction number, peaking time, final epidemic size, and number of severe infections, to assess transmission risk. The findings demonstrate that the optimal testing frequency is highly sensitive to factors such as vaccine efficacy, transmission rate, test accuracy, and vaccination coverage. The results highlight the importance of designing testing strategies that consider these parameters and align with specific public health control objectives; (6) The manuscript "Infection-induced host extinction: deterministic and stochastic models for environmentally transmitted pathogens" was published in Mathematical Biosciences 380 (2025) 109374. This study investigated the role of pathogen infection, particularly the chytrid fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, in amphibian decline and extinction. Deterministic and stochastic susceptible-infectious-bacteria epidemic models were developed to assess how pathogen characteristics influence host species extinction. Key epidemiological indices, including host and pathogen reproduction numbers and transmission rates, were derived. Theoretical analysis addressed equilibrium stability, host persistence and extinction in the deterministic model, and extinction probability and average extinction time in the stochastic model. Numerical simulations quantified the effects of pathogen traits and host-pathogen interactions on extinction risk. The findings highlight two critical conditions for pathogen-driven host extinction: (i) the pathogen’s ability to reproduce independently in the environment, and (ii) its impact on host fecundity and survival. These results provide valuable insights for designing effective amphibian conservation strategies; (7) The manuscript "Effectiveness evaluation of mosquito suppression strategies on dengue transmission under changing temperature and precipitation" was published in Acta Tropica 253 (2024) 107159. In this work, a mathematical model was developed to assess the effectiveness of releasing Wolbachia-infected male mosquitoes as a dengue control strategy under varying temperature and precipitation conditions. The model incorporates key biological processes, including larval competition, mosquito maturation, and both extrinsic and intrinsic incubation periods. Mosquito and disease persistence were analyzed using two basic reproduction numbers and the release ratio of Wolbachia-infected males. Numerical simulations and sensitivity analyses were conducted to validate theoretical findings and identify effective control measures. The results demonstrate that the success of Wolbachia-based suppression is highly sensitive to climatic factors, with control being most challenging at optimal temperature (27–30°C) and precipitation (5–8 mm/day) ranges, where the reproduction number is highest and increased release efforts are required; (8) The proof of the manuscript "A seasonal succession model for frog population dynamics with mating behaviors" has been submitted and will appear in the Journal of Mathematical Biology. In this work, a stage-structured mathematical model with periodic time delay was developed to investigate the dynamics of frog populations, incorporating seasonal changes, two-sex structure, mating interactions, and adult competition. The model tracks male and female populations across active and hibernation phases. The global dynamics were analyzed by establishing strong monotonicity of the solution semiflow in both the natural and a newly defined quotient phase space. Numerical simulations assessed the impact of maturity mortality rates and mating pair numbers on population trajectories. Results show that populations decline before hibernation, while higher numbers of mating pairs support larger stable populations during the active phase.

An extensive review will be performed on the current studies of various physiologically structured models with seasonal effects, as well as updated biological advances on tick ecology.

Formulate a physiologically structured model with seasonal effects, in particular, the seasonal diapause. The model will be reduced into a periodic delay integral form, with the aid of general inverse functions, which is suitable for describing population growth of two-stage species.

The well-posedness of the model system, in terms of existence and positiveness of solutions, will be established. The basic reproduction number will be determined and the global dynamics of the model will be investigated through developing periodic dynamical system theories for the periodic delay integral equations.

The model framework will be justified with field data, in particular: (i) the modeling framework will be extended to be suitable for ticks, in particular, to accommodate more growth stages; and (ii) model simulation with the annual pattern of staged-population sizes and tick distribution will be compared with data collected from field observations to validate theoretical modeling frameworks.

Based on the data-validated model, it will be used to address the following ecological problems: (i) the effect of diapause on the tick seasonal patterns in a specific habitat; (ii) the contribution of diapause on the ticks' northward range expansion in eastern Canada; and (iii) possible impacts of climate change on tick seasonality and range distribution.

15304821.label: Major findings and research outcome
15304821.value: With the support of the grant, a total of eight manuscripts have been published or accepted in leading journals, including Journal of Nonlinear Science, Nonlinear Analysis: Real World Applications, Journal of Dynamics and Differential Equations, Journal of Mathematical Biology, Studies in Applied Mathematics, Bulletin of Mathematical Biology, Mathematical Biosciences, and Acta Tropica. The major findings and research outcomes are as follows: (a) Comprehensive reviews and new theoretical developments have clarified the strengths and limitations of integral and partial differential equation frameworks for modeling population dynamics, especially under density-dependent and stage-structured scenarios. (b) Novel models have been developed to capture spatial spread, annual synchronization, and the effects of environmental heterogeneity and seasonal factors on species persistence and disease transmission. (c) New mathematical models have evaluated the effectiveness of mosquito control strategies (such as Wolbachia releases and insect growth regulators) under realistic environmental and biological conditions, providing insights into optimal intervention strategies. (d) New impulsive and stochastic models have been used to study COVID-19 testing strategies and the extinction risk of amphibians due to environmentally transmitted pathogens, identifying key factors that drive host extinction and optimal public health interventions. (e) The research has provided actionable recommendations for pest management, amphibian conservation, and understanding the ecological impacts of climate change on species distributions and disease risks.

15304821.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15304821.value: The research outcomes lay a strong foundation for further interdisciplinary studies. Potential directions include: (a) The developed frameworks can be extended to other species, ecosystems, and diseases, incorporating additional biological complexity such as multi-host or multi-pathogen systems. (b) Future work will focus on closer integration with field and laboratory data, enabling parameter estimation, model validation, and real-time forecasting. Policy and Management Applications: The models can be adapted to inform public health and conservation policies, such as optimizing vector control programs, designing adaptive testing strategies, and predicting the impacts of climate change on disease emergence. Collaborative and Translational Research: There is significant potential for collaboration with ecologists, epidemiologists, and public health officials to translate theoretical findings into practical interventions.

15304821.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15304821.value: This research project used mathematics to help solve real-world problems in ecology, public health, and conservation. By building and analyzing mathematical models, we gained new understanding of how animals and insects grow, spread, and interact with their environment and diseases. For example, we studied how to best control mosquitoes that spread diseases like dengue, how to protect frogs from deadly infections, and how to design effective COVID-19 testing strategies. Our work helps scientists and policymakers make better decisions about managing pests, protecting endangered species, and controlling disease outbreaks. In total, ten scientific papers were published in respected journals, showing the wide impact and value of this research. The journals where these papers appeared include: (a) Journal of Nonlinear Science, (b) Nonlinear Analysis: Real World Applications, (c) Journal of Dynamics and Differential Equations, (d) Journal of Mathematical Biology, (e) Studies in Applied Mathematics, (f) Bulletin of Mathematical Biology, (g) Mathematical Biosciences, and (h) Acta Tropica.

15305221.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15305221.value: 自旋电子的操纵是目前自旋电子学的一个重要研究领域，因为它可以带来更快的计算和增加的存储容量。为了扩展带宽和存储容量，需要以更快的速度和更低的能量产生和检测自旋的新方法。 因此，进一步提高数据存储和计算能力自旋电子器件将带来巨大的经济和社会效益。迄今为止，在自旋电子学中找到一种易于制造并具有高电荷自旋转换效率的自旋源仍然具有挑战性。另一个存在于电流开关自旋电子学的关键障碍是对于外部磁场的要求，这不仅增加了额外的能耗，而且增加了器件制造的复杂性。该提案旨在开发本质上可以用作高效自旋源的材料。我们提出的二维杂化有机无机杂化钙钛矿因其强自旋轨道耦合，较长的自旋扩散长度，潜在的多铁性和本征量子肼结构而具有室温自旋电子应用的潜能。精心设计的二维杂化钙钛矿可产生Rashba自旋分裂，这种现象是指注入材料的电荷可以极化为自旋；它还可以同时具有铁电性，这是一种由于静电荷（即偶极子）的自发排列而存在内部电场。因此，可以利用铁电的内部电场来控制和增加Rashba劈裂能，以低能量损失实现器件操纵。然而，关于可以允许铁电和Rashba效应的2D钙钛矿的结构知之甚少，而且这些的铁阶相互作用很少被展示。在此，我们建议合成具有Rashba 效应和铁电特性的杂化 2D 钙钛矿并且通过光学和电学的手段来探究和表征其Rashba铁电特性。本研究结果将为自旋电子学相关的二维杂化钙钛矿的应用和性质奠定基础。

15305221.label: Realisation of objectives
15305221.value: The proposed three objectives have been fully achieved (100% completion). Below is the explanation of the objectives and their realization: 1. To design and synthesize 2D perovskites with both ferroelectric and Rashba properties How it was achieved: We successfully synthesized uddlesden-Popper (RPP) phase 2D hybrid perovskites, which exhibit both ferroelectric and Rashba properties. Ferroelectricity was confirmed through piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) and P-E loop measurements. The Rashba effect was verified using circularly polarized excitation, photoluminescence (PL) studies, and two-PL excitation measurements. 2. To achieve a fundamental understanding of the structure-property correlation relating to molecular ferroelectricity (i.e., in-plane or out-of-plane polarization) How it was achieved: We synthesized different phases of 2D hybrid perovskites by selecting suitable organic molecules. The RPP phase exhibits in-plane ferroelectric polarization. The Dion-Jacobson (D-J) phase demonstrates out-of-plane ferroelectric polarization. This structural manipulation allowed us to establish a clear correlation between molecular structure and ferroelectric behavior. 3. To carry out circular photogalvanic spectroscopy and photo-voltage microscopy studies to verify and investigate charge-to-spin conversion efficiency using 2D perovskites as a spin source How it was achieved: Using scanning photovoltage microscopy, we verified the rashba effects in n > 1 2D hybrid perovskites. There were no under-achievements or problems encountered during the completion of these objectives.

15305221.label: Major findings and research outcome
15305221.value: We successfully synthesized 2D hybrid perovskites that exhibit both ferroelectricity and the Rashba effect. Until now, the charge-to-spin conversion efficiency in 2D hybrid perovskites has remained unknown. In this study, we are the first to construct a Hall-bar device and demonstrate highly efficient electrically driven charge-to-spin conversion in enantiopure chiral perovskites. Using scanning photovoltage microscopy, we reported: A spin Hall angle and A spin lifetime at room temperature in the n = 4 chiral perovskites. These values are significantly higher than those observed in the racemic counterpart and in lower n homologs, highlighting the superior performance of 2D hybrid perovskites in charge-to-spin conversion.

15305221.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15305221.value: The research on 2D hybrid perovskites with both ferroelectricity and Rashba properties has significant potential for further development, both in fundamental science and practical applications. The key areas of potential growth based on this proposal including Expansion of Material Systems and Spintronic Device Optimization. The versatility of hybrid perovskites provides opportunities to explore new material systems by incorporating alternative organic and inorganic components. These systems could yield enhanced Rashba splitting, stronger ferroelectricity, or improved thermal and chemical stability. Optimizing charge-to-spin and spin-to-charge conversion efficiency is critical for practical spintronic applications. Enhancing spin lifetime and reducing spin scattering in 2D hybrid perovskites are key areas of improvement. For example, optimize device interfaces (e.g., perovskite-graphene heterostructures) to reduce resistance and improve spin injection efficiency and explore multi-functional devices that combine spintronic and optoelectronic functionalities.

15305221.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15305221.value: This research focuses on creating a new type of material called 2D hybrid perovskites, which combine special properties like ferroelectricity (materials that can hold an internal electric field) and the Rashba effect (a way to control electron spins). These materials could revolutionize spintronics, a field of electronics that uses the spin of electrons instead of their charge to process and store information. Spintronics promises faster devices that consume less energy, which is essential for the future of computing and data storage. Our goal is to design and study these materials to understand how their structure influences their ability to generate and control spins. By doing so, we aim to create spin-based transistors and other devices that are efficient, low-cost, and work at room temperature. This project could pave the way for next-generation electronics, including faster computers and greener technologies, while also contributing to fundamental scientific knowledge about these cutting-edge materials.

15305321.label: Project Title(Chinese)
15305321.value: 非線性Wasserstein分佈式魯棒優化

15305321.label: Project Objectives
15305321.value: Motivated by its appearance in a wide range of applications and attractive theoretical properties, distributionally robust optimization (DRO) with a Wasserstein ambiguity set and a nonlinear objective in the embedded problem is studied. We call this class of problems nonlinear Wasserstein DRO. Fundamental questions such as optimality conditions, finiteness of the optimal value and existence of optimal solutions to the embedded problem, which is an infinite-dimensional nonlinear constrained optimization over the space of probability distributions, are addressed. Tractable reformulations and approximations for the embedded problem are derived for several classes of well-structured nonlinear functionals of probability distributions that arise from applications. For situations where a tractable reformulation is not available, an iterative algorithm for solving the challenging embedded problem, called the Wasserstein Frank-Wolfe algorithm, is developed. The convergence behavior of the proposed algorithm, such as convergence rate, will be analyzed.

15305321.value: 在管理及工程學，很多決策、估计、及預測的計算過程都涉及以某個概率分佈作為輸入的優化問題。具體例子包括機會約束規劃和隨機規劃。許多實際場景下，由於無法為優化問題輸入一個理想的概率分佈，我們常以分佈樣本作為近似。通过這一近似分布所求得的決策、估计或預測皆會受到樣本誤差的影響。分佈式魯棒優化是一個减小這一影響的有效途徑。分佈式魯棒優化的原理是首先建構一個跟理想分佈相近的分布集合，然後在該分布集合中選取對决策者最不利的分佈作為優化問題的輸入。分佈魯棒優化已被廣泛應用到包括机器學習、信号處理和能源在内的多個領域。 選取最不利分佈這過程稱之為分佈式魯棒的嵌入問題。嵌入問題本身就是一個優化問題，並且是求解分佈式魯棒優化問題中重要的一步。項目的主要和合作研究者希望探討嵌入問題為非線性優化問題的分佈式魯棒優化模型。此類問題為非線性的無限維優化問題，極具挑戰性。項目將會有三個主要貢獻。第一，項目的主要和合作研究者會研究此類非線性嵌入問題的理論特性。第二，他們會探討此類優化問題有沒有有限維的特價模型。最後，對於沒有良好特價模型的嵌入問題，主要和合作研究者亦會設計Frank-Wolfe演算法去求得最優解，並且會分析此演算法的收斂性質。

15305821.value: 人类基因组中的很大一部分能够被转录，这些转录本通常被认为是“非编码RNA”。而近年来，一系列研究证实非编码RNA也能够进行翻译。核糖体图谱和生物信息分析表明40%的长非编码RNA和伪基因RNA可能是会被翻译的“小开放阅读框”。同时，质谱分析证明了数千条这种小开放阅读框编码肽段（SEPs）的存在。尽管这些肽段逐个被报道，绝大多数的SEPs功能仍未知。我们迫切地需要一种系统性的方法来研究SEPs的功能。 我们曾报道过一种叫做OPP-ID的技术，用来分析在某种刺激下细胞内新合成的蛋白质。在本研究中，我们将会建立一个基于OPP-ID的技术平台用來发现新的SEPs。我们将利用这个平台研究肿瘤缺氧环境。在我们的预实验中，数目可观的SEPs能够从细胞质和细胞外被检测到。其中有些肽段是肿瘤特异性的MHC肽段。本研究将会提供一个用于发现SEPs生物功能的技术平台。考虑到非编码RNA数量巨大而且具有较高的细胞、组织特异性，新发现的SEPs有望在疾病的诊断和治疗中发挥重要作用。

15306021.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15306021.value: 掃描透射電子顯微（STEM）技術是目前最有效的結構表徵工具之一。球差矯正掃描透射電子顯微鏡的空間解析度已經被提升至亞埃級別，足以揭示材料的精細原子結構。此外，對功能材料在使役條件下的動態行為的認知對於構-效關係的探索具有基礎意義。原位透射電鏡技術可以在透射電鏡中對樣品施加外場並同時記錄樣品的動態回應，因此已經被廣泛應用於過程及機制的研究中。同時，隨著諸如高能量解析度電子能量損失譜、超快相機和四維掃描透射電鏡等表徵技術的快速發展，目前的先進掃描透射電子顯微鏡有能力揭示樣品結構資訊之外的更多物理細節。 氧化物鈣鈦礦材料具有諸多重要的功能特性，為電子器件的研發提供了豐富機遇。例如，對外場下鐵電與疇物理行為的探索已經對非動態記憶體的開發起到了積極作用。而近期實現的超薄自支撐氧化物鈣鈦礦薄膜進一步為探索材料納米尺度的力電和光電特性提供了理想的平臺。儘管原子分辨掃描透射電子顯微技術已經有效推進了氧化物鈣鈦礦的結構及物理性能研究，但是傳統靜態觀察的局限性仍舊阻礙了對相關材料動態性能和相關機制的深入理解。 因此，基於我們開發的高穩定性透射電鏡原位光電測試平臺，我們計畫將原位測試與先進掃描透射電子顯微技術在這一項目中進行結合，從而實現對氧化物鈣鈦礦在電場及光照下的動態回應行為的原子尺度表徵。這一項目將對典型的氧化物鈣鈦礦材料體系，包括鈦酸鉛、鐵酸鉍和鈦酸鍶對外加電場和光照的物理回應進行系統研究，從而探索相應性能的來源。利用電子能量損失譜和四維掃描透射電鏡技術，有望實現對外場作用下電荷轉移與價態變化的原子尺度觀察，從而為材料的物理研究提供全新視角。此外，對於可以承受極大應變梯度的自支撐氧化物鈣鈦礦薄膜在光照下的光回應行為的原位觀察有望為仍備受爭議的光撓曲電效應的研究提供直接證據。我們對氧化物鈣鈦礦開展的原子尺度原位探索將促進對相關動態物理特性的深入理解，從而推動其在新型器件及系統中的潛在應用。此外，相關技術進步也將為未來原位透射電鏡技術的發展開闢更多可能。

15306021.label: Realisation of objectives
15306021.value: Objective 1: We have fully achieved the first objective with satisfactory technological breakthrough and experimental results. We have successfully developed Micro-electromechanical Systems (MEMS) chip-based in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) biasing approach able to provide uniformly distributed and adjustable external electric field for atomic-scale observations of ferroelectric domain nucleation and domain wall sideways motion in ferroelectric capacitors. We prepared the PbZr0.1Ti0.9O3/La0.7Sr0.3MnO3 (PZT/LSMO) ferroelectric heterojunction sample by pulsed laser deposition (PLD) and fabricated the capacitor-structured cross-sectional PZT/LSMO specimen onto the in situ MEMS chip using focused ion beam (FIB) for in situ scanning TEM (STEM) observations. By accurately controlling the applied electric field, the domain nucleation and propagation process can be tuned, and the lateral translational speed of the ferroelectric domain wall can decrease to less than 2.2 Å/s, enabling the atomic scale STEM characterization of domain wall dynamics in ferroelectric polarization switching process. In this study, we gathered abundant experiences in on-chip fabrication of in situ device specimens and explored the modulation of domain wall translation through the electric field, which not only addressed the objective and are enlightening for our further explorations. Objective 2: We have completely achieved the second objective with successful platform development and experiment design and conduction. For in situ STEM studies involving light illumination, we developed an on-chip light-incorporated in situ TEM platform for probing specimens at the nanoscale, which allows for real-time, site-specific tracking of light-triggered structure transformation. Compared with the traditional design, this newly developed in situ platform based on a specifically designed MEMS chip offers the capability of light illumination with adjustable intensity and tailorable multi-wavelength. We then prepared cross-sectional samples of BiFeO3 thin films grown on TbScO3 substrates onto the in situ MEMS chip. Preliminary in situ experiments were conducted based on our as-developed light-incorporated in situ TEM platform, enabling controlled light illumination during atomic-scale characterization. Through in situ STEM-electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) analysis of 71° and 109° domain walls under varying illumination conditions, we observed pronounced changes in the valence states of oxygen and iron at 71° domain wall upon blue light exposure, while the 109° domain wall exhibited negligible photo-response. We further acquired in situ 4D-STEM datasets from both domain wall types under illumination. By computing the differential center of mass (dCOM) shifts, we mapped variations in electric field and charge density. Notable charge density modulations emerged on either side of the 71° domain wall under light, whereas changes near the 109° wall remained minimal. These in situ illumination studies achieve atomic-scale characterization of ferroelectric domain wall photo-responses, furnishing critical evidence for their distinctive photoelectronic behaviors. The objective was substantially realized, with direct demonstrations of differential electric field, valence, and charge transfer dynamics between different domain walls, alongside elucidation of their photoelectric mechanisms. Objective 3: We have successfully realized the third objective with representative experimental observations and analysis. To achieve atomic-scale STEM characterization of strain and strain gradients in freestanding oxide perovskites, we introduced ultra-high strain gradients (>107 m-1) into flexible freestanding perovskite oxide thin films via engineered wrinkle structures. Employing scanning transmission electron microscopy with differential phase contrast (STEM-DPC) imaging, we mapped the relative displacements of metal cations and oxygen anions across regions of varying curvature, enabling direct atomic-scale observation and quantitative analysis of ultra-strong flexoelectric effects and mechano-electric coupling in nanometer-thick oxide perovskite films. This study leverages STEM techniques to uncover gigantic flexoelectric polarization responses in bent freestanding oxide perovskite thin films harboring ultra-high strain gradients, while unveiling an abnormal mechanical behavior identified as flexoelectric-driven bending expansion/contraction, which elucidates unconventional bending mechano-electric coupling in flexible freestanding films. The objective was fully realized, delivering high-fidelity atomic-scale strain mapping and detailed flexoelectric and electromechanical characterizations for strained freestanding BiFeO3 and SrTiO3. Objective 4: We have completely realized the fourth objective with successful experimental demonstrations. Building on the atomic-scale characterization of mechano-electric coupling in bent freestanding oxide perovskites, we prepared cross-sectional samples of wrinkled freestanding oxide perovskites onto in situ MEMS chips and conducted a series of illumination experiments using our as-developed light-incorporated in situ TEM platform. Multiple datasets of in situ STEM-EELS and DPC were acquired from both non-bent and bent regions of freestanding SrTiO3 thin films. Comparative analysis of chemical shifts and peak shape variations in the oxygen and titanium without and with light illumination revealed opposing valence state alterations at the upper and lower surfaces of the SrTiO3 thin film in bent regions. STEM-DPC mapping also indicates potential charge separation and accumulation under light illumination due to the flexoelectric effect induced internal electric field. To probe wavelength dependence, in situ experiments were performed using LED sources at 430 nm, 532 nm, and 625 nm. This objective was substantially realized through direct in situ observations, providing atomic-scale evidence of strain-gradient-mediated photo-responses and laying the groundwork for exploiting flexo-photovoltaic effects in flexible oxide devices.

15306021.label: Major findings and research outcome
15306021.value: 1. Ferroelectric domain wall dynamics. In situ STEM observations reveal that domain walls in PZT thin films exhibit creeping motion under near-critical electric fields, with morphology evolving through stretching and shrinkage stages. Atomic-scale analysis shows polarization switching via magnitude changes and 180° rotations over several unit cells. Phase-field simulations attribute this to competing gradient, elastic, and electrostatic energies, applicable to other perovskites. These insights enable precise domain control, advancing ferroelectric device design. Published in Advanced Functional Materials (Part C, 8(3)). 2. In situ TEM platform development. We engineered an in situ TEM platform using a six-electrode MEMS chip, enabling the integration of a multi-band micro-LED (625 nm, 532 nm, 430 nm). This enables wavelength-specific photo-response testing, enhancing sample adaptability and experimental versatility for perovskite studies. Published in ACS Energy Letters (Part C, 8(2)). 3. Photoelectric response in BiFeO3 domain walls. In situ STEM-EELS on BiFeO3 domain walls shows light-induced valence shifts (O K- and Fe L-edges) at 71° walls, indicating charge accumulation from efficient carrier generation and separation via built-in fields, unlike inert 109° walls. 4D-STEM confirms charge density modulations, linking superior 71° domain wall photoconductivity to narrower bandgap and field-driven dynamics. 4. Flexoelectric effects in freestanding perovskites. Atomic-scale STEM-DPC in strained freestanding perovskites demonstrates flexoelectricity boosting out-of-plane polarization in bent BiFeO3 to 146.6 μC/cm2 and inducing 35.3 μC/cm2 in SrTiO3. Extreme gradients cause asymmetric strain and bending-induced expansion/contraction in BiFeO3 (absent in SrTiO3), driven by flexoelectric-piezoelectric synergy. These findings pave the way for micro/nano flexoelectric devices. Published in Nature Communications (Part C, 8(1)). 5. Strain-Enhanced photoresponse in SrTiO3. In situ STEM-EELS/4D-STEM on wrinkled freestanding SrTiO3 reveals light-induced valence shifts and surface charge accumulation at bent regions across wavelengths, absent in flat areas due to the insulating nature. Strain gradients modulate band structure, enabling flexoelectric-enhanced carrier separation and photovoltaic-like responses in inert perovskites, highlighting mechano-photo coupling mechanisms. 6. Extended explorations by advanced STEM approaches. To enable the efficient and damage-free preparation of perovskite thin film samples for plane-view STEM observations, we developed a liquid-phase transfer method that yields intact freestanding films for high-quality imaging. Published in Adv. Optical Mater. (Part C, 8(5)). We also drafted a review that covers advanced low-dose TEM for beam-sensitive photoactive COFs/MOFs. Published in Nanoscale Horiz. (Part C, 8(4)).

15306021.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15306021.value: This research establishes atomic-scale foundations for ferroelectric domain manipulation, opto-electronic domain wall responses, and strain-flexoelectric coupling in oxide perovskites, unlocking potentials for next-generation flexible electronics, sensors, and energy harvesters. To deepen mechanistic insights, we will integrate in situ TEM characterizations with macroscopic physical measurements (photoconductive testing, Kelvin probe microscopy) and first-principles calculations to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing the enhanced photoconductivity of BiFeO3 71° domain walls. Similarly, combining experimental observations with theoretical modeling will clarify the flexophotovoltaic effects in bent SrTiO3, particularly the interplay between strain-gradient-induced band structure modulation and photogenerated carrier dynamics. Collaborative efforts with computational groups will enable quantitative correlation between atomic-scale structural features and photoelectric performance. The distinctive photoelectric properties of ferroelectric domain walls and flexoelectric responses in freestanding perovskites offer promising pathways toward novel device architectures. Potential applications include domain-wall-based photodetectors exploiting the superior photoconductivity of 71° walls, flexible photovoltaic devices leveraging strain-gradient-enhanced carrier separation, and multimodal sensors combining mechanical and optical functionalities. The developed in situ characterization methodologies will continue to serve as powerful tools for optimizing device performance and guiding the rational design of next-generation ferroelectric and flexoelectric micro/nano devices.

15306021.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15306021.value: This research explores the fascinating behavior of ferroelectric oxide perovskites whose internal electric polarization can be switched by applying an electric field. Using cutting-edge electron microscopy techniques, the project observes these phenomena at the atomic scale, essentially watching individual atoms rearranging during mechanical bending and ferroelectric switching. Significance: The research reveals hidden properties of ferroelectric domain walls (the boundaries between regions of different polarization). These walls exhibit unexpected photoelectric effects, meaning they respond to light by generating electric currents property that standard ferroelectric materials typically lack. Additionally, the team discovered that when these materials are bent or strained, they generate spontaneous electric polarization through flexoelectric effects, even in materials that are normally non-ferroelectric. Value and Applications: Understanding these phenomena at the atomic level enables the rational design of advanced devices. Potential applications include ultra-sensitive light detectors based on domain walls, flexible electronics and sensors that exploit mechanical deformation to generate electrical signals, and multifunctional devices combining optical, electrical, and mechanical capabilities. The novel in situ characterization methods developed during this work provide powerful tools for studying other emerging materials with photoelectric or ferroelectric properties, accelerating the development of next-generation technologies in energy harvesting, sensing, and information storage.
