16101821.label: Major findings and research outcome
16101821.value: 1. Characterization of plastisphere biofilm microbial communities. In Qiang et al. (2021) and Lo et al. (2024; 2025), we demonstrated that microplastics serve as distinct microhabitats, with microbial biofilms developing compositions that differ from those in surrounding water. Factors such as salinity and plastic substrate types significantly influence biofilm community composition. Over time, plastisphere biofilm communities change, with early compositions largely shaped by the surrounding environment. In later stages, compositions across different polymer types may diverge due to ecological succession but could eventually converge. Furthermore, we identified spatial heterogeneity across four coastal sites as the primary factor influencing plastisphere biofilm compositions. Within each site, microbial biofilm compositions were predominantly shaped by the type of microplastic polymer substrates. 2. Investigation of pathogen enrichment in the plastisphere. In Lo et al. (2024), we found that biofilms on PC plastics can accumulate pathogens at higher levels than the surrounding water. In Lo et al. (2024, 2025), environmental stress significantly influenced pathogen abundances on microplastic biofilms. 3. Gut microplastic retention-induced stress response and gut microbiota dysbiosis. In Ma et al. (2023), we found that acute exposure to microplastics can lead to their retention in zebrafish intestines, with the fish capable of depurating these microplastics in a diel pattern. In Lo et al. (under review), we demonstrated that acute microplastic exposure impairs gut health by inducing a stress response and microbiota dysbiosis, characterized by increased energy production and suppressed metabolic and detoxification pathways. Continued exposure leads to compromised gut barrier maintenance and defense functions. Gut microbiota dysbiosis is characterized by increased abundances of pathobionts, alongside reduced commensal bacteria and overall diversity, indicating a potential negative synergistic impact of microplastic exposure on gut health. ADVANCES IN METHODOLOGY AND APPLICABLE RESEARCH OUTCOMES In Qiang et al. (2021), we used long-read MinION Nanopore sequencing to trace the Limnobacter thiooxidans population on microplastic biofilms, distinguishing five common strains from other site/sample-specific strains. This has important implications for source accurate microbial tracking and pathogenicity assessment. Additionally, in Lo et al. (2023), we developed a curated database of over 210 aquaculture bacterial pathogens. While this database serves as a criterion for screening potential pathogens enriched on plastisphere biofilms, it also functions as a reference for a wide range of studies focused on characterizing bacterial pathogen profiles and assessing occurrence risks within microbial communities.

16101821.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16101821.value: Based on the project’s findings, some further research can enhance our understanding of emerging risks associated with microplastic-associated biofilms in coastal environments. For example, investigations are needed to elucidate the mechanisms driving pathogen enrichment on microplastics. This includes experiments to identify environmental factors that select for specific bacterial taxa and conditions that facilitate horizontal gene transfer, especially those involving antibiotic resistance genes. The interactions between plastisphere biofilms, pathogens, ARGs, and other emerging pollutants require systematic exploration to assess cumulative long-term risks. These research efforts will provide a deeper understanding of the ecological and health implications of microplastic pollution and enable more comprehensive risk assessments, ultimately informing evidence-based management and policy development.

16101821.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16101821.value: This research project studied how small-sized microplastics derived from global plastic pollution, now abundantly found in the ocean and along the coast, is potently colonized and utilized by layers of bacteria and microbes to form “plastisphere” biofilms. We revealed that these plastic surfaces selectively attract and support unique groups of microbes distinct from the those in the surrounding waters, some of which can be harmful bacteria facilitating the spread of infection and disease through their transport in water, ingestion by organisms and subsequently into humans. Experiments showed that when fish ingest microplastics, it can disturb the balance of commensal bacteria in the gastrointestinal tract and induce stress responses, potentially affecting the host’s health. The findings highlight the importance of understanding microplastic pollution not just as a physical pollutant, but also as a new microhabitat niche for microbial communities, a vector for biological contaminants such as harmful microbes to travel in the environment, and a predicted long term environmental issue to live by. This project provided new insights that benefit the comprehensive assessment of environmental risks from the growing threat of plastic pollution, necessary for future remediation strategies to protect global oceans, seafood, and public health.

16102021.label: Project Objectives
16102021.value: Characterization of alternative splicing events during SC early activation. Alternative splicing changes have been reported when comparing stem cells and their differentiated progenies. In our laboratory, we have established a robust in vivo fixation technique to preserve the molecular signature of quiescent SCs in comparison to conventional SC isolation techniques. We have observed differences in splicing variants in fixed SCs (fSCs), which we define as our quiescent cell population, freshly isolated SCs (fiSCs), and activated SCs (ASCs). Within these three SC populations, we aim to identify SC-specific splicing variants and quantitate their expression levels. Identification of these differentially spliced transcripts will provide us insights into which signaling pathways may be influenced by alternative splicing. Elucidation of the functional role of Rbfox2 during SC early activation. Rbfox2 is a splicing regulator in muscle function and organization but whether it plays a role in SC activation is unknown. We will use our established Rbfox2 conditional knockout mice model and healthy control mice (CT mice) to study SC activation. Firstly, we will assess the extent of SC activation in fiSCs and ASCs in both mice models. The tibialis anterior muscle (TA) will be subjected to BaCl2 injury for up to 28 days. We will then perform muscle fiber staining to assess the level of muscle regeneration compared to that of healthy control (CT) mice. Secondly, mRNA transcript diversity will be studied by performing RNA seq of fiSCs, fSCs, and ASCs from Rbfox2 KO mice in comparison to CT mice. Finally, once we have identified the differentially expressed transcripts, we will validate which of the transcripts are targets of Rbfox2. Investigate the role of Rbfox2-dependent splicing changes during SC activation. The purpose here is to determine the temporal expression of splicing variants within muscle and confirm that the splicing variants detected in objectives 1 and 2 are SC-specific. The use of fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) would help us to localize the expression of splicing variants. Transcript candidates identified in objective 2 may contain several potential binding sites for Rbfox2, but it is unclear which of the cis-acting elements influences the transcript diversity observed in our previous experiments. To identify the element responsible for specific splicing variants, each binding site will be assessed for Rbfox2 binding. Splicing reporters will then be transfected into the C2Cl2 myoblasts, and qPCR performed to determine levels of each splicing variant. Finally, we will use morpholinos, antisense sequences that target the recognition elements on mRNA to modulate alternative splicing, and FISH will be utilized to visualize the resulting isoforms.

16102021.value: 衛星細胞 （SCs） 是駐留在骨骼肌內的常駐幹細胞。 它們通常處於靜息狀態，並隨時準備對外部刺激做出快速反應，並被啟動以啟動肌纖維再生。 我們目前對衛星細胞靜息的瞭解主要依賴於囓齒動物模型，其中衛星細胞通過螢光激活細胞分選 （FACS） 被從肌肉中分離出來，稱為新鮮分離的衛星細胞。 然而，傳統的分離方法耗時很長，而且衛星細胞在分離過程中不可避免地會被啟動，這使對處於靜息狀態的衛星細胞和衛星細胞激活中發生的早期事件的研究變得非常困難。 在我們的實驗室中，我們建立了一種體內灌注方法來固定衛星細胞，與新鮮分離的衛星細胞的相比，該方法更忠實地保留了保留衛星細胞的中的分子靜息特徵。 靜息狀態的轉錄後調控是一個重要的研究領域。 我們對這一領域有著長期的興趣，例如，我們發現microRNA 參與Dek的調控來控制衛星細胞的啟動。 最近我們還發現了通過選擇性剪接 （AS） 調控的全域內含子保留在衛星細胞激活過程中有重要作用。 我們的轉錄組分析還揭示了靜息和啟動的衛星細胞之間的差異剪接變體，表明選擇性剪接可能在衛星細胞靜息的調控中發揮作用。 當前對肌肉特異性外顯子的全基因組分析揭示了特定順式作用元件的存在，這些元件可以被剪接因數 Rbfox2 識別。 據報導，Rbfox2 參與肌肉功能和再生的調節，但很少有人研究其在衛星細胞啟動中的作用。 我們已經確定Rbfox2 而不是 Rbfox1 的表達在衛星細胞激活過程中增加，而 Rbfox2 敲低會損害衛星細胞增殖並導致mRNA剪接發生變化。 我們還構建了 Rbfox2 條件性敲除 （cKO） 小鼠，它們表現出肌肉再生受損。 使用 Pax7-nGFP 小鼠，我們將全面分析衛星細胞啟動過程中的差異剪接變體，並確定這些剪接變體涉及哪些生物學途徑。 此外，我們將使用 cKO 小鼠來評估哪些剪接變體是 Rbfox2 的目標，並評估 Rbfox2 如何在衛星細胞激活期間影響其目標轉錄本的翻譯。 我們的研究不僅將有助於前所未有地了解選擇性剪接在衛星細胞啟動中的功能，而且還將確定Rbfox2 是否為該過程的關鍵剪接調節因數。 我們的長期目標是更好地瞭解選擇性剪接調節骨骼肌中衛星細胞啟動分子機制。

16102021.label: Realisation of objectives
16102021.value: In Aim 1, we studied the splicing changes in quiescent satellite cells (QSCs), freshly isolated SCs (fiSCs, representing early activated SCs), and fully activated SCs (ASCs) isolated from mice using two long-read sequencing techniques, Pacific Biosciences single-molecule real-time sequencing, and the Oxford Nanopore sequencing platform. This approach can identify complex isoforms but requires high-input RNA. While attempts were made to increase RNA yield following our fixation of QSCs (which retains the quiescence signatures), sequencing data quality was below par. However, short-read RNA sequencing partnered with rMATS helped to determine the exon exclusion levels. We identified differentially spliced events (DSEs) in QSCs, fiSCs, and ASCs, omitting lowly expressed DSEs and spliced events with discrepancies between replicas to remove false events. By comparing the splicing patterns of fiSCs to QSCs and ASCs, we identified critical splicing events for SC activation. 649 DSEs were found when comparing fiSCs to QSCs, indicating rapid splicing pattern changes upon SC isolation from muscle. 829 DSEs were detected when comparing fiSCs to ASCs, with 585/829 absent in the fiSC to QSC comparison, suggesting such splicing changes are needed for proliferation. Although 244 splicing changes overlapped in both comparisons, 75% of the overlapping DSEs exhibited opposite early and late activation changes. For example, Mettl3 undergoes alternative splicing (AS) during SC activation. Mettl3 encodes an enzyme that regulates SC proliferation. Exon 4 of Mettl3 was skipped more in fiSCs than QSCs but included more in ASCs than in fiSCs. Therefore, splicing changes of these exons during SC activation are likely transient, and we report the presence of early and late activation splicing signatures, supporting activation and proliferation. Bioinformatics analyses of genes regulated by AS during SC activation showed enrichment for pathways such as mRNA processing, transcription regulation, chromatin organization, and the cell cycle. Some of these changes were previously reported to be essential. For example, exon 8 of Ptbp1 is more skipped in fiSCs. Previous studies showed that the loss of exon 8 weakens its function as a splicing suppressor. Also, exon 5 of Kat5 was previously established to modulate its enzymatic functions and subcellular localization. Our data suggested exon 5 was skipped more following SC activation. Our analyses indicate that AS regulates critical pathways during SC activation and proliferation. In Aim 2, we further examined the role of Rbfox2 in SC activation and muscle repair in SC-specific Rbfox2 conditional knockout (cKO) mice. Our data indicated impaired muscle repair in Rbfox2-deficient mice at 7DPI (days post-injury). However, at 14DPI, there were no significant differences in fiber size, suggesting that Rbfox2 loss only delayed muscle repair. Interestingly, 4 weeks post-injury, the number of type 1 fibers (known as slow-twitch fibers) in the cKO tibialis anterior (TA) muscle was increased compared to the control (CT). The TA muscle typically has few slow muscle fibers. Our data suggests Rbfox2 may help to determine muscle fiber type. Rbfox2 cKO fiSCs exhibited delayed activation, as shown by reduced EdU incorporation compared to CT fiSCs. Transcriptomics analysis of Rbfox2 cKO fiSCs showed 1106 downregulated and 1449 upregulated genes compared to CT fiSCs. Loss of Rbfox2 impaired activation-related pathways, like translation, cell cycle, and ATP synthesis. Conversely, quiescence-associated genes like Pax7, Hey1, and Ezh1 were upregulated in cKO SCs. Also, upregulated genes in cKO fiSCs were enriched for Notch (e.g Hes1, Hey1) and Rho pathways. Notch signaling is well-established as essential for SC quiescence, while Rho signaling regulates quiescence and activation. Thus, Rbfox2 may regulate SC activation through Rho and Notch signaling. We probed the effects of Rbfox2 cKO on splicing changes during SC activation, using RNA-seq analysis to identify DSEs. Over 100 DSEs (mainly decreasing exon inclusion) were found when comparing cKO fiSCs to CT fiSCs, suggesting that Rbfox2 regulates mRNA splicing during early activation. In agreement with previous studies, the Rho GTPase signaling pathway was affected by Rbfox2 KO, with Rho signaling-related genes exhibiting changes in the inclusion level of exons. For example, Clip1 exon inclusion was decreased in the cKO. Surprisingly, Rbfox2 KO only affected a few genes undergoing splicing changes during early activation, indicating that most splicing changes during early activation were Rbfox2-independent. We previously proposed identifying Rbfox2 binding targets using iCLIP. However, Rbfox2 cKO only affected around 100 splicing events, most of which were identified in other studies. Moreover, only 25 DSEs overlapped with DSEs identified during SC early activation (when comparing fiSCs to QSCs). Thus, instead of performing iCLIP, we focused on selected targets for downstream validation. Our data identified a few genes that undergo Rbfox2-dependent splicing changes during early activation. We identified Numb, a known Notch signaling regulator, underwent an Rbfox2-dependent splicing change during early activation. Previous reports showed that Numb-deficient mice exhibit impaired SC proliferation and muscle repair, a phenotype also seen in our Rbfox2-cKO. Thus, in Aim 3 we opted to study the role of Numb exon 6 splicing during SC activation. Numb contains two alternative exons, exons 6 and 12, with previous studies showing Rbfox2 regulates the splicing of both exons. Our data suggested that exon 12 of Numb is skipped in SCs, while exon 6 was skipped in QSCs but was included more in fiSCs. Also, the loss of Rbfox2 led to exon 6 being skipped. We proposed using FISH to visualize the change in the splicing isoforms. However, the length of exon 6 of Numb is only 33bp, hindering us from designing an efficient FISH probe. Thus, we performed RT-PCR to quantify the exon inclusion level and confirm the Numb splicing change during activation. Also, we injured Pax7nGFP mice and pre-fixed SCs in vivo at different time points. We found that exon 6 of Numb was skipped in QSCs but was included more in SCs once activated. This splicing change was detected as early as 1-hour post-injury. This data demonstrates that Numb exon 6 undergoes rapid Rbfox2-dependent splicing switching during SC activation. We previously proposed to use splicing reporters to identify the cis-elements responsible for regulating splicing, to understand better how Rbfox2 regulates specific exons, and to help us design morpholinos (MOs) to manipulate exon splicing. However, the intron of Numb exon 6 contains multiple Rbfox2 binding sites, making it difficult to clone all of them. Thus, we designed MOs to block the binding site closest to exon 6. This did not inhibit exon 6 inclusion, suggesting that Rbfox2 may bind to multiple sites, supported by a recent Rbfox2 iCLIP study, which identified various peaks in the intron of Numb exon 6. Henceforth, we designed MOs that target the 3' splice site of Numb exon 6 to inhibit its inclusion and determine the role of splicing Numb during SC activation. MOs were applied to harvested muscle, and fiSCs were isolated for analysis. This treatment inhibited the inclusion of Numb exon 6. Numb MO-treated fiSCs led to 501 downregulated and 616 upregulated genes. Notch signaling (including Hey1 and HeyL genes) was upregulated in treated fiSCs, similar to our Rbfox2 cKO fiSCs. MO-treated SCs downregulated pathways, including translation, RNA metabolism, and the cell cycle, reminiscent of Rbfox2 cKO ASCs, with many genes encoding ribosome and proteasome-related proteins. Also, treated cells showed delayed SC activation, like the Rbfox2 cKO phenotype. Thus, we showed that Numb exon 6 regulates Notch signaling to facilitate rapid SC activation.

16102021.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102021.value: Our research findings demonstrate the role of alternative RNA splicing, one important post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism in satellite cell (SC) activation. Using our established in vivo fixation approach to preserve the quiescent signatures of SCs, we revealed rapid and extensive splicing changes in genes associated with RNA splicing, transcription regulation, chromatin organization, and the cell cycle. Importantly, we reported that Rbfox2, a major splicing factor, plays a key role in regulating alternative RNA splicing during early SC activation. In the absence of Rbfox2 expression, these cells experience delays in activation. Moreover, we demonstrated that Rbfox2 regulates the splicing of Numb, an established regulator of the Notch signaling pathway, where the inclusion of exon 6 of the Numb transcript was Rbfox2-dependent and is necessary for SC activation. Conversely, skipping Numb exon 6 delayed SC activation and upregulated the Notch signaling pathway. Altogether, our works provide an alternative splicing landscape during SC activation. Moreover, we demonstrated that manipulating the splicing of a single gene is sufficient to affect SC activation and essential signaling pathways such as Notch signaling. Interestingly, we also observed that injured skeletal muscle in Rbfox2-deficient mice shows a delay in muscle repair and a change in muscle fiber type. The TA muscle is a fast muscle with very few slow muscle fibers. However, at 1-month post-injury, there was increasingly more type I muscle fibers in Rbfox2 conditional knockout TA muscle compared to the control. These data highlight the importance of alternative splicing in regulating muscle fiber type, with Rbfox2 as a key regulator. In summary, this study provides important novel insights into the role of alternative splicing in SC activation, particularly emphasizing the alternative splicing of Numb. This work has been submitted as a manuscript to Stem Cell Reports, where reviewers have shown great enthusiasm and have given minor comments. The manuscript is under revision, and we expect to re-submit the revised version by early-September 2025.

16102021.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16102021.value: As mentioned, long-read sequencing has precisely identified splicing events and novel transcript variants. However, these techniques typically require a substantial amount of high-quality input RNA, of which quiescent SCs are renowned for having very little. Also, as the SC quiescence signature is gradually lost during SC isolation, SCs require in vivo fixation before sorting, compromising the RNA yield and quality. Over the years, several protocols and kits have been established to reduce RNA input for long-read sequencing. However, further optimization of long-read sequencing is warranted for fixed quiescent SCs. While we revealed rapid and extensive splicing changes upon SC activation, the function of most DSEs is still unknown. Gene enrichment analysis indicates that these genes that undergo splicing changes during SC activation are functionally important. The impact of these splicing events during SC is waiting for further study. Interestingly, in the absence of Rbfox2, we did not observe a significant number of splicing changes during SC activation. However, we did observe dynamic changes in the expression and splicing of splicing factors during SC activation. This suggests that other splicing factors regulate SC cell fate decisions, which may warrant further study. We also reported that Rbfox2 altered the muscle fiber type in the tibialis anterior muscle. This apparent remodeling could be further investigated in terms of how we might manipulate muscle fiber structure and function through alternative splicing. Such knowledge may inform the promotion of the repair of specific muscle groups. The mechanism by which this phenomenon occurs has not been studied in this reported study and could be an area of future development.

16102021.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102021.value: Satellite cells (SCs) are the adult stem cells responsible for skeletal muscle regeneration. Most SCs remain quiescent (a "dormant" state) in resting adult muscles but can activate (or "awaken" rapidly to repair muscle following tissue injury. Regulating SC functions is essential for muscle regeneration. Alternative splicing (AS) (which increases protein diversity from a single gene) is a key mechanism controlling gene function, but its role during SC activation remains elusive. Using our established fixation approach to preserve SCs in quiescence, we revealed rapid and extensive gene splicing changes upon SC activation. Importantly, we report that RNA Binding Fox-1 Homolog 2 (Rbfox2) regulates gene splicing in SCs and is required for SC activation and muscle repair. We specifically demonstrated that Rbfox2 regulates the splicing of a specific DNA region (exon 6) in the Numb gene. Exon 6 regulates Notch signaling (which regulates stem cell maintenance), with the loss of exon 6 delaying SC activation. Our study provides an AS landscape during SC activation, with Rbfox2 being a key splicing regulator in SCs. Moreover, we demonstrate that manipulating the splicing of a single gene could affect SC activation and Notch signaling, highlighting the importance of AS in regulating SC functions.

16102321.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16102321.value: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are short non-coding RNAs that play essential roles in gene regulation and numerous human diseases. Microprocessor initiates miRNA biogenesis by processing primary microRNAs (pri-miRNAs). Therefore, understanding Microprocessor's molecular mechanisms is essential for interpreting miRNA expression and functions in different cellular processes and diseases. The canonical pri-miRNA processing model, which has been developed over the last 15 years by many groups, depicts Microprocessor relying on the lower stem (LS) region of 13 base pairs (bp) in pri-miRNAs for its cleavage. However, we find that many human pri-miRNAs (~20% of human pri-miRNAs) have very short LS regions containing a few bp. Therefore, we hypothesize that Microprocessor might use a non-canonical mechanism to cleave these short LS pri-miRNAs. Indeed, we observe that Microprocessor can cleave many pri-miRNAs, which do not have the 13 bp-LS, just as efficiently as canonical pri-miRNAs, suggesting that Microprocessor does not require a 13 bp-LS for its action, as described in the canonical model. Besides, we also demonstrate that the deletion of the protein domain responsible for canonical mechanisms does not abrogate the Microprocessor ability to cleave short LS pri-miRNAs. These preliminary data support the existence of a non-canonical mechanism acting on short LS pri-miRNAs. In this study, we will use the high throughput pri-miRNA processing assays, including purified recombinant proteins, synthetic RNAs, and next-generation sequencing to identify the RNA elements essential for the proposed non-canonical mechanism. We aim to identify more RNA substrates cleaved by Microprocessor using the non-canonical mechanism. These RNA substrates might be distinct from the classical substrates of Microprocessor, pri-miRNAs. We will also investigate the use of short LS pri-miRNAs for improving gene silencing methods. This study will advance our understanding of the mechanisms of Microprocessor and, enlarge its substrate pools, thereby establishing broader functions of Microprocessor in RNA biology and gene-silencing techniques. MicroRNAs(miRNAs) 是在基因调控和许多人类疾病中发挥重要作用的短非编码 RNA。miRNA加工复合体通过对microRNA 初级转录本 (pri-miRNA)的加工来启动 miRNA 生物合成。因此，了解加工复合体的分子机制对于解释 miRNA 在不同细胞过程和疾病中的表达和功能至关重要。在过去的 15 年中，许多研究人员揭示了经典的 pri-miRNA 加工模型，该模型显示加工复合体对pri-miRNA 中13 个碱基(bp)长的下部茎 (LS) 区域进行切割。然而，我们发现许多人源 pri-miRNA（大约20%的人源pri-miRNA）具有非常短的只有几个碱基对的 LS 区域。因此，我们假设加工复合体可能使用非经典机制来切割这些短的 LS pri-miRNA。事实上，我们观察到加工复合体可以切割许多没有 13 bp-LS 的 pri-miRNA，而且这种非经典切割过程就像经典的pri-miRNA切割一样高效，这表明加工复合体的切割并不需要经典模型中的13 bp-LS区域。此外，我们的初步研究结果还证明删除经典切割模型中负责LS区域的蛋白质结构域不会影响加工复合体微切割短 LS pri-miRNA 的能力。这些实验数据证明加工复合体存在短 LS pri-miRNA 的非经典加工机制。在这项研究中，我们将使用高通量 pri-miRNA 加工分析，包括纯化的重组蛋白、合成 RNA 和NGS测序，以确定对非经典切割机制必不可少的 RNA 元件。我们的目标是使用非经典机制鉴定更多被加工复合体切割的 RNA 底物。这些 RNA 底物可能与之前经典切割模型中的底物 pri-miRNA有所不同。我们还将研究使用短 LS pri-miRNA 来改进基因沉默方法。这项研究将增进我们对加工复合体加工机制的理解，并扩大其底物RNA的范围，从而研究加工复合体在 RNA 生物学和基因沉默技术中更广泛的功能。

16102321.label: Realisation of objectives
16102321.value: This project pursued four objectives to define the molecular basis and functional impact of noncanonical pri-miRNA processing by the human Microprocessor (MP). Below is a succinct assessment of achievements, success level, and how challenges were addressed. Objective 1: Elucidate the molecular mechanism of noncanonical pri-miRNA processing by MP Achievement: Fully achieved. • Mechanistic insight: The study identified DROSHA dsRNA recognition sites (DRES) as the core determinant of noncanonical processing. In contrast to the canonical pathway, this mechanism operates independently of the 13-bp lower stem, basal junction, DROSHA dsRBD, and the Belt helix. • Key advances: o Role of DRES: High-throughput cleavage assays established DRES as essential for setting both efficiency and register. o Substrate class: Defined a distinct class of short stem-loop RNAs (~28 bp) with short lower stems (~6–8 bp) that are processed noncanonically. o Synergy: DRES acts independently and can synergize with canonical motifs (UG, UGU, mGHG) to boost cleavage. • Challenges and mitigation: o DRES discovery was difficult due to small size/low enrichment; overcome by randomized, barcoded pri-miRNA libraries enabling motif mapping at scale. o Remaining gap: Precise structural basis of DROSHA–DRES recognition; slated for future structural/biochemical work. Objective 2: Define the human pri-miRNA subset processed by the noncanonical pathway Achievement: Fully achieved. • Outcomes: o Systematic identification of human pri-miRNAs with short lower stems (~5–8 bp) that depend on DRES for accurate, efficient processing. o Functional validation via mutagenesis: installing/removing DRES switches substrates between canonical and noncanonical routes. • Challenges and mitigation: o Underrepresentation of short–lower-stem substrates in prior work addressed by targeted prioritization and integrative bioinformatic filtering. Objective 3: Characterize short-stem RNA loop substrates of the noncanonical pathway Achievement: Fully achieved. • Findings: o Structural envelope: lower stem 6–8 bp, upper stem 21–25 bp, apical loop >6 nt, total ~28 bp. o Critical element: presence of DRES dictates efficiency and accuracy. o Engineering: Artificial short-stem pri-miRNAs bearing DRES are robust noncanonical substrates. • Challenges and mitigation: o Iterative design–test cycles were required; guided by computational modeling and experimental screening to converge on optimal architectures. Objective 4: Engineer short artificial stem-loop RNAs for gene knockdown via the noncanonical pathway Achievement: Successfully achieved. • Outcomes: o Design: DRES-containing short stem-loop RNAs were processed efficiently in vitro by MP. o Cellular function: These precursors yielded mature miRNAs in cells that effectively repress target genes. o Proof-of-concept: Establishes DRES-guided designs as a platform for RNA-based knockdown and potential therapeutic development. • Challenges and mitigation: o Optimization for processing and cellular performance required multiple rounds of refinement, but strong cleavage and functional readouts confirmed viability. Overall conclusion The project met all four objectives, defining DRES-centered noncanonical processing, mapping its natural substrates, specifying structural requirements, and demonstrating practical gene-silencing applications with engineered precursors. Remaining gaps are primarily structural and will be addressed by future biochemical and cryo-EM studies. In this project, we spent more on general expenses and less on research staff compared with the requested budget, for the following reasons. We received additional financial support for my PhD students from HKUST and the Hong Kong PhD Fellowship Scheme. As a result, our spending on research staff was lower than the amount originally requested. We spent more on consumables due to project needs. We had to construct RNA libraries with greater complexity than anticipated (targeting approximately 0.25 million sequences), which required more oligos, reagents, and sequencing than planned. In addition, during the course of the research we discovered that DRES is a conserved element across multiple species. To make our study more comprehensive and to address reviewer questions, we expanded our experiments to include the Microprocessor from C. elegans, Drosophila, and mouse, which further increased consumables costs.

16102321.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102321.value: Our work advances understanding of Microprocessor (MP) enzymology, reveals a noncanonical pri-miRNA processing pathway, and introduces scalable methods to map cleavage determinants. Key findings and outcomes are summarized below. 1. Discovery of a noncanonical pri-miRNA processing pathway • Key finding: We identified a Microprocessor (DROSHA–DGCR8) mechanism that bypasses canonical elements (13-bp lower stem, basal junction) and instead uses DROSHA dsRNA recognition sites (DRES) to set accurate cleavage. • Outcomes: o DRES enhances cleavage efficiency and register across diverse pri-miRNAs. o The mechanism expands MP’s substrate scope, notably in C. elegans, and is conserved across animals. o MP can process pri-miRNAs with short lower stems (≈6–8 bp), broadening the regulatory space of miRNA biogenesis. 2. Structural and sequence requirements for noncanonical cleavage • Key finding: Optimal noncanonical substrates feature a short lower stem (~6–8 bp), an upper stem (~21–25 bp), an apical loop >6 nt, and DRES as a critical efficiency/accuracy determinant. • Outcomes: o High-throughput assays pinpointed sequence features (e.g., G–U at DRES positions) that boost cleavage. o Engineered short-stem pri-miRNAs bearing DRES are efficiently processed, enabling gene regulation/knockdown designs. 3. High-throughput pri-miRNA cleavage assays • Key finding: We established a radioisotope-free, scalable pipeline combining randomized pri-miRNA libraries, purified MP, processing assays, and NGS to map sites and quantify efficiency. • Outcomes: o Analysis of >260,000 randomized substrates uncovered core RNA elements and motifs required for MP cleavage. o The platform supports systematic testing of mutations, SNPs, and cofactors, and is portable across species (e.g., C. elegans). 4. Conservation and evolution of the noncanonical mechanism • Key finding: DRES-mediated noncanonical processing is conserved, with strong enrichment in nematodes. • Outcomes: o ~41% of C. elegans pri-miRNAs rely on short lower stems and DRES. o DRES-containing pri-miRNAs occur in human, mouse, fly, and worm, underscoring evolutionary conservation and functional importance. 5. Practical applications and future directions • Key finding: DRES discovery and high-throughput mapping enable rational design of artificial pri-miRNAs for knockdown and therapeutic use. • Outcomes: o DRES-bearing short-stem RNAs are efficiently processed by MP and produce functional miRNAs in cells. o This foundation supports development of RNA-based therapeutics and expanded high-throughput platforms to probe MP processing under physiological and disease contexts.

16102321.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16102321.value: • Mechanistic insights: Pursue structural and biochemical studies to define how DROSHA recognizes DRES, pinpointing residue-level contacts that enable noncanonical substrate selection. This will clarify mechanism and evolutionary adaptation. • Expanded discovery via high-throughput assays: Extend the pipeline to libraries with randomized mismatches and wobble pairs to uncover additional regulatory features and novel RNA motifs that modulate Microprocessor specificity and efficiency. • Therapeutic design: Exploit DRES-guided cleavage to engineer artificial pri-miRNAs for targeted gene silencing. Optimize constructs for human cells and evaluate efficacy and safety in disease models to advance precision RNA therapeutics. • Comparative biology: Conduct cross-species analyses of Microprocessor complexes, especially in organisms with atypical miRNA processing, to delineate conserved versus divergent biogenesis strategies. • Integrated technologies: Combine cryo-EM (structural definition), CRISPR-based screens (functional validation), and next-generation sequencing (comprehensive substrate profiling) to accelerate mechanistic mapping and translational development.

16102321.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102321.value: Our cells use tiny molecules called microRNAs (miRNAs) to fine tune how genes are turned on or off. Think of miRNAs as dimmer switches for genes, helping control growth, development, and how we respond to stress. To make miRNAs, cells rely on a protein machine called the Microprocessor, which cuts longer RNA pieces down to the right size, like precise molecular scissors. Scientists have long known the “standard rules” this machine follows. But some miRNAs didn’t fit those rules, and it wasn’t clear how they were made. In this research, we discovered an alternative way, called noncanonical processing, where the Microprocessor looks for special short signals in the RNA, termed DRES, to know exactly where to cut. These signals let the machine process tricky RNAs that the standard rules can’t explain. We also built a fast, large-scale testing method that lets us examine thousands of RNA sequences at once. This helped us spot these special signals and learn how they guide the Microprocessor. Why it matters: • It shows how cells can make a wider variety of miRNAs than we thought, helping explain differences across species and during evolution. • It provides practical tools for designing custom RNA molecules that could one day be used to treat diseases by turning specific genes up or down. • Overall, it gives scientists new ways to understand, and potentially control, gene regulation in health and disease.

16102421.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16102421.value: Blindness is a major public health issue globally. Population-based studies reported that retinal diseases are the most and second-most common cause of irreversible blindness in developed and developing countries, respectively. Retina is the tissue of fine layered structures at the back of the eye. Although the morphological and functional alterations of such tissue have been proven to be associated with a variety of ocular disorders, the pathogenesis is still largely not fully understood. In vivo longitudinal imaging of the biological processes at subcellular resolution provides powerful tools in discovering the biological basis and the influence of disease and therapies. In this proposed research, we will develop an optical imaging method for in vivo visualization of the structural and functional progression of retinal diseases. Retina is part of the central nervous system that can be noninvasively visualized via optical imaging approaches. With the rapid development of mouse models of human diseases, in vivo imaging of the mouse retina is now considered an ideal approach to unveil the mechanisms of retinal disorders. The mouse eye provides critical advantages for high-resolution retinal imaging because the numerical aperture (NA) of the mouse eye is exceptionally high (~0.5) compared with the human eye of small NA (0.1~0.2), making two-photon fluorescence microscopy at the subcellular level practical in live mouse model. However, the major challenge is the large optical aberrations of the mouse eye that significantly blur the laser focus and lowers the imaging resolution. Adaptive optics (AO) has recently been employed in microscopy to correct sample-induced aberrations and restore diffraction-limited resolution in biological tissues. In a previous study, we developed an adaptive optics two-photon excitation fluorescence microscope (AO-TPEFM) by using direct wavefront sensing for near-diffraction-limited and functional retinal imaging in living mice. Glaucoma and retinitis pigmentosa (RP) are two representative neurodegenerative disorders that target the inner and outer retina, respectively. In this proposal, we will adopt the AO-TPEFM to study these prevalent retinal diseases in the mouse models. We will conduct structural and functional imaging of the finest microvascular networks, resident immune cells, and neuronal circuits in the retina of glaucoma and RP mouse models. Various biomarkers across different retinal layers will be assessed to identify the most sensitive symptoms for the progression of diseases. Potential drug candidates will be administrated to study their effect on the biomarkers. 16102721.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16102721.value: This project aims to develop a versatile platform for in situ and localized induction of cancer immunotherapy. Malignant cells often evolve to evade immune recognition and elimination. Strategies in re-priming the immune system are promising. However, the variation in cancer mutations undermines these strategies and personalized cell-based therapies are expensive. Moreover, in modulating the complex immune system, balancing effective anti-cancer responses and severe systemic inflammation is essential yet difficult. Here we propose a biomaterial-based approach. We aim to develop an injectable hydrogel scaffold that will sequentially release multiple cytokines while presenting autologous tumor antigens and adjuvants to orchestrate the priming of immune cells for long-lasting, effective anti-tumor responses. The scaffold serves as an artificial extracellular matrix for the dendritic cells to proliferate and mature. It will hold assorted microgel particles that 1) present antigens from tumor cell lysate and adjuvants, and 2) encapsulate multiple cytokines and release them with the release profile optimized for each signal. The programmed release of multiple contents would recruit dendritic cells and create a supportive microenvironment for the dendritic cell to present specific tumor antigens. The hydrogel scaffold is expected to restrict all the dendritic cell-priming events within the artificial matrix, thereby attenuating any systemic side effects. Subsequently, the scaffold will be degraded to release the dendritic cells such that they are free to activate T cells for eliciting specific anti-tumor responses. We hypothesize that the proposed hydrogel platform can provide both spatial and temporal control of biological cues for dendritic cells in order to generate effective vaccines against cancer. 該項目旨在開發一個多功能原位局部誘導癌症免疫療法平台。處於惡性階段的癌細胞往往已進化出各種機制逃逸免疫系統的識別與清除。雖然重啟免疫系統產生特異性抗腫瘤反應的療法被寄予厚望，但癌細胞的高變異率使該策略成效受限，而且基於離體免疫細胞的個性化治療費用昂貴。再者，在調控複雜的免疫系統時，要在維持有效抗癌反應與嚴重全身性炎性反應之間取得平衡是相當困難的。我們提出了一種基於生物材料的方法開發可注射的水凝膠微粒複合平台。此平台，依次控釋多種細胞因子，自體癌細胞抗原和免疫激活劑以誘導樹突細胞啟動持久、有效的特異性抗癌反應。該平台由微米尺度的多孔基質和多種水凝膠微粒構成。多孔基質具有類胞外基質的性質，可供樹突細胞附著並增殖。水凝膠微粒封裝以下信號分子: 1) 由自體癌細胞裂解物中提取的抗原； 2) 多種細胞因子和免疫佐劑。通過在多孔基質有序釋放這些信號分子，該複合平台將富集樹突細胞，並為其創造支持性微環境以誘導特異性抗原呈遞，上述過程將被限制在該水凝膠平台內部，從而減輕全身性反應。該平台隨後會降解，釋放成熟樹突細胞回歸淋巴系統，激活 T 細胞產生特異性抗癌反應。我們的假說為該水凝膠微粒複合平台可在空間與時間兩個維度上控釋多種信號分子，以此調控樹突細胞疫苗對抗癌症。

16102721.label: Realisation of objectives
16102721.value: A) Multi-parameter Hydrogel Design for Controlled Immunomodulator Release: IFN-γ and Poly(I:C) We developed a hydrogel microparticle (HMP)-in-scaffold system to replicate the mechanical and chemical environment of subcutaneous tissue during infection, enabling controlled immunomodulatory agent delivery. The modular design allowed for independent screening of scaffold materials and cytokine release kinetics to optimize dendritic cell (DC) maturation in vitro. The scaffold, composed of non-hydrolysable dextran (DX)-based hydrogels, mimicked ECM stiffness and served as an immunostimulatory matrix. Encapsulated within fast- or slow-degrading HMPs, IFN-γ and poly(I:C) were sequentially released to modulate DC behavior. Results showed that the DX scaffold combined with fast-degrading HMPs, enabling rapid IFN-γ followed by poly(I\:C) release, maximally promoted DC maturation. Treated DCs showed increased CD86/CD40 expression, enhanced antigen presentation via MHC I/II, and higher TNF-α and IFN-γ production compared to HA or GC-based scaffolds with slower HMPs. This HMP-in-scaffold platform thus enables fine-tuning of mechanical and biochemical cues for in vitro DC vaccine development. With gelation under physiological pH and temperature, it is also amenable for in vivo injectable use. However, significant foreign body response (FBR) surrounding the bulk hydrogel post-injection was observed, limiting DC access to inner modules and indicating the need for further surface modifications. B) Zwitterionic Microgels for Vaccine Delivery: Enhanced Immunogenicity with Minimal FBR Using droplet microfluidics, we synthesized 70–80 µm microgels with varied surface charges: anionic (CMDX), cationic (DEDX), zwitterionic (PCDX), and neutral (DX), encapsulating the model tumor antigen ovalbumin (OVA). Release profiles and FBR potential were compared across microgels and corresponding in situ-forming bulk hydrogels. Bulk hydrogels induced substantial FBR, impeding DC recruitment. We thus advanced a microgel-only design. In vitro, JAWSII and RAW264.7 co-cultures confirmed the immunogenicity of OVA-loaded DX microgels—showing increased CD86/CD40 expression and secretion of IL-6 and TNF-α. These findings allowed us to exclude additional adjuvants like poly(I\:C) and IFN-γ. In vivo (non-tumor C57BL/6 model), PCDX microgels suppressed FBR and supported local recruitment and maturation of DCs (CD11c+ CD86+). PCDX also facilitated sustained antigen release and efficient redistribution to inguinal lymph nodes over 21 days. Robust T cell responses (CD4+, CD8+) and humoral responses (IgG1, IgG2) were observed, positioning zwitterionic PCDX as a potent self-adjuvanted vaccine carrier. C) Self-Adjuvanted L-Arginine Modified Nanogels for Sustained Antigen Delivery We created ~325 nm acid-labile dextran (DX)-based nanogels via water-in-oil emulsion, incorporating hydrazone crosslinks for pH-triggered degradation. Nanogels were surface-modified with amino acids—arginine, glutamic acid, or histidine—to evaluate immunomodulatory effects. Ovalbumin (OVA) served as the model antigen. Release kinetics at pH 5 and 7 confirmed acid-sensitive antigen release. In vitro, prolonged culture with JAWSII cells showed nanogels retained intracellular OVA for four days and promoted antigen presentation via MHC-I/II. DCs treated with Arg-modified nanogels exhibited higher CD86, CD40, and CCR7 expression. RAW264.7 macrophages responded with increased M1 markers and NFκB activation. These immunogenic features enabled the exclusion of additional adjuvants. In vivo, ArgDX nanogels demonstrated superior antigen depot function. Biodistribution showed persistence at the injection site and antigen transport to lymph nodes, spleen, and peripheral organs. In lymphoid organs, elevated CD11c+ CD86+ DCs were detected. Robust CD4+/CD8+ T cell activation and anti-OVA IgG1/IgG2 antibody production were also observed, confirming ArgDX nanogels as potent antigen delivery platforms for vaccination. D) TLR2-Agonist Peptide-Decorated Nanoparticles for Cancer Vaccine Delivery We engineered dextran (DX)-based nanoparticles (NPs) encapsulating OVA and poly(I:C), with surface conjugation of a TLR1/2-agonist peptide (Gly-Gly-Gly-Cys-Ser-Lys-Lys-Lys-Lys), derived from Pam3CSK4. The NPs featured pH-sensitive hydrazone crosslinks for intracellular antigen release in acidic compartments. Compared to bolus OVA or non-targeted NPs, CSK-NPs significantly enhanced DC uptake, maturation, and antigen presentation via MHC-I. As intracellular depots, they enabled prolonged antigen presentation in draining lymph nodes, resulting in efficient activation of naïve CD8+ T cells. In vivo, CSK-NPs triggered potent cellular and humoral responses, surpassing alum-based controls in the B16-OVA melanoma model. Dual-loaded CSK-NPs (OVA + poly(I:C)) showed superior tumor control without systemic toxicity. The self-adjuvanting peptide-polysaccharide conjugate design makes them ideal for cancer vaccine development by simultaneously delivering antigens and PAMP-like signals. E) Dual-Sized Hydrogel and MOF Systems for Antigen and Tolerogenic Signal Delivery in Type 1 Diabetes We developed a dual-sized particle vaccine system for inducing immune tolerance, combining dextran-based nanoparticles (NPs) and metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). NPs were loaded with OVA and coated with a Q-peptide derived from the anti-inflammatory protein Angpt-1. This setup aimed to modulate APC responses from the inside-out via receptor-mediated signaling (Tie2, integrins). Q-peptide-conjugated tL-NPs suppressed DC maturation markers (CD86, CD40) in vitro while promoting DC trafficking and Treg cell induction in vivo. The strategy effectively suppressed OVA-specific cellular and humoral responses, supporting its potential in tolerogenic vaccine development. Additionally, to further induce immune tolerance, IL-10 was loaded into zwitterionic dextran (zDX)/MOF composites to mitigate rapid cytokine burst release. The extended release of IL-10 in the local environment was hypothesized to create anti-inflammatory conditions that sustain tolerogenic responses and expand Treg populations. Together, Q-peptide NPs and IL-10-loaded zDX/MOFs present a promising co-delivery strategy for vaccines targeting autoimmune conditions like Type 1 diabetes.

16102721.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102721.value: Journal Paper 1: This study developed a novel vaccine delivery system using zwitterionic polysaccharide-based hydrogel microparticles to create a long-term antigen depot that enhances immunogenicity while suppressing foreign body responses (FBR). PCDX hydrogel microparticles were synthesized by functionalizing dextran (DX) hydrogel precursors with zwitterionic phosphorylcholine (PC) motifs and using droplet microfluidics to generate uniform microparticles with diameter of 70 µm. Compared to carboxymethyl dextran (CMDX) and diethylaminoethyl dextran (DEDX), PCDX hydrogels significantly increased dendritic cell (DC) activation, evaded FBR, evidenced by reduced macrophage adhesion and minimal fibrotic encapsulation,while providing a slower, sustained release of the model antigen, OVA. Subcutaneous PCDX resulted in local activation of DCs, their migration to lymph nodes, and antigen presentation to trigger both CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell response. PCDX also induced more durable and potent humoral responses, with higher levels of antigen-specific IgG1 and IgG2a by day 28. The findings suggest PCDX hydrogels offer a promising solution for vaccine delivery, addressing critical challenges in immunotherapy by enhancing immunogenicity and suppressing FBR, making them valuable for developing effective, long-lasting vaccines. Journal Paper 3: This study developed dextran-based nanogels modified with L-arginine (ArgDX) for intracellular antigen depot in cancer vaccine delivery. These nanogels aimed to address poor immunogenicity of tumor antigens, rapid clearance by innate immunity, and limited cross-presentation on MHC-I to activate CD8+ T-cells. ArgDX nanogels promoted antigen uptake, storage, and cross-presentation on MHC-I, directing immunogenic maturation of antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Compared with nanogels modified with L-histidine (HisDX) and L-glutamate (GlutDX), ArgDX nanogels rapidly released antigens in acidic cellular compartments, promoting greater antigen uptake and storage in DCs in vitro, leading to stronger immunogenic maturation of DCs and M1 polarization of macrophages. OVA-laden nanogels showed prolonged antigen storage and supply from endo-lysosomal compartments, with antigen retention at skin injection sites until day 21. ArgDX nanogels promoted the highest level of lymph node homing signal CCR7 on DCs and showed higher antigen presentation on both MHC-I and II than DX in vitro. In vivo immune studies showed ArgDX nanogels were more effective in inducing both cellular and humoral immunity compared to other treatment groups on day 21 post-treatment. The study concluded ArgDX nanogels represent a promising self-adjuvanted nanocarrier for vaccine delivery, enhancing immune responses through activated DCs with intracellular antigen depots and improved immunogenic maturation. These findings indicate ArgDX nanogels could be effective carriers for cancer vaccines, offering sustained antigen release and fostering robust immune responses.

16102721.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16102721.value: We propose to further evaluate our microgel and nanogel systems in animal models, focusing on both cancer immunotherapy and autoimmune disease treatment. We may assess the efficacy of these systems in solid tumor models to investigate their ability to inhibit tumor growth and induce anti-tumor immunity. Additionally, we may extend the use of these systems for treating autoimmune diseases by modifying the particle surface to induce tolerogenic DC activation. To evaluate in animal models, we propose to focus on Type-1 diabetes. We will test the nanogels' ability to promote T-regulatory cell expansion and suppress autoimmune responses. This work will provide valuable insights into the dual therapeutic potential of our platform.

16102721.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102721.value: In our research, we developed novel cancer vaccine delivery systems using engineered hydrogel platforms to enhance vaccine effects while evading undesirable inflammatory response. We designed micron-sized and nano-sized gel particles to deliver antigens and immune-modulating signals in a controlled, sustained manner upon injection. By optimizing particle size, surface properties, and degradation rates, we upregulated dendritic cell activation and their presentation of antigens, key for producing productive immune responses.

16102821.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16102821.value: Antibiotic tolerance, namely the ability of genetically susceptible bacteria to survive antibiotic treatment, plays a critical and underappreciated role in determining the clinical outcome of bacterial infections. Unlike the better understood phenomenon of antibiotic resistance, which arises from specific genetic alterations that allows cells to direct counteract the effects of antibiotics, tolerance is viewed as phenotypic states, often associated with transient dormancy. Although many genes and mutations have been associated with tolerance, none has proven to be essential for the phenotype; therefore, tolerance is evidently an emergent property of a biological network of many interacting molecules. Recently, it has been shown in numerous studies that high-tolerance mutants can emerge rapidly upon repeated antibiotic treatment. More worryingly, such tolerance is believed to be a stepping stone for the bacteria to develop resistance. Proteomics, which aims at the systematic and simultaneous identification and quantification of all proteins in a biological system, and as such, is especially well-suited to study tolerance. Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive human pathogen that is the leading cause of severe nosocomial infections, particularly due to the prevalence of resistant strains. Despite its clinical importance, tolerance in S. aureus is much less studied and understood than that in model organisms such as Escherichia coli, and so far proteomics has been scarcely employed to tackle this problem. This research proposal outlines our plan to (1) selectively enrich for high-tolerance S. aureus mutants, employing the strategy of adaptive laboratory evolution, (2) develop effective experimental and computational workflows for S. aureus proteomics, in particular for non-growing tolerant (sub-)populations, (3) apply quantitative proteomics to study these mutants under various conditions, and by cross-comparing the differential proteomes of these mutants, zoom in on proteins and molecular pathways that are critical to tolerance, while at the same time survey the diverse landscape of this phenomenon, and (4) build up a catalog of tolerance-associated proteins and develop high-throughput MS-based protein assays for them. This research project promises to deliver the key enabling experimental platform for researchers to study tolerance in S. aureus, and at the same time provide new insights and generate new hypotheses about the mechanisms of antibiotic tolerance, and contribute to the ongoing efforts to develop new treatment to fight bacterial infections and to slow the development of resistance. 抗生素耐受性，即細菌在抗生素治療中存活的能力，在細菌感染的臨床結果起著關鍵且未被充分認識的作用。這現像有別於由特定的基因突變引起，允許細胞直接抵消抗生素的影響的抗生素抗藥性。耐受性被視為表型狀態，通常與短暫休眠有關。儘管許多基因與耐受性有關，但沒有一個被證明是耐受性所必需的。 因此，耐受性顯然是許多相互作用分子的生物網絡的表徵。最近許多研究表明，在重複抗生素治療後，高耐受突變株可以迅速出現。 更令人擔憂的是，這種耐受性被認為是細菌產生抗藥性的先聲。蛋白質組學旨在對生物系統中的所有蛋白質進行系統和同步的識別和量化，因此特別適合研究耐受性。 金黃色葡萄球菌是一種革蘭氏陽性，有普遍流行抗藥菌株，可導致嚴重醫院感染的主要病原體。與模型生物如大腸桿菌相比，科學家對金黃色葡萄球菌的耐受性研究和理解要少得多，而且迄今為止，蛋白質組學幾乎沒有被用於研究這個問題。這項建議書概述了我們的研究計劃:（1）採用人工適應進化的策略，演化出高耐受性金黃色葡萄球菌突變株；（2）開發有效的蛋白質組學實驗流程，特別適用於金黃色葡萄球菌的非生長種群；（3）在不同條件下培養這些突變株，並通過交叉比較這些突變株的差異蛋白質組，聚焦於有關抗生素耐受性的關鍵蛋白質和分子途徑，同時發掘此現象多樣化的產生機制；（4）建立與耐受性相關的蛋白質的目錄，並為它們開發高通量的質譜測定方法。 該研究項目有望為研究人員提供研究金黃色葡萄球菌耐受性的實驗平台，同時開創針對抗生素耐受性機制的新研究方向，並為開發新療法對抗細菌感染，減緩抗生素耐藥性出現的努力做出貢獻。

16102821.label: Realisation of objectives
16102821.value: The captioned project has been completed with full realization of the objectives. The project has also trained 3 postgraduate students in the area of bacterial proteomics: Jordy SULAIMAN (Ph. D.), Yanrong PAN (Ph. D.) and Xing WU (M. Phil.). Please also note that a larger fraction of the funding was used for laboratory consumables than was budgeted. It is largely due to our effort to apply our proposed experimental strategy to other systems (details below), beyond antibiotic tolerance in S. aureus as described in the proposal, to demonstrate its broad applicability to the community and to maximize the impact of the project. This adjustment was also made possible because one of the Ph. D. students, Jordy SULAIMAN, was a Hong Kong PhD Fellowship awardee and did not require financial support. A summary of the achievements under each project objective is provided below. Objective 1 Our first objective is to perform adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) experiments on Staphylococcus aureus by repetitive antibiotic treatments to mine for mutants exhibiting elevated antibiotic tolerance. This objective has been completed with the following research findings. Through adaptive laboratory evolution using two antibiotics (daptomycin and rifampin) alone or in combination mimicking clinical use, more than 10 tolerant and resistant MRSA mutants were generated and characterized. Interestingly, we discovered that cyclic antibiotic treatment applied to the exponential phase cultures of MRSA all led to resistance mutations in the mprF gene (a known daptomycin resistance gene), whereas the same treatment applied to stationary phase cultures led to several tolerance mutations (in genes prkC, proP, rpsR, pgrS, among others) conferring different levels of tolerance. We also observed the interesting competition between resistant and tolerant mutants, and the tolerance-suppressing effect of an additional antibiotic. We subsequently turned to study the stochasticity of the adaptive evolution and tried to test the impact of population bottlenecks on the evolution process. More daptomycin-tolerant MRSA mutants were generated. Among them, we detected mutations on the yycH and yycI genes in multiple lineages that appeared to be responsible for daptomycin tolerance. While we focused on daptomycin for this objective because it is the commonly used last-line antibiotic against MRSA infections, we also became interested in a novel biofilm-inhibiting compound that may be employed as an adjuvant in antibiotic treatments. Elasnin is an elastase inhibitor that was found to be produced in large quantities by a biofilm-forming marine bacteria Streptomyces mobaraensis (by the group of our collaborator, Prof. Peiyuan Qian) and also possesses potent antibiofilm activity against MRSA. Since elasnin’s activity against MRSA was quite orthogonal to traditional antibiotics, we were wondering if ALE using elasnin would produce tolerant or resistant mutants in MRSA as well. As another demonstration of our approach, we were able to generate an elasnin-tolerant mutant (with a mutation in a putative phosphate transport regulator gene) and studied it by proteomics. Although the original objective has been completed and our overall approach proven effective, we continued to pursue extensions to the proposed research plan to maximize the impact, namely, to apply the same approach to other pathogenic bacteria (E. faecium, P. aeruginosa and K. pneumoniae) in mono- or co-culture systems, and to other biocides (ethanol). In one study, we were able to apply adaptive laboratory evolution to P. aeruginosa, by simulating a co-infection environment with S. aureus and K. pneumoniae. These three pathogens are commonly found in polymicrobial infections in wounds and cystic fibrosis lungs. Another direction was to study how E. faecium strains isolated in clinical settings in recent years become increasingly tolerant to alcohols, again by using the adaptive laboratory evolution approach. In both cases the bacteria were found to adapt quickly to the stimuli of the other species or to increasing concentrations of alcohols, and whole genome sequencing revealed multiple interesting mutants hinting at novel mechanisms of molecular adaptations. Objective 2 Our second objective is to develop the requisite experimental and computational workflow for effective application of proteomics on S. aureus, in particular on non-growing, tolerant (sub-)populations. This objective has also been completed in the course of Jordy SULAIMAN’s thesis work and reported in the papers we published. In particular, we fine-tuned the affinity-based cell purification protocol for removing dead cells, originally for E. coli, to work with MRSA cells. We also adjusted some sample preparation procedures to maximize the number of proteins detected. To make our methods more generally applicable, we also extended our methods to other pathogenic bacteria as well as bacterial co-culture systems. In particular, we also adapted our proteomics methods to P. aeruginosa and E. faecium , and recently developed a computational workflow for taxon-specific quantitative proteomics on constructed bacterial communities and validated it on a tri-species consortium of P. aeruginosa, S. aureus and K. pneumoniae. Unlike current metaproteomic methods which are typically designed for more complex bacterial communities (such as the gut microbiome) but are often limited to detecting functional changes at the pan-species level, our method is designed for simpler consortia and can reveal changes in species composition as well as differential protein expression in each species. This work is part of Yanrong PAN’s thesis and will be written up in a manuscript, tentatively titled “Taxon-resolved label-free quantitative proteomics for defined polymicrobial communities.” Objective 3 Our third objective is to employ state-of-the-art proteomic technology to study the high-tolerance mutants under normal growth conditions and under antibiotic challenges, in order to obtain insights into the molecular mechanisms for tolerance. This objective as stated has been largely completed. The ALE-generated mutants were subjected to proteomics analysis and reported in several papers listed in this report. Overall, these results validated our proposed strategy of using proteomic analysis and cross-comparison of multiple mutants sharing tolerance phenotypes to identify important tolerance-associated proteins. Although not in the original proposal, we also extended the research impact by applying the same strategy to elucidate the tolerance and biofilm eradication mechanism of elasnin, as well as the adaptations of P. aeruginosa in simulated polymicrobial infections and E. faecium in elevated concentrations of alcohol. To summarize the use of proteomics in antibiotic resistance and tolerance research, we also wrote a review article which we hope will encourage more researchers working on various microbiological problems to adopt this powerful approach (Sulaiman and Lam, Proteomics 22, 2100409 (2022)). Objective 4 Our modified fourth objective is to construct comprehensive spectral libraries of the S. aureus proteome, to enable the development of high-throughput MS-based protein assays for antibiotic tolerance research. The proteomics experiments we performed on various MRSA strains under different conditions led to a collection of 111 MS runs of shotgun proteomics data acquired on state-of-the-art instruments. We have submitted the data in their unprocessed form to public repositories to accompany our publications. Since the midterm progress report, we have also compiled spectral libraries from the data and released them for public use. A manuscript titled "A high-quality mass spectral library and comprehensive mass modification profiling of the Staphylococcus aureus proteome" has been written to describe this dataset, including some meta-analysis about patterns of post-translational modifications (which is attached with this report). The publication process of this manuscript is still ongoing.

16102821.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102821.value: The major research outcome of this project was the development and validation of an experimental strategy that combines adaptive laboratory evolution with proteomics to study antibiotic tolerance in Staphylococcus aureus, a phenomenon of great clinical importance due to the prevalence of this pathogen and its implication on the emergence of antibiotic resistance. Using this strategy, dozens of tolerant S. aureus mutants with minimal genotypic deviation from the non-tolerant ancestral strain could be obtained, which were then characterized by whole genome sequencing and proteomics to reveal molecular mechanisms underlying tolerance. The rich data obtained confirmed the hypothesis that tolerance is an emergent property that arise from perturbations in the network of molecular interactions associated with many genes and proteins of diverse functions, collectively known as the “tolerome.” Thus, this study was a leap forward in the effort to map the tolerome and thereby to better understand this phenomenon. The same strategy was also successfully applied to several other bacterial systems, as an extension of the project. Another outcome of the project was the training of two Ph. D. students Jordy SULAIMAN (graduated in 2022) and Yanrong PAN (expected in 2026), one M. Phil. Student, Xing WU (graduated in 2024).

16102821.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16102821.value: Given that effectiveness of the experimental approach of combining adaptive laboratory evolution and proteomics, we have already attempted to enhance the impact of this project by applying it to other bacterial pathogens, to constructed microbial communities, and to other phenomena of interest with some success. Going forward, we believe that the same approach can be adapted more broadly to other problems in microbiology. Some challenges that we foresee is in designing suitable culture conditions to sustain stable cultures (especially for microbial communities), and in obtaining more parallel lineages in the evolution experiment. To that end, high-throughput autonomous systems for bacterial culture will be crucial as they enable the researcher to explore the design space and the evolutionary landscape more efficiently. As proteomic methods advance, there is also a need to leverage the latest technologies, such as data-independent acquisition and single-cell proteomics, to reach deeper in the proteomes with improved quantitative accuracy.

16102821.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102821.value: Antibiotic tolerance, namely the ability of genetically susceptible bacteria to survive antibiotic treatment for a longer duration than expected, plays a critical and underappreciated role in determining the clinical outcome of bacterial infections, for instance, as a stepping stone to the development of antibiotic resistance. Unlike resistance, however, tolerance is viewed as phenotypic switches and is an emergent property of a biological network of many interacting molecules, which would be difficult to clarify by a reductionist approach. Therefore, proteomics, which aims at the systematic and simultaneous identification and quantification of all proteins in a biological system, and as such, is especially well-suited to study tolerance. In this project, we focused on the common pathogen Staphylococcus aureus. We first utilized adaptive laboratory evolution to mine for high-tolerance mutants, and then cross-compared their proteomes under various conditions to zoom in on proteins that are critical to tolerance. The experimental strategy was shown to be effective in generating dozens of distinct high-tolerance mutants and identifying many genes and proteins implicated in tolerance, confirming the emergent property hypothesis and contributing to the ongoing efforts to fight bacterial infections and slow the development of resistance.

16102921.label: Project Objectives
16102921.value: To further characterize SURF4-mediated ER-to-Golgi transport of ShhN. We will analyse the dynamics of the association between SURF4 and ShhN (Aim 1-1), and investigate whether proteoglycans regulate the dissociation of SURF4 from ShhN at the Golgi (Aim 1-2). To reveal the COPII machinery that regulates the packaging of Shh into transport vesicles. We will reveal the Sec24 isoform that regulates the packaging of ShhN into COPII vesicles (Aim 2-1). We will then reconstitute the packaging of ShhN into COPII vesicles using purified COPII components (Aim 2-2). To identify additional factors that regulate the sorting and secretion of Shh. We will perform proteomic analyses to reveal novel Shh-associated cellular factors (Aim 3-1) and test whether the identified Shh-associated cellular factors regulate trafficking of Shh (Aim 3-2). We will also investigate whether cholesterol medication and sphingomyelin (SM) regulate the sorting of Shh at the TGN (Aim 3-3). To test whether SURF4 and other identified cellular factors are important for Hh secretion and signaling in Drosophila wing imaginal discs. We will use the flippase-out Gal4 system to generate mosaic clones of knockdown cells. Using this system, we will test whether knockdown of SURF4 or other identified factors causes defects in Hh secretion and causes defects in Hh-activated target gene expression in wing discs.

16102921.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16102921.value: 刺猬因子 (Shh) 是一種關鍵的信號分子，在胚胎模式、細胞分化和器官發育中起著重要作用。新合成的 Shh 被導入內質網 (ER)，在那裡經歷一系列的修飾後形成熟的脂質修飾氨基末端片段。成熟的 Shh 隨後離開內質網，並沿分泌轉運途徑輸送至質膜。到達質膜後，這種信號分子就會釋放到細胞外基質中，最終被靶細胞質膜上的受體識別，從而誘導下游信號轉導。儘管刺猬因子信號通路的分子機制取得了重大進展，但調控細胞分泌Shh蛋白的分子機制仍不清楚。 我們研究了未經膽固醇修飾的 Shh N 末端片段(ShhN)的細胞內部運輸過程。我們發現 Shh 中的 Cardin-Weintraub (CW) 基序對於 ShhN 的 ER 到高爾基體轉運是必要和充分的。此外，我們發現貨物受體 SURF4 直接與 ShhN 的 CW 基序相互作用，以調節 ShhN 包裝到 ER 的 COPII 囊泡中。已知 CW 基序與在高爾基體合成的蛋白聚醣 (PG) 有相互作用。有趣的是，我們發現抑制 PG 的合成會導致 ShhN 從反式高爾基網絡 (TGN) 輸出的缺陷。 基於這些初步結果，我們假設 Shh 的分泌受 SURF4 和蛋白多醣接力機制的調節。為了驗證這一假設，我們將進一步研究 SURF4 介導的 ShhN ER 輸出。然後我們將揭示 COPII和其他調節 Shh分泌的細胞因子。最後，我們將研究 SURF4 以及其他已鑑定的細胞因子是否調控果蠅翅膀中 Hh的分泌和 Hh 信號傳導。 我們的研究將為 Shh 的生物合成運輸提供新的見解，這對於 Shh 行駛其生理功能很重要。刺猬因子信號通路的過度激活可導致癌症。我們的研究將提供通過抑制 Shh 分泌來下調 Hh 信號傳導的新的治療靶點。

16102921.label: Realisation of objectives
16102921.value: Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) is a key signaling molecule critical for embryonic patterning, cell differentiation, and organ development. While significant progress has been made in understanding the regulation of Shh expression in Shh-producing cells, as well as the receptors and downstream Hedgehog signaling pathways in target cells, the mechanisms governing the transport and secretion of newly synthesized Shh remain poorly understood. In this proejct, we aimed to elucidate how Shh is trafficked through the secretory pathway. We identified the Cardin-Weintraub (CW) motif in Shh as both necessary and sufficient for its ER-to-Golgi transport. Further investigation revealed that the cargo receptor SURF4 plays a crucial role in exporting Shh from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Knockdown of SURF4 delayed the delivery of Shh to the Golgi, and vesicle formation assays confirmed that SURF4 is essential for packaging Shh into transport vesicles. Mechanistic studies, including GST pull-down assays, peptide binding assays, and isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), demonstrated that the first luminal loop of SURF4 (aa 49-60) directly binds the CW motif of ShhN, likely through electrostatic interactions. We also observed that Shh colocalizes with SURF4 upon ER exit and travels with it to the Golgi. The CW motif is known to interact with proteoglycans (PGs), which are primarily synthesized in the Golgi. Intriguingly, inhibiting PG synthesis impaired ShhN export from the trans-Golgi network (TGN) without affecting E-cadherin surface delivery. Protein interaction analyses revealed that the proteoglycan heparin competes with SURF4 for Shh binding, suggesting that PGs displace SURF4 from Shh in the Golgi. Notably, a slightly acidic pH (6.0) did not disrupt the SURF4-ShhN interaction, but heparin still inhibited their binding, indicating that PG-mediated competition occurs even in the TGN’s mildly acidic environment. Our findings outline a multistep mechanism for Shh secretion:1) SURF4 binds the CW motif of Shh, facilitating its packaging into COPII vesicles; 2) PGs compete with SURF4 for Shh binding in the Golgi; 3) SURF4 is recycled back to the ER via COPI vesicles;4) PG association with Shh is required for TGN export. This study uncovers a novel SURF4-proteoglycan relay system that regulates Shh sorting and secretion, bridging a critical gap in understanding how Shh moves from production to function. It also provides broader insights into cargo receptor mechanisms—specifically, how they selectively capture clients in one compartment and release them at their destination. These findings were published in PNAS (1). We extended this work to other secretory proteins containing the CW motif, including Desert Hedgehog (Dhh), Indian Hedgehog (Ihh), BMP8A, and SFRP1. The polybasic motifs in these cargoes were essential for ER export, and further analysis showed that they interact with SURF4’s tri-acidic motif in its first luminal domain. These interactions were both necessary and sufficient for ER-to-Golgi trafficking. Additionally, we found that SURF4 localizes to specific ER exit sites (ERES), where it mediates the export of CW motif-bearing cargoes. This work, accepted in JBC (2), establishes SURF4 as a general regulator of CW-dependent secretion. To explore the physiological relevance of SURF4 in Hedgehog signaling, we developed a Drosophila genetic model. Using actin-y+-Gal4 (act>y+>Gal4) drivers and FLP-out Gal4 mosaics, we knocked down Surf4 in wing discs. Mosaic clones in the P compartment near the A/P boundary disrupted ptc-lacZ reporter expression, indicating that Surf4 is required for Hedgehog secretion and signaling in Drosophila. To further test the importance of the SURF4-Shh interaction in mammalian cells, we expressed synthetic mRNAs encoding a CW motif fused to a signal peptide and an ER retention (KDEL) motif. This disrupted Shh ER-to-Golgi transport and reduced GLI1 reporter expression, confirming that SURF4-mediated Shh trafficking is essential for Hedgehog signaling. References: 1. 16102921.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102921.value: The study from this project elucidates the molecular mechanisms governing the secretion of Sonic Hedgehog (Shh), a crucial signaling molecule in mammalian development. While the signal transduction pathway induced by Shh is well characterized, mechanisms mediating its secretion remains poorly understood. The research reveals that the Cardin-Weintraub (CW) motif in Shh is essential for its transport from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the Golgi apparatus. Specifically, the cargo receptor Surfeit locus protein 4 (SURF4) directly binds the CW motif of Shh, facilitating its packaging into COPII vesicles for ER-to-Golgi transport. Upon reaching the Golgi, Shh dissociates from SURF4 by Proteoglycans (PGs), synthesized in the Golgi. PGs compete with SURF4 for Shh binding. Inhibition of PG synthesis disrupts Shh export from the trans-Golgi network (TGN), indicating that PGs are crucial for TGN export of Shh. This suggests a SURF4-to-PG relay mechanism, where SURF4 mediates early ER export, while PGs facilitate later secretory stages. The study from this project further extends these findings to other secretory proteins containing the CW motif, including Desert Hedgehog (Dhh), Indian Hedgehog (Ihh), bone morphogenetic protein 8A (BMP8A), and secreted frizzled-related protein 1 (SFRP1). The polybasic motifs in these cargo proteins are critical for their ER export, with BMP8A and SFRP1 directly interacting with SURF4 via a tri-acidic motif in SURF4’s luminal domain. This interaction is both necessary and sufficient for their ER-to-Golgi transport. Additionally, SURF4 localizes to specific ER exit sites (ERES), where it selectively captures CW motif-containing cargo, highlighting its broader role as a cargo receptor for secretory proteins. In conclusion, our study provides key insights into the biosynthetic trafficking of Shh and related proteins, identifying SURF4 as a central regulator of ER export and revealing a relay system involving PGs for subsequent secretion. These findings enhance our understanding of secretory pathway regulation and have implications for developmental disorders and diseases linked to Hedgehog signaling. The majority of the work in this project is published in PNAS 2022 and JBC 2022. We submitted an international patent entitled “Disruption of Sonic hedge-Surf4 interaction for cancer treatment”. We also published one review article with support from this grant. Some of the work are been included in a manuscript published in PNAS 2023.

16102921.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16102921.value: The Shh signaling pathway is an important target for cancer treatment. Current therapies primarily focus on ligand-recipient cells by targeting plasma membrane receptors or downstream signaling components. In contrast, this project provides a foundation for a novel strategy aimed at disrupting Shh ligand secretion rather than recipient cell signaling. We demonstrate that disrupting the SURF4-Shh interaction by expressing synthetic mRNA encoding an ER-retained CW motif impairs Shh signaling in mammalian cells. Moving forward, important future directions of this project include optimizing the expression and stability of synthetic mRNA encoding this motif, as well as identifying small-molecule inhibitors that block SURF4-Shh binding. These mRNAs and inhibitors will then be tested for their ability to suppress cancer progression in mice. This approach could circumvent resistance caused by mutations in recipient cells. Moreover, combining these mRNAs and inhibitors with existing therapies targeting recipient cell signaling may offer a more robust solution to acquired resistance.

16102921.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102921.value: This study uncovers how cells properly release Sonic Hedgehog (Shh), a protein vital for embryo development and tissue patterning. While scientists knew how Shh signals to other cells, how it gets out of the producing cells was a mystery. The team discovered that Shh carries a special tag (the CW motif) that acts like a shipping address. A cellular "courier" called SURF4 recognizes this tag, packages Shh into transport bubbles, and sends it from the ER (the cell’s secretory protein factory) to the Golgi (its shipping center). There, sugary molecules called proteoglycans take over, ensuring Shh gets delivered outside the cell. Disrupting this process blocks Shh secretion, which could lead to developmental defects. The same system also helps transport other important proteins, like those involved in bone growth (BMP8A) and cell communication (SFRP1). By revealing this SURF4-to-proteoglycan relay, the study solves a long-standing puzzle in cell biology and opens doors for treating diseases linked to faulty protein secretion, such as birth defects or cancers driven by Hedgehog signaling.
