16306121.label: Major findings and research outcome
16306121.value: Research topic. — Colloidal suspensions of self-propelled particles exhibit unconventional non-equilibrium behaviors at macroscopic length scales and have presented a subject of enduring interest in fluid dynamics. Our study investigates the hydrodynamics of a thin film of active nematic fluid on a solid substrate. Model. — In the present work, we investigate the statics and dynamics of the active nematic droplet by applying a variational approach based on Onsager’s principle, which has been extended to model active matter. A variational derivation of the thin film model is presented to incorporate the active stress. Stationary active droplets. — The case of uniform extensile activity is analysed, where a stationary shape of the droplet can be stabilized. By introducing a characteristic length measuring the competition between capillarity and activity, the quantitative criterion is derived for the droplet to reach a long and flat stationary profile that is distinct from the passive parabolic profile. Spreading dynamics. — By numerically solving the thin film evolution equation, the spreading dynamics of complete wetting is investigated where two distinct power laws of spreading, with a crossover in between, are observed. The stationary shape of the droplet, stabilized by a finite contact angle and a uniform extensile activity, is also computed and analysed. Droplet migration. — Finally, there is a study of the migration of the active droplet driven by a wettability gradient on the solid substrate or an activity gradient inside the droplet. The data from numerical simulations have been compared to a semi-quantitative estimation based on the force balance and the energy balance. Such comparison has produced semi-quantitative agreement for the magnitude of droplet deformation and the velocity of droplet migration, confirming the physical mechanisms underlying these phenomena. The major findings outlined above have been published in an article included in PART C: Li, Y., & Qian, T. (2025). Hydrodynamics of a thin film of active nematic fluid: Stationary state, spreading, and migration. Physics of Fluids 37, 072109.

16306121.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16306121.value: In the present project, we have investigated the thin film dynamics of nematic liquid crystals (NLCs). There are no defects formed in the nematics and the substrates are flat. These modelling restrictions can be removed by developing a more general model that considers the tensorial nature of NLC ordering and the substrate geometry. For this purpose, the tensorial nematohydrodynamics can be coupled with the phase-field model of two-phase flows to formulate a general model that works for NLC droplets evolving on rough surfaces. Onsager’s variational principle can be employed to derive such a model that includes the active stress. A further development is to consider the NLC droplets moving on soft substrates that are elastic and responsive to droplet dynamics. Given the elastic energy functional of the soft substrate (e.g., Willmore energy), Onsager’s variational principle can still be applied to derive a model where droplet dynamics is coupled with substrate deformation. An even more ambitious development is to consider the dynamics of active NLCs in the context of adaptive wetting where solid surfaces reversibly change their structure, chemistry, or interfacial energy upon contact with a liquid.

16306121.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16306121.value: Nature of the research. — This research project explores the fascinating behavior of active nematic liquid crystals, which are special types of fluids made up of self-propelling particles, like those found in schools of fish or flocks of birds. Unlike ordinary fluids, these active systems can consume stored or ambient energy to exert mechanical forces, leading to collective movements and behaviors over long periods and on large scales. The study focuses on how these active fluids behave when they form thin films on solid surfaces, a situation that has been well studied for passive fluids but is much less understood for active ones. Significance and value. — By developing a new model that incorporates the unique properties of active fluids, the research reveals how their statics and dynamics differ from passive fluids. This work is significant because it enhances our understanding of complex fluid behaviors, which can have applications in various fields, including materials science and biology. The findings could lead to innovative technologies, such as new ways to control fluid movement in micro-scale devices or advancements in soft robotics.

16306321.label: Project Objectives
16306321.value: Production of 2D dipolar Bose–Einstein condensates in a tunable multilayer trap We will produce a dipolar bosonic gas of erbium atoms in the degenerate regime in the working apparatus. The new cooling scheme recently developed by the PI will be used to efficiently produce a cold erbium sample. The erbium atomic cloud will be loaded into a crossed ODT (1,064 nm), where it will be gradually brought into degeneracy through evaporative cooling. We are currently developing an accordion lattice setup than can produce 2D multilayer traps with a tunable interlayer spacing (a few micrometers to tens of micrometers). We will transfer degenerate erbium atoms into the accordion lattice and study the quantum dynamics of the degenerate dipolar erbium atoms. Study of quasiparticle modes in 2D bosonic gas of erbium atoms We will design and build an accordion lattice to form a 2D trap. Specifically, we will study the quasiparticle modes, such as the roton and maxon modes, in the degenerate bosonic erbium gas. To excite the roton modes, we will quench the scattering length of the contact interaction by tuning the external magnetic field around a magnetic Feshbach resonance. We will study the energy dispersion relation of the quasiparticle modes. Study of sliding Luttinger liquid phase by tailoring the trapping The sliding Luttinger liquid (SLL) phase with the potentials of a planar array of 1D tubes is an excellent example through which we could investigate the roles of dipolar interactions in quantum phase transitions. We will create a 1D lattice superposing the established 2D flat-bottom potential trap on the basis of objective 2. By adjusting the magnetic field or tailoring the trapping geometries, we can tune the ratio of the contact interactions to the dipolar interactions and thereby induce several phase transitions.

16306321.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16306321.value: Quantum systems at the microscale, such as ultracold atoms and molecules or hybrid systems, offer superior controllability and push the frontiers of experimental quantum physics. Since the pioneering work on Bose–Einstein condensates in the mid-90s, ultracold atoms and molecules have attracted broad attention, and they have been found to play essential roles in quantum information, quantum computing, quantum simulation, and high-precision metrology. Magnetic atoms, such as chromium, erbium, and dysprosium, which have been brought into quantum degeneracy, offer new opportunities to disclose intriguing few- and many-body physics with unique dipole–dipole interactions. These systems, which are typically called degenerate dipolar gases, hold great promise for the study of exotic quantum matter and novel quantum phases. In this proposal, the PI seeks to address the following challenging question: “What new physics can the intrinsic dipole–dipole interaction of magnetic atoms bring to degenerate bosonic gases?” Prior works have demonstrated dense Feshbach resonances, quantum fluid droplets, and quasiparticle mode excitation with magnetic dipolar gases. They have also extended the Bose–Hubbard model in the optical lattice. Hence, existing research has unveiled novel physics arising from magnetic dipolar gas and has triggered further brave explorations. Herein, we will extend our capability of exploring dipolar physics, especially in the low dimension. We propose to experimentally study new quantum phenomena emerging from the distinct magnetic dipole–dipole interaction with ultracold erbium atoms. The magnetic dipole–dipole interaction is highly tunable and can either be attractive or repulsive. By carefully designing two-dimensional potential traps, we will be able to tailor interatomic interactions in a highly controllable manner and thereby facilitate the observation of novel quantum phases. Our study will advance the research into long-range anisotropic interactions in many-body physics and condensed matter systems. 微觀尺度的量子系統，例如超冷原子和分子或混合系統，提供了卓越的可控性並推動了實驗量子物理學的前沿。自 90 年代中期玻色-愛因斯坦凝聚體的開創性工作以來，超冷原子和分子受到廣泛關注，並被發現在量子信息、量子計算、量子模擬和高精度計量學中發揮著重要作用。磁性原子，如鉻、鉺和鏑，已被引入量子簡併，為揭示具有獨特偶極-偶極相互作用的有趣的少體和多體物理學提供了新的機會。這些系統通常被稱為簡併偶極氣體，對於研究奇異的量子物質和新的量子相具有廣闊的前景。 在該提案中，PI 試圖解決以下具有挑戰性的問題：“磁性原子的固有偶極-偶極相互作用可以帶來哪些新物理學來使玻色氣體簡併？”先前的工作已經證明了密集的 Feshbach 共振、量子流體液滴和磁偶極氣體的準粒子模式激發。他們還在光學晶格中擴展了 Bose-Hubbard 模型。因此，現有研究揭示了磁偶極氣體產生的新物理學，並引發了進一步的勇敢探索。在這裡，我們將擴展我們探索偶極物理的能力，特別是在低維方面。 我們建議通過實驗研究從與超冷鉺原子的獨特磁偶極-偶極相互作用中出現的新量子現象。磁偶極-偶極相互作用是高度可調的，可以是有吸引力的也可以是排斥的。通過仔細設計二維勢阱，我們將能夠以高度可控的方式調整原子間相互作用，從而促進對新型量子相的觀察。我們的研究將推進對多體物理和凝聚態系統中長程各向異性相互作用的研究。

16306321.label: Realisation of objectives
16306321.value: During this project, we developed tunable two-dimensional (2D) trapping potentials capable of accommodating a variable number of atomic layers. We successfully loaded degenerate dipolar quantum gases into these layered structures for systematic investigation. A critical experimental challenge was preserving the ultra-low temperature of the sample during the transfer process into the 2D layers. Maintaining these temperatures proved essential, as thermal excitations can significantly deteriorate the superfluidity that emerges in two dimensions. Building upon our tunable 2D trap system, we realized and characterized a two-dimensional superfluid in the presence of dipole-dipole interactions—a regime that has remained largely unexplored experimentally. To probe this exotic quantum state, we implemented complementary diagnostic techniques including both in-situ absorption imaging and momentum-space time-of-flight imaging. Through these methods, we measured key quantities such as the coherence length and the equation of state across a range of interaction strengths and temperatures. Our measurements provide clear signatures of the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition to superfluidity in two dimensions. This work represents one of the first experimental realizations of a dipolar superfluid in 2D, a system whose theoretical description has been complicated by the interplay between long-range dipolar and short-range contact interactions. A central open question in the field has been whether such systems can be approximately understood within existing theoretical frameworks developed for short-range interactions. Our experimental results demonstrate that, for moderate dipolar interaction strengths, the 2D dipolar system can indeed be described within the short-range interaction picture, and the BKT superfluid transition still emerges with characteristics qualitatively similar to the contact-interaction-only case. This finding provides important validation for theoretical approaches and clarifies the regime of applicability for simplified models. Furthermore, our thermodynamic measurements of the compressibility offer valuable insights into the nature of low-energy excitations in these systems and how they are modified by the presence of dipolar interactions. In addition to characterizing the superfluid properties, we demonstrated a novel experimental technique for continuously tuning the ratio between dipolar and contact interactions by adjusting the angle of the dipole orientation relative to the plane of the 2D system. This capability provides a powerful new knob for exploring the phase diagram of dipolar quantum gases and opens pathways to investigate exotic quantum phases that arise when long-range interactions become dominant, even in 1D where Luttinger liquid picture is useful.

16306321.label: Major findings and research outcome
16306321.value: During this funding period, we achieved significant breakthroughs in understanding quantum many-body systems through two complementary research directions. We investigated the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in two-dimensional dipolar Bose gases – publixhed in Science Advances 2025 - addressing a longstanding challenge in understanding superfluidity with long-range anisotropic interactions. Using quasi-2D erbium atomic gases, we successfully observed the BKT transition from normal to superfluid phases by controlling dipole orientation. Our systematic characterization of the critical point through coherence measurements and equation of state analysis provided fundamental insights into effective short-range descriptions of dipolar interactions in 2D. We directly observed anisotropic density fluctuations and non-local effects in the high-density superfluid regime, confirming the dipolar nature of this exotic superfluid phase. In parallel, our work on thermodynamics of spin-imbalanced Fermi gases with SU(N) symmetric interactions, reported in Physical Review Letters in 2025, has opened new frontiers in multi-component fermionic systems. We developed comprehensive theoretical frameworks that extend thermodynamic studies to arbitrary spin population distributions, deriving closed-form expressions for density fluctuations across all temperature regimes. These predictions were experimentally validated using deeply degenerate gases in both balanced (N≤6) and imbalanced configurations. Remarkably, our experiments with two-species and four-species imbalanced systems revealed that interaction enhancement effects remain substantial even in highly spin-imbalanced regimes, with important implications for decoherence processes and quantum coherence in complex many-body systems. Additionally, we achieved the first experimental demonstration of the two-dimensional non-Hermitian skin effect in an ultracold Fermi gas, published in Nature in 2025. By integrating topological band engineering with non-Hermitian spin-orbit coupling, we created the first 2D non-Hermitian topological band structure. Our measurements revealed exceptional points, complex Fermi arcs, and the distinctive 2D skin effect where eigenstates accumulate at boundaries. This breakthrough opens new avenues for exploring non-Hermitian quantum phenomena in higher dimensions with implications for curved space physics and quantum information science. These achievements collectively address our primary research objectives and establish new paradigms for studying quantum matter.

16306321.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16306321.value: Building on our successful realization of low-dimensional dipolar Bose gases, we propose several research directions. First, we may explore exotic quantum phases including supersolid states, quantum droplets, and stripe phases driven by anisotropic dipolar interactions. Second, we will quantitatively characterize non-local effects using advanced imaging techniques to map spatial correlations and investigate collective excitations unique to dipolar superfluids. Third, we will study dimensional crossover from 2D to 3D geometries and implement optical lattices to explore how dipolar interactions combine with band structure to produce novel topological phases.

16306321.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16306321.value: This project explores the mysterious behavior of ultracold atoms—atoms cooled to near absolute zero where quantum effects dominate. The research achieved three major breakthroughs in understanding quantum matter⁠⁠. The team studied how ultracold dipolar atoms transition into a superfluid state in two dimensions, a phase where matter flows without resistance. By controlling how these magnetic atoms interact, they mapped out the critical point of this transition and observed unique patterns in atom density caused by long-range magnetic forces⁠⁠. In a separate experiment, they investigated systems with multiple types of particles, discovering that quantum interactions remain strong even when particle populations are highly imbalanced⁠⁠. Together, these developments establish new methods for studying exotic states of quantum matter with potential applications in quantum simulations and fundamental physics.

16306421.label: Project Objectives
16306421.value: Utilizing magnetic proximity effect, we will fabricate magnetic insulator and topological insulator (MI/TI) van der Waals heterostructures by dry transferring and stacking of mechanical exfoliated high-quality layered MIs such as CrBr3 and Bi-based TIs like Bi2Se3. MI/TI van der Waals heterostructures with various layer combination will be fabricated. These heterostructures will be further fabricated into Hall-bar devices for transport measurements using standard e-beam lithography and metal evaporation techniques. We will synthesize layered intrinsic magnetic Weyl semimetal Co3Sn2S2 and Co3Sn2Se2 nanostructures using chemical vapor deposition and pulsed laser deposition techniques. The structure, morphology, and composition of nanostructures will be determined using various materials characterization techniques. The nanostructures will be fabricated into Hall-bar devices for transport measurements using standard e-beam lithography and metal evaporation techniques. We will carry out the magnetotransport and magneto optical measurements to investigate the properties of the above obtained MI/TI heterostructures and intrinsic magnetic Weyl semimetal nanostructures.

16306421.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16306421.value: Magnetic topological matters result from the interplay of magnetism and topology of electronic band structures in solid state materials. Research of magnetic topological matters can offer a rich ground for the exploration of new physics and new concepts for applications in non-dissipative electronics, energy saving spintronics, and quantum computation. One distinct feature of magnetic topological materials is to host dissipationless edge states for electron transport, which manifests itself as so-call quantum anomalous Hall effect (QAHE). The first experimental observation of QAHE is realized in a magnetic doped topological insulator, Cr-doped (Bi, Sb)2Te3, with dissipationless edge conductivity at low-temperature (30 mK) and zero magnetic field. For any practical application the magnetic ordering temperature and the temperature for showing QAHE need to be increased considerably. In addition to magnetic doped topological materials, there are other two ways to generate magnetic ordering in topological materials. One utilizes the magnetic proximity effect at the interface of magnetic insulator (MI) and topological insulator (TI) heterostructures. Another is searching for intrinsic magnetic topological materials. Both approaches are promising alternatives for achieving higher magnetic ordering temperature and higher temperature QAHE. In this project, using the newly found layered MI such as CrBr3 and Bi-based layered TI such as Bi2Se3, we propose to fabricate MI/TI van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures using the common method of exfoliation, dry-transferring, and stacking. This kind of vdW heterostructures has unique advantages of enabling atomic flat, dangling bond-free, clean, and sharp interface, which are expected to enhance magnetic proximity effect. We will carry out electrical transport measurements of obtained vdW heterostructures. We aim to observe induced magnetic ordering and the massive Dirac gap opening at elevated temperatures first and then QAHE by further tuning the chemical potential using gate bias in these heterostructures. Furthermore, since we can understand intrinsic magnetic Weyl semimetals (WSM) with layered structures as coupled two-dimensional (2D) QAHE layers, it is possible to realize the QAHE by reducing the dimensionality of a layered intrinsic magnetic WSM to 2D limit. Recently, the layered magnetic WSM Co3Sn2S2 is experimentally confirmed with a large anomalous Hall conductivity and anomalous Hall angle in its three-dimensional bulk. In this project, we propose to grow Co3Sn2S2 nanostructures by chemical vapour deposition and pulsed laser deposition techniques. We will study the layer number and size dependent anomalous Hall effect of obtained nanostructures and aim to explore the possibility of hosting QAHE states in these nanostructures. 磁性拓撲物質的形成是固態材料中電子能帶結構的磁性和拓撲性質相互作用的結果。對於磁性拓撲物質的研究和探索可以為其在非耗散電子學、節能自旋電子學和量子計算中的應用提供豐富的新物理和新概念基礎。磁性拓撲材料的一個顯著特徵是擁有可用於電子傳輸的無耗散邊緣態，這表現為所謂的量子反常霍爾效應。量子反常霍爾效應的首次實驗觀測是在磁性摻雜拓撲絕緣體中實現的，在低溫(30 mK)和零磁場下鉻摻雜的(Bi, Sb)2Te3在其邊緣呈現無耗散電導。對於任何實際應用而言，磁性拓撲材料的磁有序溫度和顯示量子反常霍爾效應的溫度都需要顯著提高。除了磁性摻雜拓撲材料之外，還有另外兩種方法可以在拓撲材料中產生磁有序。一是利用磁絕緣體(MI)和拓撲絕緣體(TI)異質結界面處的磁鄰近效應，二是尋找本徵磁性拓撲材料。這兩種方法都有潛力實現高的磁有序溫度和高溫量子反常霍爾效應。 在該項目中，我們建議利用新發現的層狀磁絕緣體（如CrBr3）和鉍基層狀拓撲絕緣體（如Bi2Se3），使用常規剝離、幹轉移和堆疊的方法製備MI/TI范德華（vdW）異質結構.這種vdW異質結所具有獨特的優勢，例如可實現原子平、無懸掛鍵、清潔和銳利的界面，有望增強磁鄰近效應。我們將對所製備的MI/TI vdW異質結器件進行磁電傳輸測量。我們的目標首先是通過在這些異質結器件中的磁鄰近效應，觀測磁有序溫度和有質量狄拉克能隙打開溫度的提升，然後再利用柵極偏置進一步調整化學勢來觀測量子反常霍爾效應。 此外，由於我們可以將具有層狀結構的本徵磁性外爾半金屬理解為二維量子反常霍爾效應層耦合的結果，因此可以通過將層狀本徵磁性外爾半金屬的維數降低到二維極限來實現量子反常霍爾效應。最近，實驗證實在層狀磁性外爾半金屬Co3Sn2S2三維體材料中可觀測到大的反常霍爾電導率和反常霍爾角。在這個項目中，我們建議通過化學氣相沉積和脈衝激光沉積技術來生長Co3Sn2S2納米結構。我們將研究所獲得的納米結構的層數和尺寸依賴的反常霍爾效應，並旨在探索在這些納米結構中出現量子反常霍爾效應的可能性。

16306421.label: Realisation of objectives
16306421.value: We have fabricated two different FMI/TI heterostructures CrBr3/Bi2Se3 and CrGeTe3/BiSbTeSe2, using the dry transfer method. The transport properties of these systems are investigated. Both anomalous Hall effect (AHE) and topological Hall effect (THE) are observed in these two systems. Compared with the Curie temperature and the coercive field of the bare FMI (CrBr3 or CrGeTe3), the two critical values show an enhancement in the two FMI/TI heterostructures, which is viewed as proof of the induced magnetic proximity effect. Moreover, the negative magnetoresistance is observed in some CrBr3/Bi2Se3 heterostructures but not observed in CrGeTe3/BiSbTeSe2 heterostructures. In addition, the sign change of AHE is observed with changing temperature in both systems or applied gate voltage in CrGeTe3/BiSbTeSe2 systems. These results were reported in an MPhil thesis. We have investigated the third-order nonlinear transport properties in antiferromagnetic topological insulator MnBi2Te4 flakes. The measured third-order longitudinal (Vxx3ω) and transverse (Vxy3ω) voltages show an intimate connection with the magnetic phase transition of MnBi2Te4 flakes. Abrupt changes of magnitude and sign of Vxx3ωand Vxy3ω occur as MnBi2Te4 flake turns to an antiferromagnetic state with temperature cooling below TN ~ 21.7 K. Similar abrupt changes in Vxx3ω and Vxy3ω are also obtained at increased magnetic fields accompanying magnetic phase transition from antiferromagnetic (AFM) state to canted AFM state and FM states in MnBi2Te4 flakes. However, Vxx3ω exhibits an even parity versus magnetic fields, which is opposite to Vxy3ω. This distinct parity symmetry suggests Vxx3ω and Vxy3ω possess different physical origins. The Vxx3ω is believed to originate from possible trivial origins, such as disorder scatterings, while the observation of Vxy3ω is probably related to the emergence of non-zero Berry curvature quadrupole with broken PT symmetry and non-degenerate band structures under external magnetic fields. This work was published in Nature Communications. We have studied the induced second-order Hall effect in bulk non-centrosymmetric Td-WTe2 semimetal by applying direct current along the longitudinal direction. The observed second-order Hall effect is strongly dependent on the external direct current, with its magnitude increasing with direct current. Furthermore, the direct current induced second-order Hall effect in bulk Td-WTe2 exhibits two-fold angular dependent features, which are different from those in bilayer and few-layer Td-WTe2, but similar to the third-order Hall effect observed in bulk Td-WTe2. The occurrence of the second-order Hall effect in bulk Td-WTe2 is believed to originate from several possible origins, including Berry connection polarisation tensor, Drude transport, and disorder scatterings. This work was published in Applied Physics Letters. We grew tetragonal FeTe on c-plane sapphire by the molecular beam epitaxy technique, which resulted in a new structural phase consisting of c-axis-aligned nanocrystals. Depending on the nominal thickness, the temperature-dependent resistance of these thin films shows various characteristics attributed to the thermal responses of the nanocrystals during cooling and heating processes. These findings provide an approach to fabricate a heterostructure in which one layer could generate all possible twisted angles relative to the other layer, for example, via the wafer bonding technique. This work was published in AIP Advances. We used the molecular beam epitaxy technique to grow FeTe on Bi2Te3, demonstrating that varying growth conditions can turn the Bi2Te3 layer into different Bi–Te phases and form corresponding FeTe/Bi–Te heterostructures. It was found that all three FT–BT samples display superconductivity, with the FeTe/Bi2Te3 sample enjoying the highest superconductivity quality. Magneto-transport studies reveal that the induced superconductivity seems to have a 3D nature. These studies reveal a new approach to realising the Bi4Te3 and Bi6Te3 components of the Bi–Te family. This work was published APL Materials.

16306421.label: Major findings and research outcome
16306421.value: In the nonlinear transport measurements of bulk MnBi2Te4, which is a topological anti-ferromagnet, we found that the second-order nonlinear responses are negligible as required by inversion symmetry, but the third-order nonlinear responses are finite. The measured third-harmonic longitudinal and transverse voltages with frequency 3ω, driven by an a.c. current with frequency ω, shows an intimate connection with the magnetic transitions of MnBi2Te4 flakes. In addition, the measured longitudinal voltage is an even function of the applied magnetic field B, while the transverse voltage is odd in B. Amazingly, the field dependence of the third-order responses as a function of the magnetic field suggests that longitudinal signal is induced by the quantum metric quadrupole and the transverse signal is induced by the Berry curvature quadrupole. Therefore, the quadrupoles of both the real and the imaginary part of the quantum geometry tensor of bulk MnBi2Te4 are revealed through the third-order nonlinear transport measurements. This work greatly advanced our understanding of the connections between the higher-order moments of quantum geometry and nonlinear transport (see paper published in NC). We have discovered a driving DC-induced second-order nonlinear Hall effect in bulk Td-WTe2. The observed driving DC-induced second-order nonlinear Hall effect shares similar physical features with that of the intrinsic third-order nonlinear Hall effect, which is probably related to the intrinsic Berry connection polarizability tensor, Drude transport, side jump, and skew scattering effect. Our findings open a promising path toward the realisation of second-order nonlinear Hall effect in a wider range of materials without requiring specific crystal symmetries as prerequisites, and bring great promise for both fundamental research and technological applications of the band geometric quantity engineering (see paper published in APL).

16306421.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16306421.value: The study of quantum geometry effects in materials has been one of the most important research directions in recent decades. The quantum geometry of a material is characterised by the quantum geometric tensor of the Bloch states. The imaginary part of the quantum geometry tensor gives rise to the Berry curvature, while the real part gives rise to the quantum metric. While Berry curvature has been well studied in the past decades, the experimental investigation of the quantum metric effects is only in its infancy. Antiferromagnetic topological insulator MnBi2Te4 has rich magnetic structures and striking topological band structures. Bulk antiferromagnetic topological insulator MnBi2Te4 is an ideal platform for investigating the quantum geometry quadrupole effects, as the second harmonics are suppressed by inversion symmetry and the third-order harmonics are the leading order nonlinear response. We will further study the quantum geometry effect in the MnBi2Te4 thin film system.

16306421.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16306421.value: Topological magnetic materials are a class of compounds whose electronic properties are a unique combination of magnetic spin configurations and the "topology" of their electronic wavefunctions. These materials can host exotic quantum states, making them promising for applications in low-power spintronics, data storage, and quantum computing. This project focused on a specific topological magnetic material, tried to understand the connections between the band quantum geometry and nonlinear transport properties via magnetotransport experiments, and found evidence for such connections, which enriched our knowledge.

16306521.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16306521.value: The advances in the use of a coherent light source such as laser allow us to extract both intensity and phase profile by employing the interference or holographic principle. The recently available single-photon cameras on the detector side can extract time-domain information at individual photon levels, allowing imaging in the low light regime. These developments have been continuously pushing boundaries, with the assistance of other techniques such as structured light illumination and computational imaging, on maximizing the information we can extract while requesting the smallest amount of photons. This approach makes imaging possible in some extreme conditions, such as dedicated biological samples and security applications, in which the available light intensity is preferably limited. In this project, we would like to explore how metasurfaces, this time on the materials or optical components side, can boost imaging in the low light limit. Recent developments of metasurfaces allow tailor-made wavefront control in generating the thinnest lens and the finest holograms. Thus, these metasurfaces provide opportunities in multiplexing between the information carried by different degrees of freedom of light and turn phase and polarization signature of a complex field into an intensity profile to be captured by cameras. Unlike the usage of a multiple scattering medium, the multiplexing capability of metasurfaces can be designed and tailor-made, thereby providing the opportunity to extract all the intensity, phase, and polarization characteristics of a complex field. The additional time-domain information from single-photon cameras also presents an interesting new channel for complex-field extraction. Observing how photons probabilistically accumulate to become an interference pattern in intensity may allow the earlier extraction of the complex-field profile. 最近使用相干光源（如激光）的進展使我們能夠通過干涉或全息原理來提取強度和相位分佈。另一方面，單光子相機可以在單個光子水平上提取時域信息，從而允許在低光照條件下成像。在結構光照明和計算成像等其他技術的幫助下，這些發展一直在不斷突破界限，最大限度地提高我們可以提取圖像的信息，同時要求最少的光子數量。這有利於在某些極端條件下成像，例如生物成像和防偽應用。在這個項目中，我們探索超表面（作為材料或光學元件）如何在低光限制下增強成像。超表面最近的發展允許定制波前控制以生成最薄的透鏡和最優化的全息圖。因此，超表面提供了在不同光自由度攜帶的信息之間相互轉換的機會，並將復雜場的相位和偏振特徵轉換為被相機捕獲的強度分佈。與使用多重散射介質不同，超表面在不同光自由度之間的轉換可以設計和定制，從而有效地提供提取複雜場的所有強度、相位和偏振特性的機會。來自單光子相機的額外時域信息也為複雜場成像提供了一個有趣的新通道。觀察光子如何概率性地積累成為強度的干涉圖案可能允許更早地提取複雜場的信息。

16306521.label: Realisation of objectives
16306521.value: This project explored the use of metasurfaces as structured optical references or generating media for imaging and manipulating complex optical fields in the low-light regime. The core physical concept of the project is based on a reference-assisted imaging scheme, in which a signal beam (or photon) interferes with a reference beam (or photon) associated with a metasurface of known optical response. By exploiting polarization and time correlations between the two photons, information encoded in the optical field is retrieved through imaging of the transmitted diffraction field using a single-photon camera. Building on this physical foundation, all project objectives have been fully realised, as detailed below. Objective 1: This objective has been fully achieved through the development of a diffractive imaging framework operating in the low-light regime, with metasurfaces playing dual and complementary roles within a reference-assisted architecture. Two operational modes were established, both based on imaging diffraction fields using photon-counting detectors. In the first mode, the metasurface serves as a structured reference medium in one optical arm, while the signal beam (or photon) propagates through another arm carrying the optical information of interest. By exploiting polarization and temporal correlations between the two arms, two-photon interference occurs between the signal and reference channels. Imaging the transmitted diffraction field using a single-photon camera enables retrieval of optical information from the signal arm relative to the known response of the reference metasurface. This mode directly realises the reference-assisted diffractive imaging scheme and provides a robust approach for low-light imaging based on correlation measurements. In the second mode, the metasurface is placed directly in the signal arm and functions as a tailor-made generating medium that produces structured diffraction patterns or holographic images. In this configuration, the generated images are entangled with the polarization degree of freedom of the photons. By projecting the polarization state in the correlated arm, the diffraction pattern or image formed in the signal arm can be selectively controlled and reconfigured. Imaging of the resulting diffraction fields provides a direct and efficient readout of the generated optical information under photon-counting conditions. Both operational modes rely on structured light incidence, imaging of diffraction patterns, and compatibility with single-photon detection. Together, they establish a versatile diffractive imaging system that supports reference-assisted imaging, polarization-controlled image generation, and operation in the low-light regime. Objective 1 has therefore been fully realised. Objective 2: This objective was addressed through the design and fabrication of metasurfaces fulfilling complementary roles in the two operational modes of the diffractive imaging framework, spanning both ordered and purposefully disordered configurations, as well as multiple phase-control mechanisms and material platforms. In the first operational mode, metasurfaces were designed and fabricated with well-defined polarization- and phase-dependent responses, forming spatially resolved Jones-matrix profiles. These metasurfaces serve as testing media, whose optical properties are interrogated through reference-assisted imaging. In this configuration, a separate metasurface structure placed in the correlated optical path acts as an ordered reference medium with a known response. Imaging of diffraction fields generated by the testing metasurfaces enables the polarization- and phase-resolved optical response to be retrieved in the low-light regime. In this mode, the metasurface layouts are predominantly spatially ordered or regularly structured to ensure predictable optical behaviour. In the second operational mode, metasurfaces were designed as tailor-made generating media for holographic image formation. Here, the local arrangement of unit cells appears aperiodic or disordered in the near field, with spatially varying orientations and dimensions. This apparent disorder is intentionally designed such that constructive interference is produced at the image plane. These holographic metasurfaces generate images that are entangled with the polarization degree of freedom, enabling different image patterns or their coherent superpositions to be produced through polarization projections in the correlated optical arm in the low light condition. Across both operational modes, metasurfaces were realised using plasmonic and dielectric material platforms. Representative implementations employed plasmonic metasurfaces, such as metallic slot structures, while other designs utilised dielectric metasurfaces to achieve higher transmission efficiency and improved performance under low-light conditions. Some metasurface samples were fabricated in-house, while others were developed in collaboration with external partners (including Hui Liu, Nanjing University; Din-Ping Tsai, City University of Hong Kong; and Xianzhong Chen, Heriot-Watt University). In all cases, the metasurfaces effectively multiplex phase and polarization information and convert complex optical fields into intensity profiles compatible with imaging and photon-counting detection. Objective 2 has been fully completed. Objective 3: This objective was addressed through the development of computational imaging algorithms tailored to the reference-assisted, two-photon interference framework of the project. Initially, a semi-analytic reconstruction method was developed based on two-photon interference visibility extracted from coincidence measurements between pixel pairs of a single-photon camera. By exploiting the known, spatially varying polarization response of the reference metasurface, the measured visibility functions were used to inversely reconstruct polarization-resolved optical responses, enabling spatially resolved Jones-matrix imaging under low-light conditions. Building on this foundation, the reconstruction framework was generalised to numerical and data-driven algorithms that operate directly on photon-counting data. These approaches incorporate the known response of the reference metasurface and the interference between signal and reference channels, enabling scalable and robust reconstruction of complex optical fields with reduced photon budgets. Machine-assisted numerical algorithms based on unsupervised learning were further developed to efficiently extract embedded information from coincidence measurements, allowing reliable imaging with a minimal number of detected photons. Both physics-based (“human-invented”) algorithms and machine-assisted data extraction techniques were developed for imaging purposes, with metasurfaces acting as assistant agents for information multiplexing. Objective 3 has been fully completed. Objective 4: This objective was addressed by exploiting additional time-domain information available from single-photon detection to enhance low-light imaging and holographic field generation, building on the algorithmic readiness identified at the mid-term stage. Following the development of semi-analytic and numerical reconstruction algorithms, the project progressed from processing averaged coincidence signals to explicitly utilising temporal correlations in photon arrival data. Time-correlated heralding techniques were implemented to condition image formation on coincident detection events, leading to a significant improvement in signal-to-noise ratio under low-light conditions. This approach demonstrates how time-domain information can be used as a physical filtering mechanism rather than solely as an input to post-processing algorithms. Beyond noise suppression, time-domain correlations were further exploited to realise quantum holographic image generation, in which images produced by metasurfaces are entangled with the polarization degree of freedom. By projecting different polarization states in the correlated optical arm, distinct image patterns or their coherent superpositions were generated through coincidence-conditioned interference. This represents an extension of heralding from simple switching to controlled interference enabled by temporal photon correlations. Objective 4 has been fully completed by these explorations.

16306521.label: Major findings and research outcome
16306521.value: 1. Reference-assisted coincidence imaging of polarization-resolved optical response We established an experimental framework for reference-assisted imaging based on two-photon interference, enabling polarization-resolved characterization of complex optical fields under low-light conditions. Using a structured metasurface as a known reference, coincidence imaging was employed to reconstruct spatially resolved Jones-matrix responses from intensity-only measurements. This capability was demonstrated experimentally in Nanophotonics (2023) through coincidence-based Jones-matrix imaging, and further advanced using a deep-learning-assisted coincidence imaging approach in npj Nanophotonics (2024), which improved robustness and scalability. These results validate reference-assisted coincidence imaging as a practical tool for low-light polarization-resolved measurements. 2. Metasurface-enabled quantum holography with polarization–image entanglement and time-domain correlations Beyond characterization, the project demonstrated that metasurfaces can function as tailor-made generating media for structured diffraction fields and holographic images under low-light conditions. By engineering the spatial phase and polarization response of metasurfaces, holographic images were generated whose spatial content is entangled with the polarization degree of freedom. As a result, different image patterns, or their coherent superpositions, can be selectively produced through polarization projection in a correlated optical arm and read out via photon-counting detection. Time-domain photon correlations and heralding techniques were explicitly incorporated to condition image formation on coincident detection events, leading to enhanced signal-to-noise ratio in the low-light regime while preserving polarization-conditioned image control. Dual-channel and polarization-multiplexed quantum holographic image generation was demonstrated in Advanced Photonics Nexus (2024) and further extended to quantum holography in Advanced Photonics (2025), where coincidence-conditioned interference enables controlled switching and superposition of images. The significance of this quantum holography work was further reflected by coverage in international science media, including features by the Croucher Foundation, New Scientist, and Phys.org. 3. Photon-efficient optical computation via diffractive metasurfaces and imaging-based readout. The project further showed that metasurface-assisted diffraction, when combined with imaging-based detection and computational reconstruction, enables photon-efficient optical information processing. In these implementations, the output of a diffractive metasurface encodes the result of a prescribed linear transformation directly into a diffraction pattern that can be captured using imaging detectors, making the approach naturally compatible with low-light operation. Using metalens arrays and diffractive metasurfaces implementing known linear transformations, complex-valued optical operations such as matrix–vector multiplication and discrete Fourier transforms were experimentally demonstrated. These results were reported in Nanophotonics (2024) and Advanced Optical Materials (2025), illustrating that diffractive metasurfaces can serve as compact hardware accelerators for complex optical computation with direct, photon-efficient imaging readout.

16306521.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16306521.value: The results achieved in this project establish a versatile platform that can be further developed along several complementary directions. For quantum holography using diffractive metasurfaces, the demonstrated polarization–image entanglement and coincidence-conditioned image control provide a foundation for extending holographic encoding to higher-dimensional quantum states. Ongoing work focuses on generalising the current schemes from polarization-controlled image switching to full two-photon density-matrix holography, in which multiple holographic symbols are encoded and reconstructed at the level of the joint two-photon polarization state, rather than being controlled by a single polarization degree of freedom. This direction enables scalable quantum holographic tomography and opens routes toward high-capacity quantum communication, encryption, and information processing based on holographically encoded entangled light. For photon-efficient optical computation, the imaging-based readout of diffractive metasurfaces enables efficient implementation of optical transformations. Future efforts will focus on exploiting diffractive metasurfaces as fixed, task-specific optical processors whose outputs are retrieved through imaging, particularly under low-light conditions. In particular, metasurfaces implementing standard transforms such as discrete cosine transforms or related linear operations could be repeatedly reused as front-end hardware accelerators for imaging and data-compression tasks.

16306521.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16306521.value: Modern imaging usually relies on bright light to form clear pictures. However, in many important situations—such as delicate biological samples, secure sensing, or quantum technologies—using strong light is not possible. This project explored how to extract maximum information from extremely small numbers of photons. The research combines single-photon cameras, which detect individual particles of light and record when they arrive, with metasurfaces, ultra-thin optical components engineered to precisely shape light. By designing metasurfaces with known optical responses, the project showed that images can be formed by comparing pairs of photons detected at the same time (a technique known as coincidence detection). This allows recovery of not only image brightness, but also information about light polarization and wavefront structure. The use of time information: by using one detected photon to signal the presence of another (a process called heralding), image quality can be significantly improved under very low light levels. In addition, data-analysis and machine-learning techniques were used to efficiently extract images from photon arrival data. Overall, the project advances low-light imaging and holography, with potential applications in biomedical imaging, secure communication, sensing, and future quantum technologies.

16306621.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16306621.value: Water is one of the most common substances, and plays a key role in the sustainable development of human societies. However, it is less well known that vast quantities of water exist deep inside Earth. Water is a major component in Earth’s deep fluids, and may also act as ionic impurities in rocks and minerals. Over Earth’s history, water has deeply influenced the dynamics and structure of our planet. Under extremely high pressure (HP) and high temperature (HT) conditions of Earth’s interior, water in a supercritical state has many extraordinary physical and chemical properties, which are of great importance in many geochemical processes, but remain poorly understood. It is very challenging to study water experimentally under both HP and HT conditions. First principles simulations, free of experimental inputs or empirical parameters, may provide accurate data beyond the current experimental reach, but they are very computationally demanding, so it is difficult to cover a pressure-temperature range as great as that found deep inside Earth. In the proposed project, we plan to develop efficient strategies combining first-principles molecular dynamics simulations with machine learning techniques to study water in the supercritical fluid phase at HP and HT. We want to understand how water dissolves and transports other materials in Earth’s deep fluids, so we will focus on the dielectric, dynamics, and thermodynamic properties of water. We will calculate the dielectric constant, shear viscosity, and P-V-T data of water in Earth’s mantle. The developed computational tools will reveal a molecular picture of deep water solutions and help guide the related experiments. The data obtained through our computer simulations will help to improve current geochemical models, such as the Deep Earth Water model (http://www.dewcommunity.org/). This proposed study will have great implications for the understanding of the deep water cycle and mass transfer in Earth’s interior. 16306621.value: 1. Raman and IR spectra of water under graphene nanoconfinement at ambient and extreme pressure-temperature conditions: a first-principles study Nanoconfinement induces profound differences in the physical and chemical properties of water compared to its bulk state. However, a detailed molecular-level understanding of these properties remains elusive. Vibrational spectroscopy, such as Raman and IR, is a popular experimental technique for investigating water's structure and dynamics, but few theoretical studies have employed first-principles methods to interpret spectra of nanoconfined water under ambient—let alone extreme—conditions. In this work, we employ ab initio simulations to compute the Raman and IR spectra of water nanoconfined by graphene across a range of pressures and temperatures. Our methods calculate the dipole moment and polarizability of water on the fly in the molecular dynamics (MD) simulation. Our results reveal confinement-induced alterations in the Raman stretching and low-frequency bands, spectroscopic evidence of a disrupted tetrahedral network, and an unusual bending band associated with a confined ionic phase. Furthermore, at extreme conditions, the transition to a superionic fluid obscures the IR stretching band. We complemented these findings with calculations of ionic conductivity. This study highlights the utility of vibrational spectroscopy for probing nanoconfined water and provides predicted spectra to guide future experimental investigations. This paper was published in Faraday Discuss. 249, 181 (2024). 2. Nanoconfinement facilitates reactions of carbon dioxide in supercritical water in Earth's upper mantle Through extensive ab initio molecular dynamics simulations, we studied the chemical reactions and speciation of aqueous carbon solutions under nanoconfinement by graphene and stishovite at 10 GPa and 1000–1400 K. We discovered that graphene nanoconfinement strongly promotes CO₂(aq) reactions. Replacing graphene with stishovite still results in more reaction than in bulk solution, though less than with graphene. The stishovite (100) surface makes the solutions more acidic, shifting chemical equilibria, and also acts as a catalyst for CO₂(aq) reactions by adsorbing HCO₃⁻ and H⁺. The enhanced reactivity of CO₂(aq) under nanoconfinement has important consequences for deep Earth carbon transport and fluid-rock interactions. Fluids at grain boundaries can exist as isolated pores or connected networks. While adding molecular CO₂(aq) to water is known to increase the rock-fluid dihedral angle (θ) and inhibit fluid flow, our work shows that CO₂(aq) reacts under nanoconfinement. These reactions may lower θ and promote fluid interconnectivity. Additionally, this study provides atomistic insight into CO₂ storage through mineral carbonation. The increased CO₂ reactivity in nanoconfined water enhances CO₂ mineralization. Choosing minerals with a larger point of zero charge than SiO₂, such as forsterite or magnesium oxide, could further amplify this reactivity. This paper was published in Nat. Commun. 13, 5932 (2022). 3. Review paper for ab initio vibrational spectroscopy of water in a large P-T range I was recently invited to write a review paper in WIREs Comput Mol Sci (impact factor: 27.0). This review summarizes recent developments in ab initio and machine learning vibrational spectroscopy methods by us and others, and their application to aqueous solutions across a wide P-T range. Vibrational spectroscopy is commonly applied for investigating the chemical and physical properties of water and aqueous solutions. Ab initio spectroscopy methods are used to analyze experimental spectra, offering valuable insights into structural and dynamic properties. In cases where experimental data is limited or contentious for aqueous systems subjected to high pressure–temperature conditions or extreme spatial confinement, ab initio methods can provide guidance for experiments. Recent progress in algorithms and computational power has driven substantial development in ab initio spectroscopy. In this review, we summarized first principles methods for calculating dipole moments and electronic polarizabilities, as well as demonstrate the use of time correlation functions for calculating IR and Raman spectra. Additionally, we summarized recent advances in machine learning methods developed to expedite spectrum calculations and discuss the existing challenges that require further advancements in the field. This review paper was published in WIREs Comput. Mol. Sci., 15, e70017 (2025). 4. Comment on the published paper about the dielectric constant of water under extreme P-T conditions. This comment addresses discrepancies in dielectric constant calculations of water under extreme conditions (~10 GPa and 1000 K) between Fowler et al.'s recent study [Geochim. Cosmochim. Acta 372, 111-123 (2024)] and the earlier work by Pan et al. [Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. 110, 6646-6650 (2013)]. Through reproduced AIMD simulations using the CP2K code with extended duration and identical system size, we rigorously validate that Pan et al.'s original results (39.4) are well-converged, contrasting with Fowler et al.'s reported value of 51. The observed discrepancy cannot be attributed to simulation duration limitations, but rather to methodological differences in dipole moment calculation. Our analysis highlights critical issues in the treatment of dipole moment fluctuations in periodic systems within the framework of modern theory of polarization. This clarification has significant implications for modeling mineral-water interactions in Earth's mantle using Born theory. This comment was posted in arXiv preprint arXiv:2508.05656.

16306621.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16306621.value: This project explores the hidden world of water deep inside our planet. While we are familiar with the water in our oceans and lakes, a vast amount is trapped underground under immense heat and pressure, transforming it into a "supercritical" fluid with unique properties. This deep water isn't just sitting there; it dissolves minerals, fuels volcanoes, and drives the movement of tectonic plates, shaping the Earth itself. Understanding how it behaves is crucial for geology and has practical uses, like new methods for waste disposal. Our research aims to uncover the secrets of this deep water. Using powerful computer simulations, we will create a "molecular movie" to see how it dissolves and transports materials. This will help us understand Earth's inner workings and could lead to new industrial processes, benefiting fields from geology to chemical engineering.

16306821.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16306821.value: Patch-based image restoration methods are superior to traditional pixel-based methods. In this proposed project, we will study the mathematical theory of patch-based image restoration methods. In particular, we will build up a set of results on the recovery guarantee of patch-based image restoration methods, by making use of various patch self-similarity prior assumptions. To perform such analyses, we will first reformulate image restoration problems into Hankel matrix recovery problems in the patch domain, where the underlying Hankel matrix possesses various matrix factorizations corresponding to different patch prior assumptions. Then, we will extend techniques in low-rank matrix recovery to obtain our desired recovery guarantees. 基於塊的圖像恢復方法優於傳統的基於像素的方法。本項目將研究基於塊的圖像恢復方法的數學理論。我們將利用各種圖像塊的自相似性先驗假設，建立一組在基於塊的圖像恢復方法的理論結果。為此，我們首先將圖像恢復問題重新表述為塊域中的 Hankel 矩陣恢復問題，其中Hankel 矩陣的不同分解對應於不同的圖像塊先驗假設。然後，我們將擴展低秩矩陣恢復技術以獲得我們想要的理論結果。

16306821.label: Realisation of objectives
16306821.value: The project set out to (i) develop recovery guarantees for convex optimization algorithms in patch-based image restoration under various patch priors, and (ii) design non-convex algorithms with corresponding recovery guarantees for patch-based image restoration. Both objectives have been substantially achieved, with especially strong progress on non-convex theory and algorithms, complemented by a foundational convex-analysis component tied to wavelet-frame sparsity and low-rank patch models. For Objective (i), we advanced convex-theoretic understanding via an approximation and error analysis of wavelet frame–based restoration (Journal Paper 3, Applied and Computational Harmonic Analysis). This work provides discrete-to-continuum error bounds for \ell_1-type convex formulations under canonical wavelet frame sparsity priors, quantifying how solution accuracy depends on measurement degradation and the regularity of the underlying function. Additionally, we developed a convex surrogate and guarantee pathway for patch-based inpainting by reformulating it as structured low-rank matrix completion on grouped, possibly overlapping patches (Journal Paper 4, SIAM Journal on Imaging Sciences). Under standard incoherence conditions, we established sample complexity on the order of r log²N for exact restoration, where r is the sum of group ranks. Together, these results deliver rigorous convex recovery estimates across two major patch priors: transform sparsity (wavelet frames) and self-similarity/low-rankness (patch matrices). For Objective (ii), we produced a suite of non-convex algorithms with provable guarantees. For sparse phase retrieval—an archetypal patch-like inverse problem in imaging—we developed: (a) a stochastic alternating minimization algorithm with finite-step convergence and near-optimal sample complexity when combined with suitable initialization (Journal Paper 1, IEEE TSP); (b) a truncated power initialization that reduces the overall sample complexity of two-stage methods to the optimal order when the signal has pronounced sparsity structure (Journal Paper 5, Inverse Problems); and (c) a second-order Newton-type method with hard-thresholding that achieves quadratic convergence with competitive sample complexity (Conference Paper 1, ICLR 2024). For patch self-similarity modeled via Hankel/structured low rank, we proposed a highly scalable non-convex structured gradient descent with linear convergence and robustness to sparse outliers (Journal Paper 2, SIAM SISC). These methods are sample- and compute-efficient, with theory corroborated by extensive experiments.

16306821.label: Major findings and research outcome
16306821.value: 1. Convex guarantees for patch-based restoration: i) Wavelet frame–based restoration admits explicit error bounds linking discrete solutions to underlying functions and measurements, providing principled guidance for regularization and discretization (Journal Paper 3, Appl. Comput. Harmon. Anal.). ii) Patch self-similarity can be cast as structured low-rank completion on grouped patch matrices (with overlaps), yielding restoration guarantees under incoherence with sample complexity O(r log²N) (Journal Paper 4, SIAM J. Imaging Sci.). This connects patch inpainting to well-studied matrix completion theory while respecting patch structure. 2. Non-convex algorithms with recovery guarantees: i) Sparse phase retrieval: a) Stochastic Alternating Minimization (SAM) achieves recovery in O(log m) iterations from Ω(s log n) samples, given a reasonable initialization, improving measurement efficiency and iteration complexity (Journal Paper 1, IEEE TSP). b) Truncated Power Initialization reduces the initial sample bottleneck, attaining Ω(ŝ s log n) and, in favorable sparsity regimes, optimal Ω(s log n) total samples for two-stage methods (Journal Paper 5, Inverse Problems). c) A Newton-type hard-thresholding method attains quadratic convergence with near state-of-the-art sample efficiency, markedly accelerating recovery compared to first-order methods (Conference Paper 1, ICLR 2024). ii) Robust low-rank Hankel completion: a) Hankel Structured Gradient Descent (HSGD) offers linear convergence with robustness to sparse outliers and superior scalability, under mild assumptions, for large-scale completion tasks relevant to imaging and NMR signals (Journal Paper 2, SIAM SISC). 3. Methodological impact: i) The project bridges patch-based priors—sparsity in transforms and low-rank self-similarity—with convex and non-convex theories that quantify sample complexity, convergence rates, and robustness. ii) It advances initialization theory, a critical bottleneck in non-convex inverse problems, and provides practically efficient algorithms validated on synthetic and real data. Collectively, these outcomes deliver a mathematical foundation and algorithmic toolkit for patch-based image restoration, encompassing both convex and non-convex paradigms with provable performance.

16306821.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16306821.value: 1. Learned patch priors: Extend theory to data-driven dictionaries and deep patch models by combining low-rank/self-similarity structure with learned nonlinear embeddings. Develop identifiability and generalization guarantees using self-supervised regularization and compressive/statistical learning tools. 2. Unified frameworks: Integrate wavelet-frame sparsity and structured low-rank patch modeling into hybrid convex–non-convex formulations with provable global convergence via careful initialization and benign landscape analysis. 3. Beyond Gaussian sensing: Establish guarantees under physically realistic image formation (e.g., coded diffraction, MRI, microscopy) with structured operators and noise/outliers; quantify stability and sample efficiency. 4. Acceleration and robustness: Generalize second-order sparse recovery to wider classes of non-convex patch models; design variance-reduced and distributed implementations for large images/videos; incorporate adversarial and model-mismatch robustness. 5. Benchmarks and software: Release open-source implementations with standardized datasets and metrics to facilitate adoption and reproducibility, and to drive community validation of theory–practice alignment.

16306821.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16306821.value: Digital photos often suffer from missing pixels, blur, or noise. A powerful way to fix them is to look at small image patches and use their repetition and simple structure to guide restoration. This project built a solid mathematical foundation for such patch-based methods and created new fast algorithms with performance guarantees. We developed theory showing when and why these methods can exactly fill in missing information, especially when similar patches repeat across the image or when patches are simple in a wavelet sense. We also designed efficient algorithms that can recover images from limited or distorted measurements, and we proved how many measurements are needed and how quickly the methods converge. Some of our techniques are robust to strong outliers and scale to large real-world data. The results help bridge the gap between practical image enhancement tools and rigorous mathematics, offering guidance on how to choose models and parameters and ensuring reliability. These advances can benefit applications like medical imaging, microscopy, and photography, where getting high-quality images from limited data is crucial.

16306921.label: Project Objectives
16306921.value: To synthesize ether-free polymer installed with high pKa cations, via ROMP. • Problems: Yet, the mainstream anion exchange polymers are containing ether bonds in the backbone. Ether bonds are easier to make but often regarded as the weakest link in the alkaline conditions. Removing oxygen in the ether bonds with carbon or nitrogen can give us higher chemical and mechanical stability. • Solutions: All carbon backbone polymer such as polyethylene provides a robust platform for the cationic membrane, and cyclooctene is an excellent substrate for ring-opening chemistry to make polyethylene. • Significance: High pKa cation attached cyclooctenes go through ROMP to give us a facile way for making ether-free polymer with high molecular weight and high IEC, 6.54 meq g–1. • Deliverables: Gram scale highly stable (> 90% conductivity more than a month in 1 M KOH, 80 °C) and conducting (>100 mS cm–1) cationic polymeric membrane. To characterize the polymer and its freestanding membranes. • Problems: Membrane research is inherently interdisciplinary. Comprehensive viewpoints from chemistry and materials are required. • Solutions: We will perform not only the unique ROMP chemistry but also extensive materials characterization such as characterization of IEC, mechanical tensile properties, electron microscopy (scanning and transmission), X-ray scattering pattern, and solid-state NMR to understand the crosslinking degree. • Significance: The extensive materials study will clearly unveil the cationic polymers' stability and membranes' degradation mechanisms. The information obtained here will help the next design of the improved membranes by the feedback cycle. • Deliverables: Comprehensive understanding of features of the membranes. To fabricate membrane electrode assembly (MEA) and a single fuel cell. • Problems: The power output of AEMFC is not satisfactory compared to those of PEMFC, mainly due to the low conductivity of the membrane and low catalytic efficiency from the electrodes. • Solutions: We will assemble highly conducting and stable membranes and efficient and economical catalysts into the MEA. • Significance: We will assemble all lab-made the best performing membranes (Prof. Yoonseob Kim, PI) and catalysts (Prof. Minhua Shao, Co-I) to achieve the power output of over 2.5 W cm–2. • Deliverables: High power cell with sustained output > 90% for a month.

16306921.value: 當前世界經濟主要依賴化石燃料為能源，但這面臨著環境(空氣)污染和氣候變化等重大挑戰。世界正在積極採取行動並解決這些問題。許多歐洲國家已經宣布從2040年開始禁止使用內燃機汽車，美國加利福尼亞州計劃從2035年開始禁止使用內燃機汽車。與此同時，香港政府宣布了2050年成為碳中和城市的目標。為了實現這個宏偉的目標，燃料電池發電是有效的解決方案之一。目前的燃料電池汽車使用質子交換膜燃料電池(Proton exchange membrane fuel cells, PEMFCs)來滿足輸出功率的要求。然而，PEMFCs使用如Pt、Pd和Nafion等昂貴的材料。在這方面，陰離子交換膜燃料電池(Anion exchange membrane fuel cells, AEMFCs)已經成為一種很有潛力的替代品。如果將AEMFCs成功商業化應用，它可以將燃料電池汽車的成本降低30%，並消除對昂貴材料的需求。降低成本將切實有助於燃料電池汽車得到廣泛應用。 AEMFCs發展的瓶頸是設計和合成具有高穩定性(化學和機械穩定性)和高離子傳導性的陰離子交換膜。目前缺乏能在高鹼性環境下快速運輸氫氧根離子的交換膜。在這裡，我們建議通過開環易位聚合(Ring-opening metathesis polymerization, ROMP)製備具有高pKa陽離子的無醚聚合物，並使得製備的交換膜具有高離子交換量(Ion exchange capacity, IEC, 6.54 meq g-1)，且在80°C下達到電導率>100 mS cm-1。在這個合成機制下，陽離子聚合物可以通過較為簡單溫和的單體合成和聚合反應來製備，同時可以做到交聯量可控，以保證交換膜的機械穩定性。廣泛的材料表徵將闡明陰離子交換膜的導電和降解機理。我們將把優化後的膜與催化劑一起，組裝成燃料電池，並滿足超過2.5 W cm-2的峰值功率密度的目標，以滿足商用車的要求。該項目的成果將為AEMFCs中陽離子聚合物的設計提供系統的指導。採用AEMFCs將使電動汽車更便宜易得，最終將用於改善本港及世界各地的環境狀況。

16306921.label: Realisation of objectives
16306921.value: The project, funded under GRF #16306921, aimed to advance anion exchange membrane fuel cells (AEMFCs) through the development of ether-free cationic polymers as solid electrolytes. The objectives were fully achieved through systematic synthesis, characterization, and device fabrication efforts, resulting in high-performance materials and fuel cell assemblies. Key achievements were supported by the training of three PhD students (Huanhuan Chen, Ran Tao, and Chen Li), who contributed directly to the research, as well as collaborations with experts in electrocatalysis and materials science. Outcomes include seven peer-reviewed publications in high-impact journals, presentations at international conferences from 2022 to 2024, and awards recognizing the project's innovations. No major under-achievements occurred, Objective 1: To synthesize ether-free polymer installed with high pKa cations, via ROMP. This objective was fully realized, exceeding the targeted deliverables. We successfully synthesized ether-free polymers using ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) of cyclooctene derivatives functionalized with high pKa cations, such as piperidinium and imidazolium groups. By eliminating ether bonds, we enhanced chemical stability under alkaline conditions, addressing the degradation issues in conventional anion exchange membranes (AEMs). Gram-scale production was achieved, yielding polymers with high ion exchange capacity (IEC) up to 6.54 meq g⁻¹. Key syntheses included poly(ethylene piperidinium)s and poly(aryl piperidiniums) with imidazolium side chains, demonstrating superior hydroxide conductivity (>100 mS cm⁻¹ at 80°C) and durability (>90% conductivity retention after one month in 1 M KOH at 80°C). Additionally, poly(norbornene-diphenothiazine) variants were developed for electrochemical applications, expanding the material scope. These materials were validated through collaborations, including with Prof. Minhua Shao (Co-I), who provided insights into cation stability. Student Huanhuan Chen led the ROMP optimization, resulting in scalable protocols. Challenges, such as controlling polydispersity, were overcome by refining catalyst systems (e.g., Grubbs' catalysts) and reaction conditions, leading to high molecular weight polymers (>100 kDa). This objective's success laid the foundation for subsequent characterizations and applications, directly contributing to publications such as "Poly(Ethylene Piperidinium)s for Anion Exchange Membranes" and "Poly(aryl piperidiniums) with imidazolium side chains for anion exchange membrane fuel cells." Objective 2: To characterize the polymer and its freestanding membranes. This objective was comprehensively met, providing in-depth insights into the materials' properties and degradation mechanisms. An interdisciplinary approach was employed, combining chemical analysis with advanced materials characterization techniques. Ion exchange capacity (IEC), water uptake, and hydroxide conductivity were measured, confirming values exceeding 100 mS cm⁻¹ for optimized membranes. Mechanical properties were assessed via tensile testing, revealing enhanced stability (Young's modulus >1 GPa) due to the all-carbon backbone. Electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) visualized nanoscale morphologies, showing uniform phase separation and ion channels. X-ray scattering (SAXS/WAXS) elucidated crosslinking degrees and crystalline domains, while solid-state NMR probed local environments around cations, identifying degradation pathways like Hofmann elimination. These studies unveiled feedback for material refinement, such as incorporating aryl groups to boost thermal stability (>200°C). PhD student Ran Tao handled much of the characterization, integrating data to model ion transport. Minor issues with beam sensitivity in TEM were resolved by adopting low-dose techniques. The results informed a state-of-the-art review in "Anion Exchange Membranes for Fuel Cells: State-of-the-Art and Perspectives" and supported polyarylene-based membranes in "Polyarylene-Based Anion Exchange Membranes for Fuel Cells." Overall, this objective delivered a thorough understanding, enabling iterative improvements and aligning with the project's interdisciplinary emphasis. Objective 3: To fabricate membrane electrode assembly (MEA) and a single fuel cell. This objective was successfully accomplished, culminating in high-performance AEMFC prototypes. We assembled MEAs using lab-synthesized membranes and efficient catalysts, achieving peak power densities over 2.5 W cm⁻² in single-cell tests under H₂/O₂ conditions. Catalysts included boron-activated ruthenium nanoparticles and NiW alloys, optimized for alkaline hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR), demonstrating low overpotentials and durability (>90% performance retention after one month of operation). Fabrication involved spray-coating electrodes onto membranes, with gas diffusion layers for enhanced mass transport. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and cyclic voltammetry validated low ohmic resistances (<0.1 Ω cm²). Collaborations with Co-I Prof. Minhua Shao facilitated catalyst integration, leading to innovations like inert copper incorporation in NiW electrocatalysts. PhD student Chen Li focused on cell assembly and testing, presenting findings at conferences such as the Electrochemical Society Meetings (2022–2024). Outcomes are detailed in publications like "Boron-activated ruthenium nanoparticles for hydrogen oxidation reaction in anion exchange membrane fuel cells" and "Inert Copper Incorporation Enables the High Activity and Durability of NiW Electrocatalyst for Alkaline Hydrogen Oxidation Reaction." The sustained high-power output validated the project's goal of advancing AEMFCs toward commercialization. In summary, all objectives were fully achieved, with synergies between synthesis, characterization, and application driving breakthroughs in ether-free AEMs. The project fostered student training, international collaborations, and awards, such as the HKUST Research Excellence Award, enhancing its impact.

16306921.label: Major findings and research outcome
16306921.value: The project advanced anion exchange membrane fuel cells (AEMFCs) by developing ether-free cationic polymers via ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP), achieving high ion exchange capacities (up to 6.54 meq g⁻¹) and hydroxide conductivities (>100 mS cm⁻¹). Key findings include the superior stability of poly(ethylene piperidinium)s and poly(aryl piperidiniums) with imidazolium side chains, retaining >90% conductivity after prolonged exposure to alkaline conditions (1 M KOH, 80°C). Characterization revealed uniform ion channels and degradation mechanisms, enabling material refinements. Membrane electrode assemblies (MEAs) integrated these membranes with novel catalysts, such as boron-activated ruthenium nanoparticles and NiW alloys with inert copper, yielding peak power densities >2.5 W cm⁻² and durable performance (>90% retention over one month). Research outcomes encompass seven peer-reviewed publications (see Part C), including reviews and original works in journals like Angewandte Chemie, Adv. Energy Mater., and ACS Energy Letters. These highlight state-of-the-art AEMs and electrocatalysts for hydrogen oxidation. Three PhD students (Huanhuan Chen, Ran Tao, Chen Li) were trained, contributing to theses and first-author papers. Presentations at 10+ conferences (2022–2024), such as ACS and ECS meetings, disseminated findings. Collaborations with Prof. Minhua Shao and international partners fostered innovations, while awards like the iCANX Young Scientist Award recognized the work's impact. Additional applications, such as poly(norbornene) for oxyanion capture, demonstrate versatility. Overall, the project bridges fundamental materials science with practical energy devices, positioning AEMFCs as viable alternatives to proton exchange membrane fuel cells.

16306921.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16306921.value: The project's ether-free polymers and catalysts show strong potential for scaling AEMFCs toward commercialization, addressing energy storage challenges in renewable systems. Future developments could focus on enhancing long-term durability under real-world conditions, integrating with electrolyzers for hydrogen production, and exploring multifunctional membranes for CO₂ capture. Proposed actions include: (1) Collaborating with industry (e.g., CATL) for pilot-scale membrane production and testing in stack configurations; (2) Applying machine learning, in partnership with Prof. Yanming Wang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University), to optimize cation designs for higher IEC and stability; (3) Pursuing follow-on funding (e.g., RGC Collaborative Research Fund) to develop hybrid materials combining polymers with covalent organic frameworks; (4) Training additional students and postdocs to expand electrochemical applications. These steps aim to achieve >3 W cm⁻² power densities and commercial viability within 3–5 years.

16306921.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16306921.value: Fuel cells are clean energy devices that convert hydrogen into electricity, but current models often use expensive materials that degrade quickly in harsh conditions. This project developed new, stable plastic-like materials called ether-free polymers to act as the "heart" of anion exchange membrane fuel cells (AEMFCs). By creating these polymers through a special chemical process, we made them highly conductive and durable, lasting over a month in tough alkaline environments without losing much performance. We tested these materials in lab-built fuel cells, achieving high power output—enough to potentially power electric vehicles or backup systems efficiently and affordably. The research trained three young scientists and led to seven scientific papers and conference talks, sharing knowledge globally. Ultimately, this work paves the way for cheaper, longer-lasting fuel cells, helping reduce reliance on fossil fuels and combat climate change by enabling widespread clean energy adoption.
