16307221.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16307221.value: 基于全基因组关联研究 (GWAS) 的多基因风险评分 (PRS) 已被广泛用于预测人类复杂性状，包括在欧洲人群中的许多成功应用。 但是，为非欧洲人群构建准确的 PRS 仍然具有挑战性，因为大多数 GWAS 都是在具有欧洲血统的样本上进行的。 一方面，仅使用来自代表性不足的目标人群的样本构建的 PRS 的准确性受到样本大小的限制。 另一方面，由于遗传结构的差异，使用具有欧洲血统的样本构建的 PRS 在应用于非欧洲血统时变得不太准确。 优化非欧洲人群的预测准确性需要有效地从强大的欧洲数据集中借用信息。 然而，仍然缺乏从多种族数据集构建PRS同时考虑异质遗传结构的方法。 为了提高非欧洲人群 PRS 的准确性，我们提出了一个统一的框架来构建跨人群分析中的 PRS。在我们的试点研究中，我们为此开发了一种称为 XPA 的统计方法。与现有的在单一人群中构建 PRS 的方法相比，XPA 可以通过从欧洲人群（辅助人群）的 Biobank 规模数据中借用信息，在代表性不足的人群（目标人群）中大大提高 PRS 的准确性。随着数据结构和算法设计的创新，我们的方法可以处理生物样本库规模的数据集并实现准确预测，计算成本与单核苷酸多态性的数量和样本大小近似线性。沿着这个方向，我们建议首先将 XPA 扩展到摘要级数据，以便在无法访问个人级数据时使该框架更广泛地适用。然后，我们将进一步将 XPA 推广到跨群体和跨表型分析，以使该框架能够在跨群体环境中整合遗传相关表型。

16307221.label: Realisation of objectives
16307221.value: 1. Develop statistical methods for the construction of PRS in cross-population analysis using genome-wide summary statistics. We have developed a statistical method called LOG-TRAM [1] to leverage local genetic architecture for trans-ancestry association mapping. Our results demonstrate that LOG-TRAM can effectively identify ancestry-specific loci, and the output generated by LOG-TRAM can be utilized to construct more accurate polygenic risk scores (PRS) for underrepresented populations. To further enhance the accuracy of PRS construction, we introduced XMAP [6], which fine-maps genetic risk variants by exploiting the differing linkage disequilibrium patterns across populations. Additionally, we have shown that the statistical power to prioritize risk variants can be significantly improved by incorporating functional annotations. To achieve this, we developed the PAML method [3]. Building on the findings from our XMAP method [6], we illustrate that the interpretation of genetic risk can be enhanced through single-cell data analysis. For this purpose, we developed the FIRM method [2], which integrates single-cell data with genetic analysis. Recently, we have also demonstrated that disease-risk genes prioritized in genome-wide association studies (GWASs) can be mapped to their spatial context. To accurately quantify their spatial variation patterns, we developed several methods, including matrix factorization method [7] and the mixture of mixed models (MMM) [4]. 2. Implement the proposed algorithms and perform statistical inference. We have implemented the proposed algorithms and conducted statistical inference. For instance, our results demonstrate that LOG-TRAM [1] significantly enhances the statistical power for identifying risk variants in underrepresented populations while producing well-calibrated p-values. Additionally, we have shown that the mixture of mixed models (MMM) can effectively identify cell-type-specific spatially variable genes, also yielding well-calibrated p-values [4]. Importantly, we found that the heritability enrichment of these spatially variable genes identified by MMM contributes to improving the accuracy of polygenic risk score (PRS) construction. 3. Evaluate model performance using comprehensive simulation studies and compare the analysis results with those of other related methods. We conducted comprehensive simulation studies to compare our developed methods with related approaches. For instance, LOG-TRAM [1] was evaluated against standard GWAS methods for PRS construction, including MAMA, MTAG, and MANTRA, across various settings. Additionally, MMM [4] was compared with SPARK, SPARK-X, Cellina, and HEARTSVG. 4. Apply the proposed methods to real data. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods, we applied them to biobank-scale datasets. Specifically, we utilized LOG-TRAM [1] and XMAP [6] on GWAS summary statistics for various complex traits and diseases from BioBank Japan, UK Biobank, and African populations. This resulted in significant power improvements and effective correction of confounding biases in TRAM. We also applied FIRM [2] to integrate single-cell datasets across different experimental settings. For spatial transcriptomics data analysis, we conducted a systematic evaluation, as detailed in our benchmarking paper [5]. For reproducibility, all relevant code and data are available at https://github.com/YangLabHKUST/SRT_alignment_and_integration. 5. Investigate the theoretical properties of the proposed methods. We have explored the theoretical properties of our developed methods. For instance, we demonstrated that the LOG-TRAM estimator [1] is the best linear unbiased estimator without assuming normal distributions, ensuring its effectiveness in real data analysis. Additionally, we showed that the optimization algorithm for XMAP [6] can be interpreted as an empirical Bayes approach, derived within the variational inference framework, with guaranteed convergence. Furthermore, we established that the null distribution of test statistics from the MMM model [4] is a mixture of chi-square distributions. 6. Release open-source software to disseminate the results from this research. LOG-TRAM: https://github.com/YangLabHKUST/LOG-TRAM FIRM: https://github.com/mingjingsi/FIRM PALM: https://github.com/YangLabHKUST/PALM MMM: https://github.com/YangLabHKUST/MCube XMAP: https://github.com/YangLabHKUST/XMAP MFAI: https://github.com/YangLabHKUST/mfair The project commenced during the COVID-19 pandemic, which made it challenging to recruit research staff in the first year. Additionally, academic travel and visits from outside Hong Kong were severely restricted. As noted in the mid-progress report, only a small portion of the project's funding had been utilized at that time. Once the COVID restrictions eased, the Principal Investigator decided to hire additional research staff to enhance the project's research activities and better achieve its goals. The newly recruited team includes PhD students, research assistants, and postdoctoral researchers. As demonstrated in the completion report, the research outcomes have been quite fruitful.

16307221.label: Major findings and research outcome
16307221.value: The construction of polygenic risk scores (PRS) in genome-wide association studies (GWAS) is a critical step in identifying high-risk individuals for specific diseases. However, several challenges hinder the accurate construction of PRS for underrepresented populations. First, sample sizes for these populations, such as East Asians and Africans, are often limited. Second, strong linkage disequilibrium among variants complicates the identification of causal risk variants. Third, confounding biases in GWAS summary statistics can produce misleading signals. To address these challenges, we developed several statistical methods for constructing PRS in cross-population settings by leveraging genetic diversity and accounting for confounding biases. Using cross-population GWAS summary statistics from global biobanks and genomic consortia, we demonstrate that our methods (LOG-TRAM [1] and XMAP [6]) achieve greater statistical power, better control of the false positive rate, and significantly higher computational efficiency in identifying multiple causal signals compared to existing methods. Importantly, we show that the outputs of our methods can be integrated with single-cell datasets [2] and spatial transcriptomics datasets [3, 4, 5], enhancing the interpretation of putative causal variants within their cellular context.

16307221.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16307221.value: The potential for further development of this research is significant, particularly in refining polygenic risk scores (PRS) for diverse populations. Future work could focus on expanding sample sizes by collaborating with additional biobanks and genomic consortia to include more underrepresented groups. This would enhance the robustness of our methods and improve the accuracy of PRS calculations. Additionally, we can explore integrating machine learning techniques to further enhance our statistical methods, allowing for more sophisticated analyses of genetic data. This could help in identifying novel risk variants and understanding their functional implications. A proposed course of action includes conducting validation studies across various populations to ensure the generalizability of our methods. We can also develop user-friendly tools to facilitate the application of LOG-TRAM and XMAP by researchers and clinicians. Finally, we aim to publish our findings in peer-reviewed journals and present at conferences to engage with the scientific community, fostering collaborations that can drive this research forward and ultimately improve disease risk prediction and personalized healthcare strategies.

16307221.value: An individual's likelihood of developing certain diseases based on their genetic information. This is crucial for identifying high-risk individuals and enabling early interventions. However, accurately calculating PRS for underrepresented populations, such as East Asians and Africans, presents challenges. These groups often have smaller sample sizes in genetic studies, making reliable data harder to obtain. Additionally, closely linked genetic variations complicate the identification of specific risk genes, and hidden biases in the data can lead to incorrect conclusions. To address these issues, we have created new statistical methods, such as LOG-TRAM and XMAP, to improve PRS construction across diverse populations. Using genetic data from global biobanks, our methods have shown greater accuracy in identifying genetic risk factors, reduced false alarms, and faster data processing.

16307621.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16307621.value: In recent years, condensed matter and photonic/phononic systems have been used to realize novel phenomena in fundamental physics that were previously thought to be difficult or even impossible to achieve experimentally. A good example is the realization of Weyl particles that do not exist in nature as elementary particles, but can be found as quasi-particles in condensed matter and photonic/phononic crystals carrying topological nodal points (called Weyl degeneracies) in the band structures [1-9]. The 2D counterpart is called Dirac degeneracy, which can be found in various types of honeycomb lattices. The interactions between these exotic particles can be fruitfully interpreted using geometry [10-12]. The geometric phase acquired by particles while parallel transporting on a closed loop in the parameter space can offer elegant interpretations of numerous phenomena. A popular textbook example is the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which the geometric phase obtained from an integral of a gauge field around a closed loop (equivalent to the magnetic flux enclosed by the loop) results in the shift of an interference pattern. Classical wave systems are powerful platforms for realizing the analogs of exotic particles and their interaction with fields. The inhomogeneity in a Weyl or Dirac cone system is mathematically equivalent to a gauge field, hence named synthetic gauge field. The simplest example is the synthetic magnetic field in strained crystal systems and metamaterials [13-19]. However, such previously explored synthetic gauge fields are mostly “Abelian” (behaving like numbers) and more complex “non-Abelian” (behaving like matrices) synthetic fields with rich novel physics, are not actively discussed in previous works. In this project, we will realize non-Abelian gauge fields by inhomogeneously modulating the geometric parameters in Weyl or Dirac cone systems. Such platforms will enable us to explore novel effects such as the non-Abelian Aharonov-Bohm phases, chiral gauge effect, and energy quantization that cannot be experimentally observed in high-energy physics. Using the robust properties of Weyl or Dirac cones [6-9], we aim to realize various non-Abelian gauge fields and explore their consequences by engineering inhomogeneity in photonic or phononic systems. We hope that concepts in fundamental physics, in particular the knowledge of the interaction between relativistic particles and background fields, can inspire new ways to design inhomogeneous and aperiodic metamaterials which have unique wave manipulation functionalities. Our results may suggest new strategies for wave front control and at the same time provide elegant explanations for wave phenomena on the basis of fundamental physics concepts. 近幾年，科學家開始利用凝聚態，光學或聲學系統來實現基礎物理中被認為在實驗中很難或幾乎不可能實現的新奇現象。一個典型的例子便是外爾粒子，外爾粒子在自然界中並沒有作為基本粒子出現，但是在凝聚態，光學和聲學系統的能帶中以線性簡併（即準粒子）的形式出現。與之相對應的二維繫統中存在的是狄拉克簡併，該簡併常見於各種類型的蜂窩晶格結構中。現階段，這些準粒子之間的相互作用是用幾何來進行描述的。準粒子在參數空間中的一個閉合路徑上做平行移動後獲得的幾何相位可以解釋很多新奇的物理現象。一個很有名的例子便是Aharonov-Bohm效應，粒子的幾何相位等於在閉合路徑上規範場的積分（等價於閉合路徑包圍曲面的磁通量），導致干涉條紋產生空間位移。經典波系統是實現這些準粒子及其相互作用的理想平台。外爾或狄拉克系統的非均勻性在數學上等價於粒子感受到的規範場，因此被命名為人工規範場。最簡單的例子便是晶體結構中應力可以等效為人工磁場。然而，現階段探索的人工規範場都是定義在阿貝爾群上的（單值性質），但對於更複雜些的非阿貝爾規範場（矩陣性質），雖然包含著更豐富的新奇物理現象，卻很少在以往的工作中報道。在本課題中，我們將通過非均勻的調節外爾或狄拉克系統的幾何參數，實現非阿貝爾規範場。這些系統能夠幫助我們實現很多在高能物理實驗中很難觀測到的新奇現象，比如非阿貝爾Aharonov-Bohm效應，規範場手性效應，以及粒子本征態的量子化等。 利用外爾和狄拉克簡併點的穩定特性（即簡併點不容易被打開），我們將通過調節系統的非均勻性來實現不同種類的非阿貝爾規範場，並探索這些人工的規範場產生的物理效應。我們希望基礎物理中的一些理論，特別是在粒子與規範場相互作用方面的基礎知識，能夠激發新的設計靈感，即設計非均勻或非週期的超材料結構來實現對波的傳輸進行操作。我們產出的數據可能會對波前控制系統的設計提供新的策略，同時對於這些新奇的波的傳播現象給出基於基礎物理理論的完美解釋。

16307621.label: Realisation of objectives
16307621.value: This research project systematically investigated the physical manifestations of non-Abelian parallel transport gauge in both real and parameter spaces, with subsequent experimental realization through artificially engineered photonic structures. The completed works addressed four key objectives: the first and the third objectives focus on the theoretical predictions of physical phenomena associated with different forms of gauge fields; While the other two focus on the design and experimentally observing these phenomena. All research outcomes have been rigorously documented in our peer-reviewed publications. Objective 1: non-Abelian transport gauge in momentum space We investigate non-Abelian transport gauges in parity-time symmetric and pseudo-Hermitian two-band systems, where the gauge structure is defined on a Lorentzian group—analogous to gravitational field formulations. Our analysis reveals that the momentum space of these generic systems hosts intersection singularities of exceptional surfaces. To classify these singularities, we developed an intersection homotopy approach for topological characterization of exceptional-surface-embedded defects. Furthermore, this framework predicts a novel class of topological edge states in gapless systems [Commun. Phys.; paper#2]. Extending our investigation to three-band systems with identical symmetries, we discovered that the non-Abelian parallel transport gauge generates a swallowtail catastrophe degeneracy structure in momentum space for such multi-band cases. This remarkably rich degeneracy architecture combines: (1) a non-defective nodal line isolated from exceptional surfaces, (2) a non-defective intersection of exceptional surfaces, and (3) a pair of third-order exceptional lines positioned along exceptional surface cusps. These degeneracy lines converge at a single point, forming a topologically protected stable configuration. Using our eigenframe deformation and rotation method—derived from the non-Abelian transport gauge of eigenframes—we rigorously demonstrated this topological protection. Additionally, we theoretically predicted a new form of bulk-Fermi-arc that links a pair of exceptional lines of order three, distinguished from the conventional form that links paired order-two exceptional points. [Nat. Phys.; paper#4]. Objective 2: Realization in experiment: We experimentally realized the swallowtail degeneracy structure using a topological circuit platform with three nodes emulating atomic orbitals. By engineering nonreciprocal hopping between orbitals through negative impedance converters (INICs), we synthesized an effective three-dimensional parameter space. This platform enabled direct observation of the swallowtail degeneracy configuration in the synthetic parameter space, confirming our theoretical predictions [Nat. Phys.; paper#4]. By mapping closed loops encircling various degeneracy lines in the swallowtail structure to 1D Brillouin zones, we revealed a fundamental departure from conventional topological systems. Although these loops necessarily intersect exceptional surfaces—creating gap-closing at exceptional points—robust topological edge modes persist under open boundary conditions. This phenomenon challenges conventional gap-dependent topological invariant theories. Through fabricated 1D circuit models, we experimentally demonstrated these unconventional edge states. Furthermore, using non-Abelian parallel transport of eigenframes with a non-Bloch band theory incorporated, we established that edge states associated with different degeneracy lines are topologically interconnected [Phys. Rev. Lett.; paper#7]. Objective 3. Gauge fields in non-periodic systems The introduction of gauge fields breaks the system's translational invariance. Through carefully engineered non-periodic systems, we achieve physical effects equivalent to those induced by real gauge fields. Specifically, we designed two-dimensional honeycomb structures hosting Dirac quasiparticles in their band dispersions. By implementing non-periodic modulations, we created an effective mass gradient along one in-plane direction, effectively simulating out-of-plane gauge fields. These synthetic gauge fields generate chiral Landau levels that remain dispersive in the other in-plane direction [Light Sci. & Appl.; paper#1]. 4: Experimentally realize chiral zero modes in metamaterials: We engineered a three-dimensional metamaterial system augmented with two synthetic dimensions to realize a 5D Yang-monopole degeneracy—the fundamental singularity of non-Abelian Yang-Mills gauge fields. Through controlled inhomogeneous modulations, we induced synthetic 4-form gauge fields that interact with the Yang monopole, leading to the emergence of topological chiral zero modes via energy level quantization. These modes are protected by the second Chern number that stabilizes the 5D Yang monopole structure. Remarkably, we achieved direct experimental observation of these chiral zero modes in our inhomogeneous 5D system. The polarization-sensitive excitation characteristics are also experimentally demonstrated [Phys. Rev. Lett.; paper#6]. We engineered a metamaterial system hosting spin-1 Weyl degeneracy at the Γ point in momentum space. The non-Abelian parallel transport gauge of eigenstates generates a robust three-fold linear degeneracy, described by an effective Hamiltonian comprising linear combinations of spin-1 non-Abelian generators. This topological singularity carries a ±2 invariant and is bounded by oppositely charged nodal surfaces at the Brillouin zone boundary. Using our 3D metamaterial platform, we experimentally observed the predicted Fermi-arc surface states connecting the spin-1 degeneracy point to the nodal surfaces [Phys. Rev. Lett.; paper#5]. We proposed and demonstrated a novel type of photonic straight nodal lines in a D2D metacrystal, which are protected by and unusual rotoinversion time (roto-parity-time) symmetry. The Berry curvature, which is the curl of parallel transport gauge in k-space, shows a quadrupole distribution in our desgined system. we also observed degeneracy features associated with the parallel transport of eigenstates and the topologically protected surface states in experiments, which agree well with the theoretical predictions. [Phys. Rev. Lett.; paper#3].

16307621.label: Major findings and research outcome
16307621.value: Non-Abelian gauge fields fundamentally govern particle interactions in quantum systems. Remarkably, even in artificial systems, non-Abelian parallel transport gauges - whether in real space or parameter space - can give rise to novel topological phases and associated phenomena. These findings, particularly the discovery of new topological phase classifications, establish fresh platforms for investigating uncharted territories in topological physics. In our project, we systematically investigated non-Abelian geometric phases and their induced topological effects. By engineering systems with tailored symmetries, we observed novel degeneracy structures arising from eigenframe deformation and rotation, driven by non-Abelian parallel transport gauges in parameter space. Specifically, we developed non-periodic systems capable of coupling gauge fields to band degeneracies, enabling experimental observation of gauge-field-induced chiral zero modes. These results provide a platform for probing unconventional topological phenomena beyond conventional periodic systems. Our most significant finding reveals that swallowtail and other hypersurface singularities emerge naturally in systems possessing both parity-time symmetry and pseudo-Hermitian symmetry. In Papers #2 and #4, we rigorously demonstrated the stability of these degeneracy structures, which arise from non-Abelian parallel transport gauges of eigenframe in parameter space. These configurations define a previously unrecognized topological phase, whose hallmark physical manifestations include: (1) bulk-Fermi-arc that links paired exceptional lines of order three (Paper #4), and (2) robust topological edge states in gapless systems (Paper #2 and #7). Two-dimensional Dirac degeneracies and five-dimensional Yang monopoles represent fundamental singularities in band dispersions. By introducing inhomogeneous modulations to systems hosting these singularities, we engineered distinct forms of synthetic gauge fields. In 2D systems (Paper #1), these gauge fields generate chiral zeroth Landau levels with in-plane propagative behavior. For 5D systems (Paper #6), the chiral zero mode—protected by the second Chern number—exhibits polarization-dependent excitation characteristics. A key consequence of the non-Abelian parallel transport gauge is the emergence of three-fold linear degeneracies in momentum space. The resulting geometric phase gives rise to a charge-2 topological invariant, which stabilizes these degeneracies—localized at the Brillouin zone center and bounded by nodal surfaces at the zone boundary (Paper #5). This configuration provides a unique platform for investigating Fermi-arc surface states that connect singular points with nodal surfaces, offering new insights into topological quantum phenomena.

16307621.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16307621.value: Gapless systems: Symmetry-protected hypersurface singularities have opened new avenues for studying gapless topological systems. The novel topological edge states challenge conventional bulk-edge correspondence, which depends on bandgap-defined topological invariants. This necessitates the development of more sophisticated mathematical frameworks to properly characterize these phenomena. Additionally, while our current research has primarily examined edge states in 1D systems, we anticipate that higher-dimensional systems may give rise to even more remarkable topological surface states. Other catastrophes: Our research has primarily investigated surface intersections and swallowtail catastrophes, which represent the most elementary forms in catastrophe theory. However, more complex singularities - including butterfly catastrophes, umbilic catastrophes, and Whitney umbrellas - may also emerge in the band structures. The identification of such systems could provide novel platforms for exploring topological phenomena. Fermi-arc surface states: While conventional Fermi-arc surface states typically connect Weyl or Dirac points, our discovery of Fermi-arcs linking triple degeneracy points with nodal surfaces reveals more novel possibilities. Particularly in non-Hermitian systems with parity-time symmetry, exceptional surfaces exhibiting double-cone structures, which in turn generate bifurcated surface state dispersions with mutually conjugate eigenvalues. From a topological perspective, the non-Abelian parallel transport of eigenframes may offer crucial insights into understanding these unique Fermi-arc dispersion patterns.

16307621.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16307621.value: Topological physics is a captivating field that deepens our understanding of complex physical phenomena through mathematical concepts like “topological invariants”. When these “invariants” exist, they facilitate robust signal transport that is stable and resilient against external disruptions. Typically, topological invariants arise from specific features known as "degeneracies," such as "Weyl" and "Dirac" degeneracies, named after the scientists who discovered them. This project focuses on identifying these and other novel forms of degeneracies that can give rise to new and exotic topological phases. Additionally, wave transport is influenced by "gauge fields," which can be engineered using specially designed materials. We created these artificial materials and explored the wave-guiding implications of the resulting gauge fields. Our research also suggests that new types of topological phases may emerge when we investigate a novel category of non-isolated degeneracies, necessitating a specialized mathematical framework that we have developed. These discoveries could have implications beyond academic interest. Advances in this area of physics may lead to more robust signal transport, faster computers, smarter artificial intelligence, and innovative methods for secure communication. Ultimately, we are unlocking pathways to technologies that could enhance our everyday lives.

16307821.value: 1). Experimentally characterize the edge states protected by non-Abelian topological charges in quasi-1D systems We will experimentally characterize the bulk-edge correspondence of non-Abelian topological charges using transmission line networks which offer ideal platforms for characterizing both the bulk and edge states. We will first focus on theoretically analysing and experimentally characterizing the edge states of non-Abelian charge −1 in a three-band system. We will then experimentally explore the non-Abelian bulk-edge correspondence for n>3 band systems. 2). Experimentally demonstrate braiding Dirac points in 2D systems The two Dirac points of honeycomb lattices [7] carry opposite winding numbers and can annihilate in pairs [7] due to the famous no-go theorem[8]. However, when multiple bands (n>2) are involved, the annihilation of Dirac points depends on the path they travel before merging. It implies the failure of no-go theorem [9] and shows the non-Abelian braiding features. We will construct 2D lattices using transmission lines, where each unit cell consists of three particles and such three-band systems can exhibit fruitful braiding properties. We will theoretically analyse and experimentally map the braiding of Dirac points and accompanying edge states. 3). Experimentally demonstrate braiding Weyl points in 3D metamaterials If a 3D system possesses C2T symmetry, Weyl points can be braided on the C2T plane [10] and the underlying non-Abelian constraints will determine the path of Weyl point pairwise annihilation. We will use chiral hyperbolic metamaterials to experimentally characterize the whole braiding process and map the variation of Fermi arcs. 4). Experimentally map non-Abelian nodal links in 3D metamaterials Using bi-axial metamaterials, we will experimentally characterize the non-Abelian nodal links for n>3 band systems and study the underlying braiding properties. In particular, on each k-plane cutting through the origin in the 3D momentum space, nodal lines reduce to Dirac points and so we can also experimentally study the braiding features of Dirac points on such metamaterial platforms.

We will theoretically analyse and experimentally map the braiding of Dirac points and accompanying edge states.

3). Experimentally demonstrate braiding Weyl points in 3D metamaterials If a 3D system possesses C2T symmetry, Weyl points can be braided on the C2T plane [10] and the underlying non-Abelian constraints will determine the path of Weyl point pairwise annihilation. We will use chiral hyperbolic metamaterials to experimentally characterize the whole braiding process and map the variation of Fermi arcs.

4). Experimentally map non-Abelian nodal links in 3D metamaterials Using bi-axial metamaterials, we will experimentally characterize the non-Abelian nodal links for n>3 band systems and study the underlying braiding properties. In particular, on each k-plane cutting through the origin in the 3D momentum space, nodal lines reduce to Dirac points and so we can also experimentally study the braiding features of Dirac points on such metamaterial platforms.

16307821.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16307821.value: Since the 1980s, the discovery of integer quantum Hall effect and the subsequent topological interpretation took condensed matter physics into a new era [1]. To date, the notion of topological phases has gone far and beyond the original realm of condensed matter physics, and has profound impact in the discovery and understanding of all kind of new materials. The underlying principle is that the bulk property of materials can be exhaustively classified by integer groups, which can be viewed as Abelian topological charges. Furthermore, the integer bulk topological invariant determines the number of edge states through the celebrated “bulk-edge correspondence”, which itself is an elegant theory that connects the properties of an infinite periodic system and those of an exposed surface of a truncated bulk. Until now, topological phases [2-5] have provided robust platforms for a variety of applications such as dissipation-less transportation, one-way propagation and single-mode lasing. Very recently, researchers theoretically proposed the new notion of non-Abelian topological charges [6] which takes topological phase classification to another level. Within this new framework, bulk materials are classified by non-Abelian entities that behave like matrices (such as “quaternions”). In the non-Abelian topological phases, multiple (n>1) bandgaps will be tangled together and they will exhibit intriguing braiding features. The non-Abelian topological charges do not only expose a new connection between mathematics and physics, but they also show many potential applications such as topological quantum computation. In this project, we will theoretically study and experimentally characterize various braiding features of non-Abelian topological charges based on the transmission line networks and metamaterials. The transmission line network is extremely versatile and can be used to realize just about any type of lattice models while metamaterials offers an ideal platform for implementing the continuum models. Riding on the success of our previous work, we will first build a 1D lattice model and characterize the underlying bulk-edge correspondence of all non-Abelian topological charges. We will then study the path-dependent annihilation of Dirac points in 2D Lieb/Kagome lattice and the accompanying dynamics of wave-packet propagation. Finally, we will show the braiding of Weyl points in a 3D chiral hyperbolic metamaterial and study the associated non-Abelian phenomena. We will also investigate novel features such as non-Abelian nodal links in the 3D momentum space. Going beyond the conventional Abelian topological charge concept (such as Chern number), this project will make a specific contribution in material discovery and realization.

16307821.label: Realisation of objectives
16307821.value: The aim of this proposal is to realize non-Abelian topological charges in metamaterials using transmission line network systems and 3D metamaterials. We have completed our four key objectives: the first three focus on realizing non-Abelian topological characteristics respectively in 1D, 2D, and 3D systems, while the fourth objective specifically addresses non-Abelian nodal links. Part of our work has been summarized in a review article entitled 'Non-Abelian Physics in Light and Sound' published in Science [paper #6]. Objective 1: Realization in 1D: The non-Abelian bulk-edge correspondence for n>3 band systems is experimentally and theoretically investigated using a four-band non-Abelian topological insulator realized using transmission line network. Two new classes of topological charges as well as edge states are comprehensively studied. We illustrated their difference in the four-dimensional (4D) rotation sense on the stereographically projected Clifford tori. Our results showed that a system with an even or odd number of bands will exhibit a significant difference in non-Abelian topological classification [Nat. Commun.; paper#3]. Using a theoretical framework based on non-Abelian eigen-frame rotation, we realized unconventional topological edge states in one-dimensional gapless systems stemming from non-isolated hypersurface singularities. We experimentally demonstrated this new form of topological edge states with nonreciprocal circuits for the first time [Phys. Rev. Lett.; paper#13] Objective 2: Realization in 2D: A 2D Dirac point will split into two 2nd-order exceptional points (EPs) connected by bulk Fermi arcs when the system transitions to a non-Hermitian state. We extend this concept by observing bulk Fermi arcs that links third-order EPs. In these unconventional bulk Fermi arcs, three eigenvalues share identical real parts but have distinct imaginary parts. We realize these systems experimentally using topological circuits. A winding number defined from resultant vector shows that the bulk-Fermi-arc is stabilized by the exchange of Riemannian sheets. Furthermore, analysis via non-Abelian eigenframe deformation and rotation perspective reveals that the EP3 pair is topologically nontrivial [Commun. Phys.; paper#12]. We proposed the concept of 2D non-Abelian topological insulators which can explain the energy distributions of the edge states and corner states in systems with PT symmetry. From the viewpoint of non-Abelian band topology, we establish the constraints on the 2D Zak phase and polarization. We demonstrate that the corner states in some 2D systems can be explained as the boundary mode of the one-dimensional edge states arising from the non-Abelian topology of the system [Phys. Rev. B; paper#10]. We introduced non-Hermiticity to a transmission line network that supports Dirac points. The system allows for the possibility of a point gap and eigenvalue braiding in the complex plane. We experimentally observed hybrid skin-topological (HSTE) corner states using a special synthetic complex frequency excitation technique. We demonstrated that HSTE induces asymmetric transmission along a specific direction within the topological band gap. Besides HSTE, we identify corner states originating from non-chiral edge states. Furthermore, our results suggest that whether the bulk interior is Hermitian or non-Hermitian is not a key factor for HSTE. Instead, the HSTE states can be realized and relocated simply by adjusting the non-Hermitian distribution at the boundaries [Nat. Commun.; paper#7]. We proposed and experimentally realized a near-infrared monolithic on-chip photonic system based on a perovskite/silicon nitride photonic platform, developing nano-hetero-integration technology to integrate efficient light-emitting diodes, high-performance processors and sensitive photodetectors. 2D Photonic networks are implemented to perform on-chip photonic computing and can be applied to do photonic simulations and computer vision tasks [Nat. Photonics; paper#11] Objective 3. Realization in 3D: Many intriguing topological phenomena can arise from non-Hermitian degeneracies, such as bulk Fermi arcs linking exceptional points that are split from a Dirac point and the braiding of eigenvalues around the singularities. We realized a more exotic degeneracy morphology called “swallowtail”, and explained its features using non-Abelian frame rotation and frame deformation of eigenstates. For the swallowtail, three different types of singularity exist at the same time and interact with each other. Although these singularities seem independent, they are stably connected at a single point—the vertex of the swallowtail—through which transitions can occur. We implement such a system in a non-reciprocal circuit and experimentally observe the degeneracy features of the swallowtail. Based on the non-Abelian frame rotation and deformation of eigenstates, we further demonstrate that the various transitions are topologically protected. [Nat. Phys.; paper#5]. We proposed and experimentally realized 3D meta-crystals using connected coaxial waveguides. They exhibit scalar-wave-like band dispersions, and their band structure is essentially the same as that of a nearest-neighbor tight-binding Hamiltonian. This makes the search for photonic topological phases an easier task. Different kinds of exotic topological features can be easily realised experimentally, including spin-1 Weyl points and systems in which Weyl points can be braided and annihilated in pairs by changing system parameters. Their surface states have skyrmion-like electric field distributions, resulting in a high-Q surface state band inside the light cone continuum [Nat. Materials ; Paper#8]. We topologically classified the intersection singularity of exceptional surfaces for a generic pseudo-Hermitian system with parity-time symmetry. By constructing the quotient space under equivalence relations of eigenstates, we reveal that the topology of such gapless structures can be described by a non-Abelian free group on three generators. Importantly, the classification predicts a new kind of non-Hermitian gapless topological phase and can systematically explain how the exceptional surfaces and their intersections evolve under perturbations with symmetries preserved [ Commun. Phys.; paper#2] 4: Experimentally realize non-Abelian nodal links in 3D metamaterials: We designed and fabricated a 3D electromagnetic metamaterial which exhibits multiple nodal links and the topological connection between nonadjacent nodal lines are experimentally demonstrated. The linking structure in the n>3 band system can be described with non-Abelian frame charges involving adjacent bands. The results revealed the non-adjacent band gap connection in the multiple nodal links, where nodal lines from distant band pairs are topologically related. [Phys. Rev. Lett.; paper#4]. We designed and fabricated 3D phononic crystals that exhibit earring nodal links, and experimentally observed two different kinds of earring nodal links by measuring the band structures. We found that the order of the nodal chain and line can be switched after band inversion but their link cannot be severed, manifesting the stability of the quaternion charge {−1} due to the non-Abelian band topology. [Phys. Rev. Lett.; paper#1]. We use biaxial 3D metamaterial as examples to show how complex nodal line configurations can be explained as the topological consequences of the frame charge flow from the Γ point to the Brillouin zone boundaries. Our results reveal that non-Abelian band topology is intrinsically manifested in general multiband photonic systems. Interestingly, some features of these non-Abelian frame charges can be viewed as an analog of electric charges confined in conducting wires, only that they flow in momentum space along nodal lines. But different from electric charges, these frame charges are not integers, and non-Abelian signatures emerge when braiding between adjacent band nodal lines occurs, which flips the direction of the flow. The photonic Γ point serves as the source or sink of such a frame charge flow due to a hidden braiding induced by the electrostatic mode at zero frequency. This source naturally generates non-Abelian topological signatures that can be identified even in ordinary dielectric media [Phys. Rev. X; paper#9]

16307821.label: Major findings and research outcome
16307821.value: The essence of non-Abelian topological charges lies in the quantized rotation of the eigenframe in parameter space. This framework allows for topological classification from a multi-band perspective, differing from the conventional single-band approach, and it elucidates the evolution of nodal features in parameter space. In our project, we aimed to achieve both objectives, successfully addressing them. Objectives 1 to 3 focus on exploring topological characteristics in one, two, and three dimensions, respectively. We designed and fabricated systems based on the principle of eigen-frame rotation. We conducted measurements to characterize its properties, explaining the topological features using quaternions and generalized quaternions, which are essential for describing 3D and higher-dimensional rotations. The most straightforward method to implement frame rotation in momentum space is through "connectivity-defined arrays," with the transmission cable network system being the simplest and most flexible option. This approach was successfully demonstrated in Paper #3, where we realized a 4D frame rotation in a quasi-1D system, and in Paper #10 for 2D systems, as well as in Paper #7, where we observed hybrid skin-topological corner states using a novel complex frequency excitation method. The non-Abelian bulk-edge correspondence presents challenges, as the topological invariants are not integers but generalized quaternions. We established a "quotation rule" to determine boundary charges, which in turn helps identify boundary modes. Another realization of coaxial connections occurs in a "solid-state" metacrystal, as shown in Paper #5. We developed a unique fabrication method for these crystals, which, in addition to demonstrating topological phase realizations, possess remarkable properties: their topological surface modes exhibit skyrmion textures, resulting in high-Q characteristics. A third approach to implementing frame rotation involves circuit elements (Papers #5, #12, #13). This method offers advantages over passive coaxials, as circuit elements can incorporate gain, leading us into the non-Hermitian regime. The mathematics become increasingly complex when the system's eigenvectors are not orthogonal so that in addition to frame rotation, we also have frame deformation, and there are exceptional points at which eigenvectors to coalesce. Overcoming these challenges has enabled us to realize numerous new and unexpected phenomena, as detailed in Section 5.3. Objective 4 focuses on exploring and explaining the evolution of nodal features in band structures from a non-Abelian topological perspective. We fabricated samples exhibiting these features (Papers #1, #4, #9), finding that nodal features, including nodal links, can be effectively explained using non-Abelian frame charges, providing new insights previously unknown in this context.

16307821.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16307821.value: Higher Dimensions: Currently, most of our work focuses on 1D, 2D, 3D and 4D systems. We can explore higher dimensions where new phenomena related to frame rotation may emerge. Higher Frequencies: Our work primarily operates at microwave frequencies. While transitioning to higher frequencies, such as optical, poses challenges and increased costs in fabrication, it would be valuable to pursue. This shift could bring our findings closer to practical applications. Bulk-Edge Correspondence: Traditional bulk-edge correspondence relies on integer values. In the context of eigenframe rotation, topological invariants take the form of matrix-like entities rather than integers. We have established a quotient rule to demonstrate correspondence, but the proof lacks mathematical rigor and requires further development. Non-Hermiticity: The mathematics becomes significantly more complex in non-Hermitian systems. Nevertheless, this investigation is crucial, as all real systems exhibit non-Hermitian characteristics due to environmental interactions. When eigenvectors become non-orthogonal, our topological description based on frame rotation must be adapted to account for frame deformation and the challenges presented by exceptional points, where eigenvectors merge and cannot be traced. While we have made some progress, much more work remains. This might require collaborating with professional mathematicians.

16307821.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16307821.value: In recent years, topological photonics has emerged as a promising field, enabling advanced systems where the transport of electromagnetic signals is robust against disruptions. Traditional topological methods primarily focus on "band topology," which examines the properties of individual bands (or channels) one at a time. However, different channels can influence one another, leading to the exploration of a multi-band approach. This perspective allows for a more comprehensive understanding of how multiple channels interact, enhancing robust signal transport capabilities across various frequencies. In our project, we have successfully delved into the intricate realm of non-Abelian physics, employing this multi-band approach to uncover unique properties in various advanced materials called "metamaterials". By leveraging the principle of "eigen-frame rotation," we have developed and tested systems that facilitate a deeper understanding of topological phases and transport phenomena from a multi-band perspective. The implications extend beyond theoretical exploration. Applications of non-Abelian physics are poised to advance several fields, including new materials, computing, and the development of novel devices. These advancements not only enhance our technological capabilities but also pave the way for future innovations in communication and computing.

16308221.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16308221.value: Quantile regression model relates response at quantile levels with covariates. It is one of the commonly used regression models and has wide applications. Survival analysis is a branch of statistical science that focuses on time-to-events analysis with applications in biomedical studies. In survival regression models, quantile regression is an important alternative to the Cox proportional hazards and accelerated failure models. Successful methodologies have been proposed in the literature to handle censored data for quantile regression. These methods include counting process martingale, probability mass redistribution, inverse probability weighting, local weighting and self-consistency. Each method has its own unique advantage. In statistics, efficiency is always one of the most concerned issues, since it represents the most accurate estimation for any given model. In the case of quantile regression with censored data, the literature on survival analysis has not reported efficient estimation. We will use our previous research on efficient estimation for censored linear model and quantile regression with complete data as basis to focus on finding a method that leads to efficient estimation for global quantile regression in the presence of censoring. We will provide theoretical justification of the semiparametric efficiency and numerical evidence of its superiority. 16308221.label: Realisation of objectives
16308221.value: This report summarizes progress toward the objectives in our original proposal on efficient estimation in quantile regression with censored data. Theory and efficiency. We developed a semiparametric efficiency framework by deriving the score, nuisance tangent space, and efficient influence function for censored quantile models. Leveraging least favorable submodels, we defined an estimator whose influence function attains the semiparametric information bound under standard regularity. We established consistency, asymptotic linearity, and asymptotic normality, and proved local efficiency at the true data-generating mechanism. Key steps included: (i) characterizing the counting-process-based score under dependent censoring structures, (ii) orthogonal projection to the nuisance space spanned by censoring- and baseline-related martingales, and (iii) verifying stochastic equicontinuity and Donsker properties for the induced function classes. The resulting estimator admits a closed-form influence curve representation that enables valid sandwich variance estimation and inference. Computation and algorithms. We proposed a computationally feasible algorithm that translates the efficient score equations into an iteratively reweighted optimization with convex subproblems. The algorithm uses martingale residual updates from the Peng–Huang (2008) counting-process representation and a numerically stable line search to guarantee descent. Variance estimation is implemented via plug-in evaluation of the efficient influence function and a multiplier bootstrap tailored to censoring. Extensive simulations show that the estimator is accurate, displays near-efficiency across a wide range of censoring rates, and remains stable in moderate samples. The martingale representation yields improved bias control at extreme quantiles and provides accurate standard error estimates with reliable coverage. Methodological extensions. We addressed several practical issues: Quantile crossing: we incorporated monotonicity constraints via rearrangement and isotonic postprocessing, which preserve efficiency to first order while enforcing non-crossing quantile curves. Quantiles on intervals: we developed joint estimation over designated quantile ranges, improving stability and power relative to pointwise fits. Time-dependent covariates: we constructed an efficient estimating framework for covariate processes, defining predictable scores and compensators with landmarked and fully time-varying designs; this is a central contribution enabling robust inference in longitudinal settings. Cure models: we extended the approach to mixture cure settings, deriving efficient scores under latent susceptibility and proposing a two-stage estimator with identifiable tail quantiles. Dissemination. We refined and published our methodological core in Statistica Sinica [1], establishing the theoretical and computational foundations. A second manuscript under review in Statistica Sinica [2] develops correlation structures and addresses practical challenges specific to censored quantile regression. Overall, we realized the theoretical efficiency program, delivered a practical algorithm with strong numerical performance, and advanced key extensions, especially for time-dependent covariates. [1]. We find a computationally feasible algorithm to compute the estimator and its variance estimator and investage numerical performances of these estimators. We study the counting process martingale of Peng and Huang (2008), and derive an accurate estimation using martingale representation.

We investigate several important issues including a) the quantile crossing problem; b). the quantile regression assumed on an interval rather than on all quantile levels; c). time-dependent covariates; and d). extension to survival cure models. In particular, one of our main subjects is how to solve efficient quantile estimation for time-dependent covariates.

16308221.label: Major findings and research outcome
16308221.value: Our major finding is a new method to compute coefficient estimates for quantile regression, applicable both with and without censored data. This estimator is innovative in design and performance. It achieves semiparametric efficiency: under a correctly specified model, no other regular estimator can be more accurate in large samples. In practical terms, this means sharper estimates, tighter confidence intervals, and more reliable conclusions from the same data, especially at clinically important quantiles such as early risk or long-term survival. The contribution is not merely theoretical. We translate the efficiency theory into a computational procedure that is fast, stable, and feasible for real datasets. Along the way, we developed several computational tricks that markedly improve numerical stability and convergence: carefully constructed iteratively reweighted updates, martingale-based residual corrections under censoring, and robust line-search and preconditioning steps that handle extreme quantiles and high censoring rates. These refinements reduce bias and variance in finite samples and ensure the algorithm remains dependable across a wide range of settings. Applications span biomedical and public health research (survival analysis with incomplete follow-up, detection limits in lab data), economics and finance (tail risk and income distribution analysis), and engineering reliability. The method also accommodates time-dependent covariates and can be adapted to complex structures such as cure models, making it broadly useful where standard tools struggle. The results and methodology are documented in two publications: one refined and published, establishing the theoretical foundations and practical algorithm; and a second under review that addresses correlation structures and additional challenges specific to quantile regression with censoring. Ongoing work extends these ideas to richer longitudinal designs, joint modeling across quantile intervals to prevent crossing, and more scalable implementations for large datasets. In summary, we deliver an efficiency-optimal, computation-ready estimator for quantile regression under censoring, pairing best-in-class accuracy with stable algorithms and wide applicability. These results are contained in [1] - [3] and other ongoing work. [1]. Wang, Z.F., Chen, K., Lin, Y. and Ying, Z. (2025). Efficient estimation of quantile regression. Statistica Sinica, Accepted. [2]. Dai, L., Li, T. and Chen, K. (2025). A model-free correlation coefficient for censored data. Statistica Sinica, Accepted subject to a major revision.

16308221.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16308221.value: Efficient quantile estimation for censored data has strong potential to reshape inference across biostatistics, economics, and reliability by delivering near-optimal precision, valid uncertainty, and robust performance at extreme quantiles. Next steps include: (1) extend efficiency theory to time‑dependent covariates with dynamic treatment regimes; (2) develop scalable algorithms (stochastic gradients, distributed computing) and automatic tuning; (3) enforce non‑crossing via joint, monotone quantile processes; (4) integrate cure models and frailty/correlation structures; (5) create open‑source software with diagnostics and variance tools; (6) establish finite‑sample guarantees and targeted bootstrap; (7) validate on multi‑center EHR and trial datasets; (8) disseminate via tutorials and benchmarks.

16308221.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16308221.value: Quantile regression is a major method in statistics because it goes beyond the average to show how different parts of an outcome—like the median or the extremes—change with patient traits or treatments. This gives a fuller, more useful picture than “average effect” analyses. Censored data are widespread in healthcare and biostatistics. In survival studies, some patients are still alive at the end of follow‑up, so their exact survival times are unknown; lab results can be below detection limits. These partial observations are common and, if mishandled, can bias results—especially for high‑risk or long‑surviving patients. Our work provides an innovative, best‑in‑class solution for efficient quantile estimation with censoring. “Efficient” means extracting the maximum information from the data, yielding more accurate estimates and trustworthy uncertainty measures with the same sample size. We pair rigorous statistical theory with fast, stable algorithms, so the methods are ready for real use. Why it matters: Precision insight: Identify who is at early risk or who benefits most. Reliable decisions: Correctly handle censoring to avoid bias and misleading confidence intervals. Broad reach: Works with time‑varying patient data and extends to complex settings like cure models. In short, our approach is innovative, powerful, and practical for real biomedical data.

16308321.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16308321.value: Robust statistics under Huber's contamination model arose in 1960s, since then the search for both statistically optimal and computationally feasible procedures has become a fundamental problem in areas including statistics and computer science. Many depth-based estimators, although statistically optimal, suffers from the computational difficulties. On the other hand, recent developments in computer science in search of computationally tractable algorithms for robust learning, rely on prior knowledge of moments or contamination portion, which can not be adapted to general distributions such as elliptical distributions whose moments do not necessarily exist. To overcome these challenges, the PI and collaborators recently developed a novel methodology based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), a new technique developed in machine learning society. It is possible to construct statistically optimal mean and covariance (scatter) estimates from contaminated samples, under general elliptical distributions. Equipped with the rapid progress in the computational facility for deep learning, it provides us a new scalable tool for robust statistics. In this proposed project, the PI and collaborators will focus on the multi-task robust regression problem, that includes the special case of robust mean/regression and admits wide applications where robust prediction is desired against unknown data contamination. In particular, the main purposes are listed as follows. (A) A unified framework of Generative Adversarial Networks with Proper Scoring Rules is proposed for robust multi-task regression problem, that brings many popular GANs into the toolbox of robust learning. (B) Statistical optimality of such robust estimates is given under general TV-perturbation sets, that includes Huber's contamination model as special cases, and general elliptical distributions that includes Gaussian distributions and Cauchy distributions whose moments do not exist. (C) This new methodology may bing us new techniques in a variety of applications, including but are not limited to, robust factor analysis in Economics and Finance, robust Cryo-EM imaging in biomolecular engineering that will be studied here. 穩健統計學誕生於1960年代Richard Huber提出的數據污染模型，從那時候起尋找統計最優並且計算可行的程序成為統計學和計算機科學的一個基礎問題。一方面，統計學提出的很多基於深度的最優估計，在計算上都是困難的。另一方面，計算機科學近年來發展的可行算法，都基於污染數據的有限矩假設和估計，因此不能適用於一般橢球分佈，其矩可能是不存在的。為了克服這些困難，最近本項目組及合作者發展了一種新的基於生成對抗網絡的方法。該方法可以構造一般橢球分佈下均值(location)和方差(scatter)的統計最優估計，並且借助於深度學習計算技術的迅速發展處理大規模穩健統計問題。本項目則致力於發展一般性的多目標穩健回歸問題的方法，包括上述問題作為特例，並研究相關的應用問題。特別地，本項目的主要研究內容如下： (A) 建立基於對抗生成網絡的多目標穩健回歸的統一框架，包括多種網絡結構及優化方法。 (B) 提供全變差(Total Variation)擾動模型的統計最優估計，包含Huber的經典污染模型。 (C) 探索相關應用的範例，包括Cryo-EM成像和金融數據的穩健因子分析。

16308421.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16308421.value: Topology optimization has become increasingly important as a tool for engineering structural designs and has attracted considerable attention from both industrial and academic societies. Numerous applications have demonstrated the great structural performance of computed designs. New manufacturing technology has brought demand in finer structural designs. It is timely to develop more efficient and stable numerical methods. Threshold dynamics has been recognized as an efficient and powerful method to arrange phases in domain of interest in a way that decreasing prescribed energy. It has been successfully applied to many optimization problems including topology optimization in fluid flow structures. In this proposal, we plan to develop an efficient and stable threshold dynamics method for topology optimization of heat transfer systems. The method will be applied to a practical micro heat sink model. The results will be analyzed and show that topology optimization can be used as an innovative design tool for optimizing the heat transfer. 拓扑优化作为工程结构设计工具引起了工业界和学术界的广泛关注。新的制造技术带来了更精细的结构设计需求。急需开发更高效、更稳定的数值方法。阈值动力学已被公认为一种高效且能量递减的迭代方法。它已成功应用于包括流体拓扑优化在内的许多优化问题。在本项目中，我们计划开发一个高效稳定的拓扑优化的阈值动力学方法应用于弹性力学、流体力学和热力学。我们还会仔细分析相应的问题以及所提出方法的性质。

16308421.label: Realisation of objectives
16308421.value: Under the GRF Grant 16308421, our research on topology optimization has resulted in three major publications that advance the methodology and efficiency of solving key optimization problems. The minimum compliance problem in linear elasticity and the minimum heat dissipation problem in heat transfer are two classical problems in topology optimization. To address these, we reformulated them as minimization-minimization problems and developed a simple energy-decaying iterative thresholding algorithm. In this approach, the material domain is implicitly represented by its characteristic function, which is updated in each iteration by comparing a defined function with a threshold value. The energy-decaying property of the algorithm was theoretically proved. Numerical experiments demonstrated the effectiveness and robustness of the method for both types of problems. These results have been published in Communications in Computational Physics [Wei Hu, Dong Wang, and Xiaoping Wang, 2022] and Communications in Computational Physics [Luyu Cen, Wei Hu, Dong Wang, and Xiaoping Wang, 2023], respectively. To further enhance the efficiency and robustness of topology optimization, we proposed a new framework that combines the strengths of deep diffusion models and the thresholding method. Specifically, we introduced the Diffusion Model with Iterative Convolution Thresholding Method (DICTM), which leverages the power of deep generative models to produce high-quality initial configurations. This significantly accelerates the subsequent threshold dynamics process, reducing the number of iterations to about one-tenth of that required by the method starting from a uniform initial guess. The improved computational efficiency also allows for more effective hyperparameter tuning at no additional cost. By integrating the robustness of diffusion models with the precision of the threshold dynamics framework, DICTM offers a powerful new approach to structural topology optimization, producing designs that are both physically sound and computationally efficient. This work has recently been accepted by Thesis 2023 Ph.D. Mathematics [Xiaonan Peng, 2023]. The involvement of the new PI has played a significant role in the coordination of the participating students and the original PI.

16308421.label: Major findings and research outcome
16308421.value: Under GRF Grant 16308421, our research on topology optimization—finding the best structure designs for efficiency—produced three key publications with impactful results. First, we focused on two core engineering problems: making structures (like beams) as strong as possible without wasting material (minimum compliance), and designing heat-dissipating parts (like computer heat sinks) to work optimally (minimum heat dissipation). We created a new step-by-step algorithm to solve these. It works by treating the structure as a grid where each point is either part of the structure or empty. In each step, it uses a "threshold" to decide which points to keep, gradually refining the design. Critically, we proved this algorithm always improves performance over time (its "energy"—a measure of how well it works—consistently drops). Tests confirmed it’s reliable for both problems, with findings published in two 2023 journals. To make the process faster, we combined this algorithm with advanced AI called deep diffusion models, creating DICTM. These AI models act like smart sketchers, generating high-quality initial designs. This cuts the number of steps needed by 90%—only 1/10th of the steps required if starting from scratch. The speedup lets us fine-tune designs without extra cost, resulting in structures that work well and are quick to create. This work was accepted for 2025 publication. Overall, we advanced topology optimization with a proven method for classic problems and an AI-boosted, far faster approach, aiding better, more efficient engineering design.

16308421.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16308421.value: We received GRF Grant 16308421 to improve "topology optimization"—designing structures (like beams or heat sinks) to work best. We published three studies making this faster and better. First, we solved two classic problems: making structures strong without waste, and designing efficient heat-dissipators. Our new step-by-step method treats materials as a "map" of points (solid or empty). Each step uses a threshold to keep/remove points based on a "score." We proved this always improves the structure, and tests confirmed it works. Findings are in two journals. To speed things up, we combined this with AI ("deep diffusion models")—smart tools that generate good initial designs—to create "DICTM." The AI’s starting design cuts steps to 1/10th, saving time. This lets us tweak designs without extra cost, making strong, heat-efficient structures quickly. This method is soon to be published.

16308721.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16308721.value: Alkyne metathesis is a synthetically very useful reaction that can be applied for synthesis of molecules with an alkyne functional group. To perform the reaction under mild condition, a catalyst is required. There has been much interest in developing efficient catalysts for the reaction based on well-defined high valent d0 W(VI) and Mo(VI) alkylidyne (carbyne) complexes. Inspired by the great success of user-friendly non-d0 ruthenium carbenes for olefin metathesis, we propose in this project to develop alkyne metathesis catalysts based on non-d0 alkylidyne complexes. Our preliminary work shows that an air-stable d2 Re(V) alkylidyne complex bearing two PO-chelating ligands and a labile pyridine ligand could catalyze homo-metathesis of internal alkynes with a broad substrate scope, including alcohols, amines and even carboxylic acids. The catalyst can tolerate heating, air and moisture in both solid and solution states and the catalytic metathesis reactions could proceed normally in wet solvents. A major drawback of the system is that the catalytic activity is relatively low and the catalytic reactions have to be carried out at about 100 oC. The main goal of this project is to search for more active catalysts based on d2 rhenium(V) alkylidyne complexes so that alkyne metathesis reactions can be performed under milder condition. The main tasks include design and synthesis of a series of new d2 rhenium(V) alkylidyne complexes, evaluation of catalytic properties of the newly synthesized complexes and demonstration of the applicability of our new catalytic systems. The proposed work may lead us to discover new alkyne metathesis catalysts that are stable to air/water and applicable for metathesis of both internal and terminal alkynes with a variety of functional groups. The knowledge gained will be useful for future work in the development of alkyne metathesis catalysts based on non-d0 alkylidyne complexes of other metals. 炔烃复分解反应是一类能合成含炔烃官能团分子的非常有用的反应。这类反应需要催化剂来实现。现在已有的炔烃复分解催化剂为高价d(0) 钨（VI）和钼（VI）的卡拜络合物。受广泛使用的非d(0)钌卡宾烯烃复分解催化剂的启发，我们将探索利用非d(0)金属卡拜络合物实现炔烃复分解反应的催化反应。我们的初步实验表明一个d(2）铼（V）卡拜络合物可以催化多种炔烃的复分解反应。这个催化剂具有对热，空气及水不敏感的优点。但是它的催化活性较低，需要在100 oC 左右进行反应。此项目的主要目的是寻找更有效的d2铼（V）催化剂来实现温和条件下的反应。主要工作包括新的铼（V）卡拜络合物的设计及合成，催化活性的测试，及新催化剂的应用。我们期望能够发现对空气和水稳定、底物适用性广的炔复分解的催化剂。从中学习到的知识将对今后发展更好的用于炔烃复分解的催化剂有指导意义。

16308721.label: Realisation of objectives
16308721.value: The main objectives of the project are (i) to synthesize new d2 Re(V) alkylidyne complexes that are potentially active for alkyne metathesis with a broad substrate scope, and (ii) to investigate catalytic properties of d2 Re(V) alkylidyne complexes in alkyne metathesis reactions, especially for reactions involving alkynes (both internal and terminal) with protic groups and heteroatoms. To achieve the objectives, we have carried out the following research work. We have made a lot of efforts in building a library of d2 Re(V) alkylidyne complexes that are potentially catalytically active for alkyne metathesis. We have prepared a series of phenol-functionalized phosphines Ar2PC6H4OH (POH). With these ligand precursors, we have sucessfully prepared a series of d2 Re(V) alkylidyne complexes supported by PO-chelating ligands, including complexes of the type Re(≡CCH2Ph)(L)(PO)2 (L = phosphine, pyridine, H2O and SMe2). We have also tried to prepare Re(V) alkylidyne complexes supported by other LX-type bidentate ancillary ligands. Starting from Ph2P-o-C6H4SH (PSH), we were able to synthesize six-coordinated thiophenolate complexes Re(≡CR)(PMePh2)(PS)2, five-coordinated thiophenolate complexes Re(≡CR)(PS)2 and the six-coordinated sulfinate complex Re(≡CCH2Ph)(H2O)(PSO)2 (PSO = Ph2P-o-C6H4SO2). Starting from Ph2P-o-C6H4NH2 (PNH), complexes Re(≡CR)(PMePh2)(PN)2 were synthesized. We have also succeeded in making complexes of the type Re(≡CR')(PMePh2)(Ph2PCH=CRO)2 starting from phosphine-carbonyl compounds Ph2PCH2C(=O)R. As an alternative strategy for the development of Re(V)-based alkyne metathesis catalysts, we have tried to prepare Re(V) alkylidyne complexes with tridentate ligands. For example, by ligand substitution reactions of the alkylidyne complex ReCl2(≡CH2Ph)(PMePh2)3 with tridentate ligands bis(2-diphenylphosphino-4-tolyl)amine (PNHP) and 2-{(2-diphenylphosphino-phenyl)-iminomethyl}phenol (PNOH), we have successfully prepared the complexes bearing a [PNO] pincer ligand, and complexes bearing a [PNP] pincer ligand. We have searched for more convenient synthetic routes to rhenium alkylidyne complexes. for example, through direct reactions of Re(III) complexes ReCl3(PPh3)2(MeCN) and ReCl3(PR3)3 with reagents such as terminal alkynes, diazoalkanes, and phosphorus-ylides. Novel rhenium spiro bi(metallacycloprop-1-ene) complexes were obtained in the reactions of terminal alkynes with Re(III) complexes such as ReCl3(PPh3)2(MeCN) and ReCl3(PMePh2)3. To investigate metathesis activity of Re(V) alkylidyne complexes, we have studied stoichiometric reactions of a series of rhenium(V) alkylidyne complexes with internal alkynes. Through this activity, we have identified several systems that can undergo alkyne metathesis reactions and found that ligand environment is very important for the metathesis activity. New Re(V) alkylidyne complexes have been obtained from the metathesis reactions. While metathesis reactions of internal alkynes are well-documented, metathesis of terminal alkynes remains a rare accomplishment, both catalytically and stoichiometrically. To overcome this challenge, we explored reactions of terminal alkynes with non-d0 alkylidyne complexes. We found that the complex Re(≡CR)Cl2(PMePh2)3 can undergo metathesis reactions with a variety of terminal alkynes with a diverse functional groups. Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations were performed to study thermodynamic and kinetic aspect of the reaction. Using homometathesis of internal alkynes as model reactions, we have evaluated catalytic properties of a number of Re(V) alkylidyne complexes including those supported by bidentate PO-, PN-, PS-chelating ligands, and those supported by tridentate PNP and PNO-chelating ligands. Several Re(V) complexes were found to be catalytically active for the reactions with varied activity. The most effective catalysts we discovered so far are Re(V) alkylidyne complexes of the Re(≡CCH2Ph)(PO)2(L) (PO = Ph2PC6H4O-; L = H2O, SMe2) which can promote homometathesis of ArC≡CMe at room temperature. To demonstrate the versatile ability of the aqua alkylidyne complex Re(≡CCH2Ph)(PO)2(H2O), we have conducted a series of catalytic reactions with the catalyst, including alkyne homometathesis, cross-metathesis, ring-closing alkyne metathesis, and acyclic diyne metathesis macrocyclization reactions. To investigate the reaction mechanism of the metathesis reactions and to understand ligand effect on the activity for metathesis reactions, we have calculated the reaction profiles of alkyne metathesis reactions of a series of Re(V) alkylidyne complexes bearing, monodentate, bidentate and tridentate ligands.

16308721.label: Major findings and research outcome
16308721.value: (1) Pincer complexes Re(≡CCH2Ph)Cl(PMePh2)(PNP) and Re(≡CCH2Ph)Cl(PMePh2)(PNO) can be synthesized by the reactions of Re(≡CCH2Ph)Cl2(PMePh2)3 with bis(2-diphenylphosphino-4-tolyl)amine (PNHP) and 2-{(2-diphenylphosphino-phenyl)-iminomethyl}phenol (PNOH), respectively. The [PNP]- and [PNO]-pincer complexes are catalytically active for homometathesis of 1-methoxy-4-(1-propyn-1-yl)benzene at 150 °C (Publication 3). (2) A series of new Re(V) alkylidyne complexes with phoshorus-sulfur hybrid chelating ligands were prepared, including six-coordinated thiophenolate complexes Re(≡CR)(PMePh2)(PS)2 (PS = Ph2P-o-C6H4S), five-coordinated thiophenolate complexes Re(≡CR)(PS)2 and the six-coordinated sulfinate complex Re(≡CCH2Ph)(H2O)(PSO)2 (PSO = Ph2P-o-C6H4SO2). Different from complexes with phosphinophenolate ligands, the PS complexes Re(≡CR)(PMePh2)(PS)2 and Re(≡CR)(PS)2 showed only marginal alkyne metathesis activity at 100 °C, whereas the sulfinate complex Re(≡CCH2Ph)(H2O)(PSO)2 is unreactive under similar condition. DFT calculations reveal that the lower metathesis activity of the thiophenolate and sulfinate complexes compared with that of PO complexes is due to the lower affinity of the five-coordinated species for alkynes (Publication 6). (3) The reactions of terminal alkynes with Re(III) complexes such as ReCl3(PPh3)2(MeCN) and ReCl3(PMePh2)3 give novel rhenium spiro bi(metallacycloprop-1-ene) complexes. These complexes can undergo oxidation-induced coupling reactions to give h4-butadiene complexes, a unique example of coupling of two carbene ligands of biscarbene complexes (Publications 2 and 5). (4) Re(V) alkylidyne complexes Re(≡CR)Cl2(PMePh2)3 can undergo stoichiometric metathesis with a range of terminal aryl and aliphatic alkynes (HC≡CR’), yielding substituted alkylidyne complexes Re(≡CR’)Cl2(PMePh2)3 and HC≡CR. These stoichiometric metathesis reactions are compatible with functional groups such as aldehydes, alcohols, esters, and even unprotected carboxylic acids. Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations indicate that the formation of substituted alkylidyne complexes is both thermodynamically and kinetically more favorable than that of methylidyne complexes (Publication 7). (5) The Re(V) alkylidyne complexes Re(≡CCH2Ph)(PO)2(L) (PO = Ph2P(o-C6H4O, L = H2O, SMe2) are highly efficient alkyne metathesis catalysts. The aqua complex represent the first non-d0 alkylidyne catalyst capable of mediating alkyne metathesis at room temperature. The aqua alkylidyne complex Re(≡CCH2Ph)(PO)2(H2O) can effectively promote alkyne homometathesis, cross-metathesis, ring-closing alkyne metathesis, and acyclic diyne metathesis macrocyclization reactions. The catalysts tolerates a range of challenging functional groups, including primary alcohols, aldehyde, amines and even carboxylic acid (Publication 4). (6) DFT study reveals that ligands can have a significant impact on the metathesis activity of Re(V) alkylidyne complexes (PhD thesis of Dr. Lam Cheung KONG).

16308721.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16308721.value: We have successfully developed alkyne metathesis catalysts based on Re(V) alkylidyne complexes. It would be of interest to explore the possibility of developing metathesis catalysts based on non-d0 alkylidyne complexes of other transition metals. Our d² Re(V) catalysts have demonstrated effectiveness in promoting metathesis reactions of internal alkynes. It is of interest to investigate the metathesis reactions of other more challenging substrates, such as terminal alkynes and electron-rich alkynes. Additionally, the application of our catalysts in organic synthesis and materials science represents another promising area of exploration. We have successfully demonstrated alkyne metathesis reactions of substituted d2 Re(V) complexes Re(≡CR)X2L3. Moving forward, it would be valuable to prepare methylidyne complexes, Re(≡CH)X₂L₃, and study their metathesis activity.

16308721.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16308721.value: Alkyne metathesis is a valuable synthetic transformation for constructing molecules containing alkyne functional groups. Traditionally, this reaction has relied on high-valent d⁰ tungsten(VI) and molybdenum(VI) alkylidyne (alkylidyne) complexes as catalysts. However, these systems often suffer from significant limitations, including moisture sensitivity and limited functional group tolerance. The primary objective of this project is to develop more robust and versatile catalysts based on d² rhenium(V) alkylidyne complexes, enabling alkyne metathesis under milder and more practical conditions. To this end, we have designed and synthesized a series of rhenium(V) alkylidyne complexes, investigated their reactivity toward alkynes, and evaluated their catalytic performance. Our work has led to the development of catalysts that are stable in air and water. They can efficiently promote homo-metathesis, cross-metathesis, and ring-closing metathesis of internal alkynes with a diverse range of functional groups.
