Most of the results have been presented at various international conferences (e.g. International Union for Pure and Applied Biophysics, APS March Meeting, etc.) and published in leading international journals such as Journal of the American Chemical Society, Angewandte Chemie, Physical Review Letters, Nature Communications, Advanced Science, Small, as shown in Part C. While some manuscripts are currently under review, other findings are being integrated into broader applications and finalized for publication, with the goal of achieving greater impact through their combined significance.

17306221.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17306221.value: The projects have demonstrated how sequence-specific interactions can regulate condensate behavior and droplet organization, opening opportunities for synthetic organelles and multiphase bioreactors that adapt to environmental cues. In addition, the projects have also developed novel coacervate-colloids hybrid functional systems, providing new pathways for bionic and dynamic material design. These systems provide a foundation for next-generation biomaterials with programmable properties for applications such as tissue engineering and disease modeling. As a large amount of data has been generated, the next step will be to develop predictive models that map sequence/sidechain chemistry to correlate molecular interactions with phase behaviors of condensates under diverse conditions. This framework is beneficial in engineering artificial organelles or multiphase bioreactors that can dynamically reconfigure in response to environmental stimuli. Such stimuli-responsive, synthetic organelles are important building blocks for designing next-generation biomaterials with programmable properties and behaviors. We aim to develop these areas with the support of research grants including RGC and the Innovation and Technology Fund (ITF).

17306221.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17306221.value: We have shown that small differences in how molecules interact can strongly influence how droplets form, solidify, or separate into layers. For example, changes in solvent can make droplets harden or dissolve, and tiny chemical differences between DNA and RNA cause them to separate into core–shell structures. These insights explain past inconsistencies and provide simple rules for designing smart, layered materials that respond to their environment.

17306521.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17306521.value: In the era of antibiotic resistance, the development of novel potent antibiotics against highly pathogenic and resistant Gram negative bacteria is urgently desired. Klebsazolicin, a recently discovered peptide natural product showing activity against narrow spectrum of Gram negative bacteria, becomes the target molecule of interest. Till today, its total synthesis has not been reported. In this project, we aim to develop a total synthetic approach towards klebsazolicin, in which the installation of the N-terminal cyclic amidine is the challenge to address. The established synthetic approach will be used to construct a series of cyclic analogues with tunable ring sizes, which will bind to the 23S rRNA target in the optimized conformation. The analogues bearing modifications at the N-terminal cyclic amidine and backbone heterocycle moieties will be synthesized, in order to optimize the key π-π interaction revealed in the target binding model. The analogues with oligo-arginine tail installed at the C-terminus of klebsazolicin will be synthesized, which will overcome the obstacle in the uptake of klebsazolicin by bacteria and expand the antibacterial spectrum. 在抗生素抗性挑战凸显的时代，发展具有抗革兰氏阴性耐药菌活性的全新抗生素的需求尤为迫切。作为近期发现的全新抗生素分子，Klebsazolicin因其对革兰氏阴性菌具有的窄谱抗菌活性而受到我们的关注。在本课题中，我们将发展基于Fmoc多肽固相合成策略的Klebsazolicin的全合成途径，并有针对性的发展引入N端环状脒结构的新方法。在此基础上，我们将构建一系列具有可调节尺寸的环状类似物，以期优化其与23S核糖体RNA靶标结合的构象。我们亦将对N端环状脒结构和分子骨架中的杂环结构进行修饰，以优化靶标结合模型中关键的π-π相互作用。我们还将通过在Klebsazolicin的C端引入寡聚精氨酸，以克服该抗生素难以被细菌摄取的问题，进而扩展其抗菌谱。

17306521.label: Realisation of objectives
17306521.value: Objective 1_Total synthesis of klebsazolicin (KLB) As the basis of the in-depth structural modification study, we first established a facile chemical total synthesis approach towards klebsazolicin. The key structural features of this natural product include oxazole/thiazole in the peptide chain and the N-terminal cyclic amidine structure. Thus, we developed the synthetic routes for two thiazole-containing dipeptide building blocks. For the oxazole-containing building block, since the racemization of the α-carbon could not be suppressed via condition optimization, we prepared the tripeptide block via chromatographic separation of the epimers. For the N-terminal cyclic amidine formation, current methods reported in literature are not applicable due to the requirement of excess amount of amine moiety. Thus, inspired by the YcaO catalyzed cyclic amidine formation in biosynthesis of KLB, we developed a Hg(II) mediated ring-closing amidine formation from thioamide precursor via a thermodynamically and kinetically favored 6-exo-trig process. This new method showed good compatibility with solid phase peptide synthesis. The efficacy was validated by synthesizing a series of pentapeptide substrates derived from the N-terminal structure of KLB. Meanwhile, we synthesized a hexapeptide natural product streptamidine containing N-terminal cyclic amidine via our method and evaluated the stereochemistry of this compound via synthesizing both epimers and monitoring the salt-dependent epimerization process in NMR solutions. With the building blocks and ring-closing amidine formation method in hand, we finished the solid phase total synthesis of KLB. Starting from Cl-trityl resin, the sequence Ser3-Gly23 containing thiazole/oxazole units was assembled via standard Fmoc-SPPS protocols. Then, the Gln2 was installed via thioamide formation, followed by the installation of Ser1. Due to the increased acidity of α-carbon of thioamide, the Fmoc removal conditions used for the last two residues were tuned correspondingly to avoid epimerization. Finally, the synthesis was completed via on-resin ring-closing amidine formation and global deprotection. In the amidine formation step, 10 equiv of thiophene was added to suppress side reactions caused by coordination of Hg(II) to thiazole. The synthetic KLB was isolated after a single HPLC purification in 10% yield (calculated based on resin loading). The synthetic KLB was characterized by MS and NMR, and the compound showed good antibacterial activities against Bacillus cereus (0.25 μg/mL for BC107 & BC177 strains) and Vibrio cholerae (0.25 μg/mL for V1978 and 0.5 μg/mL for V1853) in M9+glucose medium. This synthetic route was quite efficient and allowed us to finish the synthesis of more than fourty analogues during the structural modification study (objective 2). Objective 2_In-depth structural modification of klebsazolicin Armed with the facile total synthetic approach, we implemented the structural modification study. According to the literature, the thiazole/oxazole rings and cyclic amidine moieties could interact with rRNA via π-π stacking and contribute to the binding. To test these proposed effects, we synthesized a series of KLB analogues by partially or totally replacing the oxazole and/or thiazole structures to corresponding ring-opened Xaa-Ser structures. Meanwhile, we also tried to replace oxazole to thiazole and replace cyclic amidine to linear Ser-Gln or N-containing heteroarenes (analogues 1-19). In general, opening two of the four azole rings led to improved bactericidal activity against B. cereus and V. cholerae. It was notable that opening all four azole rings and the cyclic amidine gave a simple linear peptide analogue 17 showing the same activity against V. cholerae as KLB (0.25 μg/mL for V1978 and 0.5 μg/mL for V1853). Based on the ring-like binding conformation of klebsazolicin reported in literature, we tested the effect of cyclization on bactericidal activity. To simplify the synthesis, we replaced Gly5 and Ser15 to Cys residues in simplified KLB structures (opening azole rings and/or cyclic amidine) and prepared the S/S-bridged analogues via introducing linkers A to F and disulfide bond. The bridged KLB analogues showed substantially improved bactericidal activities compared to linear peptide analogue 17. Notably, analogues 34 and 35 containing long linkers based on biphenyl and N,N'-bisacetyl ethylenediamine structures respectively showed even higher activities than our synthetic KLB. Objective 3_Expansion of the anti-bacterial spectrum of KLB via incorporation of uptake improving moieties According to the literature report, the narrow spectrum bactericidal activity of KLB was attributed to the limited uptake by Gram-negative bacteria. Also, the C-terminal sequence Ser15-Gly23 was found to be important for uptake by not required for rRNA binding and protein synthesis inhibition. To broaden the antibacterial spectrum, we tried to introduce oligoarginine to the truncated linear KLB analogues. We tested several truncation sites derived from analogue 21 and identified Ser13-Ala14 juncture as the appropriate truncation site. Then, we introduced Arg2, Arg4 and Arg6 to the C-terminal of truncated analogue 40. Meanwhile, since polymyxin B nonapeptide (PMBN) has been reported to be able to increase the drug penetration of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, we introduced PMBN to the C-terminal of analogue 40 via Ser/Thr ligation. Analogue 43 containing Arg4 showed improved activities against B. cereus and V. cholerae compared to analogue 40, while analogue 45 containing PMBN showed better activities than KLB. However, we failed to broaden the antibacterial spectrum of KLB. Meanwhile, based on the reported uptake improvement effect of siderophores, we synthesized the analogue 46 (Figure 5). Unfortunately, no improvement in activity as well as uptake behavior was observed.

17306521.label: Major findings and research outcome
17306521.value: Klebsazolicin is a novel thiazole/oxazole-modified microcin antibiotic isolated from a Klebsiella pneumonia strain, showing narrow spectrum anti-Gram-negative activity. The existence of N-terminal cyclic amidine structure in klebsazolicin brings challenge to chemical synthesis, where current amidine formation methodologies cannot fit the requirement. The aim of this project is to develop chemical total synthesis of klebsazolicin and identify structurally modified klebsazolicin analogues with improved activity and expanded antibacterial spectrum. In this project, we developed a biomimetic on-resin ring-closing amidine formation methodology. This 6-exo-trig cyclization was mediated by Hg(II) salt and showed good efficiency in the construction of N-terminal cyclic amidine structures on peptides. The scope of this reaction was demonstrated in the synthesis of several model peptides as well as a natural product streptamidine. Using this method, we developed a solid phase total synthesis approach of klebsazolicin. The synthesis showed high efficiency, where only a single HPLC purification was needed after achieving the full structure. This facile approach served as the basis for the subsequent modification and structure-activity relationship study. We synthesized a series of structural analogues of klebsazolicin via replacing the thiazole/oxazole rings (both partially and totally) with linear Xaa-Ser units. It was found that replacing two of the four azole rings in the klebsazolicin led to improved activities against B. cereus and V. cholerae, indicating that the azole rings mainly contributed to maintaining the binding-favored conformation rather than directly participating side chain interactions. Meanwhile, we tested the effect of N-terminal cyclic amidine by replacing it with linear dipeptide and N-containing heteroarene. It was found that the cyclic amidine only provide minor contribution to the activity. The linear peptide without cyclic amidine and azole rings could largely maintain the activity. To test the effect of conformational strain, we synthesized a series of cyclic klebsazolicin analogues by replacing two residues with Cys and implemented cyclization via thioether formation and disulfide. It was found that introducing long linker to form cyclic structure could substantially increase the activity of both azole/amidine-free klebsazolicin and unmodified klebsazolicin. To expand the antibacterial spectrum, we tried to improve the uptake of klebsazolicin via introducing uptake-enhancing moieties to replace the binding-unrequired C-terminal sequence. It was found that introducing Arg4 and polymycin B nonapeptide could improve the activity against B. cereus and V. cholerae. Unfortunately, the antibacterial spectrum could not be expanded to other Gram-negative pathogens like A. baumannii, E. coli, P. aeruginosa and K. pneumoniae.

17306521.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17306521.value: In this project, we have established the facile synthetic approach towards klebsazolicin and related cyclic amidine-containing natural products (e.g., streptamidine) based on solid-phase peptide synthesis and on-resin ring-closing amidine formation. According to our structure-activity relationship studies, we found that the sequence but not the oxazole/thiazole and amidine units dominate the antibacterial activity of klebsazolicin. Unfortunately, though we tired to introduce oligoarginine, polymycin B nonapeptide (PMBN) and siderophore to the C-terminus of klebsazolicin, we failed to identify any new antibiotic showing improved anti-Gram-negative activity and broadened anti-bacterial spectrum. In all cases we studied, the compounds only showed good activity against Vibrio cholerae (colistin sensitive and resistant) and Bacillus cereus (carbapenem sensitive and resistant). For further development of the research, we plan to involve computational tools to investigate the binding mode of the synthetic klebsazolicin analogues with improved activity. Based on the modeling results, we will try to design new analogues with high S70 subunit binding affinity, and introduce targeting moieties (e.g., Gram-negative-targeting peptide from phage display) at appropriate site to improve drug uptake. Meanwhile, we will try to develop the mirror-image form of klebsazolicin via retro-inverso technology, which will provide enhanced serum stability and benefit potential in vivo study.

17306521.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17306521.value: Our research focuses on the development of novel anti-Gram-negative antibiotics to overcome the challenge from antibiotic resistance. Natural products, especially peptide natural products derived from microorganisms, are currently an important source of novel antibiotics with new action modes. Generally, natural products do not have high enough activity as well as good pharmacokinetic properties. Thus, further optimization via structural modification is also required for obtaining antibiotics with clinical potential. Efficient chemical synthesis is an important way to facilitate natural product modification, which can break through limitations of biosynthetic machinery by freely introducing artificial structure units at any position of interest. Based on this logic, in this project, we developed a new synthetic method to construct cyclic amidine structure recently discovered in natural products. We established a facile chemical synthesis of klebsazolicin, a microcin antibiotic showing anti-Gram-negative activities. Through synthesis of modified analogues, we revealed the key contributing structural factors of the bactericidal activity and identified several compounds with improved activity against antibiotic-resistant pathogens. Those results form this project could pave the way for the development of new therapeutic compounds for infectious disease caused by resistant bacteria.

17306621.label: Major findings and research outcome
17306621.value: 1. With Yanpeng Li and Yu Li, we discovered integrable systems using cluster structures and linearization techniques, and we examined 4 classes of examples from Lie theory, including the standard Poisson structure and cluster structure on generalized double Bruhat cells, where the integrable systems are constructed using generalized minors. The results have been reported at international conferences, and the paper was posted on the archive on November 28, 2024. Since then we carried out more detailed analysis on some of the integrable systems, while my two co-authors examined the connections with the relavant symplectic groupoids. We are now preparing for journal submission (possibly splitting the results into two papers). 2. With two former postdocts and my PhD student Antoine De Saint Germain, two other papers have been written, with the respective title "Friezes of cluster algebras of geometric type" (posted in the archive in Marc 2023), and "Tropical friezes and cluster additive functions via Fock-Goncharov duality and a conjecture of Ringel" (posted in the arcive in May 2024). Both papers currently under journal review. Friezes may be understood as certain discrete sysytems of functions on the cluster variety taking positve integer values at "frieze points". A crucial tool used in the two papers is the DT (Donaldson-Thomas) transformation, which is also a modification of the inverse map of a certain symplectic groupoid over a Bruhat cell.

17306621.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17306621.value: 1. The use of the DT transformation in our study of friezes lead to a suprising dicovery in another joint paper with Antoine, posted in the archive in July 2025, in which we festablished a direct connection between the DT transformation and certain invariants of Weyl groups. Such a result also points out to a possible discrete integrable systems with the DT transfrmation as the Hamiltonian, the subject of a future paper with Antoine. 2. Another nature next step after the two papers on friezes is to investigate the quantum analogs of friezes and related dynamical sysytems. This is a new direction not forseen at the beginning of the project, and it will enrich the quantization problem identified in Onjective 4.

17306621.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17306621.value: We have investigated various connections between cluster structures, integrable systems, and symplectic groupoids through concerete examples in Lie theory, while our work on friezes point to new directions to further explore such connections, espectially those at the quantum level.

17306721.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17306721.value: This project aims to (1) develop a two-channel model beyond the lowest order of perturbation theory and (2) elucidate the population and coherence lattice thermal transport in strongly anharmonic materials. Peierls' phonon gas model has been conventionally used to describe phonon transport in solids. Recent studies revealed that this model may break down for materials with strong lattice anharmonicity and ultralow thermal conductivity. When phonon couplings are so strong that the mean free paths of phonons become shorter than their wavelengths, the phonon gas model is expected to fail because coherence lattice thermal transport must be considered. However, a fundamental understanding of this complex lattice thermal transport mechanism remains elusive. In this project, a combined experimental and theoretical study will be carried out based on a two-channel thermal transport model, quantum mechanical computations, and inelastic neutron scattering experiments. Lattice anharmonicity that induces strong phonon coupling can greatly reduce the lattice thermal conductivity and play a dominant role in determining the infrared and Raman spectra; therefore, lattice anharmonicity is highly relevant to hot carrier cooling in solar cells and technologically important materials such as thermal barrier coatings, thermoelectrics, and high-temperature ceramics. Conventionally, three-phonon scatterings are believed to dominate the thermal transport of solids, whereas the preliminary results of the Principal Investigator (PI) suggest a significant role of the higher-order four-phonon scatterings in the lattice thermal transport of Tl3VSe4. Therefore, strongly anharmonic solids are expected to exhibit unconventional phonon scattering mechanisms. In the proposed project, we will verify this hypothesis by developing a machine learning potential based on accurate quantum mechanical calculations and carrying out inelastic neutron scattering experiments. These studies build upon the PI’s recent research and are thus highly feasible. Because of the strong lattice anharmonicity and large atomic displacement of low-thermal-conductivity materials, such as Tl3VSe4, BaAg2Te2, and AgCrSe2, considering phonon scatterings within perturbation theory may not be sufficient even if higher-order terms are included. To address this issue, a nonperturbative approach including anharmonicity of all orders based on the newly developed moment tensor potential will also be applied. The theoretical results will be verified by comparing them with the experimental thermal conductivity measured using the laser flash technique. Successful implementation of this project will result in deeper insights into the anomalous thermal transport properties of technologically important materials for a wide range of applications. 本項目旨在（1）基於高階微擾理論發展雙通道熱輸運模型；（2）闡明強非簡諧材料中的布居與相乾晶格熱輸運。傳統固體中的聲子輸運一般可用派爾斯氣體聲子模型描述。近期研究表明該模型對強非簡諧極低熱導材料或許並不適用。當聲子間相互作用足夠強，聲子平均自由程小於其波長時，相乾晶格熱輸運變得更重要，因而氣體聲子模型也將失效。目前對這種復雜晶格熱輸運機理的認識還不夠充分。在本項目中，我們將基於雙通道熱輸運模型、量子力學計算與非彈中子散射進行理論與實驗研究。 由晶格非簡諧性導致的強聲子相互作用可以有效降低晶格熱導率並對紅外與拉曼光譜有重要影響；因此，晶格非簡諧性與太陽能電池中的熱載流子冷卻以及其它如熱障塗層、熱電材料與高溫陶瓷等重要工程材料密切相關。一般認為，傳統材料中的熱輸運由三聲子過程主導，然而項目申請人對Tl3VSe4的前期研究結果表明其中的高階四聲子過程有不可忽略的作用。因此，強非簡諧固體應具有不同於傳統材料的聲子散射機制。在本項目中，我們將基於精確的量子力學計算構建機器學習勢函數以及非彈中子散射實驗進一步驗證這一構想。該項目是申請人當前研究的進一步延伸，因此可行性較高。 低熱導材料如Tl3VSe4、BaAg2Te2與AgCrSe2等由於具有強晶格非簡諧性與較大的原子振動，因此高階微擾理論或不能充分描述其聲子散射。為了解決這個問題，我們將基於近期發展包含所有高階項的矩張量勢函數使用非微擾方法進一步研究。通過與基於激光閃射技術測量得到的實驗熱導率對比，可以驗證理論方法的可靠性。該項目的成功執行將有助於加深對各類具有重要工程應用背景材料熱輸運性能的理解。

17306721.label: Realisation of objectives
17306721.value: Objective 1: A computational scheme for evaluating the strength of four-phonon scattering is implemented, and the phonon lifetimes of Tl3VSe4 and BaAg2Te2 are obtained based on the calculations of the third- and fourth-order force constants and the perturbation theory. Harmonic phonon properties have been computed from first principles using the small displacement method. Machine-learned moment tensor interatomic potential of Tl3VSe4 has been obtained based on data generated from density functional theory calculations. Energies, atomic forces, and virials have been calculated for various configurations of Tl3VSe4 and compared to those obtained from first-principles calculations. A good agreement between the different computational methods suggests a high accuracy of our machine-learned interatomic potential. Objective 2: Unified theory of thermal transport that considers both the population and coherence contributions is implemented. Using the computed phonon lifetimes and frequencies, we obtain the lattice thermal conductivities of Tl3VSe4 and BaAg2Te2 under different temperatures. Theoretical results are consistent with experimental measurements. A significant contribution from the coherence term is found for both compounds, and the coherence thermal transport can become dominant at high temperatures. The effects of temperature-dependent force constants on the thermal transport properties of anharmonic crystals have been studied. It is found that phonon frequency renormalization is critical for the accurate computation of thermal conductivity of materials with strong lattice anharmonicity. Molecular dynamics simulations are performed using machine-learned interatomic potential to study phonon couplings beyond the perturbative approach. Objective 3: Due to the strong lattice anharmonicity of the materials that we focus on in this project, phonon coupling strength calculated from perturbation theory can deviate from experiments. To circumvent this issue, we carry out molecular dynamics simulations based on accurate machine-learned interatomic potentials and obtain phonon properties using the normal-mode-decomposition technique. Our results suggest that the nonperturbative phonon coupling plays an important role in the thermal transport of Tl3VSe4. Our study also find that crystals with a complex unit cell can have a large contribution of phonon coherence to the lattice thermal transport, especially at high temperatures. Although the phonons in these systems are strongly coupled, which results in a low population term in the lattice thermal conductivity, the coherence term may become predominant, limiting the thermal insulation capacity.

17306721.label: Major findings and research outcome
17306721.value: Double perovskites have been synthesized for their composition variety, structural versatility, and excellent optoelectronic properties. They have also attracted much interest in thermoelectric energy conversion for their ultralow thermal conductivity. The strong lattice anharmonicity of double perovskites is conventionally attributed to the rotations and tilts of the octahedron, which is formed by a cation and its adjacent six anions. The temperature-induced phonon renormalization and the wavelike phonon coherent transport are necessary to capture the strong lattice anharmonicity. Through first-principles-based machine learning calculations and experimental measurement, we demonstrate the strongly suppressed lattice thermal conduction in B-site columnar-ordered halide double perovskites. We also show that thermal expansion, anharmonic phonon renormalization, four-phonon scattering, and wavelike coherent transport are essential in correctly capturing the strong intrinsic lattice anharmonicity and the low thermal conductivities of these perovskites. Our findings demonstrate that strong lattice anharmonicity can be caused by unconventional atomic vibration in crystalline solids. The results of this project provide a more complete understanding of the complex thermal transport mechanisms and facilitate the design of materials with ultralow lattice thermal conductivity.

17306721.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17306721.value: The results obtained in this project suggest that high-order phonon couplings can play an important role in the thermal transport of strongly anharmonic crystals. Existing implementations allow the computation of phonon coupling only up to the fourth order. Higher-order interactions can only be studied implicitly from the comparison between theoretical results and experiments. Further development of a new computational scheme for fifth-order phonon coupling will be of great importance for understanding the thermal transport in materials with ultralow thermal conductivity. Due to the high demand on computational resources for fifth-order phonon coupling calculation, new acceleration methods also need to be developed.

17306721.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17306721.value: Different from the phonon gas model, which is conventionally used to describe the thermal transport in crystalline solids, the diffuson-like phonons must be considered when studying materials with strong thermal insulation. In this project, we demonstrate how to accurately calculate the lattice thermal conductivity of materials, where phonon mean free paths are smaller than the atomic distance. Based on the results obtained, it is found that crystals with a large unit cell and strong lattice anharmonicity can induce strong phonon coherence, leading to enhanced thermal conductivity at high temperatures. This thermal behavior contrasts with conventional crystals, indicating the invalidation of the phonon gas model. We demonstrate that this anomalous behavior can be well understood based on the recently developed Wigner transport theory.

17307221.label: Project Objectives
17307221.value: Objective 1. To design and synthesize light-activated amphiphiles colloidal motors (ACMs) with tunable shapes. The self-assembly of active, self-propelled colloidal particles (or micromotors) is an emerging approach for making materials that are dynamic and reconfigurable. Powered by external energy, the assembly process is also likely to overcome entropic limit and leads to new structures unfavored in materials at equilibrium state. Yet, the pathway to control and regulate the dynamic interactions is elusive and the types of dynamic structures that have been obtained remain very limited. One promising strategy to regulate the dynamics of active colloidal system is to tune the particle shapes, but how to relate shapes and dynamics to achieve extended assemblies is largely unexplored. The aim of this project is to explore how shapes and activity of micromotors can enable dynamic assemblies. Inspired by the extremely diverse assembly structures of amphiphilic molecules when varying the size ratio of the hydrophilic and hydrophobic part, we will design and synthesize “amphiphilic colloidal motors, ACMs”. ACMs have one photo-active component and one passive component, both tunable in size. When those interesting shapes are coupled with various particle activity controlled by light, a huge parameter space becomes available for expanding possible dynamic assemblies. Objective 1 tackles the challenges in the design and synthesis of the proposed ACMs. Objective 2. To study the shape effect on the self-propulsion of ACMs. One feature that makes active colloids distinct is their ability to autonomously propel. The propulsion can be powered by various external stimuli, which convert the energy of light, electric field and chemical reactions to the mechanical movements of the particles. The direction and magnitude of such autonomous movements are determined by the asymmetric flows generated by chemical gradients. Changing the particle shapes alter such chemical distribution and therefore their propulsion dynamics. The situation gets more complex when a substrate is involved, which is often the case as micromotor likes to surf on surface. In Objective 2, by numerical calculation and experiments, we will study how shapes of ACMs will be an effective handle to regulate the particle propulsions. This will prepare us ready for exploring their dynamic assembly. Objective 3. To explore the shape effect on the dynamic assembly of ACMs. The dynamic assembly of colloidal motor particles emerge when they bump into each other to form cluster (nuclei), creating collective local flows that may (may not) stabilize the cluster. Particles can also escape the clusters as they tend to propel. A stable cluster may further grow and develop to larger structures. It is unclear when and how a structure (and what type) will be formed. With ACMs, we will explore how to manipulate the complex dynamics via changing particle shapes, sizes, and activities as an effort to facilitate stable nuclei of assemblies. The shapes can also influence how particles pack in the assembly, while their activity may be transferred to the assembled structures. Preliminary tests show promising results that a variety of collective, extended structures can establish according to ACM shapes and activities, and more to be discovered. In Objective 3, a shape (or other parameters)-structure phase diagram will be constructed experimentally. Objective 4. To derive principles that govern the self-assembly of active particles. Unlike materials in equilibrium, active colloids with the ability to propel and interact dynamically produces structures that are otherwise possible. The principles governing such assembly is worth exploring. In this project, based on the structure formed and the various parameters we can tune, we will derive factors and pathways leading to such assemblies. We will try to elucidate the mechanisms of, for example, “orientation-enabled” crystal nucleation, and “activity-directed” structure propagation, etc., preliminary phenomena observed in our ACM systems that are directly or indirectly influenced by particles shapes. These new concepts and fundamental understanding shall guide the design of active materials that are truly unique and potential functional. Objective 4 aims to uses experimental and simulation approaches to derive and generalize such principles.

17307221.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17307221.value: Active matter has recently emerged as a new paradigm for material research, which features motile building elements that interact and collectively form dynamic structures. Such materials are driven by external energy and are out of equilibrium in essence, closely emulating those in biological and living systems like colonies of bacteria and tissues of migrating cells. In the colloidal regime, micromotors hold great promise for creating active materials thanks to their ability to self-propel and the tendency to assemble. Although numerous approaches have been developed for regulating the particle propulsion, the pathway to tune their assembly is elusive. Two key challenges are to be tackled: 1) how to tune the dynamic interactions between colloidal motors to promote various assemblies, and 2) how “activity”—the essential attribute of colloidal motors—translates to and determines the final assemblies. As of now, the kinds of structures assembled from active colloids have been severely limited. In this project, we aim to address these issues by introducing amphiphilic colloidal motors, ACMs. While conventional amphiphilic molecules exhibit rich assembly properties according to their shapes, interaction strengths, and concentrations, ACMs made to possess tunable shapes and light-activated propulsions may also lead to the formation of diverse assemblies. At the same time, the ability to systematically tune the variables (shape, size, propulsion, light intensity etc.) should allow us to unveil the important parameters that influence the assembly structures for ACMs and for active colloids in general. Preliminary results show, for example, that shapes and particles’ propulsion activity are critical for ACMs to assemble into new structures such as clusters, chains, and 2D layers. They resemble micelles and membranes of conventional amphiphiles yet reveal distinct dynamics and surprising pathways. These interesting initial observations, coupled with our expertise in colloidal design and synthesis, would encourage us to pursue more discoveries and deeper investigations, and assures that this project can be completed smoothly with success. 活性物質最近已成為材料研究的新領域，其特點是活動能力的元素相互作用並共同形成動態結構。這種材料受外部能量驅動，本質上是不平衡的，與生物和生命系統中的材料如細菌群落和遷移細胞組織密切相關。在膠體狀態下，微馬達因其自我推進的能力和組裝傾向而在創造活性材料方面具有巨大的潛力。儘管已經開發了許多方法來調節粒子推進力，但調節它們組裝的途徑是難以捉摸的。需要解決兩個關鍵挑戰：1）如何調整膠體馬達之間的動態相互作用以促進各種組裝，以及 2）“活動”（膠體馬達的基本屬性）如何轉化為並決定最終組裝。到目前為止，由活性膠體組裝的結構種類受到嚴重限制。在這個項目中，我們旨在通過引入兩親膠體馬達 ACM 來解決這些問題。雖然傳統的兩親分子根據它們的形狀、相互作用強度和濃度表現出豐富的組裝特性，但製成具有可調形狀和光激活推進力的 ACM 也可能導致形成不同的組裝。同時，系統地調整變量（形狀、大小、推進力、光強度等）的能力應該使我們能夠揭示影響 ACM 和一般活性膠體組裝結構的重要參數。例如，初步結果表明，形狀和粒子的推進活動對於 ACM 組裝成新結構（如簇、鍊和 2D 層）至關重要。它們類似於傳統兩親物的膠束和膜，但揭示了不同的動力學和令人驚訝的途徑。這些有趣的我們在膠體設計和合成方面的專業知識，將鼓勵我們追求更多的發現和更深入的研究，並確保該項目能夠順利完成。

To study the shape effect on the self-propulsion of ACMs. The propulsion can be powered by various external stimuli, which convert the energy of light, electric field, or chemical reactions to the mechanical movements of the particles. The direction and magnitude of such autonomous movements are determined by the asymmetric flows generated by chemical gradients (in our system). Changing the particle shape alters such chemical distribution and therefore their propulsion dynamics. The situation gets more complex when a substrate is involved, which is often the case as micromotors settle on a surface. In Objective 2, by experiments and numerical calculation, we have shown that the shape of ACMs provides an effective handle to regulate the particle propulsions. Under light illumination, the ion gradients and local electric field by photo-catalytical reaction only exist around the TiO2 lobe of ACMs. This creates asymmetric flows around the particle and can drive their propulsion. Our experiments showed that the ACM can indeed propel with the passive TPM lobe facing the front. As planned, we have studied the shape and size effect to the propulsion of ACMs by comparing ACM particles with various sizes of TiO2 and TPM, and the aspect ratio. For instance, particles with a larger aspect ratio propel with a greater velocity, which can be attributed to the more exposed TiO2 area for generating a stronger electric field. In another case, we have developed a solution-based synthesis of silica-based ACMs adopting straight and various tunable bent geometries. This method is based on the synthesis of bent silica rods with a tailored bending position and degree, together with the site-specific installation of a photoactive engine (TiO2). Upon light illumination, the particles propel autonomously, whereby their shape information is translated to various propulsion modes including linear locomotion, steering, and spinning. For all the ACMs, we have theoretically derived how different shapes of the motor are related with their propulsion. We have also used COMSOL simulation to derive the local electric fields and the flow patterns of the particles, which match with the corresponding propulsion modes. The study on the particle propulsion provides understanding for further exploring their dynamic assembly. Object 3. To explore the shape effect on the dynamic assembly of ACMs. The dynamic assembly of colloidal motor particles emerge when they collide into each other to form clusters (nuclei), creating collective local flows that may (may not) stabilize the cluster. Particles can also escape the clusters as they tend to propel. A stable cluster may further grow and develop to a larger structure. It is unclear when and how a structure (and what type) will be formed. With ACMs, we have explored how to manipulate the complex dynamics via changing particle shapes, sizes, and activities as an effort to facilitate stable nuclei of assemblies. The shapes can also influence how particles pack in the assembly, while their activity may be transferred to the assembled structures. Our results have shown that a variety of collective, extended structures can establish according to ACM shapes and activities, and more to be discovered. We have studied the assembly of silica-based ACMs, which do not yield dynamic assembled structures. Instead, the TPM-based ACMs show rich assembly behaviors, including bilayer crystals, chains, and clusters. Notably, we discovered the crystallization of colloidal motors via a cooperative mechanism. Such cooperative process enables the growth of clusters into bilayer crystals consisted of oriented ACMs, which resemble the membranes of amphiphilic molecules. When a short chain consisting of two standing particles is formed, the local electric field becomes anisotropic, facilitating the one-dimensional propagation of the chain. Object 4. To derive principles that govern the self-assembly of active particles. Active colloids self-propel driven by external energy and have the tendency to form superstructures by dynamic interactions. The principles governing such nonequilibrium assembly is worth exploring. In this Objective, based on the structures formed and the various parameters we can tune, we have derived factors and pathways leading to such assemblies. For example, we have elucidated the mechanisms of “orientation-enabled” crystal nucleation, “activity-directed” structure propagation, and other phenomena observed in our ACM system that are directly or indirectly influenced by particles shapes. These new concepts and fundamental understanding shall guide the design of active materials that are truly unique and potentially functional. Objective 4 aims to uses experimental and simulation approaches to derive and generalize such principles. We have decoupled the active and passive components in ACMs and quantified their flow-based phoretic/osmotic interactions. For interactions between active particles, we work on a diluted TiO2 suspension under light and obtain the pair correlation function g(r). Then the potential of the mean force W(r) can be derived as W(r) = −kBT lng(r), The effective potential between the active and passive spheres can also be obtained by this approach. Our results show that the interactions between active spheres appear more attractive than between active and passive spheres. This principle is proved in the binary assembly of active and passive spheres. The particle mixture phase separates to form liquid-crystal structures. The active spheres condense to form liquid-like assemblies while excluding passive spheres. The passive spheres crystallize in the voids between the active liquids, which is enabled by the long-range flow-based forces exerted from the active particles. Active spheres form crystals when their size increases, and the co-assembly with passive spheres forms crystal-crystal structures. In addition, larger active spheres and smaller passive spheres can assemble into a binary colloidal lattice under a low light intensity. These results indicate that particle size and activity play critical roles in the dynamic assembly of particles.We have conducted Brownian dynamic simulation to reproduce all the experimental results. We have also investigated the electric field and phoretic/osmosis flow distribution around ACM clusters of different stages.

17307221.label: Major findings and research outcome
17307221.value: This project introduces a new concept of active colloids—amphiphilic colloidal motors (ACMs)—that self-propel and assemble to form membrane, chain, and micelle structures resembling those formed by amphiphilic molecules. This system is driven by external energy (i.e., light illumination) and is nonequilibrium in essence. The structures can be controlled by the shape and activity of particles, which are the key parameters for the dynamic behaviors of ACMs. The synthetic scheme, the propulsion mechanism, and the assembly principles have been well investigated, which are valuable contribution to the field. These findings have led to two high-profile publications in peer-reviewed international journals and a manuscript ready for submission (Part C, Research Output, 8). In the first case, the investigation on the interactions between basic active and passive parts of ACMs and their nonequilibrium binary assembly are reported in “Binary Phases and Crystals Assembled from Active and Passive Colloids” in ACS Nano. In the second case, we have studied various shape-dependent propulsion modes of ACMs, including linear locomotion, steering, and spinning. The results are published in “Light-activated colloidal micromotors with synthetically tunable shapes and shape-directed propulsion” in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces. Finally, a manuscript, titled “Active Particles that Cooperate and Crystallize under Light”, has been prepared. This work investigates the unique cooperative behaviors (e.g., evolution of particles) in the crystallization of ACMs. We have also used the system for developing chemical additives that can tune the behaviour of the active particles, which results in a publication "Chemical auxiliary for photocatalytic active colloids." By working on the project, post- and under-graduate students have been trained (Part C, Research Output, 10). One student, Dr. Yijiang Mu, who primarily worked on this project, has graduated. He has published multiple papers and has conducted postdoctoral research in University of Pennsylvania in the US. Another graduate student, Mr. Wendi Duan, has also gained vigorous training and has produced first author publications and shall be graduated with PhD soon. With the demonstrated publication and promising results, the PI has been awarded National Natural Science Foundation of China Excellent Young Scientist Fund, 2020 and Outstanding Young Researcher award from the University of Hong Kong (Part C, Research Output, 12). These are all highly competitive awards. Finally, the results of the project have been discussed in local and international meetings (Part C, Research Output, 9).

17307221.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17307221.value: In this project, we have introduced the concept and synthesis of amphiphilic colloidal motors (ACMs). These active particles dynamically assemble into ordered and extended superstructures, including membranes, chains, and clusters, analogous to those from amphiphilic molecules. While we have realized the original objectives, many of the observations deserve further exploration. First, extending the Janus-shaped ACMs to multi-patch particles would open the possibility to assemble open colloidal superstructures. For example, particles containing two TiO2 patches (di-patch particles) can be used to assemble Kagome lattice through the directional bonding between the active patches. Second, tailoring the colloidal activity through molecular design would provide a fundamental control for the dynamic particle assembly. The current active system is driven by the photocatalytic reactions of active particles and the subsequent formation of local chemical flows. Thus, additional synthetic molecules or polymers can be introduced to react with the catalytic chemical products and modulate the flow-based interactions. Finally, future efforts could be directed to applying active colloids as functional materials, including photonics, cargo delivery, microrobotic, and micromachinery. These explorations would take other projects/years and shall yield interesting results.

17307221.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17307221.value: Biological systems have evolved to perform sophisticated life functions: they move, adapt, self-assemble, interact, and operate with high fidelity. Active materials are synthetic in essence but capture the key characteristics of biological and living systems; they consume energy and are motile and interactive. Among such materials, active colloids are micrometer-sized particles able to propel and self-assemble driven by external energies. They exhibit collective motions and behaviors similar to those found in nature, such as swarming and flocking. So far, the pathway to tune the dynamic assembly of active particles is elusive; particularly, the assembly of ordered, extended superstructures remains largely unexplored. In this project, we introduce a new concept of amphiphilic colloidal motors (ACMs), which assemble into ordered and extended structures such as clusters, chains, and bilayer crystals activated by light. They resemble micelles and membranes of conventional amphiphiles yet the assembly occurs in a nonequilibrium system and reveals distinct pathways. The ability to systematically tune the variables (shape, size, light intensity, etc.) allows us to derive the underlying principles governing the assembly structures for ACMs and for active colloids in general. This system has a significant impact in materials science, biophysics, and nanotechnology, and provides valuable insights for self-organization and out-of-equilibrium systems.

17307321.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17307321.value: Modern statistical inference rarely puts trust on a single statistical model. Common practice often starts with a data-driven model selection step, before inference is drawn under the assumption of the selected model. The model selection step introduces an additional level of uncertainty which may severely impair the theoretical guarantee one would have expected from a correctly selected model. Recent literature has seen considerable, albeit piecemeal, effort being diverted to develop valid inference procedures which take into account the effects of model selection. One main class of strategies is provided by the bootstrap method, which has proliferated in many different forms as potential solutions to post-model-selection inference problems in different contexts. The contemporary picture is too perplexing to be fully understood by researchers and practitioners alike. For example, in popular problem settings like regression, one may easily be confronted with more than a dozen bootstrap methods, all purporting to offer valid answers, while in other settings virtually no bootstrap solution has been explored at all. Dissatisfied with the status quo, we propose to develop a general framework to unify post-model-selection inference problems, essentialise different model selection procedures and lays down guiding principles for the design of valid bootstrap strategies. For this purpose we adopt a local asymptotic perspective in our theoretical analysis, which is known to provide a better insight than a traditional asymptotic approach into finite-sample properties of the bootstrap methods, especially under circumstances when model selection becomes unstable and post-model-selection inference becomes notoriously difficult. Both old and new application areas are to be explored under our proposed framework. For old problems to which bootstrap solutions already exist, the project outcome provides a fresh insight into the conditions essential to success and limitations of those solutions, and also facilitates a critical comparison of their theoretical properties, which helps promote better judgment in practice. For new problems, the guiding principles developed by the project can be employed to oversee a proper design of novel bootstrap solutions, supported by a clear understanding of their scope of applicability and limitations. 現代統計分析領域極少依賴於單一的統計模型。在依據選中的模型的假設進行推斷分析之前，常常需要先基於現有的數據進行模型選擇。而模型選擇的步驟將引入一種新的層面的不確定性，這可能會極大程度地削減一個正確選擇的統計模型本所能提供的理論保障。最近的文獻已經對此問題有所意識，盡管零散，相應的努力已落實於將模型選擇的影響納入建設完備的推斷分析流程中。一種主流的策略是採取bootstrap重採樣技術，在眾多背景下的後驗模型選擇的推斷問題中，這一技術已層出不窮地提供了多種形式的解決方法。當代的問題圖景紛繁複雜，以致於研究者和實踐者們一致難以透徹理解。在較為流行的問題設定下，例如回歸分析，我們將面臨多種bootstrap重採樣方法以供選擇，這些方法都旨在提供有效的問題解答。然而，當面臨其他問題設定時，事實上幾乎沒有相應的基於bootstrap技術的解決方法。基於對這種情形的不滿，我們提出了構建一種普適的框架，旨在統一匯總後驗模型選擇的統計推斷問題，精簡不同的模型選擇流程，並展示出設計有效的bootstrap技術策略的指導原則。基於這一目的，在理論分析中，我們採取了一種局部漸近的視角，針對bootstrap重採樣技術的樣本量有限特質，這一方法比傳統的漸近分析更具洞見，尤其是在模型選擇過程高度不穩定，後驗模型選擇的推斷變得極為棘手的情形下。我們對於此框架的新舊領域的應用都有所探究。對於已存在相應bootstrap解決方案的老問題，此項目將為這些方法成功的關鍵性條件和這些解決方案的局限性提供一些新的視角，並促成了這些方案之間理論性質的對比，這一點將幫助我們更有效地形成實際應用中的判斷。對於新出現的問題，在清晰了解此項目的指導綱領的適用性和局限性的情況下，這些綱領可以被用於監督形成一套全新的基於bootstrap的推斷方案。

17307321.label: Realisation of objectives
17307321.value: Objective 1. A general framework for bootstrap post-model selection inference has been developed, with particular focus on the more general condition that the estimators constructed under different models may possess different convergence rates. The latter condition is especially relevant when a choice between parametric and nonparametric models is contemplated, with the nonparametric rate markedly slower than the parametric rate. The framework also extends beyond the context of model selection to cover model averaging as well. An important special case covered by the framework pertains to regression problems, of both parametric and nonparametric types, as well as a hybrid version of the two types. Objective 2. High-level conditions have been established for bootstrap validity. The crux is to carefully design the resampling procedure by which bootstrap samples are generated from an estimated model which is sufficiently close to the true model. For this purpose we develop a generalised m out of n bootstrap method for which it suffices to take the estimated model to be any, possibly conservative, model selected by a standard selection method like AIC. Under a more stringent choice of the selection method, the bootstrap sample size m=o(n) may be further relaxed to m=n. Objective 3. Several unconventional yet important post-model-selection problem settings have been explored in detail: (a) A high-dimensional regularised linear mean regression framework which allows for existence of a large number of weak signals. Using a local asymptotic approach, we derive limiting distributions of non-convex regularised estimators, theoretical results pivotal to development of a valid bootstrap scheme. (b) A high-dimensional nonparametric regularised regression framework under a convex loss function, which covers mean regression, logistic regression, quantile regression, etc. The theoretical results established under the above setting lay the groundwork for subsequent investigations into novel problem settings pertaining to Objective 4. Objective 4. A number of problem settings have been identified to provide an appropriate context for applications of bootstrap post-selection inference. (a) Semi-supervised learning based on nearest neighbour classification --- a hybrid method inspired by bootstrap bias correction has been developed to successfully accelerate convergence rates of classification regret. (b) Semiparametric predictive Bayes --- a moment martingale posterior has been developed by optimally combining a parametric and a nonparametric predictors. (c) High-dimensional multi-index mean regression setting --- a local polynomial approach has been developed for simultaneous variable selection and dimension reduction based on regularisation of bandwidth matrix (d) High-dimensional semi-parametric mean regression setting with unspecified linear and nonlinear components --- a novel penalised regression procedure is proposed for detection and estimation of strong linear and nonlinear signals under high dimensions, based on bandwidth regularisation and SCAD penalisation. (e) Causal inference about conditional average treatment effect (CATE) under a potential outcome setting --- a hybrid estimator, which combines a parametric and a nonparametric CATE estimators, has been proposed and theoretically studied.

17307321.label: Major findings and research outcome
17307321.value: The general framework and theory developed for Objectives 1 and 2 provide a solid foundation upon which a variety of post-model selection problems can be systematically and rigorously studied, inspiring novel methodologies for statistical inference under important subclasses of problem settings, prominent among which are high-dimensional nonparametric or semiparametric regression problems. For Objective 3, we have revisited the problems of (a) high-dimensional linear mean regression and (b) high-dimensional nonparametric local linear regression under convex losses, both of which have been extensively studied in the literature. For (a), we consider non-convex penalisation as a variable selection tool and establish theoretical results from a novel local asymptotic perspective, which proves to be more relevant and adaptive to practical settings where a large number of weak signals may coexist with a small number of strong signals. The results also lay the groundwork essential for the development of a viable bootstrap strategy for conducting post-selection inference. The work led to Research Output 1. For (b), we turn to a nonparametric setting which encompasses applications beyond mean regression, and develop a novel variable selection and estimation procedure based on local linear fitting and bandwidth regularisation. We prove consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed estimator, thus facilitating development of a valid bootstrap post-selection inference procedure. The work led to Research Output 2. For Objective 4, we investigated a number of post-selection inference problems which have thus far received little attention in the relevant literature: (a) semi-supervised learning based on nearest neighbour classification --- we apply bootstrap bias correction to derive a hybrid classifier (akin to data sharpening in a standard regression context) which yields better classification accuracy (Research Output 5); (b) semiparametric predictive Bayes ---we apply a moment martingale condition to develop a Bayesian predictive procedure built upon an optimal mixture of parametric and nonparametric predictors (Research Output 6); (c) high-dimensional multi-index mean regression --- we develop a novel local polynomial fit which performs variable selection and dimension reduction simultaneously based on bandwidth matrix regularisation (Research Output 3); (d) high-dimensional semi-parametric mean regression with unspecified linear and nonlinear components --- we develop a novel penalised regression procedure for detection, classification and estimation of strong linear and nonlinear signals under high dimensions, based on bandwidth regularisation and SCAD penalisation (Research Output 4).

17307321.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17307321.value: To explore the full strength of the general framework and theory afforded by findings pertaining to Objectives 1 and 2, we propose to focus on model selection contexts where estimators are subject to vastly different convergence rates under different models (a phenomenon typical of problems requiring selection between parametric and nonparametric models). One example pertains to selection between a monotonic density function and a general density for its estimation. Another example stems from causal inference, where selection is considered between a purely parametric and a purely nonparametric models for the estimation of conditional average treatment effects (CATE). It would be of immense interest to develop methods for constructing an adaptive estimator based on either model selection or model averaging, accompanied by a valid (probably bootstrap-based) inference procedure based on the proposed estimators. Work has been in progress on these two problems.

17307321.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17307321.value: This project studies post-model-selection inference problems under a broad range of settings. Predominant attention is paid to the important problem of regression, a context which has seen an imminent demand for valid post-selection inference procedures, especially under high dimensions when model selection becomes almost an indispensable feature of any practical statistical application. Our findings provide credible, theoretically guaranteed, estimation and inference procedures for a variety of high-dimensional regression contexts including linear regression, local polynomial regression, multi-index regression, semi-parametric regression with unspecified linear and nonlinear components, as well as logistic and quantile regressions. Moving beyond regression, we also develop hybrid estimators in a nonparametric classification context and a semi-parametric predictive Bayes context.

17307521.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17307521.value: The Pearl River Estuary (PRE) is characterized by excess nutrient loading, supersaturated methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide, and low dissolved oxygen, leading to various environmental problems such as eutrophication and hypoxia. It has been recognized that these chemical characteristics are caused by terrestrial input of high nutrients and low oxygen through the river network as a result of human contamination and various biological mixing processes between the river water and saline water. We hypothesize that the nutrients and gases created by complicated geochemical processes the organic-rich sediments in the seabed under extremely reducing environment may also significantly contribute to these characteristics, an issue which is not much addressed before. The primary objective of this proposal is to study the occurrence, transport, and transformation of naturally occurring CH4 in the PRE marine sediments. Most previous studies on CH4 in the marine sediments are bounded to continental shelves and basins with relatively thick sulphate-methane transition (SMT) zone in the marine sediments continuously deposited in the recent geological time; However, the sediments in a large deltaic estuary such as the PRE are of both marine and terrestrial sources and influenced by active submarine groundwater flow, which may greatly shape the CH4 diagenesis, leading to CH4 spatiotemporal distribution distinctly different from pelagic sediments. Besides, intensive human activities, abundant macrofauna, and upward fluid flow in the seabed may enhance the non-local fluxes of CH4 and the emergence of cold seeps, enhancing CH4 release across the sediment-water interface (SWI). A three-dimensional (3D) geostratigraphic model will be constructed based on the vast number of boreholes and seismic profiles in the PRE. In order to decipher the CH4 diagenetic processes, both microscopic and macroscopic sediment cores will be collected to extracted porewater for analyzing CH4 and the associated carbon components and their isotopes. The microscopic cores will be also deployed to identify the upward fluid flow and diffusion processes and the non-local processes such as bioirrigations. One-dimensional (1D) reactive transport models of CH4 and other carbon components will be constructed to identify the flow regimes, diagenesis dynamics, and CH4 discharge fluxes at the SWI. The CH4 spatial distribution will be depicted using measured CH4 in boreholes and acoustic turbidity signals from seismic profiles. Finally, CH4 cycling and its influences on coastal ecosystem will be explored to provide scientific information to help the governments to formulate effective management options to prevent eutrophication and hypoxia in the PRE. 由於營養物質大量輸入，珠江河口及其附近海域海底沉積物中賦存有大量的CH4及CO2氣體，且溶氧量較低，導致了水體富營養化及缺氧等一系列環境問題。目前人們已經認識到，這些環境問題是由於內陸人類污染物排放和鹹淡水混合過程中各種生物地球化學反應所產生的富營養物質和低氧物質通過河網輸送所造成的。然而，海底有機沉積物在極端還原環境下會發生一系列複雜的生物地球化學反應，其產生的營養物質及氣體對缺氧現象的影響同樣不可忽視，但是這以前沒有引起注意。 本課題的主要目的在於研究珠江口海底沉積物中CH4的賦存、遷移和轉化機理。以往對海底沉積物中CH4的研究大多局限於連續沉積的且具有較厚的硫酸鹽-甲烷過渡帶的大陸架及沉積盆地。然而，在珠江口等大型河口三角洲的沉積物具有明顯的海相和陸相的雙重來源，且受到海底地下水流動的影響，這將很大程度上改變CH4的成因機制，導致CH4在時空上的分佈特徵與深海沉積物中的明顯不同。此外，密集的人類活動，大量的底棲生物以及海底地下水的排泄還可能會加劇CH4的非局部釋放及冷泉的產生，增加CH4在海水和沈積物界面的排放通量。 本課題將首先根據珠江口大量的離岸鑽孔及海上地震剖面建立三維地質體模型，為下一步數值模擬提供地質平台。為了解CH4的成因及運移機理，將採集海底沉積物岩芯並提取孔隙水，分析其中的CH4含量及相關的碳同位素。此外，某些化學組分還將被用來識別垂向上的對流及擴散過程，以及非局部的生物擾動。將構建CH4和其它碳組分的一維反應運移模型，以確定流體活動、成岩過程以及CH4在海水和沈積物界面的排放通量。利用鑽孔中測量的CH4單位含量結合地震剖面中所揭示的噪音區來進一步刻畫CH4的空間分佈及儲量特徵。最後建立起珠江口海底CH4的循環機理並評價其對海岸帶生態系統的影響，為相關部門製定有效的管理政策防止珠江口及其附近海域水體富營養化及低氧環境提供科學依據。

17307521.label: Realisation of objectives
17307521.value: 1. Investigate the controlling mechanism of CH4 diagenesis in the marine sediments During the project, we conducted four core drilling campaigns in the Pearl River Estuary and South China Sea continental shelf, collecting pore water samples. Overall, we obtained approximately 10 meters of sediment cores (62 stations), ~ 30-centimeter sediment cores (15 units), and 86 sediment and CTD water sampling profiles. Sediment cores were categorized into three main types: areas dominated by sediments, regions with natural gas hydrate deposits, and cold spring zones. Using a Rizhon sampler, we collected over 1,000 pore water samples for profile analysis, measuring basic chemical and physical parameters, methane (CH₄) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) concentrations, and their stable isotope compositions. Additionally, more than 200 sediment samples were analyzed for various parameters. Based on these data, we investigated the primary origins of methane in Pearl River Estuary pore waters. In environments with minimal terrestrial influence, the sulfate-methane transition zone (SMT) is located at greater depths. Conversely, in areas with developed offshore aquifers, interference from anaerobic oxidation of methane (AOM) significantly affects SMT depth and leads to substantial methane depletion. Below the SMT, methane production is mainly driven by anaerobic methanogenesis. In sediment interfaces and shelf pore waters, methane oxidation is influenced by AOM and also impacted by anaerobic oxidation processes. Furthermore, analysis of CO₂ concentrations and isotopic compositions indicates that in the estuarine region, methane primarily results from organic matter reduction, reflecting methanogenesis under anoxic conditions. However, in shelf and box-core samples, AOM exerts a greater influence overall. 2. Construct 3D geostratigraphic model and depict the spatial distribution of CH4 We collected a total of 1,188 boreholes across the Pearl River Delta terrestrial region and offshore areas. Using a combination of explicit calculations and machine learning, we developed a geological model of the Pearl River Delta's landforms. Additionally, extensive offshore drilling data and geophysical profiles were integrated to construct a marine geological model. Based on these, we explored a land-sea coupled groundwater dynamic model, simulating the development and distribution of key pore water solutes. This work was published in Science Advances. 3. Construct 1D reactive transport models to decipher the diagenetic processes of CH4 We developed a one-dimensional transport-reaction model for pore water profiles and carbon isotope compositions of CO₂, SO₄²⁻, and CH₄ in estuarine, shelf, hydrate-bearing, and cold spring environments. Based on our simulations, we calculated vertical methane production rates and fluxes crossing the SMT (for estuarine, shelf, and hydrate zones) and the SWI (for cold spring areas). We also noted that methane generation in offshore groundwater zones is disturbed. 4. Estimate CH4 fluxes at SWI and SMT and explore their environmental implications The 3D land-sea geological model and 1D reactive transport model provides a foundational framework for analyzing methane occurrence and development in the Pearl River Estuary's ancient delta. We identified three typical methane-bearing regions, corresponding to active and positive continental margins, which define three main types of methane occurrence: AOM-dominated environments, where methane is primarily influenced by AOM, and SMT depths ranging from a few meters to over ten meters. Environments influenced by natural gas hydrate deposits, where methane exists mainly as hydrate, notably in the southeastern Qiongdongnan Basin and Shenhu regions, with SMT depths extending to several tens of meters. Cold spring regions, characterized by strong upward methane fluxes, causing the SMT to overlap with the seawater interface (SWI). Here, methane is released at the seafloor, particularly around the cold springs in the Haima area.

17307521.label: Major findings and research outcome
17307521.value: 1. A 3D geological model was constructed based on over 1,200 terrestrial boreholes and more than 100 offshore marine drillings. 2. The origins of methane in the Pearl River Estuary and northern South China Sea sediments can be categorized into AOM-influenced zones, hydrate-affected areas, and cold spring development regions. 3. A one-dimensional transport-reaction model was developed, incorporating different sedimentary environments and groundwater conditions to simulate methane formation processes in marine pore waters. This model enabled quantification of methane flux crossing the SMT under various depositional settings. 4. Extensive borehole analyses reveal that offshore freshwater groundwater disrupts sulfate reduction and AOM gradients, leading to distinct methane anomalies in these regions.

17307521.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17307521.value: Further development of this research should involve an integrated investigation of CH₄ and CO₂ cycling across the sediment–water–air continuum in the Pearl River Estuary (PRE). Although AOM in shallow sediments consumes much of the methane produced below, a significant fraction bypasses this benthic filter and reaches the water column, where it may contribute to ecosystem‐level impacts such as acidification and hypoxia. While the present study estimates CH₄ fluxes across the sediment–water interface (SWI) and the sulfate–methane transition (SMT) zone and explores their environmental influences, the quantitative mechanistic links between methane release, water‑column biogeochemistry, and ecosystem responses remain poorly constrained. To address this gap, future work will employ a multi‑method approach—combining biogeochemical analysis, incubation experiments, and numerical modelling—to elucidate the key processes governing methane production, consumption, and transport throughout the continuum. These insights will then be integrated into a coupled biogeochemical model that incorporates carbon (and potentially sulfur) isotopic tracers. This model will enable robust quantification of methane fluxes and project the potential ecosystem impacts driven by methane under future environmental scenarios.

17307521.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17307521.value: Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, and vast quantities of it are generated within marine sediments through the decomposition of organic matter. Typically, natural chemical processes deep within the seabed act as a "bio-filter" (specifically, the anaerobic oxidation of methane), consuming most of this methane before it can escape into the ocean water and the atmospher.This project investigated the Pearl River Estuary and the northern South China Sea to understand how methane is stored, transported, and transformed in these marine environments2. By collecting extensive sediment core samples and constructing advanced 3D geological models, we mapped the distribution of methane across different environments, including shallow sediments, gas hydrate deposits, and "cold springs" where gas actively leaks.A critical discovery of this research is the significant role of "offshore freshened groundwater"—ancient freshwater reservoirs trapped beneath the seafloor. We found that these groundwater systems can disrupt the natural chemical barriers that usually trap methane, altering where and how much gas is released. This research highlights the previously overlooked connection between sub-seafloor groundwater and carbon cycling, providing essential data for more accurately predicting natural greenhouse gas emissions and their potential impact on the global climate.

17307921.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17307921.value: 降階模型和不確定性量化中的含高維參數偏微分方程的自適應計算方法研究

17307921.label: Project Objectives
17307921.value: We aim to develop computational methods to solve Helmholtz equations in random media (that is parametrized by high-dimensional random variables or parameters). We construct adaptive reduced basis functions for model reduction. In addition, we develop greedy methods and clustering methods that are efficient in sampling high-dimensional parameter spaces and extracting essential information from solution space. We aim to develop computational methods to solve convection-diffusion equations with parametric velocities and small diffusivities. We propose dynamically low-dimensional approximation methods and time-localized reduced basis methods to approximate the high-dimensional solutions. In addition, we derive a posteriori error estimates for the proposed methods and develop efficient adaptive techniques to further improve the accuracy. We will study the regularity of the solution map and dimensionality of the solution manifold of the parametric Helmholtz equations. We aim to obtain rigorous upper bounds for the errors of finite-dimensional approximations to the solution manifold. We will study the numerical accuracy, stability, and convergence analysis of the proposed computational methods. We will carry out numerical simulations to solve several application problems arising from reduced-order modeling and uncertainty quantification, such as seismic inversion, pollutants transport in atmosphere or groundwater, chemical reactions, and turbulent combustion.

17307921.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17307921.value: 科學和工程中的許多複雜現像都可以通過依賴於一組參數的含參偏微分方程來建模，其中的參數可能是高維的。這些參數可以用來描述材料的導電率或折射率、波頻率、複雜流體中的不確定性因素等等。例如，具有隨機折射率的亥姆霍茲方程可用於模擬波動在具有空間異質或隨機特性的介質中的傳播或者散射。因此設計有效的計算方法來求解這類問題將在地震波反演中有重要的應用。對於含參偏微分方程，為了研究參數對物理現象（即方程的解）的影響，人們需要對不同的參數求解含參偏微分方程，這將需要大量的計算時間。 學者們已經投入大量的努力去研究含參偏微分方程，並成功提出了許多有效的方法。這些方法包括基於網格細化或稀疏性的自適應方法、模型降階法、壓縮感知、稀疏網格和低秩張量分解方法等。然而，這個研究領域仍有許多難題值得研究，例如高維含參偏微分方程的計算，尤其是當這些偏微分方程的解具有低正則性時。由於這類問題具有的維數災難的特徵，高維參數空間給數值逼近帶來了本質上的困難。另外，解的低正則性可能會進一步降低數值逼近的收斂速度。 在本項目中，我們的目標是設計有效的計算方法來求解模型降階和不確定性量化這兩個研究領域中的高維含參偏微分方程，並分析新方法的收斂性。我們將研究兩類模型問題：（1）隨機介質中的亥姆霍茲方程； (2) 具有參數速度和小粘性係數的對流擴散方程。我們將從問題解空間中提取出問題具有的低維結構，並構建自適應縮減基函數來解決這些方程。我們還將設計貪婪方法和聚類方法來對高維參數空間進行採樣。此外，我們將推導出算法的後驗誤差估計並自適應地調整基函數，從而提高它們對於高維問題解空間的逼近性質。我們的新方法可以為求解其它含參偏微分方程，例如隨機介質中的時諧麥克斯韋方程組，提供一些借鑒和思路。 除了設計新的計算方法，我們還會研究含參亥姆霍茲方程的解空間的維數，並得到解空間的有限維逼近誤差的嚴格上限。為了進一步擴大該項目的影響，我們將使用新方法來計算模型降階和不確定性量化這兩個研究領域中的應用問題，例如地震波反演、複雜流體中的輸運現象、化學反應和湍流燃燒等等。 我們預期本項目的結果將能解決模型降階和不確定性量化領域中的一些計算含高維參數偏微分方程的困難，從而在這個研究領域取得一些新進展。使用這些新方法，我們可以模擬許多實際應用問題，例如地震波反演、大氣或地下水中污染物的傳輸以及湍流燃燒。研究內燃機的燃燒速度是湍流燃燒的一個基本問題。它可以幫助工程師製造具有高燃燒效率和低溫室氣體排放的內燃機。我們將在本項目中深入研究這個問題。因此，本項目的順利完成有望在科學和工程界產生更廣泛的影響。

17308221.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17308221.value: 地球磁層頂擾動的低空信號及電離層控制效應

17308221.label: Project Objectives
17308221.value: 1. Perform and analyze high spatial resolution (~0.05 RE at the dayside magnetopause) global simulations driven by ideal steady-state upstream boundary conditions with different IMF clock angles in order to understand the physical processes of Alfvénic wave energy generation and transport from the dayside magnetopause; 2. Use high-resolution, control numerical simulations with different ionospheric conductance models to investigate the role of the ionosphere in controlling the distribution of dayside Alfvénic wave power flowing to low altitudes; 3. Develop synoptic diagnostics that can provide key points of comparison with observations, including analysis based on select events reported in literature and statistical analysis based on a large number of event simulations to validate the statistical distribution of simulated Alfvénic wave power; 4. Provide new knowledge of the relationship between dynamic magnetopause processes and their signatures at low altitudes for use as a remote sensing tool. This capability is potentially a significant contribution for the understanding of ground measurements related to magnetospheric activities.

17308221.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17308221.value: This proposed modeling study addresses the following questions, which have broad importance in geospace science, as well as significant interest in space weather modeling: What is the physical origin of the observed dayside Alfvénic Poynting flux at low altitude? What causes significant dawn-dusk asymmetry in the observed the statistical distribution of dayside Alfvénic Poynting flux?How can simulated Poynting flux at low altitude be used to infer observed properties of magnetopause activity? The project is motivated by preliminary simulation results showing that global simulations of the solar wind-magnetosphere-ionosphere system are capable of reproducing the statistical distribution of the Alfvénic Poynting flux measured by polar-orbiting satellites, both on the dayside and nightside. Furthermore, under steady IMF By driving, intense Alfvénic power flows to low altitude on the dayside, but dawn-dusk asymmetries in its simulated pattern are opposite of those exhibited by the polar cusp. Prior research has shown that the nightside Alfvénic Poynting flux is generated through the flow brake process in the magnetotail, and the dawn-dusk asymmetry of power flowing into the nightside auroral region is regulated by the meridional gradient in ionospheric Hall conductance. However, the physical origin of the dayside Alfvénic Poynting flux observed by polar-orbiting satellites and the role of the ionospheric conductance on the dayside magnetospheric processes remain unknown. This project will investigate the physical processes of generation and propagation of dayside Alfvénic Poynting flux using global magnetosphere simulations, and it will explore the role of the ionosphere in controlling its distribution based on the hypothesis that the observed dawn-dusk asymmetry in the global distribution of dayside Alfvénic power is regulated by ionospheric conductance gradients. The GAMERA global simulation will be used as the primary tool in this project. Control global MHD simulations with constant and empirically determined ionospheric conductance patterns will be performed and analyzed to investigate the role of the ionosphere in regulating the distribution of dayside Alfvénic Poynting flux. Event studies with strong IMF By using upstream satellite data will also be completed, along with comparisons of simulation results with observations as reported in the literature. This type of study based on data-model comparison plays an important role in both validating the fidelity of global simulations and facilitating the interpretations of observations. 本研究項目致力於探究以下空間物理以及空間天氣科學的基本問題：低空觀測到的阿尔芬波動的磁層起源是什麼，以及觀測到的晨昏不對稱性是由什麼物理過程所決定的。該基礎研究將應用於觀測數據的解答，即通過低空電磁擾動的觀測來遙測地球空間所發生的物理過程及其對空間天氣的影響。本研究將使用最新開發的高精度，具有高性能計算功能的全球磁流體力學數值模型，通過設計數值對照實驗，解答空間天氣學的基本問題。該磁流體力學數值模型可以用於研究低空阿尔芬波動的磁層起源，並且通過電離層-磁層耦合模式，定量研究電離層的電導率梯度對於地球磁層物理過程的影響，例如KH不穩定性。本項目通過分析磁層阿尔芬波的產生和傳播，以及和電離層的相互作用過程，可以豐富空間天氣學中電磁能量傳輸的基本物理圖像，有助於未來空間天氣探測數據的解讀和空間天氣預報模式的開發。

17308321.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17308321.value: 基於一致性度量的生存分析和聚類問題

17308321.label: Project Objectives
17308321.value: We propose a new general class of nonparametric survival functions using the Box-Cox transformation, which include the Kaplan-Meier estimator as a special case. Such a general class provides a more flexible fit to the survival function by assigning different weights to different follow-up periods. We develop concordance-based regression with recurrent event data and quantify the concordance between progression-free survival and overall survival to provide guidance on when the former can be used as a surrogate for the later. For social network data, we propose a new clustering algorithm based on triangular concordance which can account for both the heterogeneity and transitivity within clusters.
