17503621.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17503621.value: We attempt to explain the home currency bias in the international credit market. Maggiori et al. (2020) find that investors usually hold corporate bonds denominated in their home currency, no matter which country the issuers reside in. This is an important new fact beyond the classic equity home bias. As the previous studies only rely on the holding data, we focus on the price data to understand the potential economic mechanisms behind this fact. We compile a new comprehensive dataset of prices and characteristics of international corporate bonds in major currencies. The dataset covers 69,000 bonds, 3.2 million bond-month observations. 1.8 million observations of bonds in different currencies issued by the same firm. We examine the hedging demand and investment cost as two potential resolutions of the currency bias. If home currency bonds hedge against some risk factors, investors would optimally prefer home currency bonds. We examine the hedging demand channel by estimating linear factor pricing models with global and local factors spanning stock and bond risks and liquidity, and derive several testable hypotheses. First, foreign local risks affect foreign currency bonds more than domestic currency bonds issued by a domestic firm, so domestic currency bonds are better hedges against foreign risks. Second, home currency appreciates when bond returns decrease, making home currency bonds good hedges against exchange rate risks. Third, the hedging motives can explain the cross section of corporate bond currency holding. Fourth, bonds in US dollar have unique exposures to risk factors that explain the notable willingness to hold dollar bonds. Fifth, the time-varying hedging motives explain the shifted demand from euro to dollar in the last decade. Alternatively, potentially large transaction or information costs keep investors from investing in foreign currency bonds. We estimate all the pairwise country-currency-asset-specific costs from investor i to country j equity/bond in currency c in a general equilibrium model with return and holding. We confront the results with reasonable costs in the real world. Shifting from investor’s perspective to firm’s perspective, we study the optimal currency of bond issuance. Utilizing several recent factors to estimate the long-term time-varying currency premium, we compare the costs of debt in major currencies. Based on findings in the literature, we expect a sizeable gap between costs in different currencies. We further examine whether firms optimally choose bond currencies and compute the value of optimal currency choice. 在國際債券市場中，投資者傾向于購買由本國貨幣計價的債券，即貨幣本土偏好。本課題分析貨幣本土偏好背後的經濟機制，建立具有貨幣選擇的資產組合理論框架，研究不同貨幣的債券的風險、收益、對沖特征，實證檢驗對沖動機解釋貨幣本土偏好的可能性。

17503621.label: Realisation of objectives
17503621.value: Overall, the project met the main objectives to a high extent. It explains why global investors display a pronounced home-currency bias in corporate bond portfolios and demonstrates that currency denomination is a first order determinant of cross-border corporate bond investment. The project delivered a clear economic mechanism, that is, intertemporal hedging demand in local “bad times” and showed empirically that home-currency bonds provide superior hedging benefits when domestic investment opportunities deteriorate. In relation to Objectives 1–4 and 7, the project’s achievements are strong and well-supported. It documents and interprets home-currency bias in international credit markets, and it studies differences in risk, return, and hedging properties across currencies using global corporate bond return data covering major currencies and a long sample period. It also builds a dynamic portfolio-choice framework that yields testable predictions, and it tests these predictions directly with a design that isolates currency denomination from issuer fundamentals by comparing bonds issued by the same firm in different currencies using firm-time controls. The empirical results consistently support the central hypothesis: home-currency corporate bonds have stronger hedging properties relative to local risk factors, and investors’ observed portfolio weights tilt toward bonds (and currencies) that hedge local risks more effectively, including when returns are evaluated from the investor perspective with exchange-rate movements included. Finally, the project also speaks to the “specialty” of the U.S. dollar in global credit markets by explicitly incorporating USD issuance and demand in the multi-currency setting and showing how currency denomination relates to broad global investment demand patterns. Objectives 5 and 6 were addressed to the extent required for the purposes of this paper, and in a way that supports the core hedging-demand mechanism. On Objective 5, the project integrates exchange rates where they are essential for testing the mechanism—by analyzing total holding-period returns that include FX movements, and by incorporating long-term exchange-rate related predictors and hedging frictions within the broader empirical/demand-system framework. This treatment is sufficient for evaluating how exchange-rate risk and hedging costs interact with currency denomination in investors’ actual bond allocations. On Objective 6, the project analyzes the issuer-side policies by documenting multi-currency issuance patterns and interpreting them through the lens of currency-segmented investor demand.

17503621.label: Major findings and research outcome
17503621.value: The major research outcome of this project is a unified theoretical and empirical explanation for home-currency bias in global capital allocation. The project shows a key reason investors disproportionately hold corporate bonds denominated in their own currency is through intertemporal hedging motives: home-currency corporate bonds provide better insurance in local “bad times,” when domestic investment opportunities deteriorate. A key theoretical insight is that a purely static mean–variance argument cannot generate symmetric home-currency bias across countries, whereas a dynamic portfolio-choice framework with hedging demand naturally produces investor-specific currency tilts because the value of hedging depends on the investor’s local risks. Empirically, the project validates the mechanism using global bond return data covering six major currencies over a 1997-2020 period and international portfolio holdings data. The empirical design places particular emphasis on identification that isolates the role of currency denomination from issuer fundamentals by comparing bonds issued by the same firm in different currencies using issuer-level controls and bond characteristics. The results show that home-currency corporate bonds generally exhibit stronger hedging exposures to the investor’s local factors than foreign-currency bonds, and that these hedging properties translate into portfolio choice: investors allocate higher weights to bonds and currency denominations that hedge local intertemporal risks more effectively. To quantify the broader implications, the project also estimates a global demand system that explicitly incorporates multi-currency corporate bond issuance. The structural estimates confirm that home-currency denomination is a robust predictor of global asset demand especially for corporate bonds, and the estimated hedging beta contributes positively to corporate bond demand in a manner consistent with the hedging-motive hypothesis. Collectively, these findings imply meaningful currency-based segmentation in international credit markets, with potential relevance for bond pricing, issuance incentives, and currency system.

17503621.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17503621.value: Future work will extend the demand-system framework into explicit counterfactual simulations. Using the estimated demand elasticities and hedging channels, we will quantify how global portfolios, corporate credit spreads, and firms’ issuance currency mix would change under a “loss of currency bias” scenario with weaker home-currency preference and under a “loss of USD specialty” scenario with lower USD convenience and acceptance. Comparing these counterfactual equilibria can clarify how issuance and investor bases would reallocate across currencies, and how the international currency system could evolve under reduced segmentation. On the measurement side, we will better pin down the true cost of hedging with forward-basis quotes, transaction costs, and margin and funding constraints, and by modelling the risk of rolling short-dated hedges. We will also extend the within-firm identification by tracking the relative performance of the same issuer’s bonds across denominations through distress episodes, and by linking outcomes to jurisdictional and governing-law features that may affect liquidity and recovery expectations.

17503621.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17503621.value: This project studies a new and important puzzle in global finance: when investors buy company bonds from around the world, they strongly prefer bonds that are denominated in their own currency, even when the issuing company is foreign. The research explains this “home-currency bias” using a hedging idea. Bonds in an investor’s home currency tend to hold up better in that investor’s “bad times,” when local financial conditions worsen, so they are attractive as a form of protection. The value of this research is that it helps explain why global corporate bond markets remain segmented by currency, and why currency denomination can matter as much as and more than the nationality of the issuer. Using large-scale bond return data across major currencies and international holdings data, the project shows that investors tilt portfolios toward the currency that best protects them against local risks. These findings matter for investors by improving risk management and diversification, for policymakers by clarifying the currency role in bond markets, and for firms by showing investor currency demand and potentially effects on funding conditions.

17504021.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17504021.value: This proposal plans to study a set of operational and marketplace design issues related to on-demand carpooling. Major ride-hailing platforms (Uber, Lyft, Didichuxing, Grab, and Ola) all offer on-demand carpooling service in addition to their regular non-carpool car-hailing services. A rough estimation is that every day more than two million riders use these platforms’ on-demand carpooling services. According to Didi, by 2019 its carpooling services had served 2.9 billion rider trips since its launch at the end of 2015. On-demand carpooling allows multiple strangers to share a ride; thus, it revolutionizes traditional carpooling, which requires regular pre-arrangements among acquaintances and co-workers. On-demand carpooling is made possible because a ride-hailing platform hosts a large pool of for-profit drivers and deploys real-time optimization and car navigating technologies to make efficient rider-rider and rider-driver matchings within minutes or even seconds. These modern technologies and business models significantly scale up the long-recognized social benefits of carpooling, especially in terms of alleviating fuel consumption, road congestion, and emissions. This proposal gains its motivation and research focus from the challenges and dynamics in DiDi Pool, which is offered by the largest Chinese platform, Didichuxing. The platform recently (in July 2020) launched an overhaul of its system, including new pricing and pooling policies. I plan to develop mathematical and economics models based on data from Didichuxing to (1) analytically evaluate pricing mechanisms in such marketplaces, (2) study how such a platform’s matching/pooling mechanism affects its market thickness and hence efficiency, and (3) study how such a platform can optimally allocate supply capacity to carpooling to mitigate capacity constraint. This proposed research aims to make novel and important contributions to the academic literature in addition to informing the business practice of related platforms. It will contribute to the ride-sharing literature, by studying two pricing mechanisms for carpooling; the recent literature on dynamic matching, by studying the context of on-demand carpooling; and to the capacity allocation literature in revenue management, by introducing an intriguing equilibrium feature in carpooling. 本课题研究网约车平台拼车系统相关的一系列运营与市场设计问题。全球领先的网约车平台，如，北美的Uber，中国的滴滴，东南亚市场的GrabTaxi，印度市场的Ola，都广泛提供拼车服务。据滴滴出行披露的数据，2015-2019年之间该公司服务了多达29亿人次的拼车服务；粗略估计每天有多于二百万人在全球各个网约车平台上使用拼车出行。 传统上的拼车限于熟人之间，通过相互预约实现。相较之下，网约车平台上每时每刻都运营着大量的司机和车辆；通过数据的分析和算法匹配，平台可以优化导航和路径，实时向互为陌生人的用户提供拼车选项。实际运营中，平台最主要的手段是通过实时调整拼车和非拼车选项的价格来对需求进行引导，从而实现运力更高效的使用，实现降低交通拥挤，人均油耗和碳排放。 本研究集中考察网约车平台拼车系统的定价方式，以及一系列相应的匹配效率和运力分配的市场设计问题。我们考察发现，全球各大平台采用了两类不同的定价方式：1）一口价；2）实际服务价。在2020年，某大平台从一口价方式转向了围绕实际服务定价的方式，并对匹配模式进行了广泛的调整。本课题计划深入了解这一案例，通过建立经济学的模型，结合平台的实际数据，分析并刻画出这两类定价方式对用户选择，供需平衡，以及平台效率和服务指标的影响。从而确定两种定价方式何种情况下更优，从而增进学术界对平台定价和匹配方式等市场设计问题的理解，并为相关的教学提供案例材料。

17504021.label: Realisation of objectives
17504021.value: Objective 1: This objective has been fully achieved. We built a modular, tractable framework that links rider demand, the real time matching technology, and the driver labor market into a single optimization problem. The model supports both descriptive analysis (what happens under a given policy) and prescriptive design (what policy should be chosen). It yields closed form characterizations in several important special cases and delivers comparative statics theorems that can be tested numerically. The same framework also underpins two prescriptive mechanisms—pre matching and matchability screening—and accommodates welfare and emissions accounting. • Completeness: The framework covers all elements named in the objective—pricing (two modes), matching, pooling, dispatch, and capacity allocation—within a single, internally consistent model. • Analytical tractability: We obtain closed form demand splits in canonical cases, a threshold characterization of dispatch, and comparative statics (belief single crossing, volatility effects, capacity/wage behavior). • Actionability: The primitives (network effect, demand volatility, labor supply elasticity, belief calibration) are measurable from operational data, so the model produces testable predictions and implementable guidance. • Extensibility: The layers are modular, enabling researchers to swap in alternative matching functions, richer belief dynamics, or different supply curves without changing the overall logic. The project successfully delivers an analytical foundation for studying and optimizing on demand carpooling systems. It unifies marketplace design (mode choice and prices) with operations (dispatch and capacity), explains observed industry practices, and offers a platform for further research on welfare and environmental impacts. Objective 2: We built an analytical framework that nests both mechanisms under a common set of primitives: (i) a demand system in which riders choose between solo, pool, and not riding; (ii) a state dependent matching technology that captures “network effects” (the match rate rises with compatible demand and market density); and (iii) an operational layer with capacity constraints and threshold dispatch, so the model speaks to both marketplace design and driver side supply. The framework produces several robust, policy relevant findings: 1. A structural reason for the observed dominance of upfront pricing. We show that, under rational beliefs about matching, upfront weakly dominates contingent. The economic driver is what we term a coupon–matching covariance: contingent discounts are paid exactly in the high demand/high match states, so discount outlays comove with revenue rich states and reduce expected profit. Upfront “decouples” discounts from realized matching and avoids that overspending in busy times. This mechanism explains why many platforms (Uber, Lyft, and Didi post 2021) converged to upfront pool fares. 2. Belief calibration creates a single crossing rule. If riders’ beliefs about matching are miscalibrated, the ranking can flip, but in a disciplined way: pessimism favors upfront; optimism favors contingent. The threshold belief at which the ranking crosses increases with network strength, so as markets get denser or algorithms improve, the region in which upfront is preferred expands. This “single crossing” guideline turns an otherwise abstract choice into a practical test based on measurable belief bias. 3. Volatility strengthens the case for upfront. Demand volatility amplifies the covariance wedge that hurts contingent pricing. In our simulations, the gap between upfront and contingent grows monotonically with volatility. This runs counter to the popular intuition that contingent “hedges uncertainty,” and provides a coherent rationale for platforms that moved toward guaranteed pool discounts as they scaled to larger, more volatile markets. 4. Network effects and capacity interact with pricing. Stronger network effects increase the profitability of pooling under both modes, but they also alter the size of the gap between the modes. By solving the capacity constrained version of the model, we connected the pricing decision to driver hiring and dispatch thresholds. This linkage is essential for platform level evaluation and for interpreting pricing pivots during periods of supply scarcity. Evaluation framework for platform changes: We developed a modular framework that lets a platform (or researcher) quantify the consequences of switching from baseline pricing/dispatch to pre matching. It consists of five linked components: In sum, the project equips researchers and practitioners with a principled way to compare upfront and contingent pricing, understand the consequences of platform policy changes such as Didi’s pivot, and design complementary information policies to realize the full value of pooling. Objective 3 We developed a full analytical framework to study this mechanism within our stochastic demand, capacity constrained model. The framework nests the baseline (single ex ante menu) as a special case and adds two elements: 1. Information structure: A binary signal that partitions realized requests into matchable vs. non matchable. We explicitly model the signal’s quality via a parameter that captures how much the match rate for the matchable group improves relative to the baseline. 2. Menu conditioning and dispatch: Prices are optimized by segment; riders best respond given beliefs; the platform dispatches via the same threshold rule as in the baseline, so screening interacts coherently with capacity allocation. We delivered clean, testable comparative statics and welfare results that together identify when the mechanism helps and why. We paired the theory with numerical experiments that (i) replicate the short run profit gains, (ii) trace the long run performance as beliefs adjust, and (iii) map how gains vary with signal quality, network strength, and demand volatility. The analysis is intentionally lightweight to implement: a platform needs only a real time matchability score (which many already maintain for ETA pooling) and a pricing/UX switch to present a solo only menu for low score requests. We provide a decision checklist that a product team can use. This objective has been fully achieved. We: (1) formalized a novel, implementable pre pooling mechanism; (2) delivered rigorous short run and long run performance guarantees, including boundary cases; (3) quantified gains and trade offs numerically; (4) provided an operational playbook that a platform can apply with existing data pipelines; and (5) articulated welfare and environmental implications (per rider emissions fall as sharing improves, while aggregate emissions follow capacity). The resulting toolkit enables both researchers and practitioners to evaluate, tune, and responsibly deploy matchability screening to improve pooling efficiency and marketplace health. Objective 4 This objective targets the supply side of pooled ride hailing: how many drivers (or service minutes) a platform should field and when pooling meaningfully reduces the amount of capacity required to meet demand. We developed a capacity allocation policy by extending our basic model to include the driver side decisions including wage and capacity. We delivered a complete, decision oriented framework that: • Specifies a concrete dispatch rule (threshold dispatch) and shows how to coordinate it with pricing. • Identifies the market conditions under which pooling eases supply pressure, not just shifts demand. • Provides regime specific guidance for scaling capacity up or down and for setting prices that unlock real sharing. • Quantifies expected impacts on platform profit, driver earnings, rider surplus, and emissions across the full range from weak to strong matching. In short, the project moves capacity allocation for pooled ride hailing from ad hoc tuning to a principled policy with clear diagnostics, levers, and performance targets, and it explains when and why carpooling mitigates supply constraints in practice.

17504021.label: Major findings and research outcome
17504021.value: Ride-hailing platforms have embraced carpooling as a promising innovation to address urban mobility challenges and achieve sustainability goals. However, these platforms have struggled to reap the rewards, as evidenced by Lyft's recent removal of this service. We explore the conditions under which carpooling can be profitable and examines the impact of different pricing and matching mechanisms on profitability and operational efficiency. We develop a stochastic demand model that incorporates the probability of successful carpool matches, a factor influenced by rider demand and network effects. Our analysis reveals that profitability requires sufficiently strong network effects and an adequate market density. We demonstrate two key findings regarding pricing mechanisms. First, when riders form rational expectation beliefs about the carpool match probability, upfront pricing consistently dominates contingent pricing because demand volatility causes coupon overspending under the latter. This dominance strengthens as demand volatility increases. Second, when riders beliefs are miscalibrated, the platform would prefer continent pricing when riders sufficiently overestimate the carpool match probability, but stronger network effects expand the region in which the platform prefers upfront. These results explain real-life industry practice. Finally, we study two innovative matching mechanisms: one that pre-matches carpool requests and another one that screens riders’ carpool matchability in real-time before offering price menus. We find that the pre-matching mechanism is generally outperformed by either upfront or contingent pricing, and the matchability screening mechanism can improve profit in short run but the profit advantage decreases when riders' belief converges to the long term average.

17504021.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17504021.value: There are four high‑value extensions. (1) Richer operating realism. Generalize from a single‑period aggregate model to a dynamic, spatial framework that captures time‑of‑day variation, pickup/detour geometry, deadheading, and heterogeneous riders/drivers (patience, value of time, vehicle capacity). (2) Learning and beliefs. Endogenize belief formation and miscalibration via online learning/bandits, allowing the platform to co‑optimize pricing and information (e.g., matchability prompts) while beliefs converge. (3) Labor and policy. Add wage floors, surge caps, and driver multi‑homing to study incidence across stakeholders; incorporate equity constraints (e.g., service access by zone). (4) Emissions and welfare. Calibrate a modular emissions/VKT layer with city‑specific energy mix and modal diversion to evaluate climate targets alongside profit. Proposed course of action. Phase A (0–6 months): Secure data partnerships; build a calibration pipeline for “city archetypes”; release a reproducible toolkit (code + dashboards) for threshold dispatch, pricing mode choice, and screening. Phase B (6–12 months): Run platform pilots: A/B test matchability screening and pre‑matching; measure short‑ vs long‑run impacts on profit, rider surplus, driver earnings, and emissions. Phase C (12+ months): Publish benchmarks and policy playbooks (deployment thresholds, fallback rules when networks are weak), and open‑source the calibrated simulator to enable broader adoption.

17504021.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17504021.value: Ride‑hailing apps (like Uber or Didi) can let strangers share a car going in the same direction. This can cut traffic and emissions, but many companies struggle to make it pay. Our project built a simple, realistic way to “test drive” carpool ideas on paper before changing the app. We compared the two prices riders commonly see: (1) an upfront, guaranteed discount for choosing “pool,” and (2) a contingent discount that applies only if a match actually happens. We show why, in steady conditions, upfront usually earns more: when demand is busy, contingent pays more discounts exactly when many people are already matching, so the platform overspends. If people’s beliefs about matching are off (too optimistic or too pessimistic), the better option can flip—helping platforms time their pricing switches. We also designed a lightweight “matchability screening” step: after requests arrive, separate trips that can realistically be shared from those that cannot, and only offer pooling (and discounts) to the first group. This boosts profit, especially when sharing is possible but not guaranteed. Finally, we studied driver supply. As matching gets easier, platforms can serve the same riders with fewer cars, lowering costs and emissions. Our framework turns these insights into practical guidance for pricing, matching, and capacity decisions.

17504721.label: Project Objectives
17504721.value: It has been documented in the existing literature that mutual funds with environmental and social objectives do more selection than treatment. Therefore, what is the meaning of this selection? How much do both passive and active funds really deviate from their optimal strategy (SP500/value funds/growth funds/other classification)? What is the overall outcome at society level? We want to analyze this question in a systematic way. We make a conjecture that the vast majority of selection is done in a superficial way---choosing firms at industry level but not firm level. The ESG score of funds might look good, nevertheless, it is not because they choose best firms with respect to ESG performance in each of the industries (including brown industries), but because they simply avoid brown industries as a simple outcome. This might differ from passive funds, who invest following an ESG index, to active funds, who select their own portfolio. We also want to look into how much funds deviate from their non-ESG benchmark. Maybe even when they deviate, it would still be super marginal deviation because of the diversification requirement. If this is true, then it puts even more doubt of whether the free capital market forces can really move the dial with respect to environmental issues at the end of the day. This may go back to the green washing story and helps explain the investor flows arising from funds' career concern. Lastly, we want to bring in the two-fund separation theory. If there are two representative funds in a fund family which both hold polluting and non-polluting industry. After one fund becomes ESG and the other remains non-ESG, based on their filtration at industry level (conjecture one), it turns out that ESG fund holds non-polluting industry only and non-ESG fund holds polluting industry only. But at fund family level it is just the same composition. If this is true, at society level these selections do not make much changes, because at cross-sectional fund family level it is regarded as recombination. We will use data to test the theory and to see to what extent this recombination holds.

17504721.label: Realisation of objectives
17504721.value: 1. Meaning of Selection, Deviation, and Societal Outcome The paper addresses the premise that ESG funds primarily rely on stock selection rather than corporate treatment, fundamentally questioning what this "selection" actually entails. The authors systematically analyze this by comparing ESG funds to benchmark indices (such as the Morningstar Category index) as well as to identical non-ESG counterpart funds. They reveal that the deviation from optimal, standard strategies is surprisingly minimal. On average, ESG funds exhibit a mere 0.05% holding deviation per stock compared to their non-ESG peers. In essence, the "meaning" of their selection is largely symbolic; they preserve the primary components of traditional benchmarks to ensure they do not compromise on financial performance, diversification, or systematic risk. Consequently, the overall outcome at the societal level is highly limited. The paper documents that while ESG portfolios successfully reduce overall absolute emissions by 36%, over 90% of this reduction is achieved simply by eliminating a tiny, concentrated subset of companies—specifically, the top 25 corporate emitters, which make up less than 2% of total portfolio holdings adjustment. Outside of this extreme extensive-margin exclusion, ESG portfolios are statistically indistinguishable from non-ESG counterparts. Because this divergence is so narrow, the authors conclude that ESG selection translates into negligible pressure on the broader corporate landscape. The lack of meaningful portfolio deviation explains why these funds fail to generate sufficient capital market pressure to alter firms' cost of capital or incentivize real-world environmental improvements. 2. Superficial Selection and Active vs. Passive Strategies The paper provides robust empirical evidence confirming the conjecture that much of ESG selection is indeed superficial, while also highlighting a crucial divergence between active and passive (index) fund strategies. The authors demonstrate that active ESG funds heavily rely on "across-industry" selection. Rather than diligently identifying the best-in-class ESG performers within brown industries, active funds achieve 57% of their emission reduction simply by divesting from entire heavily polluting sectors (like utilities and energy). This superficial avoidance strategy is starkly illustrated by the fact that nearly 39% of active ESG funds hold absolutely zero shares in the market's top 25 emitting companies. Conversely, passive ESG index funds employ a fundamentally different, more granular approach due to their inherent structural rules. Because index funds have strict diversification and tracking error constraints, they cannot simply abandon entire sectors of the economy. The paper reveals that 82% of the emission outperformance in ESG index funds is driven by "within-industry" stock selection. They are forced to de-weight the worst polluters within a sector while maintaining a balanced overall industry exposure. As a result, only 4.5% of index funds completely avoid the top 25 emitters. This proves that the depth of ESG selection is highly dependent on a fund's operational flexibility, with active funds opting for simple industry exclusion and index funds forced into firm-level optimization. 3. Marginal Deviation, Market Forces, and Greenwashing The study thoroughly investigates the magnitude of deviation from non-ESG benchmarks, confirming the hypothesis that ESG funds engage in only "super marginal" deviations to satisfy diversification requirements. The authors point out that the top 25 heavy emitters—the primary targets for ESG exclusion—rarely overlap with the market's largest components. In fact, when measured by absolute emissions, only four of the top 25 emitters overlap with the top 25 stocks by market capitalization; when measured by emission intensity, zero overlap. This structural market reality allows ESG funds to drop heavy polluters and drastically improve their "green" metrics without taking on substantial tracking error or disrupting their standard return profiles. This incredibly marginal deviation casts serious doubt on the ability of free capital markets to drive systemic environmental change, tying directly into the greenwashing narrative. The paper aligns with existing theories suggesting that because ESG funds barely deviate from market consensus, they exert no meaningful impact on corporate behavior or capital allocation. Asset managers are able to cater to investor demand for sustainable products—driven by career and asset-gathering concerns—by simply dropping a handful of high-profile polluters to market a "green" fund. Ultimately, they collect ESG-related fees without undertaking the difficult, risky task of fundamentally reallocating capital to force a genuine environmental transition. 4. Two-Fund Separation Theory and Family-Level Recombination The specific objective of testing the "two-fund separation theory"—the idea that a fund family simply redistributes polluting stocks to its non-ESG funds while allocating clean stocks to its ESG funds, resulting in a net-zero impact at the family and societal level—is mostly achieved in this paper. The study effectively employs fund family fixed effects to isolate within-family variations and control for shared management styles. When examining different green window dressing behaviors, the authors also considered the fund family effect but ultimately conclude that it is determined by where the fund is domiciled. In fact, the authors ultimately uncover empirical evidence that challenges a perfect "zero-sum" family recombination: they document that non-ESG mutual funds also hold portfolios that are greener than their underlying benchmarks. This implies that institutional investors broadly prefer lower-emission portfolios across the board, making it highly unlikely that non-ESG sibling funds are intentionally hoarding the heavily polluting stocks dumped by their ESG counterparts. There are reasonable, data-driven explanations for why the paper does not fully validate this family-level recombination theory. First, the AUMs of ESG funds are relatively small as compared to non-ESG funds within a single fund family, rendering this story somewhat invalid. Second, testing this hypothesis would require tracking dynamic portfolio shifts and internal capital flows across all sibling funds within a family exactly when a fund transitions to an ESG mandate, which falls outside the scope of this paper's holdings analysis as we already have a very rich set of empirical results. Therefore, while family-level dynamics are controlled for, proving a strict societal-level net-zero recombination is not supported by the paper's scope or baseline findings.

17504721.label: Major findings and research outcome
17504721.value: The Mechanism of Emission Reduction: The study systematically anatomizes the stock selection processes of US equity ESG funds to evaluate their environmental and financial outcomes. The central finding is that while ESG portfolios successfully achieve a 36% reduction in overall absolute emissions compared to their benchmarks, this "greenness" is achieved through highly concentrated, superficial means. Over 90% of the observed emission reduction is driven by the strategic exclusion of just the top 25 corporate emitters. Because these extreme polluters represent less than 2% of total portfolio holdings, ESG funds are able to drastically improve their climate metrics through an extensive-margin exclusion strategy, while keeping the remaining 98% of their portfolio virtually identical to standard non-ESG funds. Active vs. Passive Selection Strategies: The research uncovers a crucial divergence in how active and passive ESG funds execute their selection. Active ESG funds rely heavily on across-industry exclusion, completely divesting from heavy-polluting sectors like energy and utilities. In fact, nearly 39% of active ESG funds hold zero shares in the market's top 25 emitters. Conversely, ESG index funds, bound by strict tracking-error and diversification constraints, cannot simply abandon entire economic sectors. Instead, they rely on within-industry selection, optimizing their portfolios by underweighting the worst polluters within a given industry to achieve their emission targets. Financial Performance and Risk Profiles: Crucially, this targeted divestment strategy comes with minimal costs to investors. The holding deviations between ESG funds and identical non-ESG peers average a mere 0.05% per stock. Consequently, ESG funds do not severely compromise on diversification, systematic risk, or financial performance. Net of fees, ESG funds perform on par with conventional benchmarks, and ESG index funds consistently outperform both active ESG and non-ESG counterparts. Furthermore, while ESG funds demonstrate significantly lower exposure to ESG-related reputational risks, their structural underweighting of energy stocks makes them less effective as a hedge against macroeconomic shocks, such as energy-driven inflation. Disconnect with ESG Scores and Societal Impact: Finally, the authors highlight a stark disconnect between tangible emissions reductions and commercial ESG impact scores. Despite massive carbon reductions, ESG portfolios show less than a 1% improvement in aggregate third-party ESG scores, underscoring the noisy, broad nature of these ratings. Ultimately, the paper implies that because ESG funds rely on such marginal, symbolic portfolio deviations, they exert negligible capital market pressure on corporate cost of capital. Their narrow scope effectively preserves standard financial returns but strictly constrains their ability to drive systemic environmental impact.

17504721.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17504721.value: Future research must pivot from analyzing portfolio selection to evaluating the systemic impacts of ESG investing, particularly regarding firms' cost of capital. Because current ESG exclusion strategies are too marginal to significantly raise corporate financing costs, future studies should determine the threshold of capital shifting actually required to genuinely penalize heavy polluters. Furthermore, at the societal level, the paper's finding that mutual funds broadly maintain greener-than-average portfolios raises a fundamental market question: if public institutional investors are systematically avoiding "brown" assets, who is holding them? Identifying these buyers of last resort—whether they are retail investors, private equity firms, or state-backed entities—is essential to understanding why divestment consistently fails to starve polluters of capital. Given the real-world limitations of simple exclusion, a proposed course of action is to shift both academic and industry focus from passive divestment toward active engagement. Future research must investigate how to execute effective corporate "treatment." This includes exploring how investors can successfully leverage proxy voting, shareholder resolutions, and direct boardroom negotiations to force actual corporate decarbonization, rather than merely dropping brown stocks from their portfolios and passing the emissions onto less socially conscious owners.

17504721.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17504721.value: This research looks under the hood of "green" (ESG) mutual funds to see if they truly live up to their eco-friendly promises. By comparing the stocks held by sustainable funds to those in regular funds, the researchers discovered a surprising truth: green funds are almost identical to conventional ones. To achieve a significantly lower carbon footprint, these funds do not drastically overhaul their investments to support innovative green technologies. Instead, they take a shortcut by simply dropping a tiny fraction—about 2%—of the absolute worst polluting companies. The significance of this study is that it exposes the illusion behind much of today’s sustainable investing. By only avoiding a handful of heavy polluters, these funds look great on paper but fail to create real-world environmental change. Because they barely deviate from standard market practices, they apply almost no financial pressure on heavy polluters to clean up their operations. The value of this project lies in empowering everyday investors with the truth about where their money goes. It highlights that to genuinely help the planet, the financial industry must move beyond simply ignoring a few dirty companies and instead actively push businesses to adopt greener practices.

17505221.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17505221.value: The proposal studies the effect of employee litigation on financial reporting quality. Employment litigation originates from disputes with the employees, which can be costly, time-consuming, and damaging to the firm. The number of employment-related litigation filings has been steadily increasing over the last decade, ranging from large-scale class actions to individual complaints. Employers are facing greater challenges and financial exposure from both current and former employees than ever before, and such changes have a great impact on firm operations. However, there is no study on the effect of employee protection on financial reporting choices. I fill the gap in the literature by answering two questions: 1) whether and how enhanced employment protection affect a firm’s accounting accruals; and 2) how accounting choices moderate the impact of employment protection in firm investments. I hypothesis that better employee protection is associated with better employee welfare, but lower capital expenditures, lower R&D investment, and less innovation output. In response, firms use more income-increasing accruals, because it eases the working pressure of meeting performance targets and improve employees’ career prospect, which improves employee welfare and reduces the negative effects of increases litigation risks on firm investments. This project has important academic and practical value. Academically, the proposal contributes to the earnings management literature. Specifically, at one side, employees are better off if managers can better utilize accounting methods to reduce their pressure to beat the targets (Caskey and Ozel 2017). Financial strength is also an important consideration when employees form career prospects. Both effects deter workplace disputes and thus employee litigation risks. On the other side, firms use low earnings performance to negotiate with employees in terms of pay and other benefits, which may reduce their liability in employee litigations. As such, I contribute to the theory that understands the effect of employee litigation on financial reporting. In addition, while prior literature focuses largely on labor unions, our study is distinct in two ways. First, labor unions negotiate with employers through collective bargaining, while employee litigation is intended to protect individual employees. Second, both the existence and activities of labor unions are endogenously determined. On the contrary, our setting of regulatory changes is exogenous of firm performances and managerial decisions. Practically, this study has insightful policy implications. By examining the effects on business operations and welfare, this study helps regulators, managers, and investors weigh the costs and benefits of employee litigation on firm decisions. 該提案研究了員工訴訟對財務報告質量的影響。僱傭訴訟源於與員工的糾紛，成本高昂，費時費力，對公司不利。就業相關人數在過去十年中，訴訟申請一直在穩步增加，從大規模集體訴訟到個人投訴。雇主面臨更大的挑戰，財務風險比以往任何時候都高，例如變化對企業的經營有很大的影響。但是沒有研究員工訴訟對財務報告的選擇。 我填補了文獻中的空白回答兩個問題：1) 加強就業保護是否以及如何影響公司的會計應用； 2) 會計選擇如何緩和企業投資中的就業保護。我假設更好的員工保護導致更好的員工福利，但較低的資本支出、較低的研發投入和較少的創新產出。作爲回應，公司使用更多增加收入的財務報告的選擇， 因為它減輕了工作實現績效目標和改善員工職業前景的壓力，改善員工福利，並減少訴訟風險增加對於公司投資的負面影響。 該項目具有重要的學術和實用價值。在學術上，該提案對盈餘管理文獻有貢獻。具體而言，一方面，管理者能更好地利用會計方法來減輕訴訟的壓力。公司前景也是員工形成職業前景時重要的考慮。兩種影響都會減少工作場所糾紛，從而引發員工訴訟風險。另一方面，企業使用低收益業績與員工在薪酬和其他福利方面進行談判，這可能會減少他們在僱員訴訟中的責任。因此，我對以下理論做出了貢獻了解員工訴訟對財務報告的影響。 此外，先前的文獻主要關注工會，我的研究在兩個方面有所不同。第一，工會通過集體談判與雇主談判，而僱員訴訟旨在保護個別僱員。二、存在工會的活動是內生決定的。相反，我們的設置監管變化是公司業績和管理決策的外生因素。實際上，這項研究具有深刻的政策含義。通過檢查對商業運營和福利，這項研究有助於監管者、管理者和投資者權衡員工訴訟對公司決策的成本和收益。

17505221.label: Realisation of objectives
17505221.value: To conduct our empirical investigation, we use California’s Labor Code Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA) as a plausibly exogenous shock to employee litigation risk. PAGA was enacted in the state in 2004 as a cost-saving measure and is often referred to as the “Sue Your Boss” law. It authorizes aggrieved employees to bring representative actions in the name of the state and recover civil penalties for violations of the California Labor Code. PAGA has had a major effect on employee litigation, as illustrated by the fourfold increase in the number of labor-related claims filed in the years following its enactment. We expect that firms experiencing an increase in employee litigation risk will subsequently incur additional expenses to minimize such risks. This may negatively affect their profitability and thus jeopardize their ability to secure inputs from stakeholders such as investors, employees, and trade partners, which make decisions based on reported performance. One potential response by firms is to conceal reductions in profitability through accounting choices, which can result in a sustained difference between underlying “structural” and reported cumulative earnings over a potentially extended period (e.g., Bowen et al., 1995). Consistent with our expectations, we find that employee welfare is of greater interest to firms after the enactment of PAGA. The quality of employee relations (as measured by the KLD database) improves and firms spend more on employee compensation. We also show that firms’ underlying profitability (i.e., after adjusting for the effect of accounting choices) declines after the adoption of PAGA. We then relate these findings to accounting choices. Consistent with our expectation, we find that treatment firms use significantly more income-increasing accruals than control firms after the enactment of PAGA. Furthermore, although underlying profitability is reduced after the enactment, we find that reported profitability is unaffected if we do not adjust for the effect of income-increasing accruals. Other measures (e.g., accounting restatements) also suggest a decrease in reporting quality. We then improve the internal validity of our results through cross-sectional tests. We find that the effect of PAGA on reporting is more significant when the benefit of reporting high profitability is greater (e.g., a greater liquidity constraint, larger and more concentrated customers, more short-term-oriented employees) and when the cost of inflating profitability is lower (e.g., low levels of unionization, and weaker governance). Finally, we demonstrate the impact of the accounting choices induced by PAGA on firms’ real operation decisions. We focus on the decision to invest, in which reassuring stakeholders is the main consideration. We expect investment and innovation to be negatively affected by the implementation of PAGA. However, if accounting strategies successfully mitigate stakeholders’ concerns, firms that use more income-increasing accruals should experience a smaller decline in investment and innovation. Consistent with the idea that stakeholders are concerned by a decline in profitability, we find that both capital expenditures and R&D decline after the implementation of PAGA, especially among firms that experience a greater decline in post-PAGA financing cash flows. However, firms that engage in more income-increasing accruals are significantly less likely to suffer from a reduction in their capital expenditures and R&D after the enactment of PAGA. Overall, our findings suggest that firms adopt accounting choices to mitigate the negative effect of higher employee litigation risk, and these choices have real effects on firm operations. The findings are robust to alternative specifications and robustness checks.

17505221.label: Major findings and research outcome
17505221.value: We study the effect of employee litigation on financial reporting choices and the consequences for firm investment. Using the enactment of PAGA as a plausibly exogenous shock to labor-related litigation risk, we provide evidence that an increase in this risk has led firms to devote more resources to ensuring good labor relations, which leads to a decline in their underlying profitability. Firms use more income-increasing accruals and report more restatements following PAGA. Comparative statics suggest that firms with greater benefits and lower costs follow this approach to a greater degree. These firms also experience a decrease in R&D and innovation. However, those that have made accounting choices to mitigate the reduction in reported profitability experience a smaller drop in investment and innovation. Our evidence thus provides important insights into how accounting choices are affected by employee litigation environments, and in turn how such choices can have a real impact on operations.

17505221.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17505221.value: Academically, these findings contribute to the earnings management literature, which offers mixed predictions in the context of labor relations. Employees may be better off if managers use income-increasing accounting methods to reduce the pressure to meet or beat financial reporting targets (Caskey and Ozel, 2017). However, firms may use low reported earnings to negotiate better terms for pay and other benefits (DeAngelo and DeAngelo, 1991). While we weigh on these issues, we consider employee litigation, which is intended to protect individual employees, and thus our study is distinct from much of the accounting literature that focuses on labor unions, which negotiate with employers through collective bargaining. Our setting also uses a shock that is plausibly exogenous with respect to firm performance and managerial decisions, while both the existence and activities of labor unions may be endogenously determined. From a more practical perspective, our findings suggest that while PAGA provides employees with better protection, firms can partly mitigate the costs of the increased litigation risk through careful accounting decisions.

17505221.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17505221.value: We study the effect of employee litigation on financial reporting quality and firm investment. In 2004, California adopted the Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA), significantly increasing employee legal protection. Firms covered by the act spend more to improve employee welfare and experience a decline in profitability. In response, they engage in more income-increasing accruals to ease stakeholders’ concerns about firm performance. This strategy successfully mitigates the real consequences of heightened litigation risk. Firms that engage in more income-increasing accruals do not experience a reduction in financing cash flows, capital expenditures, and R&D compared with other affected firms after the enactment of PAGA. Overall, our study documents how firms use accounting choices to counter the negative impact of employee litigation risk on their operations.

17600121.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17600121.value: 金文是指鑄或刻在青銅器上的文字。金文大致出現於殷商晚期，至西周時期長篇銘文普遍，春秋金文承接西周發展，戰國時期銘文字數開始減少，進入式微的階段。就語言發展的軌跡而言，殷周金文的使用時間涵蓋了上古漢語的多個主要階段，加上語料的數量龐大，材料大多為前人未有機會目睹，所以是上古漢語研究不可或缺的重要材料。 隨著近世紀科學考古的迅速發展，出土材料與日俱增，不少研究者已注意到出土文獻於古漢語研究具有重要意義和價值。傳世先秦古書的成書問題複雜，不少更存在年代與真偽問題。相對來說，出土文獻的年代較為明確，可以避免古籍因歷代傳抄而出現的竄改和譌誤問題，能夠比較準確地反映當時語言的實況。不過，雖然過去學者曾經運用金文描寫和分析上古漢語語言特徵，但不少著作的出版年代較早，當時所見的金文語料數量有限，加上此類論著大多是針對個別語言形式或現象的專題討論，金文於研究中僅用為舉例性質，並非窮盡式的多角度考察。 本計劃選取商周金文虛詞為研究課題，擬融合古文字學、語法學、文獻學等多個學科的專業知識、理論及方法，就虛詞的語言現象進行跨學科的研究。首先，本計劃運用古文字學考釋方法，分析金文虛詞反映的異體、同形、通假等文字現象，考究字形的發展演變，釐清銘文存在的同詞異形、同形異詞等複雜關係，闡明金文與傳世古書間虛詞的對應關係，為準確的金文釋讀提供意見；然後，本計劃從語法角度，描寫金文虛詞的共時與歷時特徵，分析金文虛詞在上古漢語實詞虛化過程的表現和特點，總結金文虛詞的系統，從而勾勒上古前期漢語的語言發展歷史；本計劃總結金文虛詞時代及地域特徵，以此為參照標準討論青銅器斷代和分域問題，為先秦文獻年代和真偽的討論提供意見，最後通過不同語料中虛詞形式和特徵的比較，分析金文與其他出土材料間語言親屬的關係。 Bronze inscriptions commonly refer to the archaic writings inscribed or incised on early Chinese bronze vessels. Chinese bronze inscriptions initially emerged from the late Shang period. Lengthy inscriptions were extensively used in the Western Zhou. They kept a thriving development in the Spring and Autumn, but experienced a striking decline in the late Warring States period. Bronze inscriptions, which broadly spanned the different evolutionary stages of Old Chinese, have provided researchers with significant sources of Old Chinese that were unavailable or inaccessible by previous research. The rapid advancements of scientific excavations in Mainland China have brought a vast number of unearthed textual sources over the recent decades. Researchers have addressed various important aspects of excavated texts in the study of classical Chinese. Generally, early Chinese texts had undergone a prolonged process of textual transmission, causing more or less problems in dating and authenticity. By contrast, the excavated sources are more precisely datable and largely restrained from textual variations and corruption as a result of centuries of transmission, and thus have been widely recognized as more reliable sources for the studies of Old Chinese. Researchers have made attempts on the linguistic studies of bronze inscriptions to various extent. Nevertheless, these studies were either published long ago when the abundant corpus of newly excavated sources were unavailable or focused on a small topic, that is, bronze inscriptions were merely used for exemplification. An extensive and thorough language survey of bronze inscriptions remains unavailable. The present project relies on early bronze inscriptions as the principal source of investigations in undertaking a comprehensive language research on the function words from the interdisciplinary perspectives of paleography, grammar, and philology. First, it will examine the graphic variants as seen from inscriptional function words, and discuss related paleographic phenomena, such as phonetic loans and homoglyphs, in detail. Second, it will analyze the grammatical features of function words synchronically and diachronically to explore the linguistic features associated with Old Chinese grammaticalization process. Finally, on the basis of diachronic and regional variations, it will revisit the dating and provenance problems of bronze vessels, as well as philological questions, such as the compilation and authenticity of early Chinese texts. Furthermore, by comparing function words among different language sources, it will shed new light on the discussions of genetic affiliation of bronze inscriptions by bringing in new linguistic evidence.

17600221.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17600221.value: 權力基礎與組織環境：釘釘的使用如何影響中國工作場域的人際關係

17600221.label: Project Objectives
17600221.value: Empirical contribution 1: Understanding key characteristics of DingTalk use in Chinese urban middle-class workplaces and variations across different organizational contexts Developed by Chinese multinational technology company Alibaba Group, DingTalk is a comprehensive e-work app with communication, collaboration, and office administration features. The app also enables geolocation tracking which means, for instance, that employees can be located and contacted if they venture beyond their allocated workspace. According to DingTalk’s developer and the Chinese company owners and managers who have adopted the app, its functions enhance efficiency. At the same time, DingTalk may be “the most hated app in China”. Its borderline authoritarian features are considered a “catastrophe for office staff” because of the coercive influence managers are enabled to exert over employees beyond conventional workspaces and times (https://medium.com/@hypp.johnstone/the-dark-side-of-alibabas-dingtalk-fb6b9ed7614a). Given this gulf between employers and employees in perceptions of DingTalk, this project seeks to uncover the various ways in which the two groups use the platform, and how this use varies across organizations. Empirical contribution 2: Exploring how DingTalk’s surveillance functions influence workplace interaction This project seeks to understand how DingTalk use influences workplace social interactions and how individuals at different hierarchical levels perceive DingTalk. Generally, e-work apps have extended work to online venues and facilitated the greater intrusion of work into the private sphere. In particular, the technical features of these apps have provided the means to reach, monitor, and micro-manage workers to a much greater extent than before, and surveillance has increased to inconceivable levels. From the standpoint of theory, of course, surveillance and observability are important for employee compliance. How then does this unprecedented capability influence worker compliance in the workplace? The project will attempt to answer this question by examining how DingTalk influences workplace social interactions between managers and workers and among workers in both conventional FTF and online venues. Empirical contribution 3: Investigating worker coping strategies Literature on the pervasiveness of technology in the workplace emphasizes worker agency by investigating their resistance and control. However, the PI’s previous study on WeChat use in Chinese middle-class workplaces concluded that most workers engaged in cynical performances of compliance when employers used apps to demand affective labor. This phenomenon has not been fully explored, and nor has worker resistance been examined. This study will focus on how workers cope with the enhanced monitoring of their work processes and content through DingTalk. For example, they might appropriate DingTalk to their advantage because such extensive documentation could make it easier for workers to make a case for protection of their labor rights in disputes with employers. Theoretical contribution 1: Examining how digital technology influences the social relations of workplace subordinates and supervisors Most studies on digital technologies in the workplace and organizational culture are based on Western contexts and focus on how technology blurs work and personal boundaries. There is little theoretical examination of how digital media use influences day-to-day workplace social interactions. In a non-Western context, this study field discusses how the increased observability and surveillance afforded by DingTalk influence the power dynamics between workplace subordinates and superiors. Examining DingTalk use in the Chinese context provides a Weberian ideal case because: 1) the use of monitoring technology in the workplace is a global trend and China is at the frontier of its adoption, 2) DingTalk’s comprehensive and invasive feature set is typical of many other similar Chinese e-work apps, and 3) there is a traditional emphasis on hierarchy and a particular style of authoritative relationships in Chinese culture. Theoretical contribution 2: Examining how online interaction characteristics influence workplace power dynamics when daily office communication is digitized DingTalk records conversations, tracks work time, produces work logs, and quantifies worker data for managers. A previous study by the PI suggested that the distinctive features of online interaction, such as the elimination of physical interaction spaces and the unlimited nature of online disclosures, have transformed the workplace into a panoptic environment that transcends time and space. Here, subordinates are compelled to constantly express loyalty and show public deference to superordinates. This project extends the previous study by examining how the distinctive features of digital communication, especially the recordability and quantification capacities of DingTalk, influence workplace social interactions, power differentials between subordinates and superordinates, and interactions between workers.

17600221.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17600221.value: 有關工作場域內技術應用的研究主要集中在資訊和通信技術如何模糊了工作和個人生活的界限，侵犯了私人空間。同時，新興技術也有可能使組織部門扁平化，從而提高工作人員的勞動生產力和自主性，並加強了工作人員對工作和生活需求的管理。 研究發現，在西方語境下，工作場域內資訊和通信技術的使用既可以成為壓迫的工具，也可以實現勞動者的賦權。相比之下，本項目負責人的先前研究認為中國的工作場域中，微信的使用加劇了權力等級關係，它的普遍存在意味著，與面對面的情境相比，下屬需要不斷被動地服從上級，並進行更多的情感勞動。目前尚不明確中國中產工作者為何會順應日益增長的勞動需求，甚至是有辱人格的需求，也不清楚在不同的組織環境中，資訊和通信技術方面對工作者的影響是否不同。 此研究通過聚焦應用程式釘釘在中國工作場合的使用，探討數位技術如何改變工作場域的互動過程。目前，中國大陸內有超過1500萬家企業、地方政府和學校(包括大學)使用釘釘，它具有強大的記錄和量化功能，便於監控工作場合。這個項目將聚焦於工作人員的釘釘使用經驗，以期理解：1) 釘釘如何改變工作場所的社會互動；2)組織環境和不同的權力基礎如何影響數位技術的使用；3)員工如何運用策略來應對類似釘釘這樣的應用程式帶來的日益增長的監管和強化的需求，以及員工是否能利用這項技術為自己謀利。 本項定性研究項目將基於先前有關微信和職場社會互動的研究經驗，包括焦點小組和訪談等。該研究將有助於從實證和理論層面理解有關工作場合內數位技術的使用情況。實證層面上，該項目將呈現，在中國，新興電子工作應用程式的普及對工作場合互動與工作關係產生了怎樣的影響。理論層面上，該項目將在五種權力基礎的經典模型（強制性權力、獎賞性權力、專家性權力、法定性權力和參照性權力）和Goffman的符號互動理論的基礎上，探討人們在工作中如何適應一項新興的技術，以及這種技術如何改變社會規範、自主性、工作與生活關系和面對面互動。對中國中產工作者相關行為的研究將進一步揭示新興電子工作應用程式對後製造業時代勞動力的勞動需求和工作場域內權力關係的影響和改變。

17600621.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17600621.value: 通過經顱直流電刺激誘導的神經可塑變化減少在慢性壓力下的高危行為

17600621.label: Project Objectives
17600621.value: Continuous and on-going political conflicts and the persistent COVID-19 pandemic in the past year have caused high levels of chronic stress to the whole Hong Kong society. An important mechanism by which chronic stress negatively impacts physical and mental health is via its association with high-risk behaviours such as addiction, suicide and antisocial acts, which have resulted in huge medical and financial costs in Hong Kong. High-risk behaviours may be initiated in response to or as a way to adapt to chronic stress, which in turn lead to further increase in stress, forming a vicious cycle. Breaking this cycle by cutting the association between chronic stress and high risky tendency is essential for the general population to maintain psychological integrity and resilience during the periods of adversity. In the proposed research, we aim to explore the efficacy of non-invasive neuromodulation method, specifically the transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), on reducing risk taking among non-clinical individuals experiencing high chronic stress. The findings would have important implications on the potential utilization of tDCS as a therapeutic tool for reducing high risky tendency on subclinical populations, and have high translational values for correcting behaviours in clinical settings among individuals with mental conditions implicating excessive risk taking. Chronic stress may enhance risk-taking tendency through altering behavioural regulations in situations where both the size and probability of rewards and punishments need to be considered, and high-level cognitive processes when evaluating the value of risky options. These processes may respectively depend on functioning of the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) in the brain. Past research has generated encouraging evidence on the effectiveness of single-session tDCS stimulation on the DLPFC or the OFC on reducing risk taking. Compared to other neuromodulation methods such as the Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS), the tDCS method is relatively safe, easy to administer, convenient and cheap, boosting its potential for large-scale applications in more extended populations for promoting mental health. Currently, evidence on the effectiveness of multi-session tDCS on reducing risk taking over extended time periods is still lacking. This is a critical gap given demonstrating persistent tDCS effect is fundamental to its usefulness in therapeutic and clinical settings. Thus, we propose to initiate a randomized control study (RCT) to systematically evaluate whether 10-session tDCS on the right DLPFC or the OFC could lead to reduction in risk taking compared to the sham control group, and whether the effect is still observable at 1-month and 3-month follow-up. Risk taking is a complex and multi-domain construct. An important limitation of existing empirical studies on risk taking is that most studies exclusively measured risk taking using artificial laboratory tasks, while the connection between the laboratory risk tasks and real-life risky behaviours is tentative. As a result, the implications of the findings from those studies on real-life risk taking are limited. To remedy this issue, we propose to measure risk taking using both an established laboratory task, and a widely-used questionnaire assessing risky decision making in hypothetical real-life scenarios. Furthermore, the ecological validity of the risk task and the questionnaire will be further ascertained by correlating them with participants’ self-reported lifetime engagement in common high-risk behaviours, such as addiction, unhealthy diet, unsafe sex, suicide, impulsive, violent and socially defiant behaviours. When being applied as a therapeutic tool, knowledge on the neurocognitive and emotional mechanisms by which tDCS intervention reduces risky tendency are important for understanding why the intervention may work on some but not other individuals, and for predicting the intervention outcome across different individuals. Based on existing literature, we formulated an a priori framework which generated formal predictions that tDCS on the right DLPFC reduces risk taking through altering the high-level cognitive bias (i.e. illusion of control), whereas the effect of tDCS on the right OFC on risk taking is mediated by its facilitatory effect on inhibition control over cognitive, emotional and motor processes. Hence, our proposed project further aims to delineate the potentially distinct mechanisms by which tDCS on two different scalp locations, both of which were found to be effective in reducing risky tendency, exert their influences. Towards formulating individual-based intervention protocols in therapeutic settings, it is also important to explore key individual characteristics that may determine the effectiveness of the intervention. In the proposed research, we will examine whether the effect of tDCS intervention on risk taking would be modulated by several traits that are closely associated with risky tendency, including impulsivity, reward and punishment sensitivity, and locus of control. These findings would importantly inform on the selective application of the tDCS protocols on individuals with particular characteristics, which could help with further evaluation of the tDCS method in reducing risk taking among special populations.

Furthermore, the ecological validity of the risk task and the questionnaire will be further ascertained by correlating them with participants’ self-reported lifetime engagement in common high-risk behaviours, such as addiction, unhealthy diet, unsafe sex, suicide, impulsive, violent and socially defiant behaviours.

When being applied as a therapeutic tool, knowledge on the neurocognitive and emotional mechanisms by which tDCS intervention reduces risky tendency are important for understanding why the intervention may work on some but not other individuals, and for predicting the intervention outcome across different individuals. Based on existing literature, we formulated an a priori framework which generated formal predictions that tDCS on the right DLPFC reduces risk taking through altering the high-level cognitive bias (i.e. illusion of control), whereas the effect of tDCS on the right OFC on risk taking is mediated by its facilitatory effect on inhibition control over cognitive, emotional and motor processes. Hence, our proposed project further aims to delineate the potentially distinct mechanisms by which tDCS on two different scalp locations, both of which were found to be effective in reducing risky tendency, exert their influences.

Towards formulating individual-based intervention protocols in therapeutic settings, it is also important to explore key individual characteristics that may determine the effectiveness of the intervention. In the proposed research, we will examine whether the effect of tDCS intervention on risk taking would be modulated by several traits that are closely associated with risky tendency, including impulsivity, reward and punishment sensitivity, and locus of control. These findings would importantly inform on the selective application of the tDCS protocols on individuals with particular characteristics, which could help with further evaluation of the tDCS method in reducing risk taking among special populations.

17600621.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17600621.value: The persistent political conflicts and COVID-19 pandemic have led to elevated chronic stress levels in Hong Kong, with far-reaching and profound negative impacts on the citizen’s mental health. An important pathway via which chronic stress negatively impacts health is through promoting high-risk behaviours, such as addiction, suicide, and antisocial acts. Therefore, testing means to break the association between chronic stress and high-risk behaviour is essential to reducing the adverse consequences of stress and promoting stress resilience. The transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) may be a viable method for reducing risky tendency in high-stress individuals, through modulating brain functions and plasticity. Although single-session tDCS has been shown to reliably reduce risky decision making and behaviours acutely, its efficacy over extended periods of time has not been demonstrated, particularly among non-clinical samples. Being able to show that tDCS could lead to long-lasting reduction of risky tendency is necessary for promoting the wide application of this method in therapeutic settings. In this project, we aim to conduct a randomised control trial to systematically and comprehensively test whether 10 sessions of tDCS on either the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex or the orbitofrontal cortex would lead to reduction in risky tendency not only immediately after treatment, but also at 1 month and 3 months after treatment. Participants will be healthy male and female adults (21-40 years old) under relatively high levels of chronic stress, as selected from an online survey prior to the study. Participants will be randomly allocated to one of 3 treatment groups: DLPFC tDCS, OFC tDCS, and sham control. At baseline, participants will complete several risk-taking assessments, including an established computerised task that measures both risk taking and a cognitive bias that was shown to increase irrational risky tendency (illusion of control), an established questionnaire that measures risky decision making in real-life scenarios, and a scale measuring past engagement in common risky activities. Participants will also complete various personality and mood questionnaires, along with assessments on important cognitive abilities. We hypothesized that both DLPFC and OFC tDCS would reduce risk taking across the 3 timepoints, but the effect of DLPFC tDCS would be mediated by reduction in cognitive bias, whereas that of OFC tDCS would be mediated by increase in inhibition functions. These hypotheses will be tested by linear mixed models and mediation analyses. Additional exploratory analyses also test whether the tDCS effect would be moderated by relevant personality factors such as impulsivity. 近年來，持續的政治衝突以及新冠病毒流行導致香港社會整體的慢性壓力水平不斷上升，對市民的心理健康產生了深遠的負面影響。一個慢性壓力損害健康的重要途徑是通過促進高風險行為，例如成癮，自殺以及反社會行為。因此，探索有望打破慢性壓力和高風險行為關聯的途徑對於降低壓力導致的惡性後果以及促進壓力抗性有重大意義。通過調節大腦功能和可塑性，經顱直流電刺激（tDCS）可能是降低高壓力群體高風險行為的可行方法。儘管單次tDCS已被證明可以可靠地短期減少風險決策及行為，但其長期療效尚未得到證實，尤其是在非臨床樣本中。能夠證明tDCS可以長期降低風險傾向對於將這種方法廣泛應用在醫療場景中是非常必要的。在本項目中，我們將開展一項隨機對照實驗，以系統全面地測試10試次針對背外側前額葉皮層（dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, DLPFC）或眶額皮層（orbitofrontal cortex, OFC）的tDCS是否會造成風險傾向降低的即時效果，以及1個和3個月後的持續效果。正式實驗前，我們將利用在線調查方式挑選處於相對較高慢性壓力水平下的健康男女成年人（21至40歲）。每一個實驗參與者將會被隨機分配到DLPFC tDCS, OFC tDCS, 或假性刺激對照組。在基準時間點，實驗參與者將會完成數個風險傾向的測試，包括一個已被前期工作證實可以有效測量風險傾向以及和高風險行為相關的認知偏差（控制錯覺）的電腦範式，一個已被證實可以有效測量現實生活場景中風險決策的問卷，以及一個測量曾經參與高風險行為的量表。參與者還將完成各種人格和情緒問卷，以及對重要認知功能的評估。我們假設針對DLPFC或OFC的tDCS都會降低3個時間點的風險傾向，但DLPFC tDCS的影響將由認知偏差的減少中介(mediate)，而OFC tDCS的影響將由抑制功能的增加中介。這些假設將通過線性混合模型和中介分析進行檢驗。附加的探索性分析還將測試tDCS的效應是否會受到相關人格因素（如衝動性人格）的調控(moderate).

17600721.label: Project Objectives
17600721.value: Demonstrate the necessity of approaching the historical study of Protestantism in Korea from a transnational perspective. Specifically, this project will explore how the language of ecumenical cooperation informed relationships among Protestants across political and denominational lines. In this manner, it will contribute to a growing body of work that has increasingly recognized the importance of moving beyond national frameworks when examining the history of Protestantism in Asia (H. J. Kim 2017; Hollinger 2017; Kim 2007; Lee 2014). In particular, it will build on the work of Robert Wuthnow (2010), who has argued for the necessity of understanding American Christianity from a transnational or global perspective. Because Protestant denominations and organizations from the United States dominated Korea for much of the first-half of the twentieth century, an important corollary of Wuthnow’s study is that the history of Protestantism in Korea must also be understood from a transnational or global perspective. Challenge a long-standing belief in the field of Korean Studies that attributes the “success” of Protestantism in Korea to the alignment of this religion with the social and cultural practices of the country or the political interests of its people (Yi 1973; Lee 2000; Park 2003; Oak 2013). While these studies of Korean Christianity have done much to further our understanding of this religion’s role in shaping modern South Korea, they tend to focus on how Christianity became “Korean.” Yet Christianity is a world religion, and what is missing from this inward-facing question is an understanding of Korean Christianity’s place in the global history of the transnational development of Christianity. Reveal how and why the international Protestant community became involved in the human and labor rights movement of the 1970s and the democracy and reunification movement of the 1980s (Cha 2019; Chang 2015; Stenzel 2008; Yi 2006; Chang 1998). This project will demonstrate that the roots of this involvement lay in the outbreak of the Korean War. In particular, it will argue that the transnational scope of Christianity gives its adherents a theoretical (or theological) reason to engage in international politics and social reform movements (Lehmann 2016; Haynes 2001; Thomas 2001; Rudolph 2005). Show that the Korean War and the Cold War sparked a diversification of the types of Protestant actors in South Korea. In particular, it will spotlight how the Korean War accelerated the entrance of the World Council of Churches (WCC) into South Korea, which the Western Protestant community of the time viewed as a “mission field” and hence a country to be overseen by the International Missionary Council (IMC). The WCC’s involvement in South Korea encompassed more than simply Christian solidarity or support. It subtly involved issues of colonialism and (in)equality, as Western Protestant leaders confronted postcolonial concerns regarding the missionary movement’s ties to imperialism. This project will discuss how these concerns affected Western Protestant leaders’ work with Korean leaders under the banner of ecumenism. Investigate how transnational Christian organizations like the WCC negotiated the political and diplomatic pitfalls of their work. Michael Barnett has observed that humanitarian aid organizations operating in authoritarian countries often publicly declare themselves to be “neutral” and distribute aid based solely on need out of concern that any indication of partiality could jeopardize access to these countries (Barnett 2011). This project will demonstrate that a similar concern shaped the work of Christian groups seeking to support protest movements in South Korea. In short, it will show how foreign Christian organizations negotiated the political hazards of operating under the authoritarian conditions of South Korea. Historicize the formation of a religious “global civil society” centered on South Korea. In particular, this project will extend recent studies that have examined the diverse roles that religions have played in constructing a “global civil society” (Schäfer 2017; Juergensmeyer 2005). It will investigate how the transnationality of Christianity facilitated the activities of adherents across state borders (Haynes 2001). In this manner, it will call attention to the strategies Christians in Asia have used to be active in the political and civil spheres (Bautista and Lim 2009). Prepare one scholarly monograph and at least two articles for publication in high-impact journals that demonstrate the historical origins and development of the complex links that exist between international and Korean Christian communities. This project will illuminate the competing interests of various groups and show how the language of ecumenism provided spaces for cooperation even while tensions generated by systematic inequalities between various groups persisted. In addition, these findings will be shared with the public through public talks, open forums, and short Internet lectures in order to foster discussion of the global reach of religions today.
