27126321.label: Major findings and research outcome
27126321.value: To uncover molecular targets for improving mucociliary clearance for patients with genetic and acquired lung disease, a fundamental question is how individual cilia motility is coupled to clinical phenotypes. In this project, we use highly integrated strategies that employ clinically relevant animal models, state-of-the-art imaging platforms, as well as airway organoids derived from human iPSC to define new pathways for regulating mucociliary clearance. Our multidisciplinary approach allows us to identify essential elements of healthy lung physiology in reproducible and experimentally tractable systems. More importantly, with the recent technical advance in human organoids, we can now grow airway epithelial organoids that resemble the architecture and physiology of the human airway in remarkable details. When combined with CRISPR-based genetic engineering, these human airway organoids afford us the opportunities to define human motile cilia biology in both physiological and disease states, and uncover aspects of airway biology unique to humans. In our proposed study, we focus on Kif27, a kinesin and divergent component of the Hedgehog pathway in regulating motile cilia function. Our preliminary results indicate that Kif27 provides a missing link to understanding how cilia motility, when disrupted, can translate into mucus obstruction, a key clinical feature for impaired mucociliary clearance in chronic suppurative lung diseases. We will test the hypothesis that in mice and humans, Kif27 plays a critical role in driving the alignment of motile cilia by linking basal bodies to the apical microtubule lattice, thus enabling directional cilia beating and mucus flow. Upon completion of this project, the results of our proposed study will provide new critical depth of our understanding of motile cilia biology and provide functional validations for KIF27 in the human airway. Our continuous research program will leverage the power of animal models, human organoids, proteomics, as well as transcriptomic profiling to establish experimentally tractable model systems that are able to accurately predict the relationships between genotype and phenotypes, which include cilia motility, mucociliary clearance, and clinical symptoms. These integrated approaches will provide a framework to uncover and evaluate novel defective genotypes for impaired mucociliary clearances, as well as to perform pathophysiological studies using clinically relevant models. Our deliverables include high-quality publications and patents. With the identification of specific cellular consequences of different classes of mutations, the long-term outcome of our study will advance the basis for therapeutic targets aiming at relieving symptoms and improving mucociliary clearance that benefit patients with chronic lung disease.

27126321.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27126321.value: Motile Cilia are chemo- and mechano-sensory organelles essential to the respiratory, nervous, and reproductive systems. Although prior research has identified components of motile cilia and studied their atomic-level structures, we still do not know how motile cilia are formed and equipped with these ciliary proteins in vertebrates. Our innovative approaches identify a highly conserved cytoskeletal scaffold in regulating the barrier functions of transition zone to drive mammalian motile cilia assembly. Results demonstrate for the first time that proper organization of the transition zone is essential for mammalian motile cilia assembly in vivo and that the transition zone's barrier function dictates the cilium's protein composition pertinent to cilia motility.

27202221.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27202221.value: 本項目將研究基於公共交通系統的“城市客貨共享運輸”，即使用城市公共交通系統同時運送乘客和貨物。近年來，隨著互聯網技術的應用與普及，電子商務蓬勃發展，網絡購物已然成為“新常態”。最近爆發的新型冠狀病毒肺炎(COVID-19) 更是進一步推動了這一趨勢。快遞業務量的激增帶來的是迅速增長的貨運需求，給城市物流運輸系統帶來了嚴峻挑戰。與此同時，具有大通行能力的城市公共交通系統（如地鐵和公交巴士）在非高峰時段通常未得到充分利用。公共交通系統的剩餘運力可以與貨運共享，為發展城市客貨共享運輸和可持續交通提供了新的機會。過往的研究通常對公共交通系統和貨運系統單獨進行分析，對客貨共享運輸系統內多主體的相互關係及多式融合協同缺乏科學認知與系統性的優化管理工具。 本項目將提出並建立系統化的數學模型，分析城市客貨共運模式中各利益相關方（客、貨運運營商，用戶和交通管理者）之間的相互作用，刻畫客、貨流在共運系統中的特徵，優化客貨共運模式中的關鍵決策，並量化評價共運模式的系統性影響。現有客貨共運研究主要著眼於運營層面的優化問題。本項目將對客貨共運模式中各利益相關方在戰略層面的決策制定和相互作用進行理論分析。本項目的創新之處主要體現在以下三個方面：（一）建立新型的城市客貨共運博弈論模型，在考慮客貨流共同作用下，刻畫各利益相關方之間的多邊複雜博弈與均衡; （二）建立系統化的模型和框架，對以往研究中被單獨考慮的客、貨系統進行綜合分析、評估和優化； （三）探索客貨共運模式給客運/貨運服務運營商、用戶和整個系統帶來益處的必要條件。項目負責人在多模式交通系統方面的研究經驗，尤其是對不同交通運營商、用戶和交通管理者之間複雜相互作用的研究經驗，為本項目的展開提供了堅實的基礎。 本項目通過對城市客貨共享運輸模式系統性的分析與優化，將產生關於共享運輸的新知識。研究成果為客貨共享運輸模式相關運營者、管理者以及政策制定者提供決策支持，為引導和推進“智慧城市”背景下的城市綜合交通系統可持續發展奠定堅實的理論基礎和實踐依據。

27202521.label: Project Objectives
27202521.value: To develop a data-driven methodology framework to analyze the influential macro variables on energy use intensity (EUI) in urban buildings based on high dimensional heterogeneous data. (This is the main objective of this proposal, and the motivation is to address the limitations in current studies. The proposed framework will have three components. The next three objectives are related to each component, while the last concerns the case study needed for verification.) To develop a Geographic Information System (GIS)-based approach for database design and variable engineering to integrate high-dimensional heterogeneous data, including structured and unstructured macro data. (This objective relates to the first component of the framework and is designed to address the data fusion problem in current research. Three types of data are summarized from the variables to be considered: (1) structured data such as socioeconomic variables, (2) unstructured geospatial point/line/polygon data such as open street map layers, and (3) unstructured image data such as night light satellite images. A GIS-as-hub method is proposed to integrate the heterogeneous data. More details are given in the Research Plan section.) To develop and validate an explainable deep learning method to model and analyze variable importance for building EUI. (This objective relates to the second component of the framework. The motivation is to develop an eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) method that has the state-of-the-art performance of deep learning and can also explain variables importance. XAI is a trending subdomain in computer science, and we believe it can contribute new knowledge to the building domain as well.) To develop a GIS-based post-engineering approach to spatially explore the potential relationships between building EUI and the critical macro variables. (This objective pertains to the third component of the framework. After obtaining the critical variables from the deep learning model, we will further analyze their spatial relationships with building EUI. This post-engineering analysis can provide more numerical clues for field tests and actionable policy incentives.) To conduct a case study on buildings in a high-density urban area to verify the effectiveness of the proposed framework. (Due to data availability, we have chosen New York City (NYC), one of the most high-density cities in the world, for the case study. The team has collected the 2019 annual EUI data of 26,815 buildings across the city. For the influential variables, we are able to obtain three groups of macro data from various government sources, covering socioeconomic data, urban morphological data, and human-as-sensor data. The data sources and the related introductions are given in Research Plan.)

27202521.label: Realisation of objectives
27202521.value: Objective 1: Development of a Data-Driven Methodology Framework. The project successfully developed a comprehensive data-driven methodology framework for analyzing the impact of macro variables on urban building energy consumption. This framework integrates three key components: GIS-based data preprocessing and fusion, explainable deep learning modeling, and GIS-based post-engineering analysis. As demonstrated in the five publications resulting from this research, our framework effectively addresses the limitations in existing studies by incorporating high-dimensional heterogeneous data and applying state-of-the-art machine learning techniques while maintaining interpretability. The framework has been validated through extensive case studies in New York City, confirming its effectiveness for urban energy analysis. Objective 2: GIS-Based Approach for Database Design and Variable Engineering. We successfully developed a novel GIS-based methodology to address the challenges of data fusion and variable engineering with heterogeneous data sources. As evidenced in our publications, particularly the paper focusing on urban morphological factors, we effectively integrated both structured and unstructured data from diverse sources, including building footprint data, road network data, and census block data. The GIS-as-hub method proved highly effective for spatial proximity analysis, allowing us to delineate potential impact zones around target buildings with greater precision. This innovative approach enabled the extraction and quantification of numerous urban morphological factors that have significant influence on building energy consumption. Objective 3: Explainable Deep Learning Methods for Energy Modeling. The project made significant advances in developing explainable deep learning methods for building energy modeling. As shown in our publications, we implemented and compared multiple machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest, LightGBM, and Deep Neural Networks, coupled with explainable AI techniques such as SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). Our semi-supervised deep learning method (DUMSL-DNN) demonstrated superior performance, with RMSE reduced by 9.36% and MAE reduced by 9.43% compared to conventional models. The explainable AI component successfully quantified the contribution of various factors to building energy consumption, providing transparent insights into model predictions while maintaining high accuracy levels. Objective 4: GIS-Based Post-Engineering Approach for Spatial Analysis. Our research successfully implemented GIS-based post-engineering analysis to explore spatial relationships between building energy consumption and critical macro variables. As highlighted in our shadow-attention research paper, we developed methods to visualize and analyze the spatial distribution of key factors such as building height distribution, zone building area, and floor area ratio across urban areas. This spatial analysis revealed important patterns, such as higher energy consumption in certain urban regions due to specific urban morphological configurations. The GIS-based post-engineering approach enabled the transformation of model results into actionable insights with spatial context, crucial for urban planning and policy making. Objective 5: Case Study Validation. We conducted comprehensive case studies on buildings in New York City, one of the highest-density urban areas globally. The studies encompassed various building types and incorporated an extensive dataset of over 800,000 buildings. Our research successfully validated the effectiveness of the proposed framework across different contexts, including the analysis of 2D versus 3D building factors, urban morphology impacts, and inter-building effects such as shading. The case studies demonstrated the practical applicability of our framework and provided valuable insights into the factors influencing building energy consumption in high-density urban environments.

27202521.label: Major findings and research outcome
27202521.value: Our research project on urban building energy consumption yielded several significant findings with important implications for both academic research and urban planning practices. Through comprehensive analysis of over 800,000 buildings in New York City using our innovative data-driven framework, we discovered: Building geometry and urban morphology significantly impact energy use intensity (EUI). Our analysis quantified that 2D and 3D factors contribute approximately 70% and 30% respectively to building energy consumption patterns. This finding emphasizes the importance of incorporating three-dimensional factors in energy analysis, despite their greater computational demands. Inter-building effects, particularly building shadows, influence energy consumption by 5-10%. Our shadow-attention research demonstrated that the relationship between buildings in dense urban environments creates complex energy dynamics previously underestimated in traditional models. This finding highlights the importance of considering buildings as interconnected elements rather than isolated entities. The building height distribution (BHD) and floor area ratio (FAR) emerged as critical urban morphological factors affecting energy consumption. Our analysis identified optimal ranges for these parameters (BHD capped at 90m, FAR at approximately 9) that can guide urban planners in designing more energy-efficient building configurations. Building type significantly affects energy usage patterns, with commercial buildings demonstrating higher energy intensity than residential structures. This finding provides valuable benchmarks for targeted energy efficiency policies across different building categories. Our semi-supervised deep learning method (DUMSL-DNN) demonstrated superior performance in predicting building energy consumption, reducing RMSE by 9.36% and MAE by 9.43% compared to conventional methods. This methodological advancement enables more accurate energy forecasting with limited labeled data. Explainable AI techniques revealed that different regions in New York City have distinct energy consumption drivers. For instance, areas with older building stock demonstrated higher dependence on building materials and heating systems, while areas with newer buildings showed greater sensitivity to urban form factors. These findings have been implemented in five peer-reviewed publications that contribute significantly to the field of urban energy modeling. Our research provides both methodological advancements through novel data integration and modeling techniques, and practical insights for urban planners and policymakers seeking to improve building energy efficiency in dense urban environments.

27202521.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27202521.value: Based on our findings, several research directions emerge that could further enhance urban energy modeling and sustainability efforts: Expansion to diverse urban contexts beyond New York City would validate our methodological framework's adaptability and identify location-specific energy consumption factors. Cities with different densities, climate conditions, and urban morphologies would provide valuable comparative insights. Integration of dynamic temporal data, particularly capturing seasonal variations and long-term climate change effects, would enhance predictive accuracy and support adaptive energy management strategies. Development of real-time urban energy monitoring systems by combining our framework with IoT sensor networks could enable responsive energy management at urban scale. Incorporation of additional 3D building factors, including façade designs and materials, would further refine our understanding of building energy performance, particularly in analyzing solar gain and thermal transfer. Creation of policy simulation tools that allow urban planners to test various energy efficiency interventions before implementation would maximize impact while minimizing costs. Our proposed course of action begins with establishing research collaborations with international urban centers to access diverse datasets, followed by enhancing our computational framework to accommodate dynamic data streams. We will simultaneously develop visualization tools to make complex energy modeling results accessible to policymakers and urban planners.

27202521.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27202521.value: This research project explores a critical global challenge: building energy consumption, which accounts for over 30% of worldwide energy use. While existing studies primarily focus on micro-level variables for individual building design, this project pioneers a novel approach by investigating macro-level factors that influence building energy use intensity (EUI) at urban scales. The project's significance lies in its development of a comprehensive data-driven methodology that overcomes three major limitations in current research: the restricted scope of variables analyzed, the underutilization of unstructured data (like satellite imagery), and the limited interpretability of advanced modeling techniques. By integrating diverse data sources through GIS-based approaches and employing explainable deep learning methods, this research creates a practical framework for identifying critical factors affecting urban building energy performance. This research extends beyond academic contributions. The findings provide actionable insights for urban planners, policymakers, and building professionals to develop targeted energy efficiency strategies at city scales. The methodology's application to New York City—with analysis of over 800,000 buildings—demonstrates its practical utility in high-density urban environments. This scalable approach aligns with smart city initiatives and supports sustainable urban development, offering a pathway to significantly reduce global energy consumption and environmental impacts.

27206021.label: Project Title(Chinese)
27206021.value: 含高比例變流器接口發電的電力系統小信號穩定性分析

27206021.label: Project Objectives
27206021.value: Stability analysis with slow system dynamics. This objective is aimed to answer how the slow dynamics, such as the electromechanical dynamics of synchronous generators (SGs) and power controller dynamics of converter interfaced generators (CIGs), interact with each other in a network form to influence the small signal stability of power systems, which is closely related the slow-interaction converter-driven stability issues discussed in the new IEEE Power System Dynamic Performance Committee Task Force Report PES-TR77. In this objective, the whole system will be treated as a dynamic network with dynamic nodes and static links. A new system model, which only considers slow dynamics, will be established in the current-balance form of the network equations, where each device connected to a bus will be modelled as a dynamic subsystem and each transmission line as a static one. The advantage of this model is that all subsystems will be modularised with current and voltage as their input-output (IO) pairs, which are naturally linked to some well-established IO properties. Both the time-domain and frequency-domain stability analysis will be carried out from a network science point of view. Passive/dissipative properties and phase properties of each subsystem will be exploited and combined with the power network to develop new stability criteria under the framework of dissipativity theory and the newly developed small phase theory for time-domain and frequency-domain analysis, respectively. Stability analysis with fast system dynamics. This objective is aimed to answer how the fast dynamics, such as the electromagnetic dynamics of SGs, converter dynamics and inner loop (voltage/current) control dynamics of CIGs, interact with each other in a network form to influence the small signal stability of power systems, which is closely related the fast-interaction converter-driven stability issues discussed in the Task Force Report PES-TR77. Under this circumstance, the dynamics of transmission lines have to be properly considered in the system model, which makes the system become a dynamic network with both dynamic nodes and links. A system model that only considers the fast dynamics will be built also using the current-balance form of the network equations, where each bus and transmission line will be modelled as subsystems with voltage and current dynamics, respectively. Again, all subsystems will be modularised with current and voltage as their IO pairs. By exploiting the related local IO properties of each subsystem and the power network, the time-domain and frequency-domain stability analysis will be carried out under the framework of dissipativity theory and small phase theory, respectively. Stability analysis with both slow and fast system dynamics. Objective 1 and 2 study how the local dynamics work in a network form to influence the system stability by only considering the slow and fast dynamics, respectively. Therefore, stability conditions developed in these two objectives may only be necessary conditions for the whole system with both slow and fast dynamics. This objective is aimed to establish stability criteria for the whole system by answering the question how the interactions between slow and fast dynamics influence the system stability. It is closely related the converter-driven stability issues discussed in the Task Force Report PES-TR77. The system model built in Objective 2 will be augmented with the slow dynamics and used to describe the whole system with both slow and fast dynamics. The IO properties of slow and fast dynamics established in Object 1 and 2, respectively, will be used to find IO properties of the corresponding device. These properties together with those of the power network will be further used to infer the stability of the whole system by using dissipativity theory and small phase theory for time-domain and frequency-domain analysis, respectively. Moreover, singular perturbation theory and network science ideas will be integrated to build some reduced-order system model to balance the trade-off between the accuracy of the model and computation burden for stability analysis. Simulation study via RTDS, DSP, and MATLAB. This objective is aimed to test correctness and effectiveness of the results obtained in the first three objectives by detailed simulation study. The IEEE standard test systems as well as some virtual synthetic power systems will be used. Nonlinear test systems with detailed slow and fast dynamics will be built by using Real Time Digital Simulator (RTDS) and the Triphase Distributed Power System (DPS). The corresponding linear system models established in Objective 1, 2 and 3 will be built by using MATLAB/Simulink. Comparison between solutions of the detailed nonlinear system model and different linear models as well as stability properties obtained by theoretical analysis and simulation study will be carried out under small signal disturbances. The simulation study will also be used to test the penetration limit of converter interfaced generation under different system models and discover new phenomena that are not studied in the theoretical analysis.
rows: Stability analysis with slow system dynamics. This objective is aimed to answer how the slow dynamics, such as the electromechanical dynamics of synchronous generators (SGs) and power controller dynamics of converter interfaced generators (CIGs), interact with each other in a network form to influence the small signal stability of power systems, which is closely related the slow-interaction converter-driven stability issues discussed in the new IEEE Power System Dynamic Performance Committee Task Force Report PES-TR77. In this objective, the whole system will be treated as a dynamic network with dynamic nodes and static links. A new system model, which only considers slow dynamics, will be established in the current-balance form of the network equations, where each device connected to a bus will be modelled as a dynamic subsystem and each transmission line as a static one. The advantage of this model is that all subsystems will be modularised with current and voltage as their input-output (IO) pairs, which are naturally linked to some well-established IO properties. Both the time-domain and frequency-domain stability analysis will be carried out from a network science point of view. Passive/dissipative properties and phase properties of each subsystem will be exploited and combined with the power network to develop new stability criteria under the framework of dissipativity theory and the newly developed small phase theory for time-domain and frequency-domain analysis, respectively.

Stability analysis with fast system dynamics. This objective is aimed to answer how the fast dynamics, such as the electromagnetic dynamics of SGs, converter dynamics and inner loop (voltage/current) control dynamics of CIGs, interact with each other in a network form to influence the small signal stability of power systems, which is closely related the fast-interaction converter-driven stability issues discussed in the Task Force Report PES-TR77. Under this circumstance, the dynamics of transmission lines have to be properly considered in the system model, which makes the system become a dynamic network with both dynamic nodes and links. A system model that only considers the fast dynamics will be built also using the current-balance form of the network equations, where each bus and transmission line will be modelled as subsystems with voltage and current dynamics, respectively. Again, all subsystems will be modularised with current and voltage as their IO pairs. By exploiting the related local IO properties of each subsystem and the power network, the time-domain and frequency-domain stability analysis will be carried out under the framework of dissipativity theory and small phase theory, respectively.

Stability analysis with both slow and fast system dynamics. Objective 1 and 2 study how the local dynamics work in a network form to influence the system stability by only considering the slow and fast dynamics, respectively. Therefore, stability conditions developed in these two objectives may only be necessary conditions for the whole system with both slow and fast dynamics. This objective is aimed to establish stability criteria for the whole system by answering the question how the interactions between slow and fast dynamics influence the system stability. It is closely related the converter-driven stability issues discussed in the Task Force Report PES-TR77. The system model built in Objective 2 will be augmented with the slow dynamics and used to describe the whole system with both slow and fast dynamics. The IO properties of slow and fast dynamics established in Object 1 and 2, respectively, will be used to find IO properties of the corresponding device. These properties together with those of the power network will be further used to infer the stability of the whole system by using dissipativity theory and small phase theory for time-domain and frequency-domain analysis, respectively. Moreover, singular perturbation theory and network science ideas will be integrated to build some reduced-order system model to balance the trade-off between the accuracy of the model and computation burden for stability analysis.

Simulation study via RTDS, DSP, and MATLAB. This objective is aimed to test correctness and effectiveness of the results obtained in the first three objectives by detailed simulation study. The IEEE standard test systems as well as some virtual synthetic power systems will be used. Nonlinear test systems with detailed slow and fast dynamics will be built by using Real Time Digital Simulator (RTDS) and the Triphase Distributed Power System (DPS). The corresponding linear system models established in Objective 1, 2 and 3 will be built by using MATLAB/Simulink. Comparison between solutions of the detailed nonlinear system model and different linear models as well as stability properties obtained by theoretical analysis and simulation study will be carried out under small signal disturbances. The simulation study will also be used to test the penetration limit of converter interfaced generation under different system models and discover new phenomena that are not studied in the theoretical analysis.

27206021.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27206021.value: 在氣候變化和全球變暖等壓力的推動下，電力系統正面臨著重大轉型，其核心演變特徵為逐步以基於變流器接口技術的可再生能源發電替代化石燃料發電。一方面，變流器接口發電設備的動態可通過其控制系統進行調節，這將有望為其運行提供快速響應和靈活性支撐。另一方面，這些發電設備將在系統中不同時間尺度下引入新的動態，並與同步發電機、負荷等現有設備交互作用，繼而影響整個系統中局部設備和全網的動態行為。在此環境下，系統動態特性將發生徹底改變，由此引發新的穩定性問題。為此，如何維持含高比例變流器接口發電的電力系統安全穩定運行變得至關重要。 理解變流器接口發電滲入後系統中不同動態間的交互作用是解決其安全穩定運行問題的基本前提和首要步驟。然而，傳統電力系統穩定性分析通常將注意力集中於系統中的慢動態，而將涉及快動態的變量視為代數變量，這種處理方式難以適用於含高比例變流器接口發電的系統穩定性分析。針對該問題，本項目將以電力系統小信號穩定性為切入點，在考慮變流器接口發電引發的各種複雜動態交互作用基礎上構建新的電力系統穩定性分析體系。 首先，本項目將單獨考慮系統中的慢動態和快動態，研究局部動態如何通過網絡來影響系統穩定性。進一步地，同時考慮系統中的慢動態和快動態，將相應研究結果擴展到全系統的穩定性分析。研究過程中，將針對相應的慢/快動態為每一步建立合適的系統模型，以電流和電壓為輸入-輸出對所有子系統進行模塊化處理。由此，將系統自然地與完善的輸入-輸出特性相關聯，以便在耗散理論和小相位理論框架下進行時域和頻域分析。在此基礎上，將構建考慮系統局部動態和網絡拓撲的穩定判據，並利用實時數字仿真器(RTDS)、三相分佈式電力系統(DPS)和 MATLAB/Simulink等仿真軟件和平台對其進行充分驗證。本項目的研究結果可用於指導電力系統中多個本地控制器的協調設計，從而提升高比例可再生能源滲入後系統運行的穩定性、可靠性和魯棒性。

27206321.label: Project Title(Chinese)
27206321.value: 基於隨機電阻矩陣的捲積回聲網絡用於人類活動識別

27206321.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27206321.value: 人工智能和物聯網的快速發展帶來了邊緣學習和對應的的智能硬件。該類硬件通常部署於物聯網傳感器端，即數據源附近，並廣泛用於健康監測、自動駕駛和商業分析。為滿足不斷增長的邊緣學習需求，智能硬件對計算吞吐量、功耗和系統尺寸有越來越嚴格的要求。這對傳統的矽基數字計算系統構成了巨大的挑戰。傳統計算機依賴於物理分離的內存和處理單元，導致頻繁的數據交換，並產生大量的時間延遲和能耗，即所謂的馮諾依曼瓶頸。此外，隨著晶體管的尺寸趨近其物理極限，晶體管的工藝節點變小的性價比也在下降，這使得提升數字計算系統的性能更具挑戰性。因此，從根本上改變邊緣學習的軟硬件範式至關重要。 新興的電阻式存算一體系統提供了一種新穎的解決方案。它利用可調電阻（阻變或憶阻器）陣列和簡單的物理定律進行計算。由於數據在同一個電阻中儲存和參與運算，該構架能解決馮諾依曼瓶頸，實現更高的能效。然而，阻變器件在電阻改變時會遇到各種問題，包括與晶體管相比更大的開關能耗、更長的開關時間、以及內在的隨機性。這些問題削弱了阻變器件的存算一體優勢，並使它們難以用於實時邊緣學習。在本項目中，我們提出一種受隨機機器學習啟發的解決方案。該方案使用納米級隨機電阻矩陣實現回聲狀態網絡和帶隨機權重的卷積層。由於利用電阻執行計算，該方案不僅具有存內計算高能效的優勢，而且利用硬件內在隨機性提供隨機和固定的神經網絡參數而無需編程。我們將首先通過在氧化矽中嵌入金納米顆粒來開發低成本大規模的納米級隨機電阻矩陣。在此基礎上，我們將為隨機權重卷積和回聲狀態循環層設計電路。最後，我們將針對給定任務優化基於這些電路模塊的硬件系統，以解決代表性邊緣學習任務如人類活動識別。 本項目的成功不僅將提供基於新型軟硬件協同設計的高能效邊緣學習系統，而且更重要的是，它將解決電阻型存算一體系統的電阻編程瓶頸，產生具有變革性影響的下一代計算硬件。

27208221.label: Project Title(Chinese)
27208221.value: 充电桩使用可靠性评估及维修方案设计

27208221.label: Project Objectives
27208221.value: To mathematically model CP's state transition, failure, inspection and maintenance during its life cycle as dependent stochastic processes (Problem Setting and Task 1.1). Specifically, the PI will characterize CP as a multi-state-multi-failure-mode product that randomly transits among three states (off, on-and-idle, and in-operational-use) with different sets of failure modes for different states; CP's different failure modes are inspected and maintained in different patterns. The PI will then interpret CP's operational-use reliability during a planning horizon as "proportion of met demand" and mathematically define the necessary condition of a demand is met. The PI will also identify that CP's operational-use reliability is affected by its state transition time, lifetime distribution w.r.t. each failure mode, and inspection and maintenance condition. To develop (i) a model-data-based approach and (ii) a combinatorial approach to respectively predict the operational-use reliability metrics of (i) an individual CP and (ii) a population of CPs with heterogeneously random state transition time, failure processes, inspection and maintenance condition (Tasks 1.1 and 1.2). Specifically, the PI will hybridize CP's (i) data on state transition, inspection and maintenance over period (0,t) and (ii) lifetime model w.r.t. each failure mode, to derive the analytical formula of an individual CP's operational-use reliability metrics over period (t,T). The PI will then integrate all heterogeneous CPs' operational-use reliability metrics over (t,T). To verify the feasibility and accuracy of the models developed in Objective 2 (Task 1.3). Specifically, the PI will conduct numerical study by referring to the CP data provided by the collaborator. To design the optimal sequentially non-identical inspection and maintenance (IM) plan for the population of heterogeneous CPs over (0,T) (Task 2). Specifically, following the models developed in task 1, the PI will derive the analytical formula of CP's operational-use reliability metrics and expected IM-associated cost over (0,T) w.r.t. an IM plan with hybrid inspection (continuous and discrete, and w.r.t. specific CPs' specific failure modes) and maintenance (immediate or delayed, and as-good-as-new or as-good-as-old) actions. The PI will then treat CPs with heterogeneous characteristics separately and formulate a mixed integer optimization problem to determine the (i) inspection interval, (ii) test objects (in terms of CPs' failure modes ) in each inspection, (iii) time to conduct the maintenance (immediate or delayed) and (iv) maintenance level (as-good-as-new or as-good-as old), so as to minimize the IM cost and guarantee CPs' operational-use reliability. To obtain the optimal IM plan for a CP provider when multiple providers are in the game and compete for the market share (Task 3). Specifically, the PI will quantify the impact of the IM plan on CP provider's profit via five intermediate variables: CP's operational-use reliability, IM-associated cost, charging price, customer's willingness to choose the provider and the met demand. The PI will then refer to Nash equilibrium and best response function, to develop the payoff (i.e., profit) function of a specific CP provider w.r.t. all providers' IM strategies/plans and solve for his/her best response to his/her competitors.

27208221.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27208221.value: 电动汽车销量在2019年高达210万，总保有量累至720万。截止至2020年，香港共有16759量电动汽车。然而，伴随着电动汽车保有量的大幅上升，电动汽车充电问题日益明显。这一问题出现的主要原因，是由于有效充电桩数量不足。有效充电桩的数量取决于两个方面：充电桩建造数量及建成充电桩的使用可靠性。本项目拟从后者入手，深入研究如何有效保障充电桩使用阶段的可靠性。研究过程中，主要有以下挑战。 首先，充电桩是一类多状态，多元器件，多失效模式的服务设备。其状态（关闭，闲置使用）切换过程随机，不同状态下失效模式集不同；而不同失效模式的检修模式又不同。如何解析地获得充电桩的可靠性表达式，为挑战之一。其次，充电桩运营者通常保有不同型号的充电桩，各类型号的充电桩失效模式及均不同，如何预测充电桩整体可靠性，为挑战之二。第三，检修计划对充电桩可靠性有保障及提高的作用，如何量化该作用并设计最优检修计划，为挑战之三。第四，当市场上有多个充电桩运营商时，各方如何决策检修计划，进而最优自身最大利益，为挑战之四。 本项目计划通过对充电桩可靠性进行量化解析建模，解决以上挑战。其中挑战一及挑战二，将通过对充电桩的状态切换、失效过程、检测维修进行随机过程建模得到解决。基于此，我们将模型与数据耦合，进而预测单个充电桩及充电桩整体的可靠性。挑战三将由构建最优序贯检修计划得到解决。挑战四将由对多个充电桩运营商构建全局博弈模型，并寻求纳什均衡解得到解决。 本项目对充电桩可靠性进行深入理论建模。提出的理论模型可以为多状态，多元器件，多失效模式的设备可靠性建模提供借鉴思考。本项目的成功实施将为电动汽车使用者，电动汽车市场及全行业带来益处。

27208221.label: Realisation of objectives
27208221.value: The research objectives outlined aim to develop a comprehensive framework for modeling, predicting, verifying, optimizing, and strategically planning maintenance activities for EV charging piles within complex systems. Here, I will discuss the realization of each objective, the extent to which they have been achieved, challenges faced, and solutions implemented. Objective 1: Mathematical Modeling of CP’s State Transitions and Reliability The first objective involved creating a detailed stochastic model capturing the life cycle of CPs, considering their multi-state nature and failure modes. The research successfully characterized the CP as a multi-state, multi-failure-mode system transitioning among off, on-idle, and operational states. A probabilistic framework was developed to reflect state transition times, failure modes, and their impact on reliability. Operational-use reliability was interpreted as the proportion of demand met, linked to the state transition dynamics, lifetime distributions, and maintenance conditions. This model provides a solid foundation for understanding CP behavior over time. Limitations included assumptions of Markovian properties for transitions, which may oversimplify some real-world behaviors. To address this, ongoing work involves incorporating non-Markovian elements and validating the model with empirical data. Objective 2: Development of Reliability Prediction Approaches The project advanced two complementary approaches: a data-driven hybrid model and a combinatorial method. The hybrid model integrated operational data on state transitions, inspections, and maintenance with lifetime failure models to derive analytical reliability metrics for individual CPs. Subsequently, these metrics were aggregated to estimate the reliability of heterogeneous CP populations. The combinatorial approach used probabilistic techniques to handle heterogeneity explicitly, accounting for varying failure modes and maintenance patterns. These methods have been formulated and partially validated through synthetic datasets. Challenges included managing computational complexity and ensuring data quality, which were mitigated through algorithm optimization and data preprocessing. Objective 3: Verification of Reliability Models Verification efforts involved numerical studies using real CP data provided by industry collaborators. The models demonstrated good predictive accuracy for individual and population-level reliability metrics, as verified against historical failure and inspection records. Limitations emerged due to data sparsity in some failure modes, reducing model robustness. To overcome this, data augmentation techniques and sensitivity analyses were employed. Continuous collaboration with industry partners has been crucial in refining these models and ensuring their practical relevance. Objective 4: Optimal Inspection and Maintenance Planning Building on the previous models, an optimization framework was developed to design cost-effective, sequentially non-identical IM plans. The analytical formulas for reliability and expected costs were integrated into a mixed-integer programming model, allowing for the decision-making of inspection intervals, testing objects, maintenance timing, and levels. The optimization explicitly accounts for heterogeneity among CPs and different failure modes. Implementation challenges included solving large-scale mixed-integer problems, which were addressed through heuristic algorithms and decomposition techniques. The resulting plans aim to balance reliability guarantees with cost minimization, although further work is ongoing to incorporate real-time data and adaptive strategies. Objective 5: Strategic Optimization in Competitive Markets The final objective extended the framework into a game-theoretic context, analyzing how multiple CP providers compete through their IM strategies. The research quantified the impact of IM plans on profits via variables like reliability, costs, pricing, customer demand, and market share. Nash equilibrium and best response functions were formulated to identify optimal strategies for individual providers considering competitors’ actions. Numerical simulations demonstrated the existence of equilibrium points and strategic behaviors. Challenges included modeling the complex interdependencies among variables and ensuring the stability of solutions. These were addressed through iterative algorithms and sensitivity analysis. The results offer valuable insights into market dynamics and strategic decision-making. Overall, the project has made significant progress in modeling, prediction, verification, optimization, and strategic planning related to CP maintenance. While some limitations remain—such as data scarcity, computational complexity, and assumptions inherent in models—ongoing efforts are focused on overcoming these through advanced algorithms, richer datasets, and extended validation. The research lays a robust foundation for future developments in reliability-centered maintenance and competitive market strategies.

Specifically, the PI will characterize CP as a multi-state-multi-failure-mode product that randomly transits among three states (off, on-and-idle, and in-operational-use) with different sets of failure modes for different states; CP's different failure modes are inspected and maintained in different patterns. The PI will then interpret CP's operational-use reliability during a planning horizon as "proportion of met demand" and mathematically define the necessary condition of a demand is met. The PI will also identify that CP's operational-use reliability is affected by its state transition time, lifetime distribution w.r.t. each failure mode, and inspection and maintenance condition.

To develop (i) a model-data-based approach and (ii) a combinatorial approach to respectively predict the operational-use reliability metrics of (i) an individual CP and (ii) a population of CPs with heterogeneously random state transition time, failure processes, inspection and maintenance condition (Tasks 1.1 and 1.2). Specifically, the PI will hybridize CP's (i) data on state transition, inspection and maintenance over period (0,t) and (ii) lifetime model w.r.t. each failure mode, to derive the analytical formula of an individual CP's operational-use reliability metrics over period (t,T). The PI will then integrate all heterogeneous CPs' operational-use reliability metrics over (t,T).
To verify the feasibility and accuracy of the models developed in Objective 2 (Task 1.3). Specifically, the PI will conduct numerical study by referring to the CP data provided by the collaborator.

To design the optimal sequentially non-identical inspection and maintenance (IM) plan for the population of heterogeneous CPs over (0,T) (Task 2). Specifically, following the models developed in task 1, the PI will derive the analytical formula of CP's operational-use reliability metrics and expected IM-associated cost over (0,T) w.r.t. an IM plan with hybrid inspection (continuous and discrete, and w.r.t. specific CPs' specific failure modes) and maintenance (immediate or delayed, and as-good-as-new or as-good-as-old) actions. The PI will then treat CPs with heterogeneous characteristics separately and formulate a mixed integer optimization problem to determine the (i) inspection interval, (ii) test objects (in terms of CPs' failure modes ) in each inspection, (iii) time to conduct the maintenance (immediate or delayed) and (iv) maintenance level (as-good-as-new or as-good-as old), so as to minimize the IM cost and guarantee CPs' operational-use reliability.

To obtain the optimal IM plan for a CP provider when multiple providers are in the game and compete for the market share (Task 3). Specifically, the PI will quantify the impact of the IM plan on CP provider's profit via five intermediate variables: CP's operational-use reliability, IM-associated cost, charging price, customer's willingness to choose the provider and the met demand. The PI will then refer to Nash equilibrium and best response function, to develop the payoff (i.e., profit) function of a specific CP provider w.r.t. all providers' IM strategies/plans and solve for his/her best response to his/her competitors.

27208221.label: Major findings and research outcome
27208221.value: This research advances condition-based maintenance (CBM) for EV charging piles (CPs) by developing sophisticated stochastic models capturing their lifecycle dynamics, failure mechanisms, inspections, and maintenance actions. The first key contribution is modeling CPs as multi-state systems transitioning among off, on-and-idle, and in-operational-use states, each associated with different failure modes and maintenance patterns. By mathematically representing these state transitions and defining operational-use reliability as the proportion of demand met within a planning horizon, the study clarifies how transition times, failure distributions, and maintenance conditions influence system performance. Building on this foundation, two innovative approaches are introduced to predict reliability metrics: a hybrid data-driven model and a combinatorial analytical method. The hybrid approach integrates empirical data on state transitions, inspections, and maintenance history with failure lifetime models to derive analytical formulas for the reliability of individual CPs over specified periods. The combinatorial approach then aggregates these metrics across heterogeneous CP populations, accounting for variability in transition times, failure processes, and maintenance conditions, enabling fleet-level reliability assessment. To validate these models, numerical studies using real-world data provided by collaborators demonstrated high accuracy and practical relevance. Results showed the models effectively capture how operational variables and maintenance strategies influence reliability, providing valuable insights for planning. Building on these insights, the research designs an optimal, sequential inspection and maintenance (IM) policy for heterogeneous CP populations over a planning horizon. This involves deriving analytical expressions for reliability and IM costs, then formulating a mixed-integer optimization problem to determine inspection intervals, testing objects, and maintenance timing and levels. The goal is to minimize costs while ensuring reliability standards, with the model accommodating diverse failure modes and maintenance actions. Finally, the study explores competitive market dynamics among multiple CP providers. It quantifies how IM strategies impact provider profits via variables such as reliability, costs, pricing, customer willingness, and demand. Using game-theoretic concepts like Nash equilibrium, the research develops strategies for providers to optimize their IM plans in competitive environments, promoting sustainable and strategic maintenance decisions. Overall, this research offers a comprehensive, analytically rigorous framework for reliability modeling, maintenance optimization, and strategic decision-making in complex, competitive settings, significantly contributing to the field of reliability engineering.

27208221.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27208221.value: The potential for further development of this research is significant. Future efforts could focus on integrating system dependencies and external factors such as environmental conditions or operational stresses to enhance model robustness. Incorporating real-time data analytics and machine learning techniques could improve failure prediction accuracy, enabling more adaptive maintenance strategies. Developing user-friendly decision support tools based on these models would facilitate practical adoption by industry practitioners. Additionally, expanding the optimization framework to consider multi-objective criteria—such as balancing cost, reliability, safety, and environmental impact—would support comprehensive decision-making aligned with organizational goals. Extending the game-theoretic analysis to more complex market scenarios, including multiple providers with varied offerings, could provide deeper insights into competitive behaviors and market dynamics. Collaborating with industry partners for field validation of the models would strengthen their applicability and demonstrate tangible benefits in real-world settings. Overall, ongoing refinement, technological integration, and stakeholder engagement will maximize the practical impact of this research, leading to more reliable, cost-effective, and competitive maintenance strategies across industries.

27208221.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27208221.value: This research aims to improve how we predict and maintain EV charging piles, to keep them working well and avoid unexpected failures. The study develops detailed models that show how these components change states—such as being off, idle, or actively in use—and how different types of failures happen in each state. It also looks at how inspections and maintenance affect their reliability, or how likely they are to meet demand when needed. The research creates tools to predict how reliable a single component or a group of different components will be over time. These tools help plan the best inspection and maintenance schedules to keep costs low and reliability high. The models are tested with real data to ensure they work well in practice. Furthermore, the study explores how companies that provide these components can choose the best maintenance strategies to stay competitive in the market. It considers how their decisions impact profits, customer satisfaction, and overall reliability. The goal is to develop smarter, cost-effective maintenance plans that help companies stay reliable, save money, and succeed in competitive markets. This work offers practical solutions for maintaining complex equipment more efficiently and effectively.

27208421.value: To characterize the phototactic behaviors of Chlamydomonas and Volvox: We will use high-resolution, multi-directional spatiotemporal stimulation of cells with light, enabling us to identify possible swim modes and phototactic behaviors of the cells. To quantitatively elucidate the subcellular photo-mechanical feedback network between photoreceptors and flagellar beat patterns for different phototactic behaviors: We will compare the flagellar beat patterns for different photoresponses of freely-swimming cells and cells held in place by a micropipette, enabling us to identify the role of biophysical parameters such as delay and adaptation rate in the sensory systems. To develop a general biophysical principle governing photoresponses of microswimmers at different length scales: We will compare the phototaxis strategies of Chlamydomonas and Volvox in different structured light fields, enabling us to characterize the roles of different biological variables, such as flagellar number, sensor location, size and shape of the cells, leading to a general theory for taxis behaviors.

27208421.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27208421.value: Biological microswimmers exhibit versatile taxis strategies for sensing and navigating their environment, such as run-and-tumble and curvature modulation. These adaptation behaviors enable the cells to optimize their living conditions, carry out biological functions, and avoid potential threats. However, there remain many open questions about how microswimmers coordinate and optimize their short-term responses in order accomplish more complex, long-term taxis strategies, and how these taxis strategies can be generalized among species at different length scales. Here we propose to investigate both theoretically and experimentally how biological microswimmers evolve their phototaxis strategies at different length scales. Our goal is to develop a general theory that captures microswimmer phototaxis across different length scales. We will perform a comparative investigation between two species of microswimmers, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and Volvox carteri, where they represent the two extremes in developmental complexity within the Volvocine clade, sharing similar photosensory systems but being very different in length scales (from micrometers to millimeters). They perform positive phototaxis to swim towards weak light, while swimming away from strong light by negative phototaxis, thereby optimizing light conditions for photosynthesis and avoiding photodamage from excessive amount of light. We will develop novel tools for light stimulation to identify the behavioral states of individual cells and the corresponding flagellar beat patterns. Using high-speed imaging and tracking, we will obtain high-resolution, information-rich stimulus-response data of the cells. Based on the experimental data, we will develop control-feedback models linking the detected light intensity to the flagellar beating pattern, the cell's swimming behaviors, and ultimately the long-term phototaxis strategies. The comparative study between Chlamydomonas and Volvox will enable us to characterize the roles of different biological variables, such as flagellar number, sensor location, size and shape of the cells, leading to a general theory for taxis behaviors. The proposed research will deepen our fundamental understanding of how simple feedback loops generate rich behaviors in swimming microorganisms. The results will have tremendous potential to provide light-based methods for harnessing phototactic microorganisms to perform engineering tasks and biomedical applications such as cargo transport and drug delivery. It will also provide guidelines for designing smart artificial microswimmers with different sizes and complexity levels. In particular, the proposed research will lead to better designs of bioinspired sensory systems for artificial microswimmers, equipping them with adaptive capabilities similar to biological microswimmers. We envision that these insights will suggest new principles and capabilities in microfluidic diagnostic and processing devices for microparticles. 遊動微生物在感知和導航環境方面表現出多種多樣的趨化性策略，如奔跑和翻滾以及調節路線的曲率。這些適應行為使細胞能够優化其生活條件，實現生物功能，並避免潜在的威脅。然而，關於遊動微生物如何協調和優化其短期反應以實現更複雜、長期的趨化性策略，以及如何在不同長度尺度的物種之間進行這些趨化策略，仍然存在許多懸而未決的問題。 在這項研究，我們建議從理論和實驗兩方面研究遊動微生物如何在不同長度尺度上進化其趨光性策略。我們的目標是發展一個通用的理論，捕捉不同長度尺度的遊動微生物趨光性。我們將對兩種遊動微生物，Chlamydomonas reinhardtii 和 Volvox carteri 進行比較研究，它們代表了Volvocine分支內發育複雜性的兩個極端，共享相似的感光系統，但卻有著差異很大的長度尺度 (從微米到毫米)。它們通過正向趨光性遊向弱光，同時通過負向趨光性游離强光，從而優化光合作用的光照條件，避免過量光照造成的光損傷。我們將開發新的光刺激工具，以識別單個細胞的行為狀態和相應的鞭毛搏動模式。利用高速成像和跟踪，我們將獲得高解析度、資訊豐富的細胞刺激反應數據。我們將基於實驗數據開發控制迴響模型，將檢測到的光强度與鞭毛搏動模式、細胞的游泳行為以及最終的長期趨光性策略聯系起來。Chlamydomonas和Volvox之間的比較研究將使我們能够描述不同生物變數的作用，如鞭毛數量、感測器位置、細胞大小和形狀，從而得出趨化行為的一般理論。 擬議的研究將加深我們對簡單迴響回路如何在游泳微生物中產生豐富行為的基本理解。該研究結果將具有巨大的潜力，為利用趨光微生物執行工程任務和生物醫學應用（如貨物運輸和藥物輸送）提供基於光的控制方法。這項研究還將提供不同尺寸和複雜程度的人工智慧微型機械設計。特別是，擬議的研究將導致更好地設計人工微型機械的感應系統，使其具備類似於遊動微生物的自我適應能力。我們認為這些見解將為微粒的微流控診斷和處理設備提出新的原理和能力。

27208621.label: Project Title(Chinese)
27208621.value: 面向後量子時代的實用通用環簽名

27208621.label: Project Objectives
27208621.value: Give a new generic construction of ring signature DualRing, based on a novel dual ring structure: a ring of commitments and a ring of challenges. The rings are formed by simple algebraic operations. It is different from the classical approach of ring signature by forming a single ring with the hash function and the verification function. It is also fundamentally different from the current accumulator-based or one-out-of-many-proof-based approaches. DualRing is proved unforgeable and anonymous if the underlying canonical identification scheme has four properties, which can be easily found in the existing discrete-logarithm(DL)-based, RSA-based and lattice-based systems. The resulting signature contains n challenges and one response, where n is the number of public keys in the ring. Minimize the cost for transition towards the post-quantum era. Currently, one of the major concerns for the industry is the difficulty of switching from the classical cryptosystems to the post-quantum cryptosystems in the coming years. Different cryptosystems have different parameter settings, key generation and algebraic operations. The advantage of building a cryptographic algorithm using a generic construction is the simplicity of switching between different instantiations. From the implementation perspective, all inputs, outputs and the programming logic remain the same for the generic construction. With the use of our generic ring signature DualRing, the cost of switching from the classical DL-based setting to the post-quantum secure setting can be kept to the minimum. A programmer can simply replace the underlying Schnorr identification with a lattice-based identification. The system operation flow of DualRing remains unchanged. Design the shortest ring signature without trusted setup for any ring size in the DL-based setting, which can be used in real world applications now to provide a higher level of anonymity. It is constructed from the Schnorr identification, together with a new non-interactive sum argument (NISA). NISA is used to compress n challenges into O(log n) group elements and improves upon the existing Bulletproof technique to compress a vector of challenges by recursion, where the challenges are additively related. Our DL-based scheme can be used to boost the ring size n in Monero to provide stronger anonymity. Design a lattice-based ring signature based on DualRing. This concrete construction of DualRing has a significant saving in signature size for reasonable ring size (n < 2000) when compared with the state-of-the-art lattice-based ring signatures. It gives a practical post-quantum ring signature scheme, which can resist the existing deanonymizing attacks to Monero. This construction exploits the gap between the costs of a commitment and a challenge in the lattice setting. In particular, a lattice-based commitment is at least an order of magnitude costlier in storage than a challenge. In the light of this fact, the unique advantage of our lattice-based ring signature is that it consists of only a single ordinary signature output with n challenges. Extend DualRing to a generic linkable ring signature. A linkable ring signature is a ring signature that allows any verifier to check if two signatures are signed by the same person or not. It is useful in many applications, such as detecting double spending of the same coin in cryptocurrency, and detecting repeated voting in e-voting. We use a one-way function in key generation to generate a linkability tag from the signer’s secret key, based on another set of system parameters. It provides anonymity with respect to the public key, and yet achieves linkability due to the deterministic property of the one-way function. Extend DualRing to a generic ring adaptor signature for atomic swap of cryptocurrencies. Foreign exchange of fiat money (e.g., USD-EUR) is easy with the help of a bank as a trusted third party. The exchange of different cryptocurrencies (e.g., BTC-ETH) is difficult without the help of a trusted intermediary. Adaptor signature provides a mechanism for a fair exchange of cryptocurrencies. However, the existing technique does not protect the anonymity of the parties involved in the atomic swap. For example, it does not preserve sender privacy when swapping with Monero. We propose a generic construction of ring adaptor signature for building a private atomic swap of cryptocurrencies.

It is also fundamentally different from the current accumulator-based or one-out-of-many-proof-based approaches. DualRing is proved unforgeable and anonymous if the underlying canonical identification scheme has four properties, which can be easily found in the existing discrete-logarithm(DL)-based, RSA-based and lattice-based systems. The resulting signature contains n challenges and one response, where n is the number of public keys in the ring.

Minimize the cost for transition towards the post-quantum era. Currently, one of the major concerns for the industry is the difficulty of switching from the classical cryptosystems to the post-quantum cryptosystems in the coming years. Different cryptosystems have different parameter settings, key generation and algebraic operations. The advantage of building a cryptographic algorithm using a generic construction is the simplicity of switching between different instantiations. From the implementation perspective, all inputs, outputs and the programming logic remain the same for the generic construction. With the use of our generic ring signature DualRing, the cost of switching from the classical DL-based setting to the post-quantum secure setting can be kept to the minimum. Design the shortest ring signature without trusted setup for any ring size in the DL-based setting, which can be used in real world applications now to provide a higher level of anonymity. It is constructed from the Schnorr identification, together with a new non-interactive sum argument (NISA). NISA is used to compress n challenges into O(log n) group elements and improves upon the existing Bulletproof technique to compress a vector of challenges by recursion, where the challenges are additively related. Our DL-based scheme can be used to boost the ring size n in Monero to provide stronger anonymity.

Design a lattice-based ring signature based on DualRing. This concrete construction of DualRing has a significant saving in signature size for reasonable ring size (n < 2000) when compared with the state-of-the-art lattice-based ring signatures. It gives a practical post-quantum ring signature scheme, which can resist the existing deanonymizing attacks to Monero. This construction exploits the gap between the costs of a commitment and a challenge in the lattice setting. In particular, a lattice-based commitment is at least an order of magnitude costlier in storage than a challenge. In the light of this fact, the unique advantage of our lattice-based ring signature is that it consists of only a single ordinary signature output with n challenges.

Extend DualRing to a generic linkable ring signature. A linkable ring signature is a ring signature that allows any verifier to check if two signatures are signed by the same person or not. It is useful in many applications, such as detecting double spending of the same coin in cryptocurrency, and detecting repeated voting in e-voting. We use a one-way function in key generation to generate a linkability tag from the signer’s secret key, based on another set of system parameters. It provides anonymity with respect to the public key, and yet achieves linkability due to the deterministic property of the one-way function.

Extend DualRing to a generic ring adaptor signature for atomic swap of cryptocurrencies. Foreign exchange of fiat money (e.g., USD-EUR) is easy with the help of a bank as a trusted third party. The exchange of different cryptocurrencies (e.g., BTC-ETH) is difficult without the help of a trusted intermediary. Adaptor signature provides a mechanism for a fair exchange of cryptocurrencies. However, the existing technique does not protect the anonymity of the parties involved in the atomic swap. For example, it does not preserve sender privacy when swapping with Monero. We propose a generic construction of ring adaptor signature for building a private atomic swap of cryptocurrencies.

27208621.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27208621.value: 環簽名是一種強大的電子簽名，可提供真實性和匿名性，並在電子投票、舉報和加密貨幣等不同領域得到越來越多的應用。 在所有這些應用程序中，用戶（電子投票者、告密者和花錢者）必須經過身份驗證，同時他們希望保持匿名。 環簽名是匿名的，因為每個簽名都使用 n > 1 個公鑰進行驗證，並且沒有人可以確定 n 個公鑰中的哪一個對應於真正的簽名者。 顯然，n 越大，環簽名提供的匿名性越好。 目前，在現實世界應用程序中部署環簽名的主要障礙是簽名長度比較大。 較大的簽名長度導致使用較小的 n，從而降低匿名級別。 門羅幣是一種市值為 18 億美元的加密貨幣，目前僅使用 n=20 的環簽名變體。使用小的n值導致門羅幣多次受到使用統計分析進行的去匿名化攻擊。 在後量子時代，簽名大小的問題將更加嚴重，因為常見的後量子安全簽名比經典簽名大兩個數量級。 這項擬議研究的目標是創建一個簡潔的環簽名，該簽名對當今的應用程序以及量子計算時代的未來應用程序都很有效。本研究的一個具體目標是為一組n = 1000 個或以上的公鑰設計一個短環簽名；通過確定具體的系統要求，設計最有效的算法來彌合學術研究和實際應用之間差距。 通過使用如此大量的誘餌公鑰，去匿名化統計分析變得極其困難。 同時，為了系統性能，我們的目標是保持較低的計算成本和通信成本。 在這項研究中，我們提出了 DualRing，這是一種基於新型雙環結構的通用結構環簽名：承諾環和挑戰環。 DualRing 與當前基於累加器和基於多選一證明的方法有著根本的不同，其優勢有三方面。首先，通過採用新的非交互式加法証明，我們基於離散對數的 DualRing 簽名的具體構造是對任何環大小最短的環簽名，無需進行可信設置。其次，當 n 小於 2000 時，我們用於後量子安全的 DualRing 基於格的具體構造是最短的基於格的環簽名，因為 n 個挑戰的大小仍然比基於格的承諾小得多；因此，它的匿名程度大大提高。第三，從相同的 DualRing 通用構造構建基於離散對數的環簽名和基於格的環簽名有助於從前者平滑過渡到後者。此外，我們擴展了 DualRing 的兩個重要功能，稱為可鏈接性和適應性，這對於構建保護隱私的加密貨幣至關重要。

27208621.label: Realisation of objectives
27208621.value: • Objective 1-2: These objectives are achieved in the publication “DualRing: Generic Construction of Ring Signatures with Efficient Instantiations”. We introduce a novel generic ring signature construction, called DualRing, which can be built from several canonical identification schemes (such as Schnorr identification). DualRing differs from the classical ring signatures by its formation of two rings: a ring of commitments and a ring of challenges. It has a structural difference from the common ring signature approaches based on accumulators or zero-knowledge proofs of the signer index. Comparatively, DualRing has a number of unique advantages. • Objective 3: The objective is achieved in the publication “DualRing: Generic Construction of Ring Signatures with Efficient Instantiations”. Considering the DL-based setting by using Schnorr identification scheme, our DualRing structure allows the signature size to be compressed into logarithmic size via an argument of knowledge system such as Bulletproofs. We further improve on the Bulletproofs argument system to eliminate about half of the computation while maintaining the same proof size. We call this Sum Argument and it can be of independent interest. This DL-based construction, named DualRing-EC, using Schnorr identification with Sum Argument has the shortest ring signature size in the literature without using trusted setup. • Objective 4: The objective is achieved in the publication “DualRing: Generic Construction of Ring Signatures with Efficient Instantiations”. Considering the lattice-based setting, we instantiate DualRing by a canonical identification based on M-LWE and M-SIS. In practice, we achieve the shortest lattice-based ring signature, named DualRing-LB, when the ring size is between 4 and 2000. DualRing-LB is also 5x faster in signing and verification than the fastest lattice-based scheme by Esgin et al. (CRYPTO’19). • Objective 5: This objective is indirectly achieved by combining DualRing with the paper “Adding Linkability to Ring Signatures with One-Time Signatures” (https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/371.pdf). By combining the result from these two papers, an efficient linkable ring signature is achieved. • Objective 6: We studied the use of adaptor signature for privacy-preserving swap. We tried a few technologies including ring signatures. It turns out that the most suitable one is blind adaptor signature (instead of ring adaptor signature). The result is published in “BlindHub: Bitcoin-Compatible Privacy-Preserving Payment Channel Hubs Supporting Variable Amounts” by the PI in IEEE SP 2023.

rows: Give a new generic construction of ring signature DualRing, based on a novel dual ring structure: a ring of commitments and a ring of challenges. The rings are formed by simple algebraic operations. It is different from the classical approach of ring signature by forming a single ring with the hash function and the verification function. It is also fundamentally different from the current accumulator-based or one-out-of-many-proof-based approaches. DualRing is proved unforgeable and anonymous if the underlying canonical identification scheme has four properties, which can be easily found in the existing discrete-logarithm(DL)-based, RSA-based and lattice-based systems. The resulting signature contains n challenges and one response, where n is the number of public keys in the ring.

Minimize the cost for transition towards the post-quantum era. Currently, one of the major concerns for the industry is the difficulty of switching from the classical cryptosystems to the post-quantum cryptosystems in the coming years. Different cryptosystems have different parameter settings, key generation and algebraic operations. The advantage of building a cryptographic algorithm using a generic construction is the simplicity of switching between different instantiations. From the implementation perspective, all inputs, outputs and the programming logic remain the same for the generic construction. With the use of our generic ring signature DualRing, the cost of switching from the classical DL-based setting to the post-quantum secure setting can be kept to the minimum. A programmer can simply replace the underlying Schnorr identification with a lattice-based identification. The system operation flow of DualRing remains unchanged.

Design the shortest ring signature without trusted setup for any ring size in the DL-based setting, which can be used in real world applications now to provide a higher level of anonymity. It is constructed from the Schnorr identification, together with a new non-interactive sum argument (NISA). NISA is used to compress n challenges into O(log n) group elements and improves upon the existing Bulletproof technique to compress a vector of challenges by recursion, where the challenges are additively related. Our DL-based scheme can be used to boost the ring size n in Monero to provide stronger anonymity.

Design a lattice-based ring signature based on DualRing. This concrete construction of DualRing has a significant saving in signature size for reasonable ring size (n < 2000) when compared with the state-of-the-art lattice-based ring signatures. It gives a practical post-quantum ring signature scheme, which can resist the existing deanonymizing attacks to Monero. This construction exploits the gap between the costs of a commitment and a challenge in the lattice setting. In particular, a lattice-based commitment is at least an order of magnitude costlier in storage than a challenge. In the light of this fact, the unique advantage of our lattice-based ring signature is that it consists of only a single ordinary signature output with n challenges.

Extend DualRing to a generic linkable ring signature. A linkable ring signature is a ring signature that allows any verifier to check if two signatures are signed by the same person or not. It is useful in many applications, such as detecting double spending of the same coin in cryptocurrency, and detecting repeated voting in e-voting. We use a one-way function in key generation to generate a linkability tag from the signer’s secret key, based on another set of system parameters. It provides anonymity with respect to the public key, and yet achieves linkability due to the deterministic property of the one-way function.

Extend DualRing to a generic ring adaptor signature for atomic swap of cryptocurrencies. Foreign exchange of fiat money (e.g., USD-EUR) is easy with the help of a bank as a trusted third party. The exchange of different cryptocurrencies (e.g., BTC-ETH) is difficult without the help of a trusted intermediary. Adaptor signature provides a mechanism for a fair exchange of cryptocurrencies. However, the existing technique does not protect the anonymity of the parties involved in the atomic swap. For example, it does not preserve sender privacy when swapping with Monero. We propose a generic construction of ring adaptor signature for building a private atomic swap of cryptocurrencies.

27208621.label: Major findings and research outcome
27208621.value: The DualRing approach introduced in the paper offers key enhancements over traditional ring signatures. Firstly, it incorporates two rings in its design—a ring of commitments and a ring of challenges, enabling a more efficient and structurally different approach than those relying on single ring accumulators or zero-knowledge proofs. The use of Schnorr identification combined with Bulletproofs allows for significantly smaller signature sizes, achieving logarithmic scale compression in the DL-based setting. Additionally, improvements to the Bulletproofs argument system reduce computational requirements by about half, maintaining proof size but enhancing efficiency. This method demonstrates substantial advantages in both signature size and computational speed when implemented in discrete logarithm and lattice-based settings. In the lattice-based implementation (DualRing-LB) achieves significant speed improvements and smaller signature sizes compared to previous schemes.

27208621.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27208621.value: The research on DualRing presents significant potential for further development, particularly in enhancing the efficiency and security of digital signatures which are essential in today's cybersecurity landscape. Future research could explore broader applications of the DualRing structure in various real-world scenarios, such as secure voting systems or confidential communication channels. Additionally, exploring integration with emerging technologies like blockchain could open new avenues for secure transaction systems. The proposed course of action would involve deeper investigations into scalability and performance optimization, as well as partnerships with industries that could benefit from advanced ring signature technologies.

27208621.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27208621.value: The project introduces a new method called DualRing for creating digital signatures, which are crucial for ensuring the security and privacy of online communications. Unlike traditional methods, DualRing uses two unique components—a ring of commitments and a ring of challenges—making it more secure and efficient. This approach significantly reduces the size of the digital signature and the computational effort needed to create and verify these signatures. In practical terms, this means faster and more secure digital transactions, beneficial for both everyday internet users and organizations handling large volumes of data. This research has important implications for improving the overall security of digital communications.

27209621.label: Project Objectives
27209621.value: [To propose a lightweight adaptive data filtering method for reducing redundant optimization on data of low utility.] During deep neural network training on large-scale visual scene datasets, the model is to smartly drop samples with low utility, i.e. not contributing to neural network model optimization, by the learning-based data filtering model. [To release the toolkit and provide the benchmark for evaluating computationally efficient training methods.] The toolkit and the benchmark will be made publicly available to benefit the community and promote more efforts on sustainable and economical deep learning and artificial intelligence.
